docs.text: Customize the admin ¶ A ModelAdmin states only what the model does not already say. Class attributes shape the list and the form; methods change behaviour; templates and themes change the look. # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Tone , action from .models import Post site = Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" , per_page = 8 ) @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) search = ( "title" , "slug" ) readonly = ( "created_at" ,) badges = { "published" : { True : ( "Published" , Tone . OK ), False : ( "Draft" , Tone . WARN )}} tabs = ( "published" ,) # one tab per badge: Published | Draft fieldsets = { "Organization" : ( "author_id" , "published" )} @action ( confirm = "Publish the selected posts?" ) async def publish ( self , posts : tuple [ Post , ... ], principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> None : await Post . filter ( id__in = [ p . id for p in posts ]) . aupdate ({ "published" : True }) Register a model ¶ @site.admin(Post) registers a ModelAdmin class for a model. site.register(...) takes a model class, which gets the default admin, or a ModelAdmin class that names its model with model= . The slug in the URL is the table name with dashes ( blog-posts ), or the class attribute slug = "posts" . Shape the list and the form ¶ Attribute Effect Default columns Columns of the list The model's fields search Columns the search box looks in The first three text columns the list shows readonly , exclude Shown but not editable; never shown () badges Value → Badge(label, tone, icon) or (label, tone[, icon]) Plain text tabs One tab per badge of the named column None fieldsets Fieldset s, or a dict of title → field names One group per_page , show_count Page size; row count in the sidebar The site's Admin(per_page=20, show_count=False) bulk_delete Offer bulk delete where can(principal, "delete") allows True allow_hard_delete Offer physical deletion in the Deleted view False Tone ( NEUTRAL , ACCENT , OK , WARN , DANGER , INFO ) is the color role of badges, stats and events. Without configuration the label and plural come from the model, the order from @db.ordered_by and the "last modified" line from its @db.timestamps() column. Search matches a row when any search column contains the typed text, compared case-insensitively as text (a number or date matches its printed form). Naming an exclude d column in search is refused at registration, because which rows match would reveal its value. Form inputs follow the column type: text, number, checkbox, UUID, datetime, date , time (without a UTC offset), Decimal (finite values only) and Enum (a select of member names). Another type is shown read-only. A time or decimal that is retyped but means the stored value ( 09:30 for 09:30:00 , 12.5 for 12.50 ) is not saved again. Datetime fields use the app's settings.timezone (UTC without built-in settings): stored instants are shown there and edited datetime-local values are read there, then saved as UTC-aware datetimes. A time that does not exist or occurs twice during a daylight-saving change is refused for correction. Soft-deleted models ¶ For a model using @db.soft_delete() or SoftDeleteModel , the admin's Active list and default queryset(principal) contain live rows. When tabs is unset, the list shows Active and Deleted views; ?deleted=1 selects the latter. With custom tabs the Deleted view is a last tab after them. The default deleted_queryset(principal) is self.model.only_deleted() . Override it to add tenant or ownership filters; the admin always narrows it to rows with a delete timestamp, and uses that same scope for restore and hard-delete. The deleted_at and every tracked changed_at column are automatically readonly unless excluded. Deleting a row uses soft deletion. Deleted rows cannot be edited or deleted through the regular row form before restoration. The Deleted view offers restore to users allowed to change each row. Physical purging is hidden and refused unless the model admin opts in with allow_hard_delete = True ; each selected row must also pass can(principal, "delete", row) . Override behaviour ¶ Each method below is called by the framework; override what you need and call super() for the rest. # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller from hinoki.admin import Avatar , ModelAdmin , Refusal from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from .models import Post @site . admin ( Post ) # the site created above class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): def queryset ( self , principal : Caller [ Any ] ) -> QuerySet [ Post ]: # rows this caller sees, in every statement return Post . filter ( author_id = principal . user . id ) . select_related ( "author" ) def can ( self , principal : Caller [ Any ], action : str , row : Post | None = None ) -> bool : # narrows a grant, never widens it if action == "delete" and row is not None and row . published : return False return super () . can ( principal , action , row ) def display ( self , row : Post , column : str ) -> Any : # a list cell: text, a Badge or an Avatar if column == "author_id" : return Avatar ( row . author . name ) return super () . display ( row , column ) async def check ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ], row : Post | None ) -> dict [ str , str ]: # {field: message} refuses if values . get ( "published" ) and not ( values . get ( "title" ) or ( row and row . title )): return { "title" : "A published post needs a title." } return {} async def remove ( self , row : Post , principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> None : if row . published : raise Refusal ( "Unpublish the post first." ) # shown on the page await super () . remove ( row , principal ) queryset(principal) decides which rows a caller sees; counts and pages come from it. can(principal, "view", row) then trims the fetched page, so a page may hold fewer rows than per_page . save(values, principal, row=None) and remove(row, principal) are the only places that write; run a domain operation there instead of a raw write. Refusal raised in either rolls the write back and shows its message. stats(principal) returns the dashboard Stat s for the model. Mass assignment, excluded columns and out-of-scope rows are refused by the framework. Add fields that are not columns ¶ extra_fields (or an extras() method, when the choices depend on what is registered) adds form fields that are not columns: Extra("password", "Password", "password") : a masked input, never filled in again. Extra("tags", "Tags", "choices", choices=(("a", "A"), ("b", "B"))) : checkboxes; the value is a frozenset of the checked ones. They reach check and save next to the columns, so save takes them out before writing the row; extra_initial(row) returns what the edit form shows. The Users section is built this way ( hinoki.admin.users.useradmin ). Many-to-many fields ¶ A model's many_to_many field appears in its add and edit forms as a multi-select named after its ids field ( <field>_ids , or its ids_name ) when the target model is registered with the same admin and the signed-in user may view it. The options are what that target's admin lists for the user (its queryset ), at most 200, with the linked rows first. Saving replaces only the links to rows the user can see; links to rows outside that scope are kept. A key that is unknown, hidden from the user or longer than 200 characters is refused with one message ( Some choices are not available. ) and nothing is saved, so a hidden row cannot be told from a missing one. More than the field's max_items selections is refused the same way. When the options are truncated the form says so; narrow them with ?link_q_<ids_name>=text on the form URL (the text is cut at 100 characters and matched against the target admin's search columns, or its primary key). A target that is not registered or not viewable leaves the field read-only: the form shows no count and ignores any posted value. A name in readonly shows the links without changing them. The row and its links are written in the request's transaction, so a refused link rolls the row back too. Add a bulk action ¶ Mark an async method with @action . The list shows the button once rows are selected: # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py from typing import Any from hinoki import Caller from hinoki.admin import ModelAdmin , action from .models import Post @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): @action ( confirm = "Publish the selected posts?" ) async def publish ( self , posts : tuple [ Post , ... ], principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> None : ids = [ post . id for post in posts ] await Post . filter ( id__in = ids ) . aupdate ({ "published" : True }) The action name is the method name with _ written as - ; the label defaults to "Publish selected". view , add , change and delete are reserved. The name is also the permission checked by can(principal, name, row) . Every selected row is checked against the queryset and can before confirmation and again before execution; one denied row refuses the whole action. The action runs in the admin's write transaction with the selected rows locked, on at most 200 distinct rows (more answer 400 ). A failure rolls everything back; success redirects to the list with a notice. Handlers still apply their own domain conditions to writes that involve related records or external state. Replace the HTML or the stylesheet ¶ Admin(templates="admin_ui") reads admin_ui/components/NAME.html before the built-in component of the same name ( shell , sidebar , table , form , field , auth for the sign-in page, ...) and appends admin_ui/admin.css after the theme. Copy the built-in component from the package as a starting point; keep its {{ value }} (escaped) and {{{ raw }}} placeholders. /* admin_ui/admin.css */ . hn-auth-card { border-radius : 0 ; } . hn-nav-item [ aria-current = "page" ] { font-weight : 800 ; } Choose or build a theme ¶ Four built-in styles, each with light and dark modes; the system preference picks the initial mode and the toggle overrides it. Pick one with Admin(theme="bento") . Style Navigation List Edit Look Studio (default) Sidebar Cards with a table Drawer beside the list Soft violet, rounded Console Top bar Dense monospaced grid Drawer Neon cyan and teal, square Paper Quiet text index, centred column Document rows Own page Serif type, terracotta Bento Icon rail (bottom tab bar on phones) Grid of cards Own page Ink outlines, offset shadows, yellow accent Studio Console Paper Bento A Theme is a set of --hn-* design tokens for both schemes, plus edit ( "drawer" , "page" ), layout ( "sidebar" , "topbar" , "index" , "rail" ) and list_style ( "table" , "rows" , "cards" ). Start from a built-in one: # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py import dataclasses from hinoki.admin import THEMES , Admin studio = THEMES [ "studio" ] forest = dataclasses . replace ( studio , name = "forest" , label = "Forest" , light = { ** studio . light , "accent" : "#1f6f50" , "accent-hover" : "#17543c" }, dark = { ** studio . dark , "accent" : "#5cc79b" , "accent-hover" : "#7ad6b0" }, layout = "topbar" , extra_css = ".hn-brand-text strong { letter-spacing: .04em; }" , ) site = Admin ( theme = forest ) extra_css is appended after the tokens; default_mode="dark" starts dark until the user switches. The text and surface colour pairs of the built-in themes are tested against WCAG AA contrast. Bento was checked in Chromium and Firefox at 1440, 390, 360 and 320 px; WebKit was not run. Errors and edge cases ¶ All of these fail when the Admin is created or the model registered, not on a request: Mistake Error A ModelAdmin naming a different model than the one registered RegistrationError search naming an exclude d column RegistrationError A bulk action named view , add , change or delete RegistrationError A template file that is not a component, an unknown placeholder, {{ }} changed to {{{ }}} , or a form , table , confirm or auth override without {{ csrf }} TemplateError A theme with a missing token, unknown layout or bad name ValueError from the Theme , before any page is served See also ¶ Add an admin Define models Admin API reference

docs.text: Add an admin ¶ hinoki.admin gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk actions and a dashboard for your models, behind its own sign-in page, users and per-model permissions. It ships in hinoki-api (no extra to install); nothing is served until you mount it with Mount("/admin", site) , its migrations are applied explicitly, and importing it never touches a database. # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Tone from .models import Post , User site = Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" ) @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) readonly = ( "created_at" ,) badges = { "published" : { True : ( "Published" , Tone . OK ), False : ( "Draft" , Tone . WARN )}} site . register ( User ) # a model with the default admin # blog/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , Mount from .apps.blog.adminsite import site routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Mount ( "/admin" , site )] The Blog example builds a fuller site the same way, with a theme, links, a dashboard and activity; its routes.py mounts it beside the API and its hinoki.toml registers the admin's tables as the admin app. Create the admin's tables ¶ The admin keeps its users in five tables of your database (four active plus the legacy login-window table). Register them as an app, apply the migrations, then create the first user: hinoki app add admin --models hinoki.admin.users.models --migrations hinoki.admin.users.migrations hinoki migrations apply admin hinoki admin create-superuser alice # asks for the password twice Table Migration Holds hinoki_admin_users 0001-initial Username, Argon2id password hash, active and superuser flags, last sign-in hinoki_admin_sessions 0001-initial The SHA-256 of each session token, its user, expiry and last request hinoki_admin_grants 0001-initial One row per user, model and action hinoki_admin_login_windows 0002-login-windows Fixed-window counters of earlier versions; no policy reads it any more and it can stay empty hinoki_admin_rate_limits 0003-rate-limits Buckets of DatabaseLoginWindow : a digest of the client and the route, and a counter state Every other user is created from the admin's Users section. hinoki admin set-password alice resets a password from a shell; both commands are described in hinoki admin . Set the signing secret ¶ The admin signs its forms and cookies with admin.secret from the app's settings. Give it at least 32 random bytes through the environment: export BLOG_ADMIN__SECRET = " $( python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))' ) " Setting Default Meaning admin.secret none Signing key, at least 32 bytes admin.session_hours 12 A session ends this long after sign-in admin.idle_minutes 120 A session ends after this long without a request admin.min_password_length 12 Shortest password accepted admin.theme none Built-in theme ( studio , console , paper , bento ) for an Admin that sets no theme= ; studio when neither is set Admin(secret=...) overrides the secret and Admin(theme=...) the theme for one site. An admin with neither stops the app at startup. So does an admin served with allowed_hosts at its default * and debug off: the CSRF check trusts the Host header it compares the Origin with, so name the served hosts; debug only lifts the refusal for local development, and then the whole app accepts loopback Host names only ( localhost , *.localhost , 127.0.0.0/8 , [::1] ; any other Host receives 400 ) unless allowed_hosts names the hosts (see Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). The in-process test clients are not affected. Who may sign in ¶ Admin() without access= uses its own users: A superuser holds every permission. Other users hold grants per model and action: view , add , change , delete . A bulk action needs change . A model without a grant is missing from the sidebar, and its pages answer 404 . Grants wrap each model admin's can : an override can narrow what a grant allows, never widen it. An inactive user cannot sign in. To use your own identity instead (single sign-on, an existing user table), pass an access policy: Admin(access=Access(auth=..., permissions=[...])) . The admin then has no sign-in pages and no tables, and your callers' permissions decide what ModelAdmin.can allows. See authentication and access . The sign-in page ¶ login shows a centred card with the site name, the title Sign in , a username field, a password field and a full-width button, in the active theme's colours and in its light or dark mode. Every page of the admin redirects there ( 303 ) when the browser has no valid session. Request Answer POST login , correct credentials 303 to the admin root with a new session cookie; any previous session token is closed, never reused POST login , wrong username or password 401 "Wrong username or password." POST login , expired or forged form 403 "The form expired or is invalid. Reload and try again." POST login , too many attempts 429 (see limit sign-in attempts ) GET login while signed in 303 to the admin root POST logout 303 to login ; the session ends and its cookie is cleared Usernames are stored in lower case: 1 to 150 letters, digits and . _ @ + - , starting with a letter or digit. An unknown username costs the same hashing work as a wrong password and gets the same answer. password changes the signed-in user's password. The form asks for the current password, a new one (at least admin.min_password_length characters) and the new one again. A wrong current password, two different new ones or a password that breaks the length rule answer 422 with the reason on the form; an expired form answers 403 . Success ends every other session of the user and redirects ( 303 ) to the admin root ( ?done=password ) with a new session. The logo ¶ The sidebar and the sign-in card show a bookmark icon by default. logo= replaces it with another built-in icon or with an image you serve yourself: Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" , logo = "layers" ) # a built-in icon Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" , logo = "/static/logo.svg" ) # an image from your app An image path must start with a single / : the admin's content security policy only allows same-origin images, so an https:// URL or //host/... is refused with a ValueError when the Admin is built, as is an unknown icon name. The built-in icons are the i-* symbols of the admin sprite ( bookmark , layers , folder , users , tag , image , ...). Sessions and cookies ¶ The session is a random token in the hinoki_admin_session cookie: HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , scoped to the admin's path. The database stores only its SHA-256, so a copy of the table cannot be replayed. Every form carries a signed CSRF token that must equal the SameSite=Strict hinoki_csrf cookie. On the sign-in form the token is signed for signing in; on every other form it is bound to the signed-in user. A form is also refused when the browser marks it as sent from another site ( Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site or same-site ) or its Origin header names another host; a request without these headers relies on the token alone. Cookies are Secure on HTTPS. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, set server.trusted_proxies so the forwarded scheme is believed, or pass Admin(secure_cookies=True) : cookies are then always Secure and named __Secure-hinoki_admin_session and __Secure-hinoki_csrf , so a sibling site cannot plant them. Changing the option signs everyone out once. A session ends after admin.session_hours , after admin.idle_minutes without a request, on sign-out, on a password change and when its user is deactivated. Reactivating a user never revives an old session. Manage users ¶ A superuser sees a Users section in the sidebar: create a user, choose the models and actions it may use, rename, deactivate, change a password or delete. Only a superuser opens it. No grant does, because a user who could edit users could grant itself everything. The permission checkboxes list view , add , change and delete for each registered model. An empty password on edit keeps the current one. A new one signs the user out everywhere. Passwords are never written back into the page. You cannot deactivate yourself, remove your own superuser status or delete yourself. Every write checks that an active superuser remains; hinoki admin create-superuser recovers if two superusers demote each other at the same instant. Deleting a user removes its sessions and grants. Admin(users=AdminAccounts(), manage_users=False) leaves the section out, for a site whose users are created another way. AdminAccounts.set_active(user, False) deactivates a user from code and ends its sessions. Limit sign-in attempts ¶ The sign-in and password forms pass through a rate limit policy before any password is hashed, and hold no database connection while hashing. Policy Counts in Behaviour LoginWindow(limit=10, window=60) (default) One worker's memory Each worker counts on its own and forgets on restart: a brake, not a shared limit. Holds at most 10,000 clients and drops the oldest. DatabaseLoginWindow(limit=10, window=60) hinoki_admin_rate_limits One limit for every worker and host, the RateLimit algorithm: a burst of limit , then one attempt every window / limit seconds, and a refused attempt costs nothing. Clients are stored as digests. # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin from hinoki.admin.users import AdminAccounts from hinoki.admin.users.limits import DatabaseLoginWindow site = Admin ( users = AdminAccounts ( login_limit = DatabaseLoginWindow ())) Both count per client address and route (a flood on the sign-in never spends the password change's attempts). DatabaseLoginWindow is a RateLimit subclass, so it keeps its table within a bound, deletes expired rows while counting, and, while the table is full of live ones, counts every new address in one shared window per route, ten times as large. Separately, each user name is delayed after repeated wrong passwords, from any address: past five failures the delay doubles up to five minutes, before any hashing, in the memory of one worker. Unknown names are counted the same. An IPv6 address counts by its /64. Requests without a known address share one window ten times as large, so set server.trusted_proxies behind a proxy. With DatabaseLoginWindow , keep host clocks in sync: each host stamps the windows it opens. Any other policy works too; see rate limit an action . Serve it under another path ¶ The Mount prefix decides where the admin lives; links, assets and the cookie path follow it. Mount("/ops", site) serves it at /ops . Admin(prefix="/staff") adds a path of its own after the mount ( /ops/staff ). An admin included without a Mount is served at /admin ; Admin(prefix="") serves it at the root of its mount. Errors and edge cases ¶ When What fails Startup, no admin.secret and no secret= RegistrationError : "admin: no secret to sign its forms with; set admin.secret …" Admin(access=..., users=...) ValueError : pass one or the other register of AdminUser , AdminSession or AdminGrant RegistrationError : a plain model admin would show password hashes and let a grant holder promote itself register with a slug that is taken or reserved ( static , search , login , logout , password ) RegistrationError DatabaseLoginWindow before 0003-rate-limits is applied Sign-in fails with 503 rate_limit_unavailable on the missing table; apply the migration first One address racing many sign-ins at the same instant 429 rather than an uncounted attempt A form posting a many-to-many key that is unknown, outside the user's view or too long The form is shown again with one generic message and nothing is saved ( details ) See also ¶ Customize the admin hinoki admin commands Authentication and access Settings

docs.text: hinoki.admin gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk actions and a dashboard for your models, behind its own sign-in page, users and per-model permissions. It ships in hinoki-api (no extra to install); nothing is served until you mount it with Mount("/admin", site) , its migrations are applied explicitly, and importing it never touches a database. # blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py from hinoki.admin import Admin , ModelAdmin , Tone from .models import Post , User site = Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" ) @site . admin ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( ModelAdmin [ Post ]): columns = ( "title" , "published" , "author_id" , "created_at" ) readonly = ( "created_at" ,) badges = { "published" : { True : ( "Published" , Tone . OK ), False : ( "Draft" , Tone . WARN )}} site . register ( User ) # a model with the default admin # blog/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , Mount from .apps.blog.adminsite import site routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Mount ( "/admin" , site )] The Blog example builds a fuller site the same way, with a theme, links, a dashboard and activity; its routes.py mounts it beside the API and its hinoki.toml registers the admin's tables as the admin app.
docs.title: Add an admin

docs.text: The admin keeps its users in five tables of your database (four active plus the legacy login-window table). Register them as an app, apply the migrations, then create the first user: hinoki app add admin --models hinoki.admin.users.models --migrations hinoki.admin.users.migrations hinoki migrations apply admin hinoki admin create-superuser alice # asks for the password twice Table Migration Holds hinoki_admin_users 0001-initial Username, Argon2id password hash, active and superuser flags, last sign-in hinoki_admin_sessions 0001-initial The SHA-256 of each session token, its user, expiry and last request hinoki_admin_grants 0001-initial One row per user, model and action hinoki_admin_login_windows 0002-login-windows Fixed-window counters of earlier versions; no policy reads it any more and it can stay empty hinoki_admin_rate_limits 0003-rate-limits Buckets of DatabaseLoginWindow : a digest of the client and the route, and a counter state Every other user is created from the admin's Users section. hinoki admin set-password alice resets a password from a shell; both commands are described in hinoki admin .
docs.title: Create the admin's tables

docs.text: The admin signs its forms and cookies with admin.secret from the app's settings. Give it at least 32 random bytes through the environment: export BLOG_ADMIN__SECRET = " $( python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))' ) " Setting Default Meaning admin.secret none Signing key, at least 32 bytes admin.session_hours 12 A session ends this long after sign-in admin.idle_minutes 120 A session ends after this long without a request admin.min_password_length 12 Shortest password accepted admin.theme none Built-in theme ( studio , console , paper , bento ) for an Admin that sets no theme= ; studio when neither is set Admin(secret=...) overrides the secret and Admin(theme=...) the theme for one site. An admin with neither stops the app at startup. So does an admin served with allowed_hosts at its default * and debug off: the CSRF check trusts the Host header it compares the Origin with, so name the served hosts; debug only lifts the refusal for local development, and then the whole app accepts loopback Host names only ( localhost , *.localhost , 127.0.0.0/8 , [::1] ; any other Host receives 400 ) unless allowed_hosts names the hosts (see Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). The in-process test clients are not affected.
docs.title: Set the signing secret

docs.text: Admin() without access= uses its own users: A superuser holds every permission. Other users hold grants per model and action: view , add , change , delete . A bulk action needs change . A model without a grant is missing from the sidebar, and its pages answer 404 . Grants wrap each model admin's can : an override can narrow what a grant allows, never widen it. An inactive user cannot sign in. To use your own identity instead (single sign-on, an existing user table), pass an access policy: Admin(access=Access(auth=..., permissions=[...])) . The admin then has no sign-in pages and no tables, and your callers' permissions decide what ModelAdmin.can allows. See authentication and access .
docs.title: Who may sign in

docs.text: login shows a centred card with the site name, the title Sign in , a username field, a password field and a full-width button, in the active theme's colours and in its light or dark mode. Every page of the admin redirects there ( 303 ) when the browser has no valid session. Request Answer POST login , correct credentials 303 to the admin root with a new session cookie; any previous session token is closed, never reused POST login , wrong username or password 401 "Wrong username or password." POST login , expired or forged form 403 "The form expired or is invalid. Reload and try again." POST login , too many attempts 429 (see limit sign-in attempts ) GET login while signed in 303 to the admin root POST logout 303 to login ; the session ends and its cookie is cleared Usernames are stored in lower case: 1 to 150 letters, digits and . _ @ + - , starting with a letter or digit. An unknown username costs the same hashing work as a wrong password and gets the same answer. password changes the signed-in user's password. The form asks for the current password, a new one (at least admin.min_password_length characters) and the new one again. A wrong current password, two different new ones or a password that breaks the length rule answer 422 with the reason on the form; an expired form answers 403 . Success ends every other session of the user and redirects ( 303 ) to the admin root ( ?done=password ) with a new session.
docs.title: The sign-in page

docs.text: The sidebar and the sign-in card show a bookmark icon by default. logo= replaces it with another built-in icon or with an image you serve yourself: Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" , logo = "layers" ) # a built-in icon Admin ( site = "Blog Studio" , logo = "/static/logo.svg" ) # an image from your app An image path must start with a single / : the admin's content security policy only allows same-origin images, so an https:// URL or //host/... is refused with a ValueError when the Admin is built, as is an unknown icon name. The built-in icons are the i-* symbols of the admin sprite ( bookmark , layers , folder , users , tag , image , ...).

docs.text: Build with a coding agent ¶ A project made by hinoki new is ready for a coding agent: rules already on, an AGENTS.md with the conventions, and an MCP server that describes the app. This page shows the loop and where the agent's authority ends. hinoki new shop # asks for the directory, database, server, agent files, skills, git and uv sync cd shop uv sync # unless you answered yes to uv sync uv run pytest uv run hinoki check The generated tests pass and hinoki check exits 0; this repository's own test suite generates a project and runs both on every change. Hinoki at a glance ¶ A model that has seen other Python web frameworks tends to write their code. This summary is the part of these docs that corrects that; it is also the first block of llms.txt . Import from hinoki : Hinoki , Schema , Access , RouteGroup , http , db and crud . A model class comes from hinoki.orm ( from hinoki.orm import Model, field, pk ). Declare actions with @http.get , @http.post , @http.put , @http.patch , @http.delete or @http.query , then pass them to Hinoki(include=[...]) . Parameters and the return type are annotations. Name an Access policy with access= ; leave it out only for an action that is public on purpose. Writes use atomic=True , alone or on a RouteGroup . Request bodies and responses are Schema classes. Never return a Model : convert it with XOut.from_model(row) . Load relations explicitly with select_related(...) or prefetch_related(...) ; nothing loads lazily. crud(Model, ...) generates list, retrieve and write actions for a model. Run hinoki check after each change; hinoki mcp serves the real registry, rules and models to the agent. Does not exist here: BaseModel , Depends , APIRouter , @app.get(...) and with get/post blocks. from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http class Greeting ( Schema ): message : str class GreetingIn ( Schema ): name : str @http . get ( "/greeting" ) async def read_greeting () -> Greeting : return Greeting ( message = "hello" ) @http . post ( "/greeting" , atomic = True ) async def create_greeting ( body : GreetingIn ) -> Greeting : return Greeting ( message = f "hello { body . name } " ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ read_greeting , create_greeting ]) assert "/greeting" in app . openapi ()[ "paths" ] A test runs this block against the installed package, so the names and syntax above stay true. See function-based APIs for RouteGroup and structure an application for the conventions. What the project contains ¶ File Purpose AGENTS.md Commands, conventions, a pointer to Hinoki's docs for agents and where the agent's authority ends; CLAUDE.md points to it rules.py Eight rules on from the start (below), listed in hinoki.toml as [project] rules = ["<package>.rules:project_rules"] so the application loads them without a rules= argument; the model rules HNK-DB-001 and HNK-DB-002 commented out until the first model exists, because a model rule that matches no model fails .mcp.json Starts the development MCP hinoki-rules.toml The owner's waivers Rule Promise HNK-ACC-001 , HNK-ACC-002 Every action names an access policy and a permission HNK-API-001 , HNK-API-002 Responses are concrete Schema types HNK-API-003 Lists are paginated HNK-TXN-001 Writes run in a transaction HNK-SCH-001 Fields such as password_hash never appear in a response Schema HNK-SCH-002 Request text has a length limit AGENTS.md states the same conventions as structure an application : public only on purpose, atomic=True for writes, Schema classes in responses, explicit relation loading, server values win on create, migrations as reviewed SQL. Give the agent tools ¶ The development MCP lets the agent read the real registry, rules and models, explain one action or error code, check the project and draft a model. It never writes source code, rules or waivers; only run_scenario , when you enable it, runs real handlers. See development MCP . Skills (optional): hinoki skills install writes four playbooks under .claude/skills/ : hinoki-add-endpoint , hinoki-fix-rule , hinoki-review-api and hinoki-test-api . Each names the MCP tool or command to run and what belongs to the owner. See hinoki skills . Errors that say what to do : validation errors list every problem with a path and a stable code, and a registration error names the action and parameter. The loop ¶ The agent reads the project with inspect_project . It makes one small change: a model, a Schema , an action. It runs pytest , ruff , mypy and hinoki check . A violation is a stable rule ID, a location and an explanation; the fix is a code change. Waivers are the owner's decision. hinoki-rules.toml is read by the tools, never written, and a waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target. An agent that edits it to pass a check breaks AGENTS.md ; the framework cannot stop someone with write access, but the change is visible in review. Put the file under CODEOWNERS . Check a change against clients ¶ hinoki openapi --output openapi-baseline.json hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json Take the baseline from the released version. The second command exits 1 and lists each change that breaks an existing client: removed operations or response fields, new required input, narrowed enums, changed types. See hinoki openapi . hinoki llms renders the same document as an llms.txt text of your application's own operations, for an agent that works on a client of it; Hinoki(llms_url="/llms.txt") serves it. Neither is on by default. Generate request bodies ¶ request_cases reads an OpenAPI document and returns one RequestCase per operation with a JSON body: method , path , a valid body , and invalid , a list of (description, body) pairs that each break one constraint. # tests/bodiestest.py from hinoki.ai.samples import request_cases from shop.main import app CASES = request_cases ( app . openapi ()) # one per operation with a JSON body Parametrize a test over CASES : send case.body and expect a 2xx , then send each body in case.invalid and expect 422 . It raises CannotSample for a schema it cannot build a value for, such as a regular-expression pattern. Fill path parameters with real values before sending, and use a disposable database. Docs for agents ¶ Every build of this site also publishes the documentation as plain Markdown, in the layout of llmstxt.org : File Content llms.txt An index: the block above, then one link and description per page, grouped like the guides. Reference, project pages, the changelog and benchmarks are under Optional llms-full.txt Every page except the Optional ones, concatenated in navigation order <page>.md One page as Markdown, for example crud.md or tutorial/1-models.md ; links inside it are absolute, and a reference/ page lists each documented name with its signature and a link to the rendered page The generated AGENTS.md points an agent at llms.txt and tells it to prefer these files and the development MCP over guessing from other frameworks. Each documentation version has its own copy, for example https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/llms.txt and https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md ; the root https://hinoki.caspel.dev/llms.txt follows the default version (see documentation versions ). The files come from the same pages as the site, and the build fails when a link or a description is missing. Limits ¶ The development MCP describes and checks a project. To let an agent use a running app, expose selected actions over MCP . Rules check declarations, not what a function body does. Import rules read the project's own files and report dynamic imports as unverifiable. propose_model is a starting point: owner scoping, pagination and unique_together , but no business rules, state transitions or other relations. This workflow was verified by generating a project and running its tests and check , and by one fresh agent adding an owner-scoped resource from AGENTS.md alone. One run by one agent is evidence, not a benchmark. See also ¶ Development MCP Rules Structure an application

Each documentation version has its own copy, for example https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/llms.txt and https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md ; the root https://hinoki.caspel.dev/llms.txt follows the default version (see documentation versions ). The files come from the same pages as the site, and the build fails when a link or a description is missing.

docs.text: The development MCP describes and checks a project. To let an agent use a running app, expose selected actions over MCP . Rules check declarations, not what a function body does. Import rules read the project's own files and report dynamic imports as unverifiable. propose_model is a starting point: owner scoping, pagination and unique_together , but no business rules, state transitions or other relations. This workflow was verified by generating a project and running its tests and check , and by one fresh agent adding an owner-scoped resource from AGENTS.md alone. One run by one agent is evidence, not a benchmark.

docs.text: Expose actions over MCP ¶ expose_as_mcp publishes selected HTTP actions as tools for a remote MCP client. Each tool call is dispatched through the app like an HTTP request, so the action's authentication, access policy, validation and transaction still apply. # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from hinoki.ai.mcpapp import expose_as_mcp from notes.security import billing_staff from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , title = "Notes" , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , ) # routes and rules come from hinoki.toml mcp = expose_as_mcp ( app , tools = [ "notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices" ], access = billing_staff , ) app . include ( * mcp ) # POST /mcp Hinoki(...) has already included the routes listed in hinoki.toml ; expose_as_mcp selects among those, so call it after the app exists. It raises ExposureError right away when the patterns select no allowed action (for example only writes with allow_writes=False ), a streaming action or one left out of the OpenAPI document. The Blog example does the same for one read-only action of an API class ( blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.drafts , with the editor policy). Choose the tools ¶ tools are fnmatch patterns over qualified action names, the same names rules match: module.function , or module.Class.method for an action of an API class. "notes.apps.billing.api.*" selects every action of that module. Generated CRUD actions are named after the module that declares the crud(...) value ( notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list , see Generated CRUD ), so a module pattern selects them too. Only GET , HEAD and QUERY actions are exposed by default. A QUERY tool takes the request body as its input. allow_writes=True also exposes POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE actions. Use it only when write tools are intended and access permits them. The tool name, description, path and query parameters and JSON body shape come from the action's OpenAPI operation. Unknown arguments are rejected and path values are encoded as path segments. The MCP route never exposes itself. Protect the endpoint ¶ access is required. An intentionally public endpoint says so twice: access=None, public=True . Prefer bearer credentials for a remote client; cookie authentication with write tools needs particular care. The endpoint accepts JSON POST requests. Set allowed_origins to the exact browser origins when browser clients are expected; other cross-site browser requests are refused. Tool output is capped at 100,000 bytes (longer text is cut and marked truncated ); a request message over 1,000,000 bytes answers 413 . Errors and edge cases ¶ When What happens tools=[] ExposureError at the call access=None without public=True ExposureError A pattern matches no included action, or the action is not in the OpenAPI document ExposureError naming it An action that returns Stream , EventStream or File matches tools ExposureError naming it: a tool returns one complete result, so a streamed response cannot be exposed Transactions.require_atomic() is enabled The MCP endpoint is a POST without a transaction of its own; exclude it with except_=["hinoki.ai.mcpapp.*"] . Each tool call still runs the action's own transaction. The endpoint does not provide MCP resources, prompts, sessions or OAuth discovery. See also ¶ Development MCP : a local server that describes the project to coding agents Authentication and access Rules

docs.text: Protect endpoints with authentication and access ¶ Every endpoint is public until you attach an Access policy. A policy pairs an authentication provider (how a request proves who it is) with the permissions an action needs. Write both once and name the policy on each private action. # blog/apps/blog/security.py import hashlib from hinoki import Access , BearerAuth , Caller , Permission from .models import User def hash_token ( token : str ) -> str : return hashlib . sha256 ( token . encode ()) . hexdigest () class BlogPermission ( Permission ): WRITE = "posts:write" class TokenAuth ( BearerAuth [ User ]): """Looks the token's digest up in ``blog_users``; editors get the write scope.""" async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ User ] | None : user = await User . aget_or_none ( token_hash = hash_token ( token )) if user is None : return None scopes = frozenset ({ BlogPermission . WRITE }) if user . is_editor else frozenset () return Caller ( id = str ( user . id ), user = user , permissions = scopes ) auth = TokenAuth () editor = Access ( auth = auth , permissions = [ BlogPermission . WRITE ]) reader = Access ( auth = auth ) This is the Blog example's security module . Name your permissions ¶ Subclass Permission , an empty string enum, and use its members in policies and callers. Access and Caller store each permission as its string value, so BlogPermission.WRITE and "posts:write" match each other in checks, reprs and logs; plain strings are still accepted. Passing one string instead of a collection ( permissions="posts:write" ) is a TypeError . Define a provider ¶ Pick the base class for where the credential travels and implement one hook: Base class Credential Implement BearerAuth[User] Authorization: Bearer <token> resolve_token(token) APIKeyAuth[User] the x-api-key header resolve(value) HeaderAuth[User] the header named by header resolve(value) The hook returns a Caller with a stable id , your user object and its permissions, or None when the credential is unknown. It may be async def or def ; a synchronous hook runs on the bounded sync executor, so it may use blocking libraries. Attach a policy ¶ Name the policy with access= on the HTTP decorator and annotate a Caller[User] parameter to receive the authenticated caller: # blog/apps/blog/drafts.py from hinoki import Caller , http from .models import Post , User from .schemas import PostCreate , PostOut from .security import editor @http . post ( "/drafts" , status = 201 , access = editor , atomic = True ) async def create_draft ( data : PostCreate , caller : Caller [ User ]) -> PostOut : post = await Post . acreate ( data , author_id = caller . user . id , publication_id = caller . user . publication_id , ) return PostOut . from_model ( post , author_name = caller . user . name ) Take the owner from caller.user , never from the request body. Permissions say what a caller may do; whether a given row is theirs is still your query (the Blog's owned_post helper in api.py shows one way). To protect a whole group, set the policy once on a RouteGroup ( RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_staff) ); an action may override it, and access=None makes one action public on purpose. What clients receive ¶ Request Answer No credential 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge A credential the hook rejects (returns None ), or a value that is not Bearer <token> 401 with the challenge A valid caller without a required permission 403 A policy without permissions ( reader above) any authenticated caller passes A policy without permissions is legitimate ("any signed-in user"), and it is easy to write by accident; the rule HNK-ACC-002 asks you to list such actions explicitly. Hash passwords ¶ hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher hashes and verifies with Argon2id in Rust, off the event loop. Create it where you own its lifetime (a factory or a module) and call close() at shutdown, or use it as a context manager ( with or async with ). Its worker threads start on first use; a closed hasher starts them again if it is used, and a hasher that is garbage-collected shuts them down. # blog/apps/blog/passwords.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from dataclasses import dataclass from hinoki import Module , Resource from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher from hinoki.modules import ModuleContext @dataclass ( frozen = True , slots = True ) class PasswordService ( Resource ): hasher : PasswordHasher class Passwords ( Module ): name = "passwords" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( self , ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ]: hasher = PasswordHasher () ctx . provide ( PasswordService , PasswordService ( hasher )) try : yield finally : hasher . close () Inject PasswordService into handlers (see Application modules ): async def change_password ( new_password : str , passwords : PasswordService ) -> str : return await passwords . hasher . hash ( new_password ) async def password_matches ( password : str , stored : str , passwords : PasswordService ) -> bool : return await passwords . hasher . verify ( password , stored ) hash_sync and verify_sync exist for scripts and seeds; needs_rehash(stored) tells you when to rehash after a parameter change, and random_token() returns a URL-safe random token for opaque credentials. When the hashing queue is full, the hasher raises HashingBusy , a 503 . The Blog's accounts module shows a complete login with constant-time behaviour for unknown users. Verify JSON Web Tokens ¶ Subclass JWTAuth[User] , list the keys and implement resolve_claims , which turns verified claims into a Caller (or None ). Read secrets from a settings.Secret field and pass it as the key: JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", app_settings.jwt_key) accepts bytes , text or a Secret , and the key never appears in its repr . For JWTAuth , Rust verifies the signature and registered claims using the current key snapshot. now() and the configured issuer, audience, leeway (0 to 120 seconds; a provider with another value fails when it is built) and expiry policy are read for each verification. A request already verifying with a captured key snapshot finishes with that snapshot; a later verification observes key rotation. Rust does not turn token claims into a Caller : the application's resolve_claims hook still runs for every valid token, and remains responsible for loading or rejecting the identity and deciding its permissions. Sync, async and sync functions returning awaitables follow the normal hook execution path. Claims-only tokens on the native lane ¶ ClaimsJWTAuth is a JWTAuth whose caller comes from the token alone: sub (a non-empty string) becomes Caller.id , the claim named by scope_claim (default scopes , a list of strings) becomes the permissions, and Caller.user is None . No database lookup happens, so a token cannot be revoked before it expires: keep lifetimes short. # notes/tokens.py from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import ClassVar from hinoki import Access , Caller , Permission , Schema , http from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth , JWTKey class NotesPermission ( Permission ): WRITE = "notes:write" class Tokens ( ClaimsJWTAuth ): keys : ClassVar [ Sequence [ JWTKey ]] = ( JWTKey ( "2026-11" , "HS256" , b "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef" ), ) # read the key from a Secret in a real application issuer = "https://api.example.com" audience = "notes" class WhoAmI ( Schema ): id : str permissions : list [ str ] tokens = Tokens () writer = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ NotesPermission . WRITE ]) @http . get ( "/me" , access = writer ) async def me ( caller : Caller [ None ]) -> WhoAmI : return WhoAmI ( id = caller . id , permissions = sorted ( caller . permissions )) tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["notes:write"]}, ttl=900) signs with the first key that can sign and sets iat , exp , and iss / aud when configured. The policies of the billing examples ¶ The endpoint, CRUD and transaction guides import billing_staff and billing_admin from one module. Declare the policies once and import them wherever an action or RouteGroup names them: # notes/security.py from collections.abc import Sequence from typing import ClassVar from hinoki import Access , Permission from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth , JWTKey class BillingPermission ( Permission ): MANAGE = "billing:manage" ADMIN = "billing:admin" class StaffTokens ( ClaimsJWTAuth ): keys : ClassVar [ Sequence [ JWTKey ]] = ( JWTKey ( "2026-11" , "HS256" , b "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef" ), ) # read the key from a Secret in a real application tokens = StaffTokens () billing_staff = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ BillingPermission . MANAGE ]) billing_admin = Access ( auth = tokens , permissions = [ BillingPermission . ADMIN ]) A token from tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["billing:manage"]}, ttl=900) passes billing_staff ; without a token the answer is 401 , and with a token that lacks the permission it is 403 . Generated CRUD routes protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth can run on the native lane. Rust only admits requests: a single Authorization: Bearer <token> header whose token verifies (signature, expiry, issuer, audience, sub ) and carries every required permission goes straight to the native action. Every other request, including a missing, malformed, expired, forged or under-privileged one, is handed to the Python pipeline, which answers exactly as it does without the native lane ( 401 with the challenge, or 403 ). With owner and identity_key = caller_id , create, update and delete are native too: Rust sets the owner column from sub , and update/delete are constrained to rows that sub owns. Foreign or missing rows, and MySQL/MariaDB, are answered by the Python pipeline. A subclass that overrides a method, a modified instance, or any other auth class keeps the route on Python. The route's key, issuer, audience, leeway and permission snapshot is rechecked about once per second; reassigning them disarms the native plan until the worker restarts, so a rotation reaches native routes after that interval, not per verification. hinoki routes --lanes shows which lane each route uses. Rust verifies the token on these routes too: a handler route protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth (not generated CRUD) is authenticated by Rust, which admits the caller or answers 401 or 403 itself with the same body and WWW-Authenticate challenge as Python, in the same order relative to path/query errors, the rate limit and body validation. Rust defers to Python for anything it cannot decide identically: several Authorization headers, a value that is not a plain Bearer <token> , or a request Rust already found malformed. A rate limit still runs afterwards in Python, with the admitted caller. Error handlers registered with app.errors do not apply to these answers, on either path, because they translate other exceptions. The provider and policy are checked about once per second as for CRUD routes. Errors and edge cases ¶ Return None for an unknown credential; let unexpected exceptions propagate, they are server errors, not 401 . JWTAuth leeway must be 0–120 seconds; another value fails when the provider is built. Providers hold no per-request state: one instance serves every request and worker thread. Hinoki does not create users, sessions or permission rules: those remain your application's data and policy. A refusal by an access policy emits an AuthRejected event ( missing , invalid or forbidden , the route template and the method; never credentials or the requested path) when the application has a handler for it. The handler cannot change the answer. On Kiso, a route that Rust would authenticate is authenticated by Python while such a handler is registered, so the event can fire. See also ¶ Rules : make "every private action has a policy" a checked promise. Hosts, CORS and HTTPS : the browser-facing side of security. Authentication reference

docs.text: FIELD NOTE · 2026-11-25 15:49:11 +0000 · Linux-7.0.0-44-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.43 Benchmarks ¶ Measured: requests per second and latency of 9 stack setups on 7 request types of one small API backed by PostgreSQL, with 8 workers (multi-process) and 1 worker (single-process). Where: AMD EPYC-Milan Processor, 16 logical CPUs, Linux-7.0.0-44-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.43, 2026-11-25, 100 concurrent connections, median of 2 samples per cell. Pre-alpha software, one host, warm data, loopback network: this is not a ranking and not a production claim. 8 workers multi-process 1 worker single-process Results with 8 workers (multi-process) Summary 8 workers, 100 connections. Median requests per second of Hinoki (Kiso, native server) and how many times faster or slower it is than each framework (ratio of medians). A gap under 10% is a tie. Test Hinoki Kiso, native server Litestar Uvicorn FastAPI Uvicorn Django Ninja Uvicorn Django Bolt Actix, native server JSON 1 KB 176,301 req/s 2.4× faster than Litestar (Uvicorn) 3.0× faster than FastAPI (Uvicorn) 32× faster than Django Ninja (Uvicorn) Tie within 10% with Django Bolt (Actix, native server) 10 rows from PostgreSQL 49,860 req/s 6.1× faster than Litestar (Uvicorn) 7.1× faster than FastAPI (Uvicorn) 15× faster than Django Ninja (Uvicorn) 4.3× faster than Django Bolt (Actix, native server) Articles with JWT auth (ORM) 6,111 req/s 3.4× faster than Litestar (Uvicorn) 3.3× faster than FastAPI (Uvicorn) 7.1× faster than Django Ninja (Uvicorn) 3.8× faster than Django Bolt (Actix, native server) Hinoki (Kiso, native server) against Hinoki (Granian): ahead in 4 of 7 request types, tied (within 10%) in 3, behind in 0. Each result is the median of 2 samples. With so few samples a gap can be noise, so a gap under 10% is a tie and a larger one counts only when the sample ranges do not overlap. Python frameworks Hinoki (Kiso) is Hinoki's own Rust server and its default (started with hinoki serve --server kiso), as Actix is Django Bolt's; Hinoki (Granian) runs the same application on Granian, a third-party ASGI server. Every other framework runs on the server its documentation uses. The stacks were measured in 2 separate runs on the same machine (2026-11-25 17:13: Hinoki (Granian), Django Bolt (Actix, native server), Litestar (Uvicorn), FastAPI (Uvicorn), Django Ninja (Uvicorn); 2026-11-25 16:53: Hinoki (Kiso, native server)). The host load was not controlled between runs, so read a difference between stacks from different runs with that in mind. Scenario Request What the service does json-1k GET /json-1k A fixed JSON body of about 1 KB (1,171 bytes), no database. json-10k GET /json-10k A fixed JSON body of about 10 KB (10,864 bytes), no database. db GET /db Ten users read from PostgreSQL: one SELECT. articles GET /articles?page=1&page_size=20 A page of articles with their author and tags and the total: a COUNT, the page joined with its author, then the tags of the page. article GET /articles/1 One article with its author, tags and comments: the article joined with its author, its comments, then its tags. auth-me GET /auth/me Validate the HS256 JWT in the access_token cookie and return its user: one SELECT. auth-articles GET /auth/articles?page=1&page_size=20 The articles page behind the same JWT check: the user's SELECT, then the articles page. Stack ORM and driver Server Versions Hinoki Hinoki ORM (Rust, tokio-postgres) Granian (ASGI); or Kiso, Hinoki's own server granian 2.8.8 Django Bolt Django async ORM, psycopg 3 pool its own Actix server django-bolt 0.13.0 Litestar SQLAlchemy async, asyncpg, pool_pre_ping Uvicorn with uvloop and httptools litestar 2.25.0, sqlalchemy 2.1.8, asyncpg 0.32.0, uvicorn 0.54.0 FastAPI SQLAlchemy async, asyncpg, pool_pre_ping Uvicorn with uvloop and httptools fastapi 0.162.7, sqlalchemy 2.1.8, asyncpg 0.32.0, uvicorn 0.54.0 Django Ninja Django ORM on a bounded thread pool, psycopg 3 pool, django-ninja-jwt Uvicorn with uvloop and httptools django-ninja 1.8.0, django 6.1.3, psycopg 3.3.9, django-ninja-jwt 5.4.4 Elysia on Bun Bun.SQL (built in), prepared statements Bun.serve, processes sharing the port (SO_REUSEPORT) above one process elysia 1.4.32, Bun 1.4.5 Hono on Bun Bun.SQL (built in), prepared statements Bun.serve, processes sharing the port (SO_REUSEPORT) above one process hono 4.13.21, Bun 1.4.5 Hono on Node.js node-postgres (pg), named prepared statements @hono/node-server on Node.js, node:cluster above one process hono 4.13.21, @hono/node-server 2.1.11, pg 8.23.1, Node.js 26.13.1 How the numbers are computed All listed stacks passed the response and SQL statement-count verifier before measurement. Samples are pooled across server starts and none is discarded. Each sample is a fixed duration; bombardier counts non-2xx responses and failed requests as unexpected. Requests per second and latency are one measurement. Every sample keeps the stated number of connections busy, so higher latency means fewer requests per second; the two do not confirm each other. Bars start at 0 and show the median requests per second. Within a request table every stack shares one scale, and the reference stack comes first, then the others in a fixed order, so the page is not sorted into a ranking. The lowest to highest sample is in the last column. The comparison column is the ratio of two medians , always at least 1 and worded in the direction it points ( 2.4× faster , 1.4× slower ). It is computed from the same raw samples as the medians. 8 workers and 1 worker are separate runs. Each stack is started with that many server processes (and the same pool per process); the two groups are not added together and a 1-worker number says nothing about scaling. Samples are pooled, none is discarded. A stack is started several times; the median, the range and the CV are computed over every sample of every start, and an unstable result lists them all. The exact tables also give the upper median, sorted(samples)[len // 2] , the statistic Django Bolt's comparison publishes; with an even number of samples it is the higher middle sample. p50 and p99 are medians of per-sample percentiles , not percentiles of all requests pooled together. A range is descriptive, not a confidence interval. A gap under 10% between two medians is a tie. Differences that small are inside what this setup resolves, so no order is claimed. A larger gap is called a difference only when the sample ranges do not overlap. CV is the coefficient of variation of requests per second across samples. Above 15% the result is labelled Unstable: its median and samples stay on the page, but it is not given the highest or tied mark and no comparison with it is claimed. What this does not cover: TLS, proxies, compression, writes, cold data, larger tables, container memory limits or other hardware. Pool sizes are equal per process, but each library schedules work differently. It is not a ranking and not a production claim. docs.text: Best practices ¶ Practical defaults for building, securing, optimizing, testing and operating a Hinoki application in production. Each recommendation below matches behavior the framework implements and checks; see Structure an application for the three-layer architecture and architectural rules behind them. 1. Project structure and modules ¶ Separate HTTP, operations and persistence ¶ Keep route handlers thin and push business rules into plain async operations that take typed values ( Caller , Schema , IDs) rather than Request objects. That lets HTTP actions, management commands, admin hooks, MCP tools and tests share the same logic without duplicating checks. Use function-based APIs grouped with RouteGroup by default so shared access= , atomic= and errors= declarations live in one place. Use API classes when you need @crud(...) resources, lifecycle hooks or shared inheritance. Declare routes in each app's routes.py and keep URL prefixes in hinoki.toml ( register routes ). Enforce layer direction with Imports.forbid in your project rules ( rules ). Own worker resources with Module , never at import time ¶ Importing a Python module must not open sockets, pools or files, and must not hold global mutable per-request state. Wrap every long-lived client or pool in a Module whose lifespan opens the resource per worker, exposes it via ctx.provide(...) , and closes it in finally : # notes/passwords.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from hinoki import Module , ModuleContext , Resource from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher class Passwords ( Module ): name = "passwords" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( self , ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ]: hasher = PasswordHasher () ctx . provide ( PasswordHasher , hasher ) try : yield finally : hasher . close () Declare requires = (...) when one module depends on another so startup and shutdown order stay explicit. If handlers need a worker-owned dependency directly, subclass Resource , provide it from a Module , and annotate it on the handler signature ( application modules ). For the database, declaring database: settings.DatabaseSettings on your settings class automatically installs DatabaseModule per worker. Type configuration with AppSettings and Secret ¶ Subclass settings.AppSettings once for the project, give it a prefix, and type every credential as settings.Secret : # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "settings.toml" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings jwt_key : settings . Secret Never hardcode secret defaults or commit secrets in settings.toml (TOML rejects Secret fields at load). Supply secrets through environment variables ( NOTES_JWT_KEY ) or container secret files ( NOTES_JWT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt_key ). Call .reveal() only at the boundary that constructs the client or key ( JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", app_settings.jwt_key) accepts Secret directly without revealing it). Secret redacts itself in str , repr , logs and hinoki settings . Keep strict=True (the default) so typos in prefixed environment variables fail at startup instead of silently falling back to defaults. See settings . 2. API contracts and Schema ¶ Separate input, patch and output Schema classes ¶ Models describe tables; Schema classes describe the public wire contract. Never return a Model instance directly from an action. Define separate Schema classes by role: # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from datetime import datetime from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated from uuid import UUID from hinoki import UNSET , Field , Schema , Unset , derive from .models import Invoice class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 64 )] amount : Annotated [ Decimal , Field ( gt = 0 , max_digits = 10 , decimal_places = 2 )] due_at : datetime class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 64 )] | Unset = UNSET paid : bool | Unset = UNSET @derive ( Invoice , exclude = ( "internal_notes" ,)) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): pass Omit server-assigned fields ( id , author_id , tenant_id , created_at ) from input Schema classes, and pass them explicitly as keyword arguments to Model.acreate(data, author_id=caller.user.id) so server values always win. Use UNSET defaults on patch Schema classes and apply them with await row.aupdate_from(patch) so only sent fields are written. Turn on Actions.forbid_model_responses() and Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", ...) in your rules to prevent accidental leaks. See schemas and schemas from models . Keep validate_response=True enabled ¶ @http.* and RouteGroup enable validate_response=True by default. Leave it enabled: Hinoki checks the handler's return value against its return annotation before encoding the response, catching contract drift early and rolling back an atomic=True transaction instead of committing after a broken answer. Reach for validate_response=False only for intentional escape hatches where the return type cannot be checked ( requests and responses ). Use strict, explicit scalar types and avoid lazy I/O ¶ Use timezone-aware datetime (and time with an offset on the wire), UUID for opaque identifiers, Decimal with max_digits / decimal_places for money (never float ), and Enum or Literal for closed sets ( scalar field types ). Never trigger I/O during Schema serialization. Relations in Hinoki are never lazy, so load every related row before calling from_model(...) or projecting. 3. Security, authentication and Access ¶ Centralize authorization in reusable Access policies ¶ Endpoints are public by default. Define authentication providers ( BearerAuth , JWTAuth , ClaimsJWTAuth , APIKeyAuth , HeaderAuth ) and Permission enums once, compose them into named Access policies, and attach them on the RouteGroup or action: # notes/security.py from hinoki import Access , BearerAuth , Caller , Permission class BillingPermission ( Permission ): READ = "billing:read" WRITE = "billing:write" class TokenAuth ( BearerAuth [ User ]): async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ User ] | None : ... auth = TokenAuth () billing_reader = Access ( auth = auth , permissions = [ BillingPermission . READ ]) billing_writer = Access ( auth = auth , permissions = [ BillingPermission . WRITE ]) Keep Actions.require_access ( HNK-ACC-001 ) and HNK-ACC-002 enabled so every public or permissionless action is an explicit decision ( authentication and access , rules ). Enforce ownership and tenant scoping everywhere ¶ Permissions control what a caller may do; your queries control which rows they may touch. Enforce the same scope across manual actions, generated CRUD, MCP tools and admin: Manual writes: fold ownership or tenant checks into the write statement itself ( await Invoice.aupdate_where({"id": invoice_id, "tenant_id": caller.user.tenant_id}, {"paid": True}) ) to avoid check-then-write races. Generated CRUD: configure owner= / own_rows(...) or override get_queryset(self, principal) on the API class ( generated CRUD ). Admin and MCP: override ModelAdmin.queryset(self, principal) and ModelAdmin.can(...) in the admin ; MCP tools reuse the action's Access policy and handler directly. Apply rate limits, CORS, host checks and safe errors ¶ Rate limiting: attach RateLimit(limit, window, ...) to sensitive actions such as login or token issuance ( @http.post("/auth/login", rate_limit=RateLimit(5, 60, headers=True), atomic=True) ). The default DatabaseLimits() storage shares counters across every worker and host via the hinoki_rate_limits table (apply its migration at deploy time); use MemoryLimits() only in development or tests. Keep on_error="closed" (the default) on security-critical endpoints so a storage outage fails closed with 503 ( rate limiting ). Hosts, CORS and HTTPS: before deploying, narrow allowed_hosts from * to the exact host names you serve, list explicit browser origins in cors.origins (or per-route http.Cors(...) , never * with credentials=True ), and enable security.redirect_https and security.hsts_seconds alongside exact server.trusted_proxies CIDRs when behind a reverse proxy ( hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). Safe errors: keep debug = false in production so unhandled exceptions return 500 internal_error with a request_id and no traceback or exception message. Raise declared APIError subclasses ( errors=(InvoiceAlreadyPaid,) ) and do not catch broad Exception inside handlers — let the framework roll back and translate the error ( errors ). 4. ORM, queries and transactions ¶ Eliminate N+1 queries and use bulk writes ¶ Hinoki never lazy-loads relations; accessing an unloaded relation raises RelationNotLoaded . Load exactly what the response needs in the query that fetches the rows: Use select_related("customer") for forward foreign keys (one LEFT JOIN ). Use prefetch_related("invoices") (or scoped prefetch_related(tags=...) ) for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many relations (bounded chunked queries). See relations . For multi-row writes, prefer bulk methods over loops: # Batch writes instead of awaiting inside a loop created = await Invoice . abulk_create ( items , returning = False ) updated = await Invoice . abulk_update ( modified_rows ) deleted = await Invoice . abulk_delete ( obsolete_ids ) count = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False , overdue = True ) . aupdate ( { "reminded" : True }, returning = False ) Pass returning=False on abulk_create and QuerySet.aupdate when you do not need the written rows back ( query and write rows ). Scope transactions tightly and respect service boundaries ¶ Put atomic=True on multi-step write actions (or on the RouteGroup , setting atomic=False on pure reads and no-write POST actions). atomic=True commits only after the response is validated and encoded, and rolls back before error translation. Never return Response(status=4xx) to signal an error from an atomic=True action: a returned Response commits the transaction. Raise an APIError instead. Use async with db.atomic(): or @db.atomic inside reusable operations; nested scopes automatically become savepoints. Never perform irreversible external side effects (sending email, publishing messages) inside an open transaction. Register them with current_database().after_commit(...) so they run only after the outermost commit ( transactions , send email ). Never join across service databases or pretend a local transaction spans a remote HTTP call. Store foreign service IDs as plain values, wrap remote calls in operations with explicit timeouts, and design multi-service writes to be idempotent ( more than one service ). Paginate every list and choose the right strategy ¶ Never return an unbounded table scan; enforce Actions.require_pagination in your project rules. PageNumberPagination() when clients need page numbers and a total count. On read-only endpoints ( atomic=False ) backed by PostgreSQL or MySQL with database.max_size >= 2 , pass concurrent=True to run the COUNT(*) and page-row queries in parallel (inside a transaction or on SQLite, Hinoki automatically runs them sequentially). CursorPagination() for deep or rapidly growing feeds where constant-time pages matter and total is unnecessary. Set a 32+ byte pagination.cursor_secret via the environment or *_FILE , index the sort columns in sort order, and never order by a sensitive column (cursors are HMAC-signed, not encrypted). See pagination . 5. Performance and Rust fast paths ¶ Project read-only lists and pages directly in Rust ¶ When a read-only endpoint returns a list or page of a Schema without mutating the items in Python, use aproject(Schema) or apaginate_as(Schema, page, concurrent=True) : # notes/apps/billing/api.py from hinoki import RouteGroup from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_reader ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: return ( await Invoice . all () . select_related ( "customer" ) . apaginate_as ( InvoiceOut , page , concurrent = True ) ) aproject and apaginate_as (and their sync twins project and paginate_as ) encode eligible scalar and select_related schemas directly from Rust rows into JSON bytes without constructing intermediate Python Model or Schema objects. Accessing .items or iterating materializes Python Schema instances lazily from the owned rows without a second query, and schemas with computed fields, hooks, validators or prefetch_related fall back to normal hydration transparently ( pagination , queries ). Keep hot routes on Kiso's native lane ¶ On Kiso , eligible routes skip Python routing and request binding, and plain async def handlers whose await s are stock ORM calls can run on the native handler lane without an asyncio task. Use built-in parsers and renderers ( JSONParser , JSONRenderer , etc.) and plain async def handlers without wrapper decorators when you want native dispatch. For stateless bearer tokens, ClaimsJWTAuth verifies tokens and answers 401 / 403 refusals in Rust without entering Python ( claims-only tokens ). Inspect every route's lane and why any route falls back to Python with: uv run hinoki routes --lanes See inspect an application and Kiso server . Never block the event loop; size workers and pools together ¶ Write async def handlers with a... ORM methods by default. Never call blocking network, file or database libraries inside an async def handler. If you must call a blocking library, make the handler a plain def and use the sync ORM twins ( get , create , paginate , with db.atomic(): ) so Hinoki runs it on the bounded sync executor ( execution.sync_workers , default 8 ; execution.sync_queue , default 64 ). Beyond both, requests answer 503 overloaded ( sync and async code ). Size server.workers , server.runtime_threads and database.max_size together. Each worker owns its own database pool, and a rolling SIGHUP reload on Kiso runs at most one extra worker at a time, so budget: replicas × (server.workers + 1) × database.max_size <= database max connections Keep server.runtime_threads (default 1 ) small unless profiling shows the Rust runtime threads are saturated, and measure changes against a baseline instead of guessing ( settings ). 6. Testing ¶ Use disposable databases, synthetic fixtures and ASGIClient ¶ Tests must never touch production data, real accounts or external mail servers. Point test settings at a throwaway database (an isolated per-test SQLite file migrated with migrator.apply , or disposable PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB servers via HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL , HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL ) and drive requests in-process through ASGIClient (or SyncClient for synchronous tests) from hinoki.testing : # tests/billingtest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import create_app async def test_invoice_access_and_validation ( test_settings ) -> None : app = create_app ( test_settings ) async with ASGIClient ( app , strict_errors = True ) as client : # Anonymous and unauthorized callers are refused assert ( await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" )) . status == 401 assert ( await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" , token = viewer_token )) . status == 403 # Invalid payloads fail with 422 before hitting the handler bad = await client . post ( "/billing/invoices" , token = staff_token , json = { "reference" : "" , "amount" : "-5.00" }, ) assert bad . status == 422 Pass strict_errors=True to ASGIClient so any error response missing from an action's errors= declaration fails the test before OpenAPI can drift. Test every Access policy with denial cases ( 401 missing/invalid credential, 403 missing permission, and cross-tenant or non-owner access) as well as happy paths. Inject ManualClock from hinoki.testing for deterministic timestamps, token expiry and rate-limit windows, and use EmailBackend.MEMORY to assert on mailer.outbox without network I/O ( test an application ). 7. Production and operations ¶ Run migrations as a dedicated deploy step ¶ Never run migrations from a worker lifespan or startup hook. Plan and review SQL migrations during development, then apply them once per deployment from a single release job before rolling the new application workers: uv run hinoki migrations plan billing uv run hinoki migrations apply Check for pending or destructive changes in CI before deploying ( migrations ).
