Sending SIGHUP to the Kiso supervisor (when server.sighup = "reload" , the default) replaces workers one by one without closing the listening socket ( Kiso server ). Startup probe: opt in with Hinoki(startup_url="/health") to expose a fixed GET / HEAD endpoint returning 200 {"status":"ok"} once worker startup completes ( 503 not_ready before startup or during shutdown). Treat it as a startup probe — it does not query the database or downstream services ( optional startup probe ). Metrics and structured logs: enable Kiso's dedicated Prometheus listener via metrics.listen (protected by metrics.allow or metrics.token whenever bound off loopback; never exposed on the application port), emit JSON application logs with logging.format = "json" and logging.include_request_id = true , and emit JSON access logs with server.access_log_format = "json" ( export Prometheus metrics , serve an application ). Pre-deploy checklist ¶ Before shipping a release: Run uv run hinoki check and uv run pytest with zero failures. Run uv run hinoki routes --lanes to confirm critical routes take the expected serving lane. Confirm debug is off, allowed_hosts is narrowed, and all Secret values come from the environment or *_FILE . Apply migrations once ( uv run hinoki migrations apply ) before starting or reloading workers. Verify GET /health (if enabled) and the Prometheus /metrics scrape after rollout.
docs.title: Best practices

docs.text: Practical defaults for building, securing, optimizing, testing and operating a Hinoki application in production. Each recommendation below matches behavior the framework implements and checks; see Structure an application for the three-layer architecture and architectural rules behind them.
docs.title: Best practices

docs.text: Keep route handlers thin and push business rules into plain async operations that take typed values ( Caller , Schema , IDs) rather than Request objects. That lets HTTP actions, management commands, admin hooks, MCP tools and tests share the same logic without duplicating checks. Use function-based APIs grouped with RouteGroup by default so shared access= , atomic= and errors= declarations live in one place. Use API classes when you need @crud(...) resources, lifecycle hooks or shared inheritance. Declare routes in each app's routes.py and keep URL prefixes in hinoki.toml ( register routes ). Enforce layer direction with Imports.forbid in your project rules ( rules ).
docs.title: Separate HTTP, operations and persistence

docs.text: Importing a Python module must not open sockets, pools or files, and must not hold global mutable per-request state. Wrap every long-lived client or pool in a Module whose lifespan opens the resource per worker, exposes it via ctx.provide(...) , and closes it in finally : # notes/passwords.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from hinoki import Module , ModuleContext , Resource from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher class Passwords ( Module ): name = "passwords" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( self , ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ]: hasher = PasswordHasher () ctx . provide ( PasswordHasher , hasher ) try : yield finally : hasher . close () Declare requires = (...) when one module depends on another so startup and shutdown order stay explicit. If handlers need a worker-owned dependency directly, subclass Resource , provide it from a Module , and annotate it on the handler signature ( application modules ). For the database, declaring database: settings.DatabaseSettings on your settings class automatically installs DatabaseModule per worker.
docs.title: Own worker resources with Module, never at import time

docs.text: Subclass settings.AppSettings once for the project, give it a prefix, and type every credential as settings.Secret : # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "settings.toml" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings jwt_key : settings . Secret Never hardcode secret defaults or commit secrets in settings.toml (TOML rejects Secret fields at load). Supply secrets through environment variables ( NOTES_JWT_KEY ) or container secret files ( NOTES_JWT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt_key ). Call .reveal() only at the boundary that constructs the client or key ( JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", app_settings.jwt_key) accepts Secret directly without revealing it). Secret redacts itself in str , repr , logs and hinoki settings . Keep strict=True (the default) so typos in prefixed environment variables fail at startup instead of silently falling back to defaults. See settings .
docs.title: Type configuration with AppSettings and Secret

docs.text: Models describe tables; Schema classes describe the public wire contract. Never return a Model instance directly from an action. Define separate Schema classes by role: # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from datetime import datetime from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated from uuid import UUID from hinoki import UNSET , Field , Schema , Unset , derive from .models import Invoice class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 64 )] amount : Annotated [ Decimal , Field ( gt = 0 , max_digits = 10 , decimal_places = 2 )] due_at : datetime class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 64 )] | Unset = UNSET paid : bool | Unset = UNSET @derive ( Invoice , exclude = ( "internal_notes" ,)) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): pass Omit server-assigned fields ( id , author_id , tenant_id , created_at ) from input Schema classes, and pass them explicitly as keyword arguments to Model.acreate(data, author_id=caller.user.id) so server values always win. Use UNSET defaults on patch Schema classes and apply them with await row.aupdate_from(patch) so only sent fields are written. Turn on Actions.forbid_model_responses() and Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", ...) in your rules to prevent accidental leaks. See schemas and schemas from models .
docs.title: Separate input, patch and output Schema classes

docs.text: @http.* and RouteGroup enable validate_response=True by default. Leave it enabled: Hinoki checks the handler's return value against its return annotation before encoding the response, catching contract drift early and rolling back an atomic=True transaction instead of committing after a broken answer. Reach for validate_response=False only for intentional escape hatches where the return type cannot be checked ( requests and responses ).
docs.title: Keep validate_response=True enabled

docs.text: Use timezone-aware datetime (and time with an offset on the wire), UUID for opaque identifiers, Decimal with max_digits / decimal_places for money (never float ), and Enum or Literal for closed sets ( scalar field types ). Never trigger I/O during Schema serialization. Relations in Hinoki are never lazy, so load every related row before calling from_model(...) or projecting.
docs.title: Use strict, explicit scalar types and avoid lazy I/O

docs.text: Endpoints are public by default. Define authentication providers ( BearerAuth , JWTAuth , ClaimsJWTAuth , APIKeyAuth , HeaderAuth ) and Permission enums once, compose them into named Access policies, and attach them on the RouteGroup or action: # notes/security.py from hinoki import Access , BearerAuth , Caller , Permission class BillingPermission ( Permission ): READ = "billing:read" WRITE = "billing:write" class TokenAuth ( BearerAuth [ User ]): async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ User ] | None : ... auth = TokenAuth () billing_reader = Access ( auth = auth , permissions = [ BillingPermission . READ ]) billing_writer = Access ( auth = auth , permissions = [ BillingPermission . WRITE ]) Keep Actions.require_access ( HNK-ACC-001 ) and HNK-ACC-002 enabled so every public or permissionless action is an explicit decision ( authentication and access , rules ).
docs.title: Centralize authorization in reusable Access policies

docs.text: Permissions control what a caller may do; your queries control which rows they may touch. Enforce the same scope across manual actions, generated CRUD, MCP tools and admin: Manual writes: fold ownership or tenant checks into the write statement itself ( await Invoice.aupdate_where({"id": invoice_id, "tenant_id": caller.user.tenant_id}, {"paid": True}) ) to avoid check-then-write races. Generated CRUD: configure owner= / own_rows(...) or override get_queryset(self, principal) on the API class ( generated CRUD ). Admin and MCP: override ModelAdmin.queryset(self, principal) and ModelAdmin.can(...) in the admin ; MCP tools reuse the action's Access policy and handler directly.
docs.title: Enforce ownership and tenant scoping everywhere

docs.text: Rate limiting: attach RateLimit(limit, window, ...) to sensitive actions such as login or token issuance ( @http.post("/auth/login", rate_limit=RateLimit(5, 60, headers=True), atomic=True) ). The default DatabaseLimits() storage shares counters across every worker and host via the hinoki_rate_limits table (apply its migration at deploy time); use MemoryLimits() only in development or tests. Keep on_error="closed" (the default) on security-critical endpoints so a storage outage fails closed with 503 ( rate limiting ). Hosts, CORS and HTTPS: before deploying, narrow allowed_hosts from * to the exact host names you serve, list explicit browser origins in cors.origins (or per-route http.Cors(...) , never * with credentials=True ), and enable security.redirect_https and security.hsts_seconds alongside exact server.trusted_proxies CIDRs when behind a reverse proxy ( hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). Safe errors: keep debug = false in production so unhandled exceptions return 500 internal_error with a request_id and no traceback or exception message. Raise declared APIError subclasses ( errors=(InvoiceAlreadyPaid,) ) and do not catch broad Exception inside handlers — let the framework roll back and translate the error ( errors ).
docs.title: Apply rate limits, CORS, host checks and safe errors

docs.text: Hinoki never lazy-loads relations; accessing an unloaded relation raises RelationNotLoaded . Load exactly what the response needs in the query that fetches the rows: Use select_related("customer") for forward foreign keys (one LEFT JOIN ). Use prefetch_related("invoices") (or scoped prefetch_related(tags=...) ) for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many relations (bounded chunked queries). See relations . For multi-row writes, prefer bulk methods over loops: # Batch writes instead of awaiting inside a loop created = await Invoice . abulk_create ( items , returning = False ) updated = await Invoice . abulk_update ( modified_rows ) deleted = await Invoice . abulk_delete ( obsolete_ids ) count = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False , overdue = True ) . aupdate ( { "reminded" : True }, returning = False ) Pass returning=False on abulk_create and QuerySet.aupdate when you do not need the written rows back ( query and write rows ).
docs.title: Eliminate N+1 queries and use bulk writes

docs.text: Put atomic=True on multi-step write actions (or on the RouteGroup , setting atomic=False on pure reads and no-write POST actions). atomic=True commits only after the response is validated and encoded, and rolls back before error translation. Never return Response(status=4xx) to signal an error from an atomic=True action: a returned Response commits the transaction. Raise an APIError instead. Use async with db.atomic(): or @db.atomic inside reusable operations; nested scopes automatically become savepoints. Never perform irreversible external side effects (sending email, publishing messages) inside an open transaction. Register them with current_database().after_commit(...) so they run only after the outermost commit ( transactions , send email ). Never join across service databases or pretend a local transaction spans a remote HTTP call. Store foreign service IDs as plain values, wrap remote calls in operations with explicit timeouts, and design multi-service writes to be idempotent ( more than one service ).
docs.title: Scope transactions tightly and respect service boundaries

docs.text: Never return an unbounded table scan; enforce Actions.require_pagination in your project rules. PageNumberPagination() when clients need page numbers and a total count. On read-only endpoints ( atomic=False ) backed by PostgreSQL or MySQL with database.max_size >= 2 , pass concurrent=True to run the COUNT(*) and page-row queries in parallel (inside a transaction or on SQLite, Hinoki automatically runs them sequentially). CursorPagination() for deep or rapidly growing feeds where constant-time pages matter and total is unnecessary. Set a 32+ byte pagination.cursor_secret via the environment or *_FILE , index the sort columns in sort order, and never order by a sensitive column (cursors are HMAC-signed, not encrypted). See pagination .
docs.title: Paginate every list and choose the right strategy

docs.text: When a read-only endpoint returns a list or page of a Schema without mutating the items in Python, use aproject(Schema) or apaginate_as(Schema, page, concurrent=True) : # notes/apps/billing/api.py from hinoki import RouteGroup from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_reader ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: return ( await Invoice . all () . select_related ( "customer" ) . apaginate_as ( InvoiceOut , page , concurrent = True ) ) aproject and apaginate_as (and their sync twins project and paginate_as ) encode eligible scalar and select_related schemas directly from Rust rows into JSON bytes without constructing intermediate Python Model or Schema objects. Accessing .items or iterating materializes Python Schema instances lazily from the owned rows without a second query, and schemas with computed fields, hooks, validators or prefetch_related fall back to normal hydration transparently ( pagination , queries ).
docs.title: Project read-only lists and pages directly in Rust

docs.text: On Kiso , eligible routes skip Python routing and request binding, and plain async def handlers whose await s are stock ORM calls can run on the native handler lane without an asyncio task. Use built-in parsers and renderers ( JSONParser , JSONRenderer , etc.) and plain async def handlers without wrapper decorators when you want native dispatch. For stateless bearer tokens, ClaimsJWTAuth verifies tokens and answers 401 / 403 refusals in Rust without entering Python ( claims-only tokens ). Inspect every route's lane and why any route falls back to Python with: uv run hinoki routes --lanes See inspect an application and Kiso server .
docs.title: Keep hot routes on Kiso's native lane

docs.text: Write async def handlers with a... ORM methods by default. Never call blocking network, file or database libraries inside an async def handler. If you must call a blocking library, make the handler a plain def and use the sync ORM twins ( get , create , paginate , with db.atomic(): ) so Hinoki runs it on the bounded sync executor ( execution.sync_workers , default 8 ; execution.sync_queue , default 64 ). Beyond both, requests answer 503 overloaded ( sync and async code ). Size server.workers , server.runtime_threads and database.max_size together. Each worker owns its own database pool, and a rolling SIGHUP reload on Kiso runs at most one extra worker at a time, so budget: replicas × (server.workers + 1) × database.max_size <= database max connections Keep server.runtime_threads (default 1 ) small unless profiling shows the Rust runtime threads are saturated, and measure changes against a baseline instead of guessing ( settings ).
docs.title: Never block the event loop; size workers and pools together

docs.text: Cache values ¶ Cache stores bounded byte values or JSON-compatible values with an explicit finite TTL. Install a backend module and request Cache in the handler: from datetime import timedelta from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http from hinoki.cache import Cache , CacheModule , MemoryCache class Summary ( Schema ): total : int @http . get ( "/summary" ) async def summary ( cache : Cache ) -> Summary : cached = await cache . get_schema ( "summary" , Summary ) if cached is not None : return cached fresh = Summary ( total = await calculate_total ()) await cache . set_schema ( "summary" , fresh , ttl = timedelta ( seconds = 60 )) return fresh app = Hinoki ( include = [ summary ], modules = [ CacheModule ( MemoryCache ( max_entries = 5_000 , max_bytes = 32 * 1024 * 1024 ))], ) The API includes async get , set , delete , get_bytes , set_bytes , get_schema , set_schema and get_or_set , plus get_sync , set_sync , delete_sync , get_bytes_sync and set_bytes_sync . A sync handler can use the sync methods. The memory backend calls its Rust cache directly; the database backend bridges its sync methods to the worker event loop, so use those only in a Hinoki sync handler or another Hinoki sync execution context. get returns None for a miss or expired value. None cannot be stored as a JSON value because that would make a stored null indistinguishable from a miss; use a tagged object if the application needs that distinction. set always requires a TTL between a positive value and 366 days. Keys are UTF-8 strings of 1–256 bytes without NUL. cache.namespace("users") returns a view that prefixes keys and enforces the same full-key limit. The view delegates to its cache, so a namespace taken from a DatabaseCache follows that cache's worker binding and cleanup. set_schema stores the schema's declared fields only: @computed_field values are omitted and recomputed when get_schema validates the value again, so schemas with the default extra="forbid" round-trip. A schema containing a Secret field, including in a nested schema, is rejected with ValueError instead of caching a masked or plain secret. get_or_set reads, calls its factory on a miss and writes the result. It does not coalesce concurrent misses, so applications with expensive factories may need their own single-flight or locking policy. Schema validation mismatches in get_schema delete the stale value and return a miss; malformed JSON raises CacheDecodeError . Backends and ownership ¶ Backend State and visibility Limits and expiration MemoryCache(max_entries=10_000, max_bytes=64 MiB) Rust hinoki.core.MemoryCache , owned by one worker process; not shared by other workers Both entry count and encoded bytes are bounded; each value defaults to at most 1 MiB; monotonic TTL and clock-style eviction DatabaseCache() Uses the worker's Database ; visible across processes sharing that database Default value limit 1 MiB; TTL is checked on read; call purge_expired() from scheduled maintenance The native memory cache is guarded by a Rust mutex, copies bytes at the Python binding, and uses a second-chance clock for eviction. Its state is process-local; multiple workers do not share or invalidate each other's entries. The database backend is shared through the selected database, but has higher I/O cost and no configured global table-size quota. Values are stored as hex text, so database storage uses more bytes than the original payload. No periodic cleanup job is started by Hinoki. CacheModule(MemoryCache(...)) needs no database. CacheModule(DatabaseCache()) requires the application's DatabaseModule and uses that worker's connection pool. The database backend needs the hinoki_cache table. Apply the SQL at migrations_path() / "0001-initial.sql" through an explicit reviewed project migration; neither import nor lifespan creates a table. Failures ¶ Cache failures are visible by default. CacheUnavailable is 503, InvalidCacheKey is 400, CacheValueTooLarge is 413 and CacheDecodeError is 500. Invalid TTLs and non-JSON values raise ValueError or TypeError before the backend is called. Backend database errors become CacheUnavailable ; a route that wants a best-effort fallback should catch CacheError explicitly. Cache injection does not add a Request parameter and is excluded from the OpenAPI document and MCP input schema. A route that uses a cache still follows the normal Python handler boundary when its cache calls are ordinary Python awaitables; the Rust memory backend only moves byte storage, expiry and eviction into Rust. The cache does not implement HTTP response caching, ORM query caching, distributed invalidation, or security-sensitive rate limiting.

docs.text: Changelog ¶ Every user-facing change to Hinoki, newest first. Hinoki is pre-alpha and no release has been tagged yet, so changes are listed under Unreleased . Security schemes, page envelopes and Schema classes that would share a component name get a numeric suffix instead of overwriting each other; page envelopes of scalar items are named after the item ( Page_integer ). Decimal bounds are written as x-minimum / x-maximum / x-exclusiveMinimum / x-exclusiveMaximum strings and decimal examples as text. Field(description=..., examples=..., deprecated=..., discriminator=...) used as a default now reaches the schema, and its overloads type-check as a default. Kiso request heads: blank lines before the request line now count toward execution.max_header_bytes , so the head bound matches what the HTTP parser reads ( crates/kiso/src/framing.rs ). Admin forms and lists: create and edit forms accept date , time , Decimal and Enum columns (a select of member names); required columns of these types no longer make creation fail. A soft-delete model with custom tabs keeps its Deleted tab, an admin at Admin(prefix="") links to / , the bento theme keeps Sign out and Change password on phones, the bulk bar works without JavaScript, and the paper and bento lists keep column sorting and select-all. Navigation links drop a stale success banner, the search form and tab bar are omitted when there is nothing to search or choose, and the admin UI reads its component and icon files on first use instead of at import ( python/hinoki/admin/ ). hinoki admin : the command builds AdminAccounts from the project's admin settings, so admin.min_password_length applies to create-superuser and set-password ( python/hinoki/cli/admin.py ). MCP, OpenAPI diff and rules: expose_as_mcp() refuses an exposure that selects no allowed action, a streaming action or an action left out of the schema when it is built, not on the first call; hinoki openapi --breaking-against also reports a parameter that becomes required or changes type, a newly required request body and a dropped response body; generated time samples carry a UTC offset; Schemas.forbid_exposure reports a dict return as unverifiable ( python/hinoki/ai/ , python/hinoki/rules.py ). SQLite lock waits: the SQLite writer-lock wait now follows a larger Database.connect(wait=...) value instead of always ending after five seconds; the default remains five seconds ( crates/orm/src/sqlite.rs ). Long page indexes: the sticky table of contents now scrolls within the viewport instead of extending over the footer ( theme/static/css/base.css ). Security review fixes: WebSocket handshakes over ASGI route on the raw path and honour allowed_hosts and trusted proxies, and the same-origin check compares the scheme (also on Kiso over HTTPS); a duplicate Host on HTTP/1.0 is refused; a non-numeric Host port no longer breaks WSGI; the admin form uses the admin timezone; documentation URLs are escaped; a full sign-in table keeps blocked addresses, sign-in and password change count apart, and a user name is delayed after repeated failures; MySQL require_ssl precedes a URL fragment; Kiso's WSGI host bounds the body bytes being read; a remote PostgreSQL URL without sslmode and a world-readable TLS key log a warning. Manifests and scaffolds: names and paths with characters above the Basic Multilingual Plane (for example emoji) are written as valid TOML; they used to be written as surrogate-pair escapes, which TOML rejects ( python/hinoki/projectcli.py , python/hinoki/scaffold.py ). hinoki check : it imports the manifest's models before running the rules and warns when it ran no rules ( python/hinoki/checkcli.py , #391, #393). Migrations: a plan error no longer suggests running migrations plan (#392). Model validation: text length errors count characters, not items ( python/hinoki/orm/model.py , #396). WSGI: a plain WSGI callable reads its settings from the environment ( python/hinoki/runtime/wsgiworker.py , #400). Admin secret error: the error for an app with no admin secret names the real environment variable (for example BLOG_ADMIN__SECRET , from the settings class prefix) instead of a placeholder ( python/hinoki/admin/core.py , python/hinoki/app.py ). hinoki doctor : when the application cannot be built because of a Hinoki declaration error, the finding shows that error's message and a fix that points to it, instead of only the exception class ( python/hinoki/cli/doctor.py , docs/inspect.md ). hinoki routes : the handler column stays aligned when an access name is longer than 24 characters, in plain and coloured output ( python/hinoki/cli/routes.py , python/hinoki/cli/reportui.py ). JSON nesting limits: reading accepts exactly 128 nested arrays or objects and writing exactly 200, as documented; the 129th and the 201st are refused. An empty innermost array or object used to count as one more, and a Schema object is now counted as a container ( crates/bindings/src/request.rs ). 📚 Documentation The docs site publishes llms.txt , llms-full.txt and a Markdown copy of every page at the site root and under each version, generated at build time by docsite/llms.py and checked in CI ( docs/ai-workflow.md , .github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml ). The docsite has a new navigation, rules explorer, entry cards, footer and page transitions. The README is restructured around an animated request flow, the demo is rendered in HD at 60 fps, the comparative benchmark page is reorganized, and documentation links point at hinoki.caspel.dev (#388, #406, #409, #413, #416, #417, #419, #420, #423, #425, #426). Kiso's fuzz workflow now covers request-line framing and request-head limits with head_framing and request_head_limits ( fuzz/ , .github/workflows/fuzz.yml , docs/kiso.md ). The benchmarks page now shows a run on a dedicated 8 vCPU AMD EPYC server, with Fastify, Hono and Bun.serve as an extra group and the load average held at or below 2 before every sample. Hinoki in this run is commit 478e1452 . The benchmarks page is redesigned: 8 workers and 1 worker sit behind tabs, a Summary compares Hinoki on Kiso with the other stacks (ratios of medians, ties and unsettled results shown), and each route has its own table with the ratio, p50, p99, range and CV; the other runtimes stay a separate view (#529). The README, the site description and the docs home now use the repository description, and the README's Write an API example follows the recommended syntax: crud(...) with update and delete in routes.py and a handwritten @http.get action. The footer credits MkDocs in a compact link (#531). 🎯 Summary This is the running list of changes since the repository started. The first tagged release will be 0.1.0: Unreleased becomes [0.1.0] - date .

In the planned 0.1.x line, documented Python, CLI, settings and runtime contracts, plus migration files, stay compatible across patch releases. A later 0.y.0 may include breaking changes, described in its release notes. The same text lives in CHANGELOG.md . Unreleased New Features Improvements Fixes Documentation

docs.text: Class-based APIs ¶ A class-based API is a subclass of API whose methods carry the same @http.* decorators as functions. A class adds a path prefix, inheritance and, with @crud(...) , generated routes with hooks. For ordinary endpoints prefer functions and a RouteGroup , which also states access, transactions and errors once. When to use it ¶ Use a class for Example Generated CRUD plus hooks or extra actions @crud(Invoice, ...) with get_queryset and a pay action Actions that several resources inherit or override A base API with a counts action, reused under two prefixes A resource you ship for other projects to include The admin A class that only puts three functions under a prefix gains nothing over a RouteGroup , and each of its actions must repeat access= , atomic= and errors= . A plain class ¶ # notes/apps/billing/reports.py from hinoki import API , Schema , http from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice class InvoiceCounts ( Schema ): open : int paid : int class Reports ( API , path = "/reports" ): @http . get ( "/counts" , access = billing_staff ) async def counts ( self ) -> InvoiceCounts : return InvoiceCounts ( open = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount (), paid = await Invoice . filter ( paid = True ) . acount (), ) path= is the class prefix; each action's path is relative to it, so this action is served at /billing/reports/counts once Reports is in routes.py . Inherit and override ¶ A subclass inherits every routed method. Members are resolved by name, most derived first: # notes/apps/billing/reports.py (continued) class ArchiveReports ( Reports , path = "/archive" ): # /archive/counts, own prefix pass class PublicReports ( Reports ): # inherits path="/reports" def counts ( self ) -> None : # redefined without a decorator: no route return None In the subclass Result Nothing The route is inherited, under the subclass's path= or the inherited one The same name with a decorator Replaces the inherited route The same name without a decorator Drops the inherited route Include only the classes you serve. A base and a subclass with the same prefix are two copies of every inherited route, and the application refuses the second. Generated CRUD with hooks ¶ @crud(...) generates list and retrieve, plus the writes you give a Schema for, on a class whose only base is API . Hooks change what the generated actions do; any other decorated method is a handwritten action: # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from uuid import UUID from hinoki import API , Caller , crud , errors , http from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut class InvoiceAlreadyPaid ( errors . Conflict ): code = "invoice_already_paid" message = "The invoice is already paid." @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): def get_queryset ( self , principal : Caller [ Any ] | None ) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: return Invoice . all () . order_by ( "reference" ) @http . post ( "/ {item_id} /pay" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True , errors = ( errors . NotFound , InvoiceAlreadyPaid ), ) async def pay ( self , item_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : changed = await Invoice . aupdate_where ( { "id" : item_id , "paid" : False }, { "paid" : True } ) if not changed : await Invoice . aget ( id = item_id ) # 404 when it does not exist raise InvoiceAlreadyPaid () return InvoiceOut . from_model ( changed [ 0 ]) # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable from .api import Invoices routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Invoices ] Route Source Access GET /billing/invoices generated list (paginated) billing_staff GET /billing/invoices/{item_id} generated retrieve billing_staff POST /billing/invoices generated create ( create=InvoiceIn , atomic) billing_staff POST /billing/invoices/{item_id}/pay handwritten pay its own access= The access= of crud(...) covers generated actions only; a handwritten method states its own. pay changes the row only if it is still unpaid, in one statement, so two concurrent calls cannot both succeed. Hooks, CrudAccess , owner= and every keyword are in Generate CRUD routes . When a resource needs no code, crud(...) is a value, not a class: # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut routes : list [ Includable ] = [ crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff , ), ] To let clients filter, order and search the generated list, pass a FilterSet as filters=InvoiceFilters to @crud(...) or to the value form. The class then may define filter_queryset(self, query, params: InvoiceFilters, principal) , which runs after get_queryset and the client's filters, so it can only narrow further; see filter, order and search the list . The Tracker example's Tasks class combines filters= , owner= , a get_queryset scope, a remove hook and a handwritten complete action. One instance per request ¶ Hinoki creates the class with no arguments for every request and calls the method on that instance. Keep self empty: Take request data as parameters: request: Request , caller: Caller[Staff] , path and body values. Reach worker resources through a module , never through attributes set on self or on the class. Do not define an __init__ that needs arguments. Hinoki refuses it when the class is included. A class that keeps the stock constructor and sets no response_headers is eligible for the native handler lane like a function. hinoki routes --lanes shows the choice per route. Best practices ¶ Use a class for @crud , inheritance or a shipped resource , functions otherwise. One base, API . A @crud class accepts no other base. Share configuration with a value ( staff_crud = functools.partial(crud, access=billing_staff) ) instead of a mixin. State access= , atomic= and errors= on every handwritten action. The class carries a path only; on a protected @crud class, omitting access= on a handwritten action raises RegistrationError (pass access=None to make it public on purpose). Scope writes in the statement ( aupdate_where with the conditions), not check-then-write. Hooks build queries. get_queryset does no I/O; load relations explicitly in to_schema or written_queryset . Let crud generate or omit, not compete. To write any generated action yourself, pass it in omit= (for example omit=("list",) or omit=("update",) ), or leave create= / update= / delete=True out. Test it ¶ # tests/invoicestest.py from notes.apps.billing.api import Invoices from notes.security import billing_staff def test_invoice_routes () -> None : routes = {( r . method , r . path ): r for r in Invoices . routes ()} pay = routes [ "POST" , "/invoices/ {item_id} /pay" ] assert ( pay . access , pay . atomic ) == ( billing_staff , True ) assert ( "GET" , "/invoices/ {item_id} " ) in routes Invoices.routes() lists the class routes with its own prefix, without an application. Request tests are the same as for functions: build Hinoki(include=[Mount("/billing", routes)]) and use ASGIClient ( function-based APIs , testing ). Pitfalls ¶ Symptom Cause Fix RegistrationError: … is created without arguments per request An __init__ with required arguments Remove it; take values as parameters RegistrationError on a @staticmethod or @classmethod route Routes are instance methods Drop the decorator and keep self RegistrationError: Invoices: a crud(...) class has exactly one base, API A mixin or another base Share a functools.partial(crud, ...) or Access values RegistrationError naming create (or list , …) A method named like an action crud generates Rename it, or stop generating that action ( omit= , no create= ) RegistrationError: … is declared by two classes (/a and /b) Two different classes (often two crud(...) values for one model in one module) give an action the same qualified name Rename one class, or pass crud(..., name="ArchiveCrud") RegistrationError naming a handwritten action and access= A handwritten action on a protected @crud class omitted access= Add access=... to its decorator, or access=None to make it public on purpose A route vanished in a subclass The method was redefined without a decorator Re-declare it with its decorator

docs.text: Command line ¶ Every task in a Hinoki project has a hinoki command. Inside a project created by hinoki new , run them through uv run , which uses the project's locked environment: uv run hinoki dev uv run hinoki check uv run hinoki migrations apply Commands ¶ Group Command What it does Guide Start hinoki new [NAME] Create a project; asks for what the flags leave out, ending with "Create an app now?" ( --app NAME , --no-app ). Create a project hinoki app create\|add\|list Add an app, register an existing package, list the apps. below hinoki dev / serve Run with reload / run for production, on Kiso or Granian; --interface wsgi serves a WSGI callable. Serve hinoki shell Python shell with the app, its settings and models, top-level await . Shell Inspect hinoki check Run the architecture rules. Inspect hinoki doctor Environment, manifest and app diagnostics. Inspect hinoki routes Every route with its access policy and server lane. Inspect hinoki events Every event handler in execution order, the event limits and the apps' events targets. Inspect hinoki mail check Read and check every registered email template against its context. Email templates hinoki mail preview NAME Render one registered email template from a sample or a JSON context, without sending. Email templates hinoki settings Effective settings and their sources, secrets redacted. Inspect hinoki openapi Print, write or diff the OpenAPI document. Inspect hinoki llms Print, write or check the API as llms.txt Markdown for agents. Inspect hinoki version The Hinoki version; --verbose adds Python, platform, native core and Granian. Inspect Data hinoki migrations plan\|status\|apply\|sql Plan and apply migrations for every registered app. below hinoki admin create-superuser\|set-password Manage admin users from the terminal. below Integrate hinoki mcp Serve project context to an AI agent over MCP. below hinoki skills list\|install Write the optional agent skills. below hinoki manage [COMMAND] Run a command your application defines. below hinoki completion SHELL Print a completion script. below Targets and short commands ¶ In a project, hinoki.toml names the application ( [project] application ), so commands take no target: hinoki dev , hinoki check , hinoki routes . To use another application, pass a target, module:attribute , imported from the current directory: hinoki dev notes.main:app . A function that returns an application ( module:create_app ) is also accepted, and hinoki settings also accepts a settings class. When a target does not import, run the command from the project root (where hinoki.toml is), check that the packages have __init__.py files and that the attribute name is right. The commands report error: cannot load notes.main:ap: ... and exit with a non-zero status. Help and completion ¶ hinoki --help lists the commands in groups (Start, Inspect, Data, Integrate); hinoki COMMAND --help shows one command's options. A mistyped command or migrations action gets a suggestion: hinoki: error: argument <command>: invalid choice: 'chek' (choose from 'check', ...) did you mean 'check'? The completion script is generated from the real parser, so it follows the commands and options of the installed version: eval " $( hinoki completion bash ) " # in ~/.bashrc eval " $( hinoki completion zsh ) " # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit hinoki completion fish | source # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish It completes command, subcommand and option names; it does not complete option values or project-specific names such as apps. Terminal output ¶ On a colour terminal, doctor , check and routes print a coloured report: a status glyph per check ( ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed or violated, ? unverifiable, – skipped or waived) with the fix on its own line, and routes with coloured methods. The check summary is green only when the exit code is 0 . When output is piped or redirected, or with NO_COLOR or TERM=dumb , the text is plain and unchanged, and --format json is never styled. app ¶ The generated hinoki.toml registers no app unless hinoki new created one (the last question in a terminal, or --app NAME ): the project package keeps main.py , settings, rules and the health route, and models live in apps. It lists the generated rules in [project] rules = ["NAME.rules:project_rules"] , so main.py passes no rules= . Create each one with: uv run hinoki app create billing uv run hinoki app create gateway --no-models This creates NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,api.py,routes.py,migrations/} (or omits models.py and migrations/ with --no-models ) and registers the app in hinoki.toml , printing the Mount("/billing", billing_routes) snippet to add to NAME/routes.py if the app should be served over HTTP. Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in requires in hinoki.toml ; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order across the full app graph. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time. Both commands report hinoki.toml : hinoki new lists it among the generated files and app create says it registered the app there. --no-models creates an API-only app without persistence, and --requires (comma-separated) sets dependencies directly. app create writes no events module: to add one, create the module yourself and use app add --events or the app's events key (see Events ). Middleware and rules are project-wide lists in the [project] table that you edit by hand (see Middleware and Rules ). In a terminal, app create asks for whatever is not given — the name and, when other apps exist, requires — with the same prompts, Esc-to-cancel (exit 130, nothing created) and NO_COLOR handling as hinoki new . Without a terminal or with --no-input it never asks: the name is required (exit 2) and the default is no requires . To register a package that already exists, name its modules. Nothing is created or imported; only hinoki.toml changes: uv run hinoki app add billing --models legacy.billing.models uv run hinoki app add invoices --models legacy.invoices.models --migrations legacy.db.invoices --requires billing uv run hinoki app add gateway --requires billing --models is optional: omit both --models and --migrations to register an API-only app without persistence. When --models is given, --migrations defaults to the migrations package next to the models module ( legacy.billing.migrations ); passing --migrations without --models is rejected. --events module:attribute registers the app's event Handlers . The whole manifest is validated before it is replaced, so a duplicate name, an unknown or cyclic --requires , or a malformed module name leaves hinoki.toml untouched and exits 2. Whether the modules import is checked later, when a command such as hinoki migrations plan loads the app. List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory: uv run hinoki app list uv run hinoki app list --format json The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module and migration package (or models: none for API-only apps), the events target when set, and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields ( name , models , migrations , requires , events ) under an apps key. The command only reads and validates hinoki.toml : it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2. admin ¶ The admin's own users are managed from the admin itself, except the first one: uv run hinoki admin create-superuser ada # asks for the password twice, no echo printf '%s\n' " $ADA_PASSWORD " | uv run hinoki admin set-password ada --password-stdin A password is read from a terminal prompt or, with --password-stdin , from one line of standard input; it is never taken from the command line, where other users of the machine could read it, and it is never printed. Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D at the prompt exits with status 2 , and a refused connection is reported as such, naming the masked database and its source (status 1 ), not as missing tables. When the connection fails, the command prints error: database: … with a fix: line and exits 1; the error itself does not repeat the URL. sql NAME prints a migration's SQL. A target that does not import, or is neither an application nor a factory, stops the command with an error: line before anything runs. Commands that need hinoki.toml ( app , skills install ) exit 2 without one. Interactive prompts ( new , app create ) never appear without a terminal or with --no-input ; Ctrl-C or Esc cancels with status 130 and writes nothing. docs.text: In a project, hinoki.toml names the application ( [project] application ), so commands take no target: hinoki dev , hinoki check , hinoki routes . To use another application, pass a target, module:attribute , imported from the current directory: hinoki dev notes.main:app . A function that returns an application ( module:create_app ) is also accepted, and hinoki settings also accepts a settings class. When a target does not import, run the command from the project root (where hinoki.toml is), check that the packages have __init__.py files and that the attribute name is right. The commands report error: cannot load notes.main:ap: ... and exit with a non-zero status.
docs.title: Targets and short commands

docs.text: hinoki --help lists the commands in groups (Start, Inspect, Data, Integrate); hinoki COMMAND --help shows one command's options. A mistyped command or migrations action gets a suggestion: hinoki: error: argument <command>: invalid choice: 'chek' (choose from 'check', ...) did you mean 'check'? The completion script is generated from the real parser, so it follows the commands and options of the installed version: eval " $( hinoki completion bash ) " # in ~/.bashrc eval " $( hinoki completion zsh ) " # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit hinoki completion fish | source # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish It completes command, subcommand and option names; it does not complete option values or project-specific names such as apps.

docs.text: On a colour terminal, doctor , check and routes print a coloured report: a status glyph per check ( ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed or violated, ? unverifiable, – skipped or waived) with the fix on its own line, and routes with coloured methods. The check summary is green only when the exit code is 0 . When output is piped or redirected, or with NO_COLOR or TERM=dumb , the text is plain and unchanged, and --format json is never styled.

docs.text: The generated hinoki.toml registers no app unless hinoki new created one (the last question in a terminal, or --app NAME ): the project package keeps main.py , settings, rules and the health route, and models live in apps. It lists the generated rules in [project] rules = ["NAME.rules:project_rules"] , so main.py passes no rules= . Create each one with: uv run hinoki app create billing uv run hinoki app create gateway --no-models This creates NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,api.py,routes.py,migrations/} (or omits models.py and migrations/ with --no-models ) and registers the app in hinoki.toml , printing the Mount("/billing", billing_routes) snippet to add to NAME/routes.py if the app should be served over HTTP. Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in requires in hinoki.toml ; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order across the full app graph. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time. Both commands report hinoki.toml : hinoki new lists it among the generated files and app create says it registered the app there. --no-models creates an API-only app without persistence, and --requires (comma-separated) sets dependencies directly. app create writes no events module: to add one, create the module yourself and use app add --events or the app's events key (see Events ). Middleware and rules are project-wide lists in the [project] table that you edit by hand (see Middleware and Rules ). In a terminal, app create asks for whatever is not given — the name and, when other apps exist, requires — with the same prompts, Esc-to-cancel (exit 130, nothing created) and NO_COLOR handling as hinoki new . Without a terminal or with --no-input it never asks: the name is required (exit 2) and the default is no requires . To register a package that already exists, name its modules. Nothing is created or imported; only hinoki.toml changes: uv run hinoki app add billing --models legacy.billing.models uv run hinoki app add invoices --models legacy.invoices.models --migrations legacy.db.invoices --requires billing uv run hinoki app add gateway --requires billing --models is optional: omit both --models and --migrations to register an API-only app without persistence. When --models is given, --migrations defaults to the migrations package next to the models module ( legacy.billing.migrations ); passing --migrations without --models is rejected. --events module:attribute registers the app's event Handlers . The whole manifest is validated before it is replaced, so a duplicate name, an unknown or cyclic --requires , or a malformed module name leaves hinoki.toml untouched and exits 2. Whether the modules import is checked later, when a command such as hinoki migrations plan loads the app. List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory: uv run hinoki app list uv run hinoki app list --format json The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module and migration package (or models: none for API-only apps), the events target when set, and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields ( name , models , migrations , requires , events ) under an apps key. The command only reads and validates hinoki.toml : it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2.

docs.text: Parsers and renderers ¶ A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. Built-ins use Rust for selected parsing and JSON encoding work; Python still selects codecs, calls customization hooks and assembles framework objects. Built in Rust work Python work and options JSONParser Strict JSON decoding (no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit) prepare(data) hook and media_type Form[Schema] marker A Schema read from form text, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation XMLParser application/xml into a tree (children → dict , repeated name → list , text → str , empty → None ), parsed with the GIL released; no DTDs, custom entities, characters XML 1.0 forbids or encodings other than UTF-8; depth and element caps Rust; max_depth (default 32, at most MAX_XML_DEPTH = 1000, larger raises ValueError ), max_elements (default 10,000); attributes are not read XML[Schema] marker A Schema read from an XML body, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation Query[Schema] marker A Schema read from the query string, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation FormParser application/x-www-form-urlencoded parsing with a field cap Builds the Python mappings; max_fields MultiPartParser multipart/form-data parsing and byte/part limits Builds UploadedFile and form objects; max_parts , max_part_bytes (each part, including text fields) TextParser — Decodes UTF-8 in Python; media_type BytesParser — Hands request.data the raw bytes of an application/octet-stream body JSONRenderer Encodes dict , list , Schema , UUID, datetime and dump() objects prepare(value, request) and default callbacks run in Python; indent , sort_keys , media_type HTMLRenderer , TextRenderer — Type-check and UTF-8 encode strings in Python; media_type XMLRenderer Encodes what JSONRenderer encodes ( dict , list , Schema , UUID, datetime, dump() objects) as UTF-8 XML, with the GIL held; ASCII element names, U+FFFD for characters XML 1.0 forbids, depth limit 200 root , item Content negotiation ( Accept , quality values, wildcards) also runs in Rust; with nothing acceptable the answer is 406 before the handler runs. Upload files ¶ An action that binds an UploadedFile and has no parsers of its own gets MultiPartParser() with its default limits (100 parts, 1 MiB per part), unless the application's parsers= already include a MultiPartParser , which is then used. Other actions accept multipart only when it is listed. The parser handles bounded multipart bytes in Rust, then Python creates UploadedFile objects. For typed handler binding, annotate a parameter as UploadedFile , UploadedFile | None = None , or list[UploadedFile] ; the parameter name selects the multipart field. A single value rejects duplicates, while a list preserves repeated values. The same objects are visible through request.FILES ; text fields are available in request.POST . See endpoint upload declarations for a complete example and status-code behavior. The complete request body and every part are buffered in memory. The default body cap is 1 MiB; increasing it also increases potential memory use across concurrent requests. This parser does not stream or spool files. Keep both the runtime body cap and max_part_bytes bounded, and treat filenames and media types as untrusted client input. JSONParser , JSONRenderer , HTMLRenderer , XMLParser , XMLRenderer , FormParser , MultiPartParser and BytesParser are importable from hinoki ; TextParser and TextRenderer come from hinoki.parsers and hinoki.renderers . Choose them ¶ Per action, or for the whole application (an action's own choice wins): # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , JSONRenderer from hinoki.renderers import TextRenderer from notes.rules import project_rules from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , rules = project_rules , renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( sort_keys = True ), TextRenderer ()], ) # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) from hinoki import JSONParser , JSONRenderer , Request from hinoki.parsers import TextParser @invoices . get ( "/report" , renderers = [ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 )]) async def report () -> InvoiceReport : ... @invoices . post ( "/hook" , parsers = [ JSONParser (), TextParser ()], atomic = True ) async def hook ( request : Request ) -> HookReceipt : ... # request.data is a dict or a str Answer XML ¶ XMLRenderer renders the handler's result as application/xml; charset=utf-8 with an XML declaration. It is written by the Rust encoder, which accepts what the JSON encoder accepts: dict , list , tuple , str , int , float , bool , None , Schema instances, UUIDs, datetimes and dump() objects, at any depth. date , time , timedelta , Decimal , bytes , sets and frozensets, IP addresses and networks, PurePath , Secret (written masked) and enum members are written in their wire form at any depth, as in JSONRenderer : a Decimal as its text, bytes as base64, a set as a sorted list, an enum member as its value. A JSONRenderer 's own options ( default , prepare , sort_keys ) do not apply to it: from hinoki import JSONRenderer , XMLRenderer @http . get ( "/report" , renderers = [ JSONRenderer (), XMLRenderer ( root = "report" )]) async def report () -> dict [ str , object ]: return { "id" : 1 , "tags" : [ "a" , "b" ], "note" : None } Accept: application/xml answers <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><report><id>1</id><tags><item>a</item><item>b</item></tags><note/></report> ; without it the first renderer (JSON) answers. A mapping becomes child elements named by its keys, a list becomes repeated item elements ( item= renames them), None an empty element and booleans true / false . Keys are spelled as the JSON encoder spells them: a string as is, an integer in decimal, None as null and booleans as true / false ; any other key (a float, a UUID, a tuple) raises an error ( 500 ), as it does for JSON. A key that is not a valid XML name (a space, a leading digit, a name starting with xml , so also an integer key) is written as <item key="..."> , escaped, instead of failing the request. Tab and line breaks are written as character references so a parser keeps them, and characters XML 1.0 cannot carry are replaced by U+FFFD. Non-finite floats, which JSON refuses, are written NaN , INF and -INF ; finite floats are spelled as the JSON encoder spells them ( 1e-7 , 1e+16 ). Element names are ASCII ( [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]* , not starting with xml in any case, no colon), so root= and item= that do not match raise ValueError when the renderer is created. Nesting deeper than 200 levels (the JSON encoder's limit; the reading limit is separate: XMLParser(max_depth=) , default 32, at most 1000), an integer of more than 4300 digits or a value it cannot write raises an error ( 500 ) whose message names the type or the limit. The encoder holds the GIL, as the JSON encoder does, because it reads Python objects as it writes; it never reads the request, so an action that lists the renderer stays on the native handler lane. What a round trip keeps ¶ XMLParser is not the inverse of XMLRenderer . Reading back what was written, with XMLParser or XML[Schema] : Written Read back None , "" , {} and [] (all an empty element) None 1 , 1.5 , true the strings "1" , "1.5" and "true" (use XML[Schema] to convert per field) a list of one item {"item": "1"} (a mapping with the item name as its key) a list of two or more items {"item": ["1", "2"]} a key written as <item key="..."> the key item the root element's name lost a character XML 1.0 cannot carry U+FFFD Attributes and namespace prefixes are ignored on reading, and mixed text and elements are refused. A document of more than 32 levels needs XMLParser(max_depth=...) . Use XML for interchange, not to store Python values. Configure the Rust JSON encoder ¶ JSONRenderer ( indent = 2 , sort_keys = True ) # pretty, stable output JSONRenderer ( default = str ) # values outside a Schema the hook sees first default is a Python callback for a value the encoder does not know and must return something that is JSON (returning the same object is an error). It does not override what the encoder always handles (UUID, datetime, Schema , anything with dump() ). Without default , date , time , timedelta , Decimal , bytes , sets, IP addresses, paths, Secret and enum members are written in their wire form anywhere, including at the top level; with default , such a value outside a Schema instance is passed to the hook first, and inside a Schema the wire form always applies. A Secret is the exception: it is always written as "**********" and never passed to default . With sort_keys=True object keys are ordered by their encoded text (quotes and escapes included), which is deterministic but not always json.dumps order for unusual keys, and integer keys sort as text. The public renderer accepts indent from 0 to 16, or None for compact output. Inherit and override ¶ # notes/apps/billing/codecs.py from hinoki import JSONParser , JSONRenderer class Envelope ( JSONRenderer ): media_type = "application/vnd.myapp+json" def prepare ( self , value , request ): # reshape, then Rust encodes return { "data" : value , "request_id" : request . request_id } class SnakeCase ( JSONParser ): def prepare ( self , data ): # Rust decodes, then reshape return rename_keys ( data ) if isinstance ( data , dict ) else data For a different format write a Renderer ( media_type , render(value, request) -> bytes ) or a Parser ( media_type , parse(raw, content_type) -> Parsed ); set consumes_objects = True on a renderer that can take Schema instances directly. Every instance in a position that declares a Schema ( subclass instances )—whether a subclass or an exact instance of the declared class—reaches a custom object-consuming renderer (such as one with consumes_objects = True , or a JSONRenderer subclass overriding prepare ) as a hinoki.core.Narrowed view, never the raw instance: isinstance(value, Declared) holds, the declared fields and @computed_field values read as attributes, and dump() (with the keywords of Schema.dump : include , exclude , exclude_unset , by_alias ) gives the declared fields only; any fields a subclass added are not readable through it, and a field or computed value that holds a Schema (or subclass) reads as a Narrowed of the class its own type declares, at every depth. Narrowed(value, declared) raises TypeError unless declared is a Schema class that value is an instance of. A subclass returned for a top-level declared class that overrides dump() reaches the renderer as the dict returned by the declared class's dump() restricted to the declared fields (an exact instance of that class arrives as a Narrowed whose dump() runs the same declared dump() ). The built-in JSONRenderer , XMLRenderer and Schema.dump() narrow fields directly without wrapping exact instances in Narrowed . Media types must be distinct within one list; a failing parse raises InvalidBody(code, message) (a 400 with that stable code).

docs.text: A parser turns a request body into Python data; a renderer turns a handler's result into response bytes. Built-ins use Rust for selected parsing and JSON encoding work; Python still selects codecs, calls customization hooks and assembles framework objects. Built in Rust work Python work and options JSONParser Strict JSON decoding (no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit) prepare(data) hook and media_type Form[Schema] marker A Schema read from form text, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation XMLParser application/xml into a tree (children → dict , repeated name → list , text → str , empty → None ), parsed with the GIL released; no DTDs, custom entities, characters XML 1.0 forbids or encodings other than UTF-8; depth and element caps Rust; max_depth (default 32, at most MAX_XML_DEPTH = 1000, larger raises ValueError ), max_elements (default 10,000); attributes are not read XML[Schema] marker A Schema read from an XML body, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation Query[Schema] marker A Schema read from the query string, converted per field Rust conversion, then strict Schema validation FormParser application/x-www-form-urlencoded parsing with a field cap Builds the Python mappings; max_fields MultiPartParser multipart/form-data parsing and byte/part limits Builds UploadedFile and form objects; max_parts , max_part_bytes (each part, including text fields) TextParser — Decodes UTF-8 in Python; media_type BytesParser — Hands request.data the raw bytes of an application/octet-stream body JSONRenderer Encodes dict , list , Schema , UUID, datetime and dump() objects prepare(value, request) and default callbacks run in Python; indent , sort_keys , media_type HTMLRenderer , TextRenderer — Type-check and UTF-8 encode strings in Python; media_type XMLRenderer Encodes what JSONRenderer encodes ( dict , list , Schema , UUID, datetime, dump() objects) as UTF-8 XML, with the GIL held; ASCII element names, U+FFFD for characters XML 1.0 forbids, depth limit 200 root , item Content negotiation ( Accept , quality values, wildcards) also runs in Rust; with nothing acceptable the answer is 406 before the handler runs.

docs.text: An action that binds an UploadedFile and has no parsers of its own gets MultiPartParser() with its default limits (100 parts, 1 MiB per part), unless the application's parsers= already include a MultiPartParser , which is then used. Other actions accept multipart only when it is listed. The parser handles bounded multipart bytes in Rust, then Python creates UploadedFile objects. For typed handler binding, annotate a parameter as UploadedFile , UploadedFile | None = None , or list[UploadedFile] ; the parameter name selects the multipart field. A single value rejects duplicates, while a list preserves repeated values. The same objects are visible through request.FILES ; text fields are available in request.POST . See endpoint upload declarations for a complete example and status-code behavior. The complete request body and every part are buffered in memory. The default body cap is 1 MiB; increasing it also increases potential memory use across concurrent requests. This parser does not stream or spool files. Keep both the runtime body cap and max_part_bytes bounded, and treat filenames and media types as untrusted client input. JSONParser , JSONRenderer , HTMLRenderer , XMLParser , XMLRenderer , FormParser , MultiPartParser and BytesParser are importable from hinoki ; TextParser and TextRenderer come from hinoki.parsers and hinoki.renderers .

docs.text: Compress responses ¶ Kiso , Hinoki's Rust server, can compress the bodies it sends with brotli or gzip. It is off by default and it is Kiso only : Granian and any other ASGI server never compress what Hinoki gives them, and hinoki serve --server granian refuses compression.enabled instead of ignoring it. # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http from hinoki.settings import AppSettings , CompressionSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = AppSettings ( allowed_hosts = ( "localhost" , "127.0.0.1" ), compression = CompressionSettings ( enabled = True ), ) ) class Note ( Schema ): id : int title : str class NoteList ( Schema ): items : list [ Note ] NOTES = NoteList ( items = [ Note ( id = number , title = f "note { number } " ) for number in range ( 1 , 301 )] ) @http . get ( "/notes" , access = None ) async def notes () -> NoteList : return NOTES app . include ( notes ) hinoki serve main:app and curl show what the client asked for (headers other than the ones below are left out): $ curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "accept-encoding: br" http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes HTTP/1.1 200 OK content-type: application/json content-length: 591 vary: accept-encoding content-encoding: br For gzip the same request answers content-encoding: gzip with content-length: 1438 , and a request without accept-encoding gets the 8795 bytes unchanged. curl --compressed decodes the answer. These figures were produced by running this example; they describe this body, not a general ratio. What is compressed ¶ Kiso decides once per answer, after the application has decided it, so a plain action, Stream , EventStream and File are treated by the same rules and HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 behave alike. An answer is compressed when all of these hold: The request sends an accept-encoding that allows br or gzip (quality values and * are honoured, q=0 refuses a coding, and a malformed entry is ignored). With several acceptable codings the order of compression.encodings breaks ties. A request with no accept-encoding gets the body unchanged. The status can carry a body: 1xx , 204 , 206 , 304 and an answer with content-range are left alone. The answer has no content-encoding already and its cache-control does not contain no-transform : that directive is the way for an action to opt out. Its content-type matches compression.types . The default is text/* , application/json , */*+json , application/xml , */*+xml , application/javascript , application/x-ndjson and image/svg+xml . A response without a content-type is not compressed. A body known to be smaller than compression.min_size (1024 bytes) is left alone. A streamed body whose size is not known is compressed. text/event-stream only with compression.event_streams = True , and a File only while compression.files is True (the default). When Kiso considers an answer, it adds Vary: accept-encoding , even if the client asked for no coding, so a cache keeps the variants apart. A strong etag is weakened ( W/"..." ) on a compressed answer. How the body is sent ¶ A body of at most 64 KiB held in memory is compressed at once, and its content-length becomes the compressed size. If the result would not be smaller, the original goes out. A larger body, a Stream , an EventStream and a File are compressed as they are read, 64 KiB at a time. They have no content-length : HTTP/1.1 uses transfer-encoding: chunked and HTTP/2 uses data frames. A File is still read by the server, so its bytes do not enter Python. When the producer of a stream pauses, Kiso flushes what it has compressed so far, so a client receives each piece when the producer yields it and not at the end. An event stream's keep-alive comments are flushed too. A stream that fails after the head is cut, as without compression: the compressed body is never ended as if it were complete. HEAD receives the head its GET would get when the GET is compressed, with content-encoding and vary and without content-length . It takes no compression slot, so it does not depend on the load, and it is not a promise: the GET can still go out as it is when a body of at most 64 KiB does not get smaller or when every slot is taken, and then the HEAD named an encoding (and a weak etag ) that the GET did not use. Limits ¶ Compression runs on Kiso's runtime threads, without spawning blocking tasks, one piece of at most 64 KiB per step, and an encoder gives the thread back after four steps. Two settings bound the work: compression.max_concurrent (64) is the number of compressions in progress in one worker. An answer that arrives when all are taken is sent uncompressed at once; it never waits. The count of answers sent that way is kept by the server ( Compression::busy in the Rust crate); no setting or log line reports it yet. gzip_level (1 to 9, default 5) and brotli_quality (0 to 9, default 4) trade CPU for size. Brotli qualities 10 and 11 are refused because one 64 KiB piece would hold a runtime thread for tens of milliseconds. The brotli window is fixed at 2^18 bytes. Each compression in progress holds an encoder, which is why max_concurrent exists and is 64. The repository has no measurement of the memory of one encoder or of the CPU time per piece, so none is claimed here. benchmarks/compressionbench.py measures what a client sees over loopback, with compression off, with gzip and with brotli, and prints the body bytes and the median time per request over alternating rounds: uv run --locked python benchmarks/compressionbench.py --rounds 5 --requests 300 One run on a development machine (Apple M4 Pro, Python 3.13, debug-profile extension as built by uv sync , one synthetic JSON body of 12,980 bytes and a stream of sixteen distinct pieces of about 70 KB, five rounds of 300 sequential requests on one connection) gave these bodies and times: Scenario Identity gzip brotli small , bytes 12,980 1,911 733 small , median per request 0.145 ms 0.175 ms 0.194 ms stream , bytes (with chunk framing) 1,161,929 150,933 40,374 stream , median per request 0.426 ms 4.36 ms 3.33 ms The coefficient of variation across rounds was 0.3% to 3.2%. These are loopback numbers for one machine and one body, with the client sharing the host; they say what this body costs here, not a rate, and your content and hardware will differ. Settings ¶ Setting Default Meaning compression.enabled false Turns compression on (Kiso only) compression.encodings ("br", "gzip") Codings offered, in order of preference; each at most once compression.min_size 1024 Bodies known to be smaller are left alone; 0 to 16 MiB compression.types see above type/subtype , type/* or */*+suffix compression.event_streams false Also compress text/event-stream compression.files true Also compress a File compression.gzip_level 5 1 to 9 compression.brotli_quality 4 0 to 9 compression.max_concurrent 64 1 to 65536 compressions at once per worker A value outside its range stops the application at startup with the usual settings error. A plain WSGI callable ( --interface wsgi without WSGIAdapter ) has no settings of its own, so its compression group comes from the environment ( COMPRESSION__ENABLED=true ), and Granian refuses it the same way. The settings are declared and validated in Python; the negotiation, the rules above and the encoding run in Rust. What stays in Python ¶ Only the declaration and validation of CompressionSettings , the refusal under Granian, and passing the values to the server at start-up. No Python object is held by the compression path, and no compression runs on the asyncio loop. Not provided ¶ Compression on Granian or another ASGI server, in ASGIClient and in the test client: tests see the body the action produced. Other codings ( deflate , zstd ), and precompressed files kept next to a File . A per-route option other than cache-control: no-transform . Compression of request bodies. A compression ratio, throughput or latency figure beyond the benchmark above. A test of a WSGI callable hosted on Kiso with compression on: the same policy is passed to that server, but it has not been exercised.

A test of a WSGI callable hosted on Kiso with compression on: the same policy is passed to that server, but it has not been exercised.

docs.text: Concepts ¶ How the parts of Hinoki fit together. Each guide explains one part in detail. A model is stored data; a Schema is API data ¶ A Model describes a table and its queries (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB). A Schema validates what an endpoint accepts or returns. A response Schema exposes only the fields clients should see: @derive(Invoice) copies fields from a model, but you still decide the boundary, and a handler returns InvoiceOut.from_model(row) , never the row. A declaration is reused ¶ An action's signature and decorator options state its route, inputs, access policy, transaction ( atomic= ), declared errors and response. Routing, binding, the OpenAPI document, the rules, the admin and MCP all read that one declaration. Actions are plain functions , optionally grouped in a RouteGroup with shared options, or methods of an API class . Each app lists them in its routes.py , and the project's routes.py mounts exposed apps with Mount(...) ( register routes ). One application object ¶ A server process serves one Hinoki object: the one project.application in hinoki.toml names, or the target given to hinoki serve . Declare it at module level: # notes/main.py import stripe from hinoki import Hinoki , errors from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , title = "Notes" ) @app . error_handler ( stripe . CardError ) def card_error ( error : stripe . CardError ) -> errors . APIError : return errors . APIError ( error . user_message , status = 402 , code = "card_declined" ) Hinoki(...) loads [project] routes , app events , [project] middleware and [project] rules that hinoki.toml declares (each of include= , events= , middleware= and rules= you pass replaces its manifest value; for example, the Blog example passes include= for conditional routes) and opens nothing, so importing the module is safe: commands, servers and tests use the same app . The [[apps]] of hinoki.toml register app packages (optional models / migrations , events , requires ), not further Hinoki objects. One request ¶ The server hands each request to the compiled router and binding layer: Kiso, the default server, does so from Rust and queues matched requests for the Python pipeline; with Granian the request crosses the ASGI adapter first. Hinoki authenticates the caller, checks access, validates inputs, runs the handler, checks the return value against its annotation and renders the response. A transactional action commits after the response is prepared; a failure rolls back before it becomes an HTTP error. Handwritten handlers and hooks run in Python on both servers: the runtime is not an all-Rust server. Details: request lifecycle . Worker resources ¶ Each server worker owns its module lifespan and database pool: startup creates them, shutdown closes them. Nothing is opened at import or shared across workers. Scripts outside the server manage their own short-lived connections. See modules . Optional rules ¶ Rules check declared routes, schemas, models and imports. Hinoki ships twelve; each reports a violation, a pass, or that it could not verify its promise. They do not prove what a function body does. Turn on the ones that suit the application and run them at startup and in development. See rules . See also ¶ Request lifecycle Structure an application Sync and async code Glossary
