docs.text: Generate CRUD routes ¶ crud(...) generates model-backed routes: list and retrieve always, create, update and delete when you ask for them. Use it as a value in routes.py for plain CRUD, or apply it to an API class to add hooks and handwritten actions ( class-based APIs ). # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut , InvoicePatch routes : list [ Includable ] = [ crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , ), ] # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py (continued) @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" , "paid" ), partial = True ) class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): ... Generated actions ¶ Keyword Action Method and path Success always list GET /invoices Page[InvoiceOut] always retrieve GET /invoices/{item_id} InvoiceOut create=InvoiceIn create POST /invoices 201 , InvoiceOut update=InvoicePatch update PATCH /invoices/{item_id} 200 , InvoiceOut delete=True delete DELETE /invoices/{item_id} 204 , no body Writes run in a transaction. pagination= selects the pagination policy of the list route: PageNumberPagination() (the default) or CursorPagination() for keyset cursor pagination . omit= takes any generated action name ( "list" , "retrieve" , "create" , "update" , "delete" ) to drop it so you can omit it or write your own handler instead. The generated actions are ordinary routes, visible to OpenAPI, hinoki routes and the route registry; nothing is registered at import time. Access per action ¶ access= takes one Access , which protects every generated action including reads, or CrudAccess to set actions apart. An action without its own entry uses default ; None means public: # notes/apps/billing/routes.py (variant) from hinoki import CrudAccess from notes.security import billing_admin , billing_staff access = CrudAccess ( default = billing_staff , list = None , retrieve = None , delete = billing_admin ) Here list and retrieve are public, create and update need billing_staff , delete needs billing_admin . Unknown action names raise TypeError . Generated writes always need a policy: a write left without one raises RegistrationError (when a @crud class is declared, or when a crud(...) value is included) unless you pass public_writes=True on purpose. The access= of crud(...) covers generated actions only; on a protected @crud class (any resource where at least one generated action has an Access policy), every handwritten action must declare access=... explicitly (or access=None to make it public on purpose), and omitting access= raises RegistrationError when the class is declared. Rules see a generated action under the module that declares the crud(...) value: the value in notes/apps/billing/routes.py produces notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list , .retrieve , .create , .update and .delete , and the class form uses its class ( notes.apps.billing.api.Invoices.list ). So the scaffold's match="notes.*" rules check them, and a public list goes in except_ like any other action: Actions . require_access ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" , "notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list" ], ) The same names select MCP tools : tools=["notes.apps.billing.*"] also publishes the generated reads, and the writes with allow_writes=True . How the name is chosen: A shared helper that wraps crud(...) and is called at the top level of a feature module names the actions after that feature module, not after the helper's module. name="ArchiveCrud" sets the class name; name="notes.apps.archive.ArchiveCrud" sets the module too. Pass it when the value is built deeper (a factory that calls another factory, or a function run from main.py ), or when one module declares two crud(...) values for the same model. name= is for the function form only. Two different classes whose actions would share a name raise RegistrationError when included, naming both paths, so one except_ entry, waiver or MCP pattern never covers both by accident. One value mounted twice ( Mount("/a", notes) and Mount("/b", notes) ) keeps one name, as any API class or function does: an exception for it covers both mounts. Filter, order and search the list ¶ Declare what a client may ask for in a FilterSet and pass it as filters= . It works for crud(...) as a value and as @crud(...) on an API class. # notes/apps/billing/filters.py from datetime import date from typing import Literal from hinoki.filters import Eq , FilterSet , In , Range , Search class InvoiceFilters ( FilterSet ): paid : Eq [ bool ] status : In [ Literal [ "open" , "paid" , "overdue" ]] issued : Range [ date ] search = Search ( "reference" , "customer_name" ) ordering = ( "issued" , "reference" ) # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import crud from notes.apps.billing.filters import InvoiceFilters invoices = crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , access = billing_staff , filters = InvoiceFilters , ) Declaration Request Meaning paid: Eq[bool] ?paid=false equals the value status: In[...] ?status=open,overdue equals any of at most 50 comma-separated values issued: Range[date] ?issued.from=2024-01-01&issued.to=2024-03-31 inclusive bounds, either one optional discount: Eq[int \| None] ?discount.null=true no value ( true ) or a value ( false ); only for a nullable column and a T \| None argument search = Search("reference", "customer_name") ?search=acme the text is contained in any of the columns, ignoring case; % and _ are literal ordering = ("issued", "reference") ?ordering=-issued,reference sort keys from the list, - for descending Each attribute name is the column it filters. Types are bool , int , float , str , UUID , date , datetime (an RFC 3339 instant, read as UTC), Decimal and Literal[...] of strings; an Eq , In or Range is also what the typed OpenAPI parameter documents. A bool, UUID or Literal has no Range . An empty value ( ?paid= ) is ignored. Without filters= a generated list ignores query parameters it does not know ( ?name=x returns the unfiltered page); with filters= an unknown one is a 422 , as described below. A name that is not declared, an operator that the field does not have ( ?paid.from=1 ), a value of the wrong type or outside the Literal , a repeated parameter, an ordering key outside ordering , or a value that is too long is a 422 listing every problem with its path and a code ( type , choice , unknown , operator , duplicate , too_long , too_many ); the message never repeats the client's value. Values are parsed and coerced in Rust, bound as parameters and never become SQL text, and column names come only from the declaration, checked against the model when the routes are declared. SQLite keeps a Decimal column as text, which compares by spelling and orders alphabetically, not numerically. A Range[Decimal] filter ( ?amount.from=... / ?amount.to=... ) or an ordering entry naming a Decimal column is a 422 there, with code unsupported and path naming the field (or ordering ); only equality ( Eq , In , .null ) is checked against a Decimal column on SQLite. PostgreSQL and MySQL compare and order a Decimal numerically and accept the full Range . A filter's produced names (its own name, .from / .to for a Range , .null when nullable, plus search and ordering when declared) must not collide with the pagination parameters ( page / page_size , or cursor / limit ): a FilterSet that does is refused when the routes are declared, for crud(...) and for a manual @http.get action alike. The list applies, in this order: get_queryset(principal) (tenant and visibility), the client's filters combined with AND on top of it, the filter_queryset hook, the client's ordering and then pagination. A client filter can only narrow what get_queryset returned. The client's ordering replaces the order that get_queryset or the model set, always ends with the primary key so pages are stable, and without it that order stays. filter_queryset(self, query, params, principal) is an optional hook of the class form; params is the InvoiceFilters instance ( params.paid , params.status as a list, params.issued as Bounds(from_, to) , params.search_term , params.is_null("discount") , each None when the client did not send it): # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from hinoki.orm import QuerySet @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , access = billing_staff , filters = InvoiceFilters , ) class Invoices ( API ): def filter_queryset ( self , query : QuerySet [ Invoice ], params : InvoiceFilters , principal : Caller [ Any ] | None , ) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: if params . paid is None : return query . filter ( archived = False ) return query The Tracker example's TaskFilters and its Tasks class in api.py show a filtered, owner-scoped list. The filters belong to the list action: omit=("list",) with filters= is refused. With CursorPagination the ordering columns must be non-null int , str , UUID , datetime or float columns, and a cursor is bound to the filters and ordering of the request that issued it ( details ). On Kiso, a filtered list with PageNumberPagination and no custom get_queryset or filter_queryset hook runs on the native generated-CRUD list lane (with CursorPagination or custom hooks staying on the Python lane, where rows are still encoded in Rust); the admin lists have their own filters and do not use this one. A FilterSet also works on its own: InvoiceFilters.parse({"paid": ["true"]}) returns the typed instance or raises ValidationError . Hooks in the class form ¶ Apply @crud(...) to a class whose only base is API . These methods change what the generated actions do; every other decorated method is a handwritten action: Hook Called for Purpose get_queryset(principal) every action The base query: tenant or visibility filters. Builds a query, does no I/O filter_queryset(query, params, principal) list Narrows the list after the client's filters ; params is the FilterSet instance to_schema(item) every answer A response shape that needs loaded relations written_queryset(principal) after a write Loads response relations of the written row store(values, principal) create Creates the row change(item, scoped_queryset, values, principal) update Updates the row remove(item, scoped_queryset, principal) delete Deletes the row # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut def normalised ( reference : str ) -> str : return reference . strip () . upper () @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): async def store ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> Invoice : values [ "reference" ] = normalised ( str ( values [ "reference" ])) return await Invoice . acreate ( ** values ) Each hook may be def or async def . Sync hooks run on Hinoki's bounded executor and use the sync ORM methods ( Invoice.create(**values) ); async hooks run on the event loop and use the async ones. A sync hook must not return an un-awaited coroutine. When reads are public, principal is None ; when the action has an access policy, it is the authenticated Caller . When every generated action that calls a hook has an access policy, you can annotate the parameter with a non-optional Caller[User] (no | None guard needed). At class declaration Hinoki checks that no public generated action can call a hook expecting a non-optional Caller[...] , and that Caller[User] matches the user type of a parameterized BaseAuth[User] provider; any mismatch raises RegistrationError . For mixed public/protected resources, annotate Caller[User] | None (or Caller[Any] | None ). # notes/apps/billing/api.py (protected CRUD with typed Caller) from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from notes.security import StaffUser , billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ StaffUser ]) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: return Invoice . filter ( account_id = caller . user . account_id ) Apply visibility filters (such as archived=False ) in get_queryset or filter_queryset , and enforce mandatory tenant or account boundaries with RowScope via scope= ; owner= is an independent write safeguard, not read authorization. Relations are never loaded implicitly: load them in to_schema , and in written_queryset for the answer to a write, independently of filters that might hide the changed row from later list requests. Writes are constrained by the mandatory scope= , the query of get_queryset , the primary key and the owner column inside the mutation statement. change and remove must write through that scoped_queryset (call super() to keep the default mutation). With owner= and generated reads, Hinoki issues a UserWarning when neither scope= nor a get_queryset override bounds the reads. The warning is attributed to the resource declaration. Set scope= , override get_queryset , or omit the read actions. For intentionally public reads, a standard-library warning filter matching <Model>: owner=<column> constrains writes only preserves native-lane eligibility. Mandatory row scope ¶ Use RowScope ( from hinoki import RowScope ) to declare a reusable row boundary shared by generated CRUD, handwritten actions and many-to-many links: RowScope.by(Invoice, "tenant_id", from_user("tenant_id")) : reads an attribute from Caller.user (or calls a function key(user) ). RowScope.by_claim(Invoice, "tenant_id", "tenant_id") : reads a verified JWT claim from Caller.claims (compatible with ClaimsJWTAuth ). RowScope.by_caller(Invoice, "account_id") : matches a text column against Caller.id . from hinoki import API , Caller , RowScope , crud , from_user from hinoki.orm import QuerySet invoice_scope = RowScope . by ( Invoice , "tenant_id" , from_user ( "tenant_id" )) tag_scope = RowScope . by ( Tag , "tenant_id" , from_user ( "tenant_id" )) @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , owner = "owner_id" , scope = invoice_scope , links = { "tags" : tag_scope }, ) class Invoices ( API ): def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ StaffUser ]) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: # Presentation filter only; scope= still enforces the tenant boundary. return Invoice . filter ( archived = False ) Passing scope= to crud(...) guarantees: Every active generated action requires an Access policy; create assigns scope.column on the server, and create= / update= schemas, assign= and owner= cannot write it. A missing, empty or type-incompatible scope value stops the request with 403 Forbidden before any database query runs. Hinoki validates that get_queryset , filter_queryset and written_queryset return a QuerySet of the CRUD model, then re-applies scope= with AND after each hook and in post-write reloads. A hook that replaces the query with Invoice.all() can still adjust presentation filters inside the tenant, never across tenants. Reuse invoice_scope.apply(query, caller) , invoice_scope.for_caller(caller) and invoice_scope.value_for(caller) in handwritten actions and domain operations. Write hooks ( change , remove ) must mutate the scoped_queryset provided by the framework rather than an unscoped query. Hooks run inside the transaction and before the commit, so do not send mail or publish external events from them. They are trusted application code: do not bypass the scoped query with an unscoped write or raw SQL. Hinoki checks the persisted item after create and update for model identity and server-assigned fields, but cannot sandbox arbitrary side effects. Generate or hand-write ¶ Each action is generated or handwritten, never both. Omit any action via omit= (or leave create= , update= , or delete=True out) and declare an explicit method on the class: from uuid import UUID from hinoki import API , Caller , crud , http from hinoki.errors import Forbidden , NotFound from notes.security import StaffUser from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut , InvoicePatch from .scopes import billing_staff , invoice_scope , tag_scope @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , owner = "owner_id" , scope = invoice_scope , links = { "tags" : tag_scope }, omit = ( "update" ,), ) class Invoices ( API ): @http . patch ( "/ {item_id} " , access = billing_staff , atomic = True , errors = ( NotFound , Forbidden ) ) async def update ( self , item_id : UUID , data : InvoicePatch , caller : Caller [ StaffUser ] ) -> InvoiceOut : row = await invoice_scope . for_caller ( caller ) . filter ( id = item_id ) . aget () if row . owner_id != caller . id : raise Forbidden ( "You cannot change this item." ) # apply domain updates inside the transaction using invoice_scope ... When omit=("update",) (or any other subset) drops a generated action, the remaining generated actions keep their behavior and native-lane eligibility. A method named like an action that crud(...) still generates ( list , retrieve , create , update , delete ) raises RegistrationError when the class is declared. A handwritten route at the same method and path as a still-generated one fails when the class is included. Reuse ¶ CRUD configuration is plain Python values. Share one Access or CrudAccess , or bind your defaults once: # notes/apps/billing/resources.py from functools import partial from hinoki import crud from notes.security import billing_staff staff_crud = partial ( crud , access = billing_staff ) staff_crud(Invoice, path="/invoices", read=InvoiceOut) works as a value and as a class decorator. A @crud class accepts no base other than API , so mixins do not apply. Many-to-many fields ¶ A model with many_to_many(...) ( relations ) exposes an ids field named <field>_ids by default: tags gives tags_ids . ids_name= overrides the default. The examples below declare tags: ClassVar[ManyToMany[Tag]] = many_to_many(Tag, ids_name="tag_ids") , so their schemas say tag_ids ; without ids_name they would say tags_ids . The field is a bounded set of the target's keys. Declare it in the schemas and give the targets a scope with links= ; all_rows(Tag) is the explicit way to allow every row: class PostOut ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str tag_ids : Annotated [ set [ UUID ], Field ( max_length = 20 )] class PostPatch ( Schema ): title : str | Unset = UNSET tag_ids : Annotated [ set [ UUID ], Field ( max_length = 20 )] | Unset = UNSET @crud ( Post , path = "/posts" , read = PostOut , update = PostPatch , access = writer , links = { "tags" : lambda user : Tag . filter ( owner = user )}, ) class Posts ( API ): ... links= is required for every relation whose ids field appears in a schema; pass a RowScope , own_rows(Target, column) , all_rows(Target) , or a callable taking Caller.user ( None on public routes). The class form can override link_queryset(relation, principal) instead. A write replaces the whole set; an omitted field keeps it and [] clears it. Only the links inside the scope are replaced, so links to targets the caller cannot see are neither shown nor removed. An id that does not exist and an id outside the scope give the same 422 (type unknown_reference ) without echoing the id; more ids than the field's max_length is a 422 too. The owner row is checked against get_queryset and the owner policy first, and the row and its links are written in one transaction. A read schema includes the ids through a prefetch bounded by the field's limit: one joined target-and-bridge query per owner chunk and relation. Each statement reads that chunk under the database's transaction isolation, and shared targets appear once per link in its rows. Rust builds eligible models; Python orchestrates the prefetch and handles custom row builders. See many-to-many prefetch . The max_length of every ids field in a create or update schema is required. own_rows(Tag, "owner") scopes the targets to those whose text owner column equals the caller's id ( Caller.id ); all_rows(Tag) allows every row. The owner value is checked again inside the write's transaction, after the owner row is locked. Native lane ¶ A route with scope= or an ids field runs on the native lane when the scopes are RowScope.by_claim(...) or RowScope.by_caller(...) on text columns with ClaimsJWTAuth , and every relation it exposes is scoped with all_rows(...) , own_rows(...) , RowScope.by_caller(...) , or RowScope.by_claim(...) ( identity_key=caller_id when the resource also sets owner= ), the target's key is an int , UUID or str , the read field is a non-nullable set whose only constraint is max_length (at least the relation's max_items ), with plain items (no item constraints, enums or literals), the create field is required with a max_length and the update field is ... | Unset = UNSET . Rust checks every required RowScope before querying ( 403 on missing or non-string claim), reads the ids of a page with one SELECT on the bridge (a row with more links than max_items is a 500 : the stored data broke its bound), and on create and update it parses and bounds the set, assigns server scope= / owner= , locks the owner row inside the row scope, checks the targets inside the link scope and replaces the links in the same transaction as the row; the answers ( 403 , 404 , 422 unknown_reference , max_length ) match the Python lane. A key Rust cannot read (a string longer than the key's max_length , for example) is answered by the Python lane. RowScope.by(...) , a scope callable, a link_queryset override, a model or lifecycle hook, or a Linked / Unlinked handler keeps the route on the Python lane, which accepts the same schemas and also an optional create field and any other rule the schema states. Security and validation ¶ Set owner="author_id" to assign that column from the authenticated caller on create and constrain update and delete. identity_key extracts the owner value from Caller.user ; its default reads .id . assign maps additional server-owned columns to functions of the caller's user object. Use from_user("publication_id") (from hinoki ) to declare an attribute (or dotted attribute path such as from_user("org.id") ) read from Caller.user ; any callable such as operator.attrgetter also works: from hinoki import crud , from_user posts = crud ( Post , path = "/posts" , read = PostOut , create = PostCreate , access = editor , owner = "author_id" , assign = { "publication_id" : from_user ( "publication_id" )}, ) Client schemas cannot accept server-assigned fields. Generated writes require an access policy even when owner is configured. With ClaimsJWTAuth there is no user object, so use identity_key=caller_id (from hinoki.resources ): the owner value is then the caller's Caller.id (the token sub ). A foreign update or delete answers 403 and a missing row 404 . This is the only owner declaration that can run natively; see authentication . At declaration Hinoki rejects abstract models, unknown schema fields, unsafe nullable fields, missing required create values, update schemas that can overwrite omitted fields, primary-key updates, unknown assigned columns and incompatible derived schemas. only= and exclude= schemas remain subject to the same checks. A stored row that the read= schema refuses (for example a max_length that the data exceeds) is a server fault: the action answers 500 , the response does not repeat the stored values, and the server log names the model, the read schema, the field and the code. Client input that fails a create or update schema answers 422 . A create that breaks a unique constraint answers 409 unique_conflict unless an error handler you register says otherwise. Model hooks and Kiso ¶ Generated create and PATCH update write through the model, so its lifecycle hooks run: create calls acreate , and update saves the item with the scoped query's conditions in its UPDATE, so a row that left the caller's scope since it was read is refused ( 403 / 404 ). A model that defines any of before_save , before_create , after_create or after_save is not eligible for the native create and update routes; they use the Python lane, while its list, retrieve and delete routes stay native. Deleting does not run hooks. A handler registered for the model's Created , Updated or Deleted event likewise moves only the matching action ( create , update , delete ) to the Python lane, where the event is emitted; update then saves the instance with the scoped UPDATE, as it does for hooks. On Kiso, eligible generated routes execute in Rust when their schemas and model are supported and the resource has no access policy (other than an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth ), owner or assignment rule (other than identity_key=caller_id ) or custom hook. Ineligible and stale plans use the Python lane. See Kiso: generated CRUD ; no switch is required. Inspect the generated routes ¶ hinoki routes --path /billing/invoices GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list POST /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.create DELETE /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.delete GET /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.retrieve PATCH /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.update Generated routes appear in the OpenAPI document with their schemas, access policies, status codes and pagination. See the CRUD API reference . Prefer a handwritten action when a workflow has its own state transitions, errors or side effects beyond one model mutation.
docs.title: Generate CRUD routes

docs.text: crud(...) generates model-backed routes: list and retrieve always, create, update and delete when you ask for them. Use it as a value in routes.py for plain CRUD, or apply it to an API class to add hooks and handwritten actions ( class-based APIs ). # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut , InvoicePatch routes : list [ Includable ] = [ crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , ), ] # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py (continued) @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" , "paid" ), partial = True ) class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): ...
docs.title: Generate CRUD routes

docs.text: Keyword Action Method and path Success always list GET /invoices Page[InvoiceOut] always retrieve GET /invoices/{item_id} InvoiceOut create=InvoiceIn create POST /invoices 201 , InvoiceOut update=InvoicePatch update PATCH /invoices/{item_id} 200 , InvoiceOut delete=True delete DELETE /invoices/{item_id} 204 , no body Writes run in a transaction. pagination= selects the pagination policy of the list route: PageNumberPagination() (the default) or CursorPagination() for keyset cursor pagination . omit= takes any generated action name ( "list" , "retrieve" , "create" , "update" , "delete" ) to drop it so you can omit it or write your own handler instead. The generated actions are ordinary routes, visible to OpenAPI, hinoki routes and the route registry; nothing is registered at import time.
docs.title: Generated actions

docs.text: access= takes one Access , which protects every generated action including reads, or CrudAccess to set actions apart. An action without its own entry uses default ; None means public: # notes/apps/billing/routes.py (variant) from hinoki import CrudAccess from notes.security import billing_admin , billing_staff access = CrudAccess ( default = billing_staff , list = None , retrieve = None , delete = billing_admin ) Here list and retrieve are public, create and update need billing_staff , delete needs billing_admin . Unknown action names raise TypeError . Generated writes always need a policy: a write left without one raises RegistrationError (when a @crud class is declared, or when a crud(...) value is included) unless you pass public_writes=True on purpose. The access= of crud(...) covers generated actions only; on a protected @crud class (any resource where at least one generated action has an Access policy), every handwritten action must declare access=... explicitly (or access=None to make it public on purpose), and omitting access= raises RegistrationError when the class is declared. Rules see a generated action under the module that declares the crud(...) value: the value in notes/apps/billing/routes.py produces notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list , .retrieve , .create , .update and .delete , and the class form uses its class ( notes.apps.billing.api.Invoices.list ). So the scaffold's match="notes.*" rules check them, and a public list goes in except_ like any other action: Actions . require_access ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" , "notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list" ], ) The same names select MCP tools : tools=["notes.apps.billing.*"] also publishes the generated reads, and the writes with allow_writes=True . How the name is chosen: A shared helper that wraps crud(...) and is called at the top level of a feature module names the actions after that feature module, not after the helper's module. name="ArchiveCrud" sets the class name; name="notes.apps.archive.ArchiveCrud" sets the module too. Pass it when the value is built deeper (a factory that calls another factory, or a function run from main.py ), or when one module declares two crud(...) values for the same model. name= is for the function form only. Two different classes whose actions would share a name raise RegistrationError when included, naming both paths, so one except_ entry, waiver or MCP pattern never covers both by accident. One value mounted twice ( Mount("/a", notes) and Mount("/b", notes) ) keeps one name, as any API class or function does: an exception for it covers both mounts.
docs.title: Access per action

docs.text: Declare what a client may ask for in a FilterSet and pass it as filters= . It works for crud(...) as a value and as @crud(...) on an API class. # notes/apps/billing/filters.py from datetime import date from typing import Literal from hinoki.filters import Eq , FilterSet , In , Range , Search class InvoiceFilters ( FilterSet ): paid : Eq [ bool ] status : In [ Literal [ "open" , "paid" , "overdue" ]] issued : Range [ date ] search = Search ( "reference" , "customer_name" ) ordering = ( "issued" , "reference" ) # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import crud from notes.apps.billing.filters import InvoiceFilters invoices = crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , access = billing_staff , filters = InvoiceFilters , ) Declaration Request Meaning paid: Eq[bool] ?paid=false equals the value status: In[...] ?status=open,overdue equals any of at most 50 comma-separated values issued: Range[date] ?issued.from=2024-01-01&issued.to=2024-03-31 inclusive bounds, either one optional discount: Eq[int \| None] ?discount.null=true no value ( true ) or a value ( false ); only for a nullable column and a T \| None argument search = Search("reference", "customer_name") ?search=acme the text is contained in any of the columns, ignoring case; % and _ are literal ordering = ("issued", "reference") ?ordering=-issued,reference sort keys from the list, - for descending Each attribute name is the column it filters. Types are bool , int , float , str , UUID , date , datetime (an RFC 3339 instant, read as UTC), Decimal and Literal[...] of strings; an Eq , In or Range is also what the typed OpenAPI parameter documents. A bool, UUID or Literal has no Range . An empty value ( ?paid= ) is ignored. Without filters= a generated list ignores query parameters it does not know ( ?name=x returns the unfiltered page); with filters= an unknown one is a 422 , as described below. A name that is not declared, an operator that the field does not have ( ?paid.from=1 ), a value of the wrong type or outside the Literal , a repeated parameter, an ordering key outside ordering , or a value that is too long is a 422 listing every problem with its path and a code ( type , choice , unknown , operator , duplicate , too_long , too_many ); the message never repeats the client's value. Values are parsed and coerced in Rust, bound as parameters and never become SQL text, and column names come only from the declaration, checked against the model when the routes are declared. SQLite keeps a Decimal column as text, which compares by spelling and orders alphabetically, not numerically. A Range[Decimal] filter ( ?amount.from=... / ?amount.to=... ) or an ordering entry naming a Decimal column is a 422 there, with code unsupported and path naming the field (or ordering ); only equality ( Eq , In , .null ) is checked against a Decimal column on SQLite. PostgreSQL and MySQL compare and order a Decimal numerically and accept the full Range . A filter's produced names (its own name, .from / .to for a Range , .null when nullable, plus search and ordering when declared) must not collide with the pagination parameters ( page / page_size , or cursor / limit ): a FilterSet that does is refused when the routes are declared, for crud(...) and for a manual @http.get action alike. The list applies, in this order: get_queryset(principal) (tenant and visibility), the client's filters combined with AND on top of it, the filter_queryset hook, the client's ordering and then pagination. A client filter can only narrow what get_queryset returned. The client's ordering replaces the order that get_queryset or the model set, always ends with the primary key so pages are stable, and without it that order stays. filter_queryset(self, query, params, principal) is an optional hook of the class form; params is the InvoiceFilters instance ( params.paid , params.status as a list, params.issued as Bounds(from_, to) , params.search_term , params.is_null("discount") , each None when the client did not send it): # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from hinoki.orm import QuerySet @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , access = billing_staff , filters = InvoiceFilters , ) class Invoices ( API ): def filter_queryset ( self , query : QuerySet [ Invoice ], params : InvoiceFilters , principal : Caller [ Any ] | None , ) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: if params . paid is None : return query . filter ( archived = False ) return query The Tracker example's TaskFilters and its Tasks class in api.py show a filtered, owner-scoped list. The filters belong to the list action: omit=("list",) with filters= is refused. With CursorPagination the ordering columns must be non-null int , str , UUID , datetime or float columns, and a cursor is bound to the filters and ordering of the request that issued it ( details ). On Kiso, a filtered list with PageNumberPagination and no custom get_queryset or filter_queryset hook runs on the native generated-CRUD list lane (with CursorPagination or custom hooks staying on the Python lane, where rows are still encoded in Rust); the admin lists have their own filters and do not use this one. A FilterSet also works on its own: InvoiceFilters.parse({"paid": ["true"]}) returns the typed instance or raises ValidationError .
docs.title: Filter, order and search the list

docs.text: Apply @crud(...) to a class whose only base is API . These methods change what the generated actions do; every other decorated method is a handwritten action: Hook Called for Purpose get_queryset(principal) every action The base query: tenant or visibility filters. Builds a query, does no I/O filter_queryset(query, params, principal) list Narrows the list after the client's filters ; params is the FilterSet instance to_schema(item) every answer A response shape that needs loaded relations written_queryset(principal) after a write Loads response relations of the written row store(values, principal) create Creates the row change(item, scoped_queryset, values, principal) update Updates the row remove(item, scoped_queryset, principal) delete Deletes the row # notes/apps/billing/api.py from typing import Any from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut def normalised ( reference : str ) -> str : return reference . strip () . upper () @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): async def store ( self , values : dict [ str , Any ], principal : Caller [ Any ]) -> Invoice : values [ "reference" ] = normalised ( str ( values [ "reference" ])) return await Invoice . acreate ( ** values ) Each hook may be def or async def . Sync hooks run on Hinoki's bounded executor and use the sync ORM methods ( Invoice.create(**values) ); async hooks run on the event loop and use the async ones. A sync hook must not return an un-awaited coroutine. When reads are public, principal is None ; when the action has an access policy, it is the authenticated Caller . When every generated action that calls a hook has an access policy, you can annotate the parameter with a non-optional Caller[User] (no | None guard needed). At class declaration Hinoki checks that no public generated action can call a hook expecting a non-optional Caller[...] , and that Caller[User] matches the user type of a parameterized BaseAuth[User] provider; any mismatch raises RegistrationError . For mixed public/protected resources, annotate Caller[User] | None (or Caller[Any] | None ). # notes/apps/billing/api.py (protected CRUD with typed Caller) from hinoki import API , Caller , crud from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from notes.security import StaffUser , billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , access = billing_staff ) class Invoices ( API ): def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ StaffUser ]) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: return Invoice . filter ( account_id = caller . user . account_id ) Apply visibility filters (such as archived=False ) in get_queryset or filter_queryset , and enforce mandatory tenant or account boundaries with RowScope via scope= ; owner= is an independent write safeguard, not read authorization. Relations are never loaded implicitly: load them in to_schema , and in written_queryset for the answer to a write, independently of filters that might hide the changed row from later list requests. Writes are constrained by the mandatory scope= , the query of get_queryset , the primary key and the owner column inside the mutation statement. change and remove must write through that scoped_queryset (call super() to keep the default mutation). With owner= and generated reads, Hinoki issues a UserWarning when neither scope= nor a get_queryset override bounds the reads. The warning is attributed to the resource declaration. Set scope= , override get_queryset , or omit the read actions. For intentionally public reads, a standard-library warning filter matching <Model>: owner=<column> constrains writes only preserves native-lane eligibility.
docs.title: Hooks in the class form

docs.text: Use RowScope ( from hinoki import RowScope ) to declare a reusable row boundary shared by generated CRUD, handwritten actions and many-to-many links: RowScope.by(Invoice, "tenant_id", from_user("tenant_id")) : reads an attribute from Caller.user (or calls a function key(user) ). RowScope.by_claim(Invoice, "tenant_id", "tenant_id") : reads a verified JWT claim from Caller.claims (compatible with ClaimsJWTAuth ). RowScope.by_caller(Invoice, "account_id") : matches a text column against Caller.id . from hinoki import API , Caller , RowScope , crud , from_user from hinoki.orm import QuerySet invoice_scope = RowScope . by ( Invoice , "tenant_id" , from_user ( "tenant_id" )) tag_scope = RowScope . by ( Tag , "tenant_id" , from_user ( "tenant_id" )) @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , owner = "owner_id" , scope = invoice_scope , links = { "tags" : tag_scope }, ) class Invoices ( API ): def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ StaffUser ]) -> QuerySet [ Invoice ]: # Presentation filter only; scope= still enforces the tenant boundary. return Invoice . filter ( archived = False ) Passing scope= to crud(...) guarantees: Every active generated action requires an Access policy; create assigns scope.column on the server, and create= / update= schemas, assign= and owner= cannot write it. A missing, empty or type-incompatible scope value stops the request with 403 Forbidden before any database query runs. Hinoki validates that get_queryset , filter_queryset and written_queryset return a QuerySet of the CRUD model, then re-applies scope= with AND after each hook and in post-write reloads. A hook that replaces the query with Invoice.all() can still adjust presentation filters inside the tenant, never across tenants. Reuse invoice_scope.apply(query, caller) , invoice_scope.for_caller(caller) and invoice_scope.value_for(caller) in handwritten actions and domain operations. Write hooks ( change , remove ) must mutate the scoped_queryset provided by the framework rather than an unscoped query. Hooks run inside the transaction and before the commit, so do not send mail or publish external events from them. They are trusted application code: do not bypass the scoped query with an unscoped write or raw SQL. Hinoki checks the persisted item after create and update for model identity and server-assigned fields, but cannot sandbox arbitrary side effects.
docs.title: Mandatory row scope

docs.text: Each action is generated or handwritten, never both. Omit any action via omit= (or leave create= , update= , or delete=True out) and declare an explicit method on the class: from uuid import UUID from hinoki import API , Caller , crud , http from hinoki.errors import Forbidden , NotFound from notes.security import StaffUser from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut , InvoicePatch from .scopes import billing_staff , invoice_scope , tag_scope @crud ( Invoice , path = "/invoices" , read = InvoiceOut , create = InvoiceIn , update = InvoicePatch , delete = True , access = billing_staff , owner = "owner_id" , scope = invoice_scope , links = { "tags" : tag_scope }, omit = ( "update" ,), ) class Invoices ( API ): @http . patch ( "/ {item_id} " , access = billing_staff , atomic = True , errors = ( NotFound , Forbidden ) ) async def update ( self , item_id : UUID , data : InvoicePatch , caller : Caller [ StaffUser ] ) -> InvoiceOut : row = await invoice_scope . for_caller ( caller ) . filter ( id = item_id ) . aget () if row . owner_id != caller . id : raise Forbidden ( "You cannot change this item." ) # apply domain updates inside the transaction using invoice_scope ... When omit=("update",) (or any other subset) drops a generated action, the remaining generated actions keep their behavior and native-lane eligibility. A method named like an action that crud(...) still generates ( list , retrieve , create , update , delete ) raises RegistrationError when the class is declared. A handwritten route at the same method and path as a still-generated one fails when the class is included.
docs.title: Generate or hand-write

docs.text: CRUD configuration is plain Python values. Share one Access or CrudAccess , or bind your defaults once: # notes/apps/billing/resources.py from functools import partial from hinoki import crud from notes.security import billing_staff staff_crud = partial ( crud , access = billing_staff ) staff_crud(Invoice, path="/invoices", read=InvoiceOut) works as a value and as a class decorator. A @crud class accepts no base other than API , so mixins do not apply.
docs.title: Reuse

docs.text: A model with many_to_many(...) ( relations ) exposes an ids field named <field>_ids by default: tags gives tags_ids . ids_name= overrides the default. The examples below declare tags: ClassVar[ManyToMany[Tag]] = many_to_many(Tag, ids_name="tag_ids") , so their schemas say tag_ids ; without ids_name they would say tags_ids . The field is a bounded set of the target's keys. Declare it in the schemas and give the targets a scope with links= ; all_rows(Tag) is the explicit way to allow every row: class PostOut ( Schema ): id : UUID title : str tag_ids : Annotated [ set [ UUID ], Field ( max_length = 20 )] class PostPatch ( Schema ): title : str | Unset = UNSET tag_ids : Annotated [ set [ UUID ], Field ( max_length = 20 )] | Unset = UNSET @crud ( Post , path = "/posts" , read = PostOut , update = PostPatch , access = writer , links = { "tags" : lambda user : Tag . filter ( owner = user )}, ) class Posts ( API ): ... links= is required for every relation whose ids field appears in a schema; pass a RowScope , own_rows(Target, column) , all_rows(Target) , or a callable taking Caller.user ( None on public routes). The class form can override link_queryset(relation, principal) instead. A write replaces the whole set; an omitted field keeps it and [] clears it. Only the links inside the scope are replaced, so links to targets the caller cannot see are neither shown nor removed. An id that does not exist and an id outside the scope give the same 422 (type unknown_reference ) without echoing the id; more ids than the field's max_length is a 422 too. The owner row is checked against get_queryset and the owner policy first, and the row and its links are written in one transaction. A read schema includes the ids through a prefetch bounded by the field's limit: one joined target-and-bridge query per owner chunk and relation. Each statement reads that chunk under the database's transaction isolation, and shared targets appear once per link in its rows. Rust builds eligible models; Python orchestrates the prefetch and handles custom row builders. See many-to-many prefetch . The max_length of every ids field in a create or update schema is required. own_rows(Tag, "owner") scopes the targets to those whose text owner column equals the caller's id ( Caller.id ); all_rows(Tag) allows every row. The owner value is checked again inside the write's transaction, after the owner row is locked.
docs.title: Many-to-many fields

docs.text: A route with scope= or an ids field runs on the native lane when the scopes are RowScope.by_claim(...) or RowScope.by_caller(...) on text columns with ClaimsJWTAuth , and every relation it exposes is scoped with all_rows(...) , own_rows(...) , RowScope.by_caller(...) , or RowScope.by_claim(...) ( identity_key=caller_id when the resource also sets owner= ), the target's key is an int , UUID or str , the read field is a non-nullable set whose only constraint is max_length (at least the relation's max_items ), with plain items (no item constraints, enums or literals), the create field is required with a max_length and the update field is ... | Unset = UNSET . Rust checks every required RowScope before querying ( 403 on missing or non-string claim), reads the ids of a page with one SELECT on the bridge (a row with more links than max_items is a 500 : the stored data broke its bound), and on create and update it parses and bounds the set, assigns server scope= / owner= , locks the owner row inside the row scope, checks the targets inside the link scope and replaces the links in the same transaction as the row; the answers ( 403 , 404 , 422 unknown_reference , max_length ) match the Python lane. A key Rust cannot read (a string longer than the key's max_length , for example) is answered by the Python lane. RowScope.by(...) , a scope callable, a link_queryset override, a model or lifecycle hook, or a Linked / Unlinked handler keeps the route on the Python lane, which accepts the same schemas and also an optional create field and any other rule the schema states.
docs.title: Native lane

docs.text: Set owner="author_id" to assign that column from the authenticated caller on create and constrain update and delete. identity_key extracts the owner value from Caller.user ; its default reads .id . assign maps additional server-owned columns to functions of the caller's user object. Use from_user("publication_id") (from hinoki ) to declare an attribute (or dotted attribute path such as from_user("org.id") ) read from Caller.user ; any callable such as operator.attrgetter also works: from hinoki import crud , from_user posts = crud ( Post , path = "/posts" , read = PostOut , create = PostCreate , access = editor , owner = "author_id" , assign = { "publication_id" : from_user ( "publication_id" )}, ) Client schemas cannot accept server-assigned fields. Generated writes require an access policy even when owner is configured. With ClaimsJWTAuth there is no user object, so use identity_key=caller_id (from hinoki.resources ): the owner value is then the caller's Caller.id (the token sub ). A foreign update or delete answers 403 and a missing row 404 . This is the only owner declaration that can run natively; see authentication . At declaration Hinoki rejects abstract models, unknown schema fields, unsafe nullable fields, missing required create values, update schemas that can overwrite omitted fields, primary-key updates, unknown assigned columns and incompatible derived schemas. only= and exclude= schemas remain subject to the same checks. A stored row that the read= schema refuses (for example a max_length that the data exceeds) is a server fault: the action answers 500 , the response does not repeat the stored values, and the server log names the model, the read schema, the field and the code. Client input that fails a create or update schema answers 422 . A create that breaks a unique constraint answers 409 unique_conflict unless an error handler you register says otherwise.
docs.title: Security and validation

docs.text: Generated create and PATCH update write through the model, so its lifecycle hooks run: create calls acreate , and update saves the item with the scoped query's conditions in its UPDATE, so a row that left the caller's scope since it was read is refused ( 403 / 404 ). A model that defines any of before_save , before_create , after_create or after_save is not eligible for the native create and update routes; they use the Python lane, while its list, retrieve and delete routes stay native. Deleting does not run hooks. A handler registered for the model's Created , Updated or Deleted event likewise moves only the matching action ( create , update , delete ) to the Python lane, where the event is emitted; update then saves the instance with the scoped UPDATE, as it does for hooks. On Kiso, eligible generated routes execute in Rust when their schemas and model are supported and the resource has no access policy (other than an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth ), owner or assignment rule (other than identity_key=caller_id ) or custom hook. Ineligible and stale plans use the Python lane. See Kiso: generated CRUD ; no switch is required.
docs.title: Model hooks and Kiso

docs.text: hinoki routes --path /billing/invoices GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list POST /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.create DELETE /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.delete GET /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.retrieve PATCH /billing/invoices/{item_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.update Generated routes appear in the OpenAPI document with their schemas, access policies, status codes and pagination. See the CRUD API reference . Prefer a handwritten action when a workflow has its own state transitions, errors or side effects beyond one model mutation.
docs.title: Inspect the generated routes

docs.text: Configure a database ¶ Hinoki's ORM runs on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. The database URL selects the backend; models and queries stay the same wherever the backends' SQL features overlap. With nothing configured, the database is local SQLite at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . Set up a database in four steps ¶ Declare it. hinoki new notes --database postgresql does this for you; otherwise add the field to your settings class. Name a TOML file only if you will use one (step 2): the file named by toml= must exist. # notes/settings.py class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Populate it. With nothing set, DatabaseSettings points at a local SQLite file, .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . To use another database, pick one source: Source Use it for Example Nothing local development on SQLite – .env one URL on your machine ( hinoki new --database postgresql writes a .env.example to copy; keep .env out of git) NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@localhost:5432/notes Environment containers and CI export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE=/run/secrets/database-url settings.toml non-secret fields ( engine , host , name , user ), with the password from the environment; add toml="settings.toml" to the class connection fields The prefix ( NOTES_ ) comes from the settings class, and __ separates the group from the field. Until you set one of them, a project created with --database postgresql still uses the local SQLite file, and so do its migrations. Check it. hinoki settings , run from the project root, shows each value with its source; the URL and the password are redacted: $ hinoki settings | grep DATABASE__URL NOTES_DATABASE__URL .env *** hinoki migrations status names the database it will use, and fails with a clear error if the server does not answer: $ hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@127.0.0.1:5432/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) status connects and records its migration ledger, so on SQLite it creates the database file. Create the tables. Hinoki never creates tables or runs migrations at startup (it only creates the local SQLite file): run hinoki migrations apply once you have models ( migrations ). The rest of this page lists every field, the URL forms and each backend. Configure the application ¶ Declare a database field on the project settings. hinoki new adds it when you choose a database. # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "settings.toml" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Each worker opens one bounded pool during startup and closes it during shutdown. The Notes example's settings are exactly this field with nothing else. Importing models or routes never opens a connection, and no modules= entry is needed. The file named by toml= must exist, even if it is empty: otherwise the settings fail to load with settings.toml: TOML file cannot be read or parsed . Configure a server database with connection fields or with one URL . Setting both is an error when settings load. Connection fields ¶ Put non-secret fields in the TOML file named by toml= . Keep the settings in their own file: hinoki.toml is the project manifest, and its tables are not settings. PostgreSQL MySQL MariaDB SQLite # settings.toml [database] engine = "postgresql" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" port = 5432 options = [ "sslmode=verify-full" , "sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem" ] max_size = 10 # per worker # settings.toml [database] engine = "mysql" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" # settings.toml [database] engine = "mariadb" name = "notes" user = "notes" host = "db.example.test" # settings.toml [database] engine = "sqlite" name = ".hinoki/local.sqlite3" The password is a secret setting. It never comes from TOML: export NOTES_DATABASE__PASSWORD_FILE = /run/secrets/db-password Field Meaning Default engine sqlite , postgresql , mysql or mariadb ( settings.DatabaseEngine ) – name database name, or the file path for SQLite – user , password credentials; password is secret ( *_PASSWORD or *_PASSWORD_FILE ) – host , port server address; for PostgreSQL host may be a Unix-socket directory such as /var/run/postgresql localhost , backend port options key=value URL query pairs, such as sslmode () max_size connections per worker 10 Hinoki builds DatabaseSettings.url from these fields and percent-encodes the user, password and name. SQLite takes only name . options cannot carry credentials or override user , host , port or the name. In an environment variable, options uses the settings sequence syntax (commas between pairs); a value that itself contains a comma belongs in the TOML array. One URL ¶ export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE = /run/secrets/database-url Backend URL SQLite sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 PostgreSQL postgresql://notes:password@db.example.test/notes?sslmode=verify-full MySQL mysql://notes:password@db.example.test/notes MariaDB mariadb://notes:password@db.example.test/notes Percent-encode reserved characters in the user name and password of a hand-written URL. Prefer NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE or a secret manager over a URL in shell history or a process argument. Hinoki redacts the URL in settings output and connection errors. Credentials settings.Secret values, url and password included, are never read from TOML. SQLite has no database credentials: protect the file and its backups with operating-system permissions. Backends ¶ Backend Security defaults Limits SQLite no network, no TLS one writer at a time; bounded connections and a busy timeout of at least five seconds, extended when Database.connect(wait=...) is larger; a relative path resolves from the server's working directory (start it from the project root; migrations anchor it beside hinoki.toml ) PostgreSQL sslmode=prefer ; use verify-full for remote servers; sslrootcert adds a PEM CA to the system roots. require , verify-ca and verify-full all verify the certificate native UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte types MySQL TLS required, certificate and host verified against the system trust store; require_ssl=false only for an isolated disposable local server InnoDB, native JSON; no RETURNING MariaDB TLS required by default separate backend, tested on MariaDB 11.4 with its own conformance job. JSON is a text alias: typed dict / list fields decode by declaration; low-level Database.fetch() returns JSON values as bytes SQL Server and Oracle are not supported. Any other scheme, such as oracle:// or mssql:// , fails when the pool is created with DatabaseError: unsupported database URL scheme ; the message does not repeat the URL. A supported scheme written without its slashes, such as sqlite:./app.db , fails with invalid database URL: the scheme needs :// . PostgreSQL TLS ¶ PostgreSQL URLs accept sslmode=disable , prefer , require , verify-ca or verify-full , and sslrootcert=/path/to/ca.pem . prefer tries TLS first and falls back to plaintext only if the server declines TLS; a certificate or handshake error fails closed. All TLS connections verify the server certificate chain and hostname: require , verify-ca and verify-full all require TLS, and Hinoki's verify-ca also verifies the hostname. Trust uses Mozilla WebPKI roots plus any PEM certificates in sslrootcert (at most 1 MiB), so sslmode=require needs a trusted certificate too. sslmode=allow is unsupported. A URL to a remote host without sslmode logs a warning at connect: prefer lets a network attacker strip TLS, so use verify-full . Mount the CA file where each worker can read it. Hinoki does not create the PostgreSQL role or database: create them once with your usual tools before the first hinoki migrations apply . SQLite storage ¶ SQLite uses bundled SQLite 3.35 or newer. UUID and timestamp columns use text storage; JSON uses JSON text. contains matching is ASCII case-insensitive. In-memory databases are not supported, because each pooled connection would have an independent database. SQLite allows one writer at a time. Its internal lock wait is the larger of five seconds and the pool's configured wait ; the pool acquisition wait itself remains bounded by wait : from hinoki.db import Database database = await Database . connect ( "sqlite://./app.sqlite3" , wait = 10 ) This gives SQLite writes up to ten seconds to acquire the writer lock. The default wait=5 keeps the existing five-second limit. Use the database from a script ¶ A script, a one-off task or a test fixture opens its own pool with Database.connect and makes it current with use_database , so model queries find it. Run it from the project root so a relative SQLite path and .env match the server's: # scripts/unpaid.py import asyncio from hinoki.db import Database from hinoki.orm import use_database from notes.apps.billing.models import Invoice from notes.settings import ProjectSettings async def main () -> None : settings = ProjectSettings . load () database = await Database . connect ( settings . database . url . reveal (), max_size = settings . database . max_size ) try : with use_database ( database ): print ( await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) finally : database . close () asyncio . run ( main ()) Database.close() is a plain call, not awaited. The script does not create tables: run hinoki migrations apply against the same database first. Replace the database module ¶ A DatabaseModule in modules= , or installed with app.install(...) , replaces the one Hinoki builds from the settings, for example to use a URL chosen at runtime: # notes/main.py (excerpt) from hinoki.db import DatabaseModule app . install ( DatabaseModule ( url , max_size = 4 )) The migration commands use this module's URL too, and print (from application: DatabaseModule) . A database module of your own whose URL Hinoki cannot read stops them; pass --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL . Migrations use the application's database ¶ hinoki migrations reads the database of the project's application (its DatabaseModule , or its database setting), so the variables above configure both the server and the migration commands. --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL override it for one run; with none of them set, the local SQLite default is anchored beside hinoki.toml : export NOTES_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status # database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ...) hinoki migrations apply Hinoki never runs migrations at startup. An application that declares no database setting and installs no DatabaseModule has no database at run time, although its migrations still fall back to the local SQLite file: declare the field before you add models. See which database for the full order, and migrations for planning, review and per-backend behaviour. docs.text: Hinoki's ORM runs on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. The database URL selects the backend; models and queries stay the same wherever the backends' SQL features overlap. With nothing configured, the database is local SQLite at .hinoki/local.sqlite3 .

docs.text: Declare it. hinoki new notes --database postgresql does this for you; otherwise add the field to your settings class. Name a TOML file only if you will use one (step 2): the file named by toml= must exist. # notes/settings.py class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Populate it. With nothing set, DatabaseSettings points at a local SQLite file, .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . To use another database, pick one source: Source Use it for Example Nothing local development on SQLite – .env one URL on your machine ( hinoki new --database postgresql writes a .env.example to copy; keep .env out of git) NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@localhost:5432/notes Environment containers and CI export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE=/run/secrets/database-url settings.toml non-secret fields ( engine , host , name , user ), with the password from the environment; add toml="settings.toml" to the class connection fields The prefix ( NOTES_ ) comes from the settings class, and __ separates the group from the field. Until you set one of them, a project created with --database postgresql still uses the local SQLite file, and so do its migrations. Check it. hinoki settings , run from the project root, shows each value with its source; the URL and the password are redacted: $ hinoki settings | grep DATABASE__URL NOTES_DATABASE__URL .env *** hinoki migrations status names the database it will use, and fails with a clear error if the server does not answer: $ hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@127.0.0.1:5432/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) status connects and records its migration ledger, so on SQLite it creates the database file. Create the tables. Hinoki never creates tables or runs migrations at startup (it only creates the local SQLite file): run hinoki migrations apply once you have models ( migrations ). The rest of this page lists every field, the URL forms and each backend.

docs.text: Give an agent the development MCP ¶ hinoki mcp starts an MCP server on stdio that describes your app, its rules and its models to a coding agent. It never writes source code, rules or waivers. The one exception to reading only is run_scenario , which you enable with --scenarios : it runs real handlers and can change data ( below ). hinoki mcp The application defaults to project.application in hinoki.toml , the rules to the app's own rules ( Hinoki(rules=...) , else the [project] rules of hinoki.toml ) and the package to the application's package; pass --models to describe models. Projects made by hinoki new contain a .mcp.json that starts this server for the agent. Protocol messages go to stdout as newline-delimited JSON-RPC; diagnostics go to stderr. Options ¶ Option Default Meaning TARGET the project application Another app, as module:app --models MODULE none Model modules to describe; repeatable --rules MODULE:NAME the app's rules Another RuleSet --package NAME the target's package Packages the rules inspect; repeatable --waivers PATH as for hinoki check ( which file ) The owner's waiver file, read only; must exist. run_scenario starts the app with it too --requests PATH .hinoki/requests.jsonl Where recent_requests reads --scenarios off\|read\|write off Registers run_scenario (see below) Tools ¶ Each result is JSON in structuredContent and in a text block, with a tool_version . A failed call sets isError and carries an error message. Tool Input Result inspect_project {} App title and version; each action's id , method , path , status , access , atomic , pagination , parsers , renderers and location ; model metadata (with --models , including a many_to_many entry per relation: to , bridge , ids_name , max_items ); the enabled rule count list_rules {} Enabled rules and the waivers with their file, target, reason, owner and expiry explain_action {"action": "module.function"} Signature, docstring, access and atomic , the OpenAPI operation and the action's diagnostics. A class method or a unique bare handler name also works explain_error {"code": "validation_error"} Meaning and fix of a framework error code, HTTP error code or rule ID check_project {} or {"phase": "static"} Rule diagnostics with waivers applied, plus ok and failing ; phase is startup or static . Effectful checks are not run propose_model {"name": "Article", "fields": [...]} ; optional table , owner , path , unique_together Source text for a model, its input, patch and output Schema classes and CRUD actions. Returned, never written. Field types: str , int , float , bool , uuid , datetime , with nullable , unique , max_length recent_requests {} or {"limit": 20, "status_min": 400, "path_contains": "/invoices"} The newest requests the development server answered ( method , path , query , status , duration_ms , lane ), oldest first; limit is 1 to 200 recent_requests reads the file Kiso writes when server.recent_requests is set; it keeps about the last 1 to 2 MiB, and without it the result is empty with a note. The query field is the raw query string and is not redacted: keep tokens out of query strings and treat the file as sensitive. Run requests against the app ¶ --scenarios read or --scenarios write adds run_scenario . Its input needs path (a plain URL path starting with / ); method (default GET ), query (without ? ), string headers and json are optional. The result holds the HTTP status , response headers , the body text (at most 20,000 bytes, with truncated ) and the parsed JSON when there is some. Mode Methods read GET , HEAD , OPTIONS , QUERY write Also POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE Scenarios run your real handlers The app's lifespan and handlers run in-process, so even read can change data (a GET handler may write). Each request has a 15-second limit. Enable scenarios only yourself, never on an agent's request, and only against a disposable database. Errors and edge cases ¶ A failed app startup is reported to the client without its message, which may contain a connection string; the details go to stderr. Rule checks with side effects are never run by this server; use hinoki check --allow-effects . The server was exercised with the official mcp Python client (initialize, tools/list , tools/call ); other clients are untested. See also ¶ Build with a coding agent Expose actions over MCP hinoki mcp options

docs.text: Documentation versions ¶ Hinoki keeps unreleased documentation separate from release documentation. Development ¶ The dev documentation follows main and may change at any time. Before the first release, the site root redirects here. Treat it as documentation for the current pre-release code. Releases ¶ Each release is built from its matching vX.Y.Z tag. Release pages remain available at their versioned path; stable and latest point to the most recent release. Changes merged to main update only dev and do not replace a released version. Use the version menu in the header to move between available docs. When a page does not exist in an older version, the menu opens that version's home page. Each version also has its own llms.txt , llms-full.txt and Markdown copy of every page, for example https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/llms.txt ; see docs for agents . The llms.txt and llms-full.txt at the site root are copies from the default version: dev before the first release, latest after. Per-page Markdown copies exist only under a version path.

docs.text: Use other libraries ¶ Hinoki has its own Schema and Model classes. It does not accept Pydantic, SQLAlchemy or Django models as request bodies, responses or tables. This page says why, what that costs, and which extension points exist today. Why the framework owns them ¶ One declaration feeds every output. Request binding, the response check, OpenAPI, application MCP, the admin and rules read the same Schema and Model classes, so they can promise the same contract. The hot paths are native. Routing, selected request parsing and ORM execution run in Rust against Hinoki's own declarations, without calling back into a validation library or a foreign ORM per request. Rules need known structure. "A response Schema never exposes password_hash " is checkable because the Schema is an inspectable Hinoki class. What this costs ¶ A library that expects its own model type does not plug in: a Pydantic-based SDK, a SQLAlchemy extension or a Django app cannot be given a Hinoki Model or Schema . There is no adapter from SQLAlchemy, Django or Pydantic models, and no plugin system. Databases are SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB through Hinoki's own drivers; another ORM's connections are not shared with its pool. Bring a library anyway ¶ Anything that works on plain Python data works with Hinoki. Schema.to_dict() and Schema.dump() return plain data, and a Schema is built from plain values: # notes/apps/quotes/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http from notes.apps.quotes.client import fetch_quote # any library returning plain data class Quote ( Schema ): symbol : str price : float @http . get ( "/ {symbol} " , access = None ) async def quote ( symbol : str ) -> Quote : raw = await fetch_quote ( symbol ) return Quote ( symbol = raw [ "symbol" ], price = raw [ "price" ]) Keep the translation at the edge of the handler, and keep a second store's connections in a module so their lifetime follows the worker. Hinoki does not time-box what that code does. docs.text: Hinoki has its own Schema and Model classes. It does not accept Pydantic, SQLAlchemy or Django models as request bodies, responses or tables. This page says why, what that costs, and which extension points exist today.
docs.title: Use other libraries

docs.text: One declaration feeds every output. Request binding, the response check, OpenAPI, application MCP, the admin and rules read the same Schema and Model classes, so they can promise the same contract. The hot paths are native. Routing, selected request parsing and ORM execution run in Rust against Hinoki's own declarations, without calling back into a validation library or a foreign ORM per request. Rules need known structure. "A response Schema never exposes password_hash " is checkable because the Schema is an inspectable Hinoki class.
docs.title: Why the framework owns them

docs.text: A library that expects its own model type does not plug in: a Pydantic-based SDK, a SQLAlchemy extension or a Django app cannot be given a Hinoki Model or Schema . There is no adapter from SQLAlchemy, Django or Pydantic models, and no plugin system. Databases are SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB through Hinoki's own drivers; another ORM's connections are not shared with its pool.
