Email templates ¶ A template turns a typed context into the subject, the plain text and the HTML of a message. The language is small and fixed, the template is parsed, checked against the context Schema and rendered in Rust ( crates/mail ), and the result is an ordinary mail.Message for mail.send . The call from Python to the renderer is one synchronous native call per message, with Python objects for the context and the three rendered strings. The code on this page is the code of examples/mailroom ; a test ( tests/mailtemplatesdoctest.py ) proves that every quoted block is a piece of that example and that every printed output is what the command prints now. Use only synthetic addresses such as example.com ; nothing here sends real mail. A template file ¶ A template file is TOML with a subject , a template (the HTML) and, optionally, a text and a description . The context it reads is a Schema : # mailroom/messages.py class Account ( Schema ): name : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 80 , examples = ( "Ada" ,))] trial_days : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 0 , examples = ( 14 ,))] class Step ( Schema ): title : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 80 , examples = ( "Create a project" ,))] url : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "url" , examples = ( "https://example.com/start" ,))] class Welcome ( Schema ): user : Account steps : Annotated [ list [ Step ], Field ( max_length = 10 )] # mailroom/templates/welcome.toml description = "Sent once, after sign-up" subject = "Welcome to Mailroom, {{ user.name }}" template = '''

Welcome, {{ user.name }}

{% if user.trial_days %}

Your trial lasts {{ user.trial_days }} days.

{% else %}

Your plan is active.

{% endif %}
    {% for step in steps %}
  1. {{ step.title }}
    2. {% endfor %}
''' mail.Template.file(path, context=Welcome) names the file and its context. Nothing is read when the module is imported; the name defaults to the file's stem ( welcome ): # mailroom/messages.py WELCOME = mail . Template . file ( HERE / "welcome.toml" , context = Welcome ) RESET_PASSWORD = mail . Template . file ( HERE / "reset_password.toml" , context = ResetPassword ) templates : list [ mail . TemplateBase ] = [ WELCOME , RESET_PASSWORD ] A template built in code takes the same parts: mail.Template(name="x", subject=..., html=..., text=..., context=Ctx) , or mail.Template.from_toml(source, name="x", context=Ctx) for TOML text. Those compile when they are built, with no I/O. Register and send ¶ List the templates when you create the application. Nothing registers by import: # mailroom/main.py def build_app ( settings : MailroomSettings ) -> Hinoki : """The application; the routes need the API key and the public base URL.""" return Hinoki ( settings = settings , title = "Mailroom" , include = build_routes ( settings ), email_templates = templates , ) The auto-installed EmailModule receives the list. If you declare the module yourself, pass EmailModule(settings, templates=[...]) . Every worker reads and checks the files in its lifespan, and the worker does not start when one fails. At most 256 templates are registered, with distinct names. A route builds the context, renders it with Template.message(context, to=...) and sends the message: # mailroom/routes.py @group . post ( "/signup" , status = 202 ) async def sign_up ( data : SignUp ) -> Sent : """Send the welcome message of a new account.""" welcome = Welcome ( user = Account ( name = data . name , trial_days = data . trial_days ), steps = [ Step ( title = "Create a project" , url = START )], ) sent = await mail . send ( WELCOME . message ( welcome , to = ( data . email ,))) return Sent ( message_id = sent . message_id ) message takes the other Message options ( cc , bcc , reply_to , headers , attachments , sender ) as keywords. A test sends through the memory backend, which keeps the message in the mailer's outbox: # mailroom_tests/mailroomsendtest.py def messages () -> list [ mail . Message ]: module = next ( m for m in app . modules if isinstance ( m , mail . EmailModule )) return [ sent . message for sent in module . mailer . outbox if sent . message ] async def test_sign_up_sends_the_welcome_message ( client : ASGIClient ) -> None : response = await client . post ( "/signup" , json = { "email" : "ada@example.com" , "name" : "Ada <1>" }, headers = KEY ) assert response . status == 202 ( message ,) = messages () assert message . to == ( "ada@example.com" ,) assert message . subject == "Welcome to Mailroom, Ada <1>" assert message . text is not None assert "Your trial lasts 14 days." in message . text assert message . html is not None assert "

Welcome, Ada <1>

" in message . html To see a message printed while developing, run MAILROOM_API_KEY=dev-key MAILROOM_EMAIL__BACKEND=console MAILROOM_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER=noreply@example.com uv run hinoki dev from examples/mailroom and POST to /signup with the header x-api-key: dev-key . The console output is not reproduced here because its Date and Message-ID headers change on every run. The language ¶ A template is text with three constructs: Construct Meaning {{ path }} Insert a value. path is one to eight identifiers joined by dots ( user.name ) {% if path %} … {% else %} … {% endif %} Render a branch by truthiness; else is optional {% for name in path %} … {% endfor %} Render the body once per item of a list; name exists only inside the body An identifier is ASCII letters, digits and _ , not starting with a digit, up to 64 bytes. if , else , endif , for , in and endfor are reserved as loop variables. A loop variable may not have the name of a field of the context or of an enclosing loop ( shadowed_name ). There are no filters, expressions, comparisons, not , elif , comments, includes, macros or inheritance: anything else inside {{ }} or {% %} is a syntax error. A literal {{ or {% cannot appear in the text; a lone { , } or % is text, so CSS works. Standalone lines. A {% … %} tag that is the only non-blank content of its line removes that line (its leading and trailing spaces and tabs, and one line ending). {{ }} lines are never removed. This is why the preview below has no blank lines where the if and for tags are. Values. The context is read as these values: Python / Schema field In the template str , Email , Url , StrEnum Text as is int , float Decimal digits (an int of any size); a float with no fractional part gets .0 ( 1.0 ), never an exponent bool true or false None Nothing (empty text); a path through a None object is also empty Decimal , date , datetime , UUID The text dump() gives nested Schema An object: use user.name list[...] Something for iterates; for over None renders nothing Secret , bytes , Any , tuple , a mapping field Refused when the template is checked An object or a list cannot be inserted with {{ }} ( not_text ); a for over a value that is not a list is not_a_list ; a path through a non-object is not_an_object . Truthiness. None , false , 0 , 0.0 , empty text, an empty list and an empty object are false; everything else is true. Escaping. In html every inserted value is escaped ( & < > " ' become & , < , > , " , ' ); the literal text of the template is not touched. subject and text insert values as they are. A value inserted into the subject that has a line break, a NUL or another control character other than a tab (including U+0085 , U+2028 and U+2029 ) is refused ( header_injection ), so a value cannot add a header. A NUL in a value inserted into text or html is refused ( control_character ). Escaping is enough in text and inside a quoted attribute, so the template is also checked for where each {{ }} sits in the HTML. A {{ }} inside

There are no filters, expressions, comparisons, not , elif , comments, includes, macros or inheritance: anything else inside {{ }} or {% %} is a syntax error. A literal {{ or {% cannot appear in the text; a lone { , } or % is text, so CSS works. Standalone lines. A {% … %} tag that is the only non-blank content of its line removes that line (its leading and trailing spaces and tabs, and one line ending). {{ }} lines are never removed. This is why the preview below has no blank lines where the if and for tags are. Values. The context is read as these values: Python / Schema field In the template str , Email , Url , StrEnum Text as is int , float Decimal digits (an int of any size); a float with no fractional part gets .0 ( 1.0 ), never an exponent bool true or false None Nothing (empty text); a path through a None object is also empty Decimal , date , datetime , UUID The text dump() gives nested Schema An object: use user.name list[...] Something for iterates; for over None renders nothing Secret , bytes , Any , tuple , a mapping field Refused when the template is checked An object or a list cannot be inserted with {{ }} ( not_text ); a for over a value that is not a list is not_a_list ; a path through a non-object is not_an_object . Truthiness. None , false , 0 , 0.0 , empty text, an empty list and an empty object are false; everything else is true. Escaping. In html every inserted value is escaped ( & < > " ' become & , < , > , " , ' ); the literal text of the template is not touched. subject and text insert values as they are. A value inserted into the subject that has a line break, a NUL or another control character other than a tab (including U+0085 , U+2028 and U+2029 ) is refused ( header_injection ), so a value cannot add a header. A NUL in a value inserted into text or html is refused ( control_character ). Escaping is enough in text and inside a quoted attribute, so the template is also checked for where each {{ }} sits in the HTML. A {{ }} inside <script> or <style> , in an unquoted attribute value, in a tag or attribute name, or in an event handler attribute ( onclick , ...) is refused when the template is compiled ( unsafe_context ). A value inside a quoted href , src , action , formaction , background or poster is checked when the template is rendered: with a scheme it must be http , https , mailto or tel , otherwise the render fails ( unsafe_url ); an address without a scheme is relative and passes. The check also covers the dict shortcut. A Schema context is not allowed Unset fields ( str | Unset ), a dump() override, or a computed field that returns a secret: the first two are unsupported_field when the template is built, the last is secret_value when it is rendered. Limits. These are fixed in crates/mail/src/template/limits.rs ; they are not settings: What Limit Reason Subject source 1 KiB too_large Text or HTML source, each 256 KiB too_large TOML file 512 KiB too_large Nodes in a template 10 000 too_many_nodes Nesting of if and for 16 too_deep Path segments, identifier 8, 64 bytes invalid_path Rendered subject 998 bytes output_too_large Rendered text or HTML, each 1 MiB output_too_large Loop iterations in one render 10 000 too_many_iterations Context depth, nodes, bytes 16, 100 000, 4 MiB context_too_large Name [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63} invalid_name Problems reported at once 20 The send path still applies max_message_bytes to the whole message.
docs.title: The language

docs.text: When a template has no text , the plain text is derived from the rendered HTML by a single scanner in Rust, not by an HTML parser. Comments and the content of head , style , script , title and template are dropped; br is a line break; paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, blocks and hr make paragraph breaks; a list item starts with - ; runs of white space collapse (except in pre ); the entities & < > " ' '   and numeric ones are decoded; every other tag is removed. A link whose href starts with http:// , https:// or mailto: becomes label (URL) , or only the label when the label is the URL. The reset_password template has no text . Printed from the sample context in examples/mailroom ( --part text prints only that part): uv run hinoki mail preview reset_password --context mailroom/samples/reset_password.json --part text Hello Ada, Someone asked to reset your password from Lisbon. Choose a new password (https://example.com/reset?token=sample) You are signed in on: - Laptop - Phone <work> If it was not you, ignore this message. The text part holds the value Phone <work> as it is; the HTML part holds Phone <work> . Write a text in the file when the derived text is not what you want.
docs.title: Text from HTML

docs.text: A template is checked against its context Schema before any message is rendered: every variable must exist in the Schema , every Schema field must be used by some part, and a variable must have the right shape (a loop over a list, a path through an object, text where text is inserted). Change {{ user.name }} in the <h1> of welcome.toml to {{ user.nickname }} and the worker does not start; the error names the template, the variable and the position in the template, never a value: template 'welcome': unknown variable 'user.nickname' in html at line 2, column 17 Removing the <ol> list from the HTML leaves the steps fields unused, which is also an error: template 'welcome': unused field 'steps[].title' (and 1 more problem) hinoki mail check [TARGET] runs the same check without starting anything. It reads every registered template, prints one line for each, and exits 1 when one is refused ( 2 when the application cannot be loaded or has no email module). With the first change above: template 'welcome': unknown variable 'user.nickname' in html at line 2, column 17 ok reset_password (mailroom/templates/reset_password.toml) The rule HNK-MAIL-001 ( from hinoki.rules import EmailTemplatesMatch ) makes the same check part of hinoki check . It is opt-in: put EmailTemplatesMatch() in your RuleSet . It reads the template files, so it declares the effect files and needs --allow-effects : uv run hinoki check --rules myproject.rules:rules --allow-effects
docs.title: Checked at startup

docs.text:
hinoki mail preview NAME [TARGET] renders a registered template from the command line, with no server and no sending. Without --context it builds a sample from the examples= of the context fields (a field that is not required and has no example is left out). Run it from examples/mailroom with the memory backend and a sender set: export MAILROOM_API_KEY = dev-key export MAILROOM_EMAIL__BACKEND = memory export MAILROOM_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER = noreply@example.com uv run hinoki mail check ok welcome (mailroom/templates/welcome.toml) ok reset_password (mailroom/templates/reset_password.toml) uv run hinoki mail preview welcome Subject: Welcome to Mailroom, Ada ----- text ----- Welcome, Ada Your trial lasts 14 days. - Create a project (https://example.com/start) ----- html -----

Welcome, Ada

Your trial lasts 14 days.

  1. Create a project
--context FILE (or - for standard input, at most 1 MiB) reads a JSON object that is validated as the context Schema ; --part subject|text|html prints one part; --format json prints the three parts as JSON. The preview opens no mailer and sends nothing.
docs.title: Preview

docs.text: Some templates live in a database table, not in a file. examples/mailroom/mailroom/notices.py builds one from strings, without a Schema : # mailroom/notices.py def notice_template ( slug : str ) -> mail . Template [ mail . Context ]: """The template of a stored notice; ``KeyError`` when there is none.""" subject , html = NOTICES [ slug ] return mail . Template ( name = f "notice- { slug } " , subject = subject , html = html ) The context is a plain dict ( mail.Context ). Only the syntax is checked when the template is built; there is no Schema to check the variables against, so a missing key is found when the template is rendered, for the message being sent. A Secret in the dict is refused ( secret_value ). The error names the variable of the template: template 'notice-maintenance': missing variable 'from' in html at line 1, column 47 The /notices/{slug} route turns that error into 400 invalid_notice , so the caller learns that the notice could not be rendered without seeing a value.
docs.title: Templates from strings

docs.text: Every failure is a mail.TemplateError , a subclass of EmailError with kind template . It carries reason , template (the name), field (the part), line , column , variable and problems (a tuple of TemplateProblem , at most 20; truncated says there were more). Its text never holds a recipient, a subject, a rendered text or a value of the context. A secret never reaches the engine: a Secret field in a Schema context is secret_field , and one in a dict is secret_value . Reason When syntax , unclosed_tag , unexpected_tag , unclosed_block , invalid_path , shadowed_name , control_character , too_large , too_many_nodes , too_deep , invalid_name , unsafe_context The template does not compile unknown_variable , unused_field , not_text , not_a_list , not_an_object , secret_field , unsupported_field The template does not match its context Schema missing_variable , header_injection , output_too_large , too_many_iterations , context_too_large , unsupported_value , secret_value , unsafe_url A render fails unreadable , invalid_file The file cannot be read or is not a valid template TOML With metrics on Kiso , a Template.message that cannot be rendered while a mailer is current is counted in hinoki_email_messages_total{outcome="template"} ( Template.render alone is not a send and counts nothing). Compile and startup failures are not sends and are not counted. See export Prometheus metrics .
docs.title: Errors

docs.text: No filters, expressions, includes, macros or inheritance, and no comments. No translation: a template is one language; choose the template or write one per language. No inline images or attachment templates; attachments are the Message option. No registration in hinoki.toml : templates are listed in Hinoki(email_templates=[...]) or EmailModule(templates=[...]) . The limits above are fixed and are not settings. Rendering does not send: delivery, retries and the lack of a queue are those of mail.send .
docs.title: What templates do not do

docs.text:
Send email ¶ Hinoki sends outbound email over SMTP from a per-worker Mailer . The message is rendered, the SMTP conversation, TLS, the connection pool, timeouts and retries all run in Rust ( crates/mail ); the Python side is the Message you build, the settings and the module that owns the mailer. The call crosses the Python/Rust boundary once per message, with Python objects for the message and its result. What it is not : there is no queue, no delivery guarantee and no HTTP provider (the SMTP and the two local backends below are all there is). send returns when the server accepted the message, or raises. The admin sends no email in 0.1.0. Set it up ¶ Declare an email: settings.EmailSettings field. Hinoki installs EmailModule for you, like the database module, and opens one Mailer in every worker's lifespan. # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" ): email : settings . EmailSettings backend is required and has no default, so nothing is sent by accident. In development use console (the message is printed) and in tests memory : NOTES_EMAIL__BACKEND = console NOTES_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER = noreply@example.com For production SMTP: NOTES_EMAIL__BACKEND = smtp NOTES_EMAIL__HOST = smtp.example.com NOTES_EMAIL__USERNAME = mailer NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD_FILE = /run/secrets/smtp-password NOTES_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER = noreply@example.com Importing Hinoki or the application opens no connection: the mailer is created when the worker starts and closed ( aclose ) when it stops. Each worker has its own pool; nothing is shared between workers or event loops. Send a message ¶ # notes/routes.py from hinoki import http , mail @http . post ( "/welcome" ) async def welcome () -> dict [ str , str ]: sent = await mail . send ( mail . Message ( to = ( "ada@example.com" ,), subject = "Welcome" , text = "Your account is ready." , html = "

Your account is ready.

" , ) ) return { "message_id" : sent . message_id } mail.send uses the mailer of the running worker. It returns a SentMail ( message_id , the envelope recipients , attempts ) and raises EmailError on failure. A Message is frozen and keyword-only. to , cc , bcc and reply_to are tuples; passing one string where a tuple is expected is a TypeError . At least one of text or html is required (both make a multipart/alternative ), and at least one recipient in to , cc or bcc . sender defaults to default_sender ; with neither set, send raises invalid_message for sender . An address given as str is a bare user@example.com . To add a display name use mail.Address("ada@example.com", "Ada Lovelace") ; "Ada " as a str is refused. bcc recipients are in the SMTP envelope and never in a header. headers=(("X-Campaign", "welcome"),) adds headers. Names and values are checked: a line break or any other control character (below U+0020 except a tab, or U+007F) in a header value, the subject or a display name is invalid_header , and the headers Hinoki writes itself ( From , To , Date , Message-ID , Subject , ...) cannot be set. Text that contains =? is always written as encoded words so a reader cannot mistake it for one. The sizes are measured before anything is copied or encoded: text, HTML and attachments over max_message_bytes are limit_exceeded for text , html or attachments . A message refused in Python (no sender, a malformed header or attachment) counts as a failed send in mailer.stats() and in the metrics, like any other refusal. On a closed mailer every send is closed . attachments=(mail.Attachment("report.pdf", data, "application/pdf"),) . A non-ASCII file name is sent with an RFC 2231 filename* parameter. Header-injection attempts (a \r or \n in the subject, a display name or an address) are refused as invalid_header or invalid_address before anything is sent. SMTPUTF8 (a non-ASCII address), XOAUTH2, DKIM signing, inline images, DSN requests and PIPELINING are not supported. Send after a commit ¶ Send once the data is durable, never from inside a transaction that can still roll back. Register the send with after_commit : it runs after the outermost commit and is dropped on rollback. # notes/apps/accounts/operations.py from hinoki import db , mail from hinoki.orm import current_database async def invite ( address : str ) -> None : async with db . atomic (): await Invite . acreate ( InviteIn ( email = address )) current_database () . after_commit ( lambda : mail . send ( mail . Message ( to = ( address ,), subject = "You are invited" , text = "Join us." ) ) ) A send that fails after the commit is logged and does not undo the commit; the callback is not retried. See after-commit callbacks . When the message must not be lost ¶ Hinoki keeps no queue and cannot promise delivery: a crash after the commit and before the send loses the message. When that matters, write the message into your own table in the same transaction (an outbox) and send it from a management command that marks each row sent. That table, its retry policy and its cleanup are yours. Send from a synchronous handler ¶ A sync handler runs on a thread. Run the send on the worker's loop with run_sync : from hinoki import http , mail from hinoki.blocking import run_sync @http . post ( "/notify" ) def notify () -> dict [ str , str ]: sent = run_sync ( mail . send ( mail . Message ( to = ( "ada@example.com" ,), subject = "Hi" , text = "Hello" )) ) return { "message_id" : sent . message_id } The mailer is also available in on_startup hooks, management commands that require EmailModule , and hinoki shell . Backends ¶ backend What it does smtp Delivers to host:port over a pooled, bounded set of connections console Writes the rendered message to standard output, followed by a line of 72 dashes. Nothing leaves the process memory Renders the message and keeps it in mailer.outbox (a bounded deque, memory_capacity messages); nothing leaves the process console and memory validate and render exactly as smtp does, so a message that is refused in one is refused in all, and SentMail.raw holds the bytes that would be sent. SMTP, TLS and authentication ¶ security Default port Meaning starttls (default) 587 Plain connect, then upgrade. The upgrade is required: a server that does not offer STARTTLS is a tls error tls 465 TLS from the first byte none 25 No encryption. On a host off the loopback it needs allow_insecure = true The server certificate and host name are always verified, against the public roots bundled with Hinoki plus the certificates of tls_ca_file (a PEM file) when set: the file adds trust, it does not replace the bundled roots, and the operating system's store is not read. There is no setting that turns verification off. An IPv6 host may be written ::1 or [::1] . username and password are set together. password is a Secret : it is read from the environment or PASSWORD_FILE , never appears in a repr , a log line or an exception, and is revealed only to hand it to the SMTP login. Authentication tries PLAIN , then LOGIN , and a password is never sent in clear text to a non-loopback peer unless allow_insecure is set. check_on_startup = true connects and authenticates while the worker starts and aborts the start on failure; await mailer.check() does the same on demand without sending a message. Both are off by default. Settings ¶ All fields are in the email group. Durations are seconds, more than 0 and at most 3600 (one hour). Field Default Meaning backend required smtp , console or memory default_sender unset The From address when a message has none host , port , security localhost , by security , starttls The server username , password unset Both or neither allow_insecure false Permit security=none off the loopback, and plain AUTH there tls_ca_file unset (bundled public roots only) PEM file of certificates trusted in addition to the bundled roots helo_name the local address as a literal ( [192.0.2.1] ) Name sent in EHLO : a domain name, localhost or an address literal ( [192.0.2.1] , [IPv6:::1] ) message_id_domain domain of default_sender (an internationalized domain in its punycode form), else helo_name , else localhost Right-hand side of the Message-ID ; same forms as helo_name connect_timeout , command_timeout , data_timeout 10 , 30 , 120 Per connect, per command and per message body timeout 60 The whole send , including the wait for a connection and the retries; at least connect_timeout max_connections 4 Connections per worker pool_wait 5 How long a send waits for a free connection before a busy error idle_timeout 60 Idle connections older than this are closed max_messages_per_connection 100 A connection is replaced after this many messages retries , backoff_base , backoff_max 2 , 0.5 , 5 See retries max_recipients , max_message_bytes , max_attachments 100 , 10 MiB, 20 Limits checked before connecting memory_capacity 1000 Size of the memory outbox check_on_startup false See above A value out of range, a duration over one hour, an empty username , username without password , a host longer than 253 characters or with a control character, a default_sender , helo_name or message_id_domain that is not valid, or security=none to a remote host without allow_insecure is refused when the settings load, with the variable named and the value never shown. tls_ca_file is read when the worker starts, not when the settings load. Errors and retries ¶ Every failure is an EmailError with a kind ( EmailErrorKind ): kind Cause invalid_address , invalid_header , invalid_message The message is refused before any connection. field names the part ( to , subject , attachments , ...) and index the entry limit_exceeded max_recipients , max_message_bytes or max_attachments closed The mailer was closed (the worker is stopping) busy No connection became free within pool_wait connect , timeout , tls , auth The connection, a timeout, the TLS handshake or the login failed rejected The server refused with a permanent 5xx reply; code and enhanced_status hold it temporary A 4xx reply that survived the retries protocol The server broke the SMTP protocol The exception text is a fixed sentence plus the field and reply code. It never contains a recipient, a subject, a body, a password or the server's reply text, so it is safe to log. Connection failures ( connect ), timeouts, 4xx replies and protocol errors are retried up to retries times, all inside timeout . The wait before a retry doubles from backoff_base up to backoff_max and is then scaled by a random factor between one half and one. attempts counts the tries. A permanent 5xx reply, a TLS or authentication failure, a validation error, a full pool and a closed mailer are never retried. possibly_sent is True when the connection failed or stalled after the end of the message data was written: the server may have accepted the message. Nothing is retried then, because a retry could send a duplicate; decide in your code whether to send again. Test with the memory backend ¶ # tests/test_invite.py from hinoki import Hinoki , mail , settings from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient class TestSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" ): email : settings . EmailSettings async def test_welcome_mail () -> None : app = Hinoki ( settings = TestSettings ( email = settings . EmailSettings ( backend = settings . EmailBackend . MEMORY , default_sender = "noreply@example.com" , ) ), include = [ welcome ], ) async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : await client . post ( "/welcome" ) [ sent ] = next ( m for m in app . modules if isinstance ( m , mail . EmailModule ) ) . mailer . outbox assert sent . message is not None and sent . message . subject == "Welcome" assert b "Your account is ready." in ( sent . raw or b "" ) outbox holds SentMail entries with message and raw ; clear_outbox() empties it. Each started application, and each worker, has its own outbox. For SMTP behaviour, point host at a fake server on 127.0.0.1 ; never send real mail from a test. Templates ¶ Instead of building subject , text and html by hand, declare a mail.Template (a TOML file or strings) with a typed context, list it in Hinoki(email_templates=[...]) and send template.message(context, to=(...)) . Rendering and escaping are Rust, the template is checked against its context Schema when a worker starts, and hinoki mail preview shows the result. See email templates . Metrics ¶ With metrics.listen on Kiso and an email module installed, three families are exported. The series are fixed at startup, so no address, subject or error text becomes a label. See export Prometheus metrics . Mailer.stats() is always available, under Granian too: it returns the counts of sent and failed messages, retries, and open and idle connections of that worker. What email does not do ¶ No queue, no scheduled sends and no guaranteed delivery; see when the message must not be lost . No template language beyond the small fixed one of email templates ; you can also build text and html yourself. No HTTP email providers (only SMTP, console and memory). No bounce or delivery tracking, no DKIM signing, no SMTPUTF8, no XOAUTH2. The admin sends no email in 0.1.0. No sharing of a mailer between workers, processes or event loops.

docs.text: Hinoki sends outbound email over SMTP from a per-worker Mailer . The message is rendered, the SMTP conversation, TLS, the connection pool, timeouts and retries all run in Rust ( crates/mail ); the Python side is the Message you build, the settings and the module that owns the mailer. The call crosses the Python/Rust boundary once per message, with Python objects for the message and its result. What it is not : there is no queue, no delivery guarantee and no HTTP provider (the SMTP and the two local backends below are all there is). send returns when the server accepted the message, or raises. The admin sends no email in 0.1.0.

docs.text: Declare an email: settings.EmailSettings field. AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" ): email : settings . EmailSettings backend is required and has no default, so nothing is sent by accident. In development use console (the message is printed) and in tests memory : NOTES_EMAIL__BACKEND = console NOTES_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER = noreply@example.com For production SMTP: NOTES_EMAIL__BACKEND = smtp NOTES_EMAIL__HOST = smtp.example.com NOTES_EMAIL__USERNAME = mailer NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD_FILE = /run/secrets/smtp-password NOTES_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER = noreply@example.com Importing Hinoki or the application opens no connection: the mailer is created when the worker starts and closed ( aclose ) when it stops. Each worker has its own pool; nothing is shared between workers or event loops.

docs.text: Requests and responses ¶ This page covers what one action receives and what it returns. How to organise actions is in Function-based APIs and Class-based APIs ; how they reach the application is in Register routes . The fragments below add actions to the invoices group of the Billing app, which supplies their access policy and transactions. Declare an action ¶ # notes/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) Use @http.get , @http.post , @http.put , @http.patch , @http.delete or @http.query ( from hinoki import http ), or the same methods on a RouteGroup . Hinoki also answers HEAD through each GET route: it runs the GET response path and returns the same status and representation headers without a body, so the GET handler runs for HEAD requests too. A 405 response's Allow header includes HEAD whenever GET is available. Option Meaning status Success status (default 200 ) access Access policy; None is public atomic True runs the action in a transaction ( transactions ); there is no transaction option pagination Page-number policy ( pagination ) parsers , renderers Body formats in and out ( codecs ) errors APIError classes the action may raise ( errors ) rate_limit A rate-limit policy ( below ) cors http.Cors(...) : this action's own CORS policy, replacing the application's ( CORS ) include_in_schema , tags , deprecated , operation_id What the OpenAPI document says about the action; include_in_schema=False leaves it out without changing how it is served or protected, and deprecated ( True or a date ) also adds a Deprecation header and a warning log ( deprecate an action ) validate_response False skips the response check Each option is checked when the route is declared or registered. The fragments below continue notes/apps/billing/api.py from function APIs . Besides its imports they use these: from typing import Annotated from hinoki import XML , Field , Form , MultiPartParser , Query , Request , UploadedFile Read with a body: @http.query ¶ QUERY is the HTTP method for a read whose input does not fit a query string: it is safe and idempotent like GET , and carries a body like POST . # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceSearch ( Schema ): text : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] limit : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 100 )] = 20 @invoices . query ( "/search" ) async def search_invoices ( data : InvoiceSearch ) -> list [ InvoiceOut ]: rows = await Invoice . filter ( reference__contains = data . text ) . limit ( data . limit ) return InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows ) curl -X QUERY http://127.0.0.1:8000/billing/invoices/search -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"text": "2026"}' The body is bound, parsed and validated exactly as for POST : the same parsers, size limit and 400 / 413 / 415 / 422 answers. A QUERY action must not change state. RouteGroup(atomic=True) applies to POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE only; pass atomic=True on the action if the read needs a transaction. @http.query inside an API class works like the other methods. A 405 answer lists QUERY in Allow where it is available; HEAD is answered through GET routes only. Hinoki sends no Accept-Query or cache headers by itself. The method is recent. Granian passes it through over ASGI and WSGI (both are tested), but a proxy, gateway, firewall or HTTP client may reject it, and browsers send a CORS preflight for it. Keep a GET or POST route beside it when clients cannot send QUERY . In the OpenAPI document a QUERY operation appears under the path's query field ( x-query with openapi_version="3.1" ); see OpenAPI . Bind request values ¶ Typed path parameters come from the path, query parameters from the query string, and a body parameter from the request body. Declare request: Request as the first parameter when you need headers, cookies or raw request data; it is injected only when that parameter is annotated. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceLabel ( Schema ): id : UUID locale : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 35 )] @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} /label" ) async def invoice_label ( request : Request , invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceLabel : locale = request . headers . get ( "accept-language" , "en" )[: 35 ] return InvoiceLabel ( id = invoice_id , locale = locale ) Request path, query and body values are validated before the handler runs; a Schema body uses Schema.validate() and reports nested field errors with its parameter prefix. Discriminated request variants belong in a wrapper Schema field ( Annotated[Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator="kind")] ); bare union body parameters are not supported. Hinoki does not coerce input values into different types, except in Query[...] , Form[...] and XML[...] . Return a Schema built from the row: InvoiceOut.from_model(row) or InvoiceOut.from_models(rows) ( model schemas ). A returned dict or Model where a Schema is declared is a 500 internal_error ( the response check ). Use a wrapper Schema for a discriminated response union too; bare union return annotations are rejected by OpenAPI generation. Query strings as a Schema ¶ Query[...] reads a whole query string into a Schema , for any method: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceFilter ( Schema ): paid : bool = False limit : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 100 )] = 20 @invoices . get ( "/recent" ) async def recent_invoices ( filters : Query [ InvoiceFilter ]) -> InvoiceRecent : rows = await Invoice . filter ( paid = filters . paid ) . limit ( filters . limit ) return InvoiceRecent ( items = InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows )) # ?paid=true&limit=5 Text is converted to the int , float and bool the Schema declares before the strict validation (a repeated key fills a list field, a single one still does). A value that does not convert, a repeated key for a scalar, a missing required field and an unknown key (by default) are 422 errors, reported with the parameter name as prefix. The Schema owns the whole query string, so the action takes no other query or page parameters, at most one Query[...] , and it cannot be a path parameter. OpenAPI lists one query parameter per field. A plain path or query parameter ( n: int , slug: str ) takes no constraints: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1)] on one is refused with a RegistrationError when the routes are declared, because nothing would enforce it. Any Field(...) is refused, even one with only description or examples : scalar parameters read none of its attributes, and refusing every form is simpler and more explicit than allowing a subset. The same holds for the path and query parameters of a WebSocket route. Put the constraints in a Schema and take it as Query[...] (above) or as the body; on a WebSocket, validate inside the handler. Form bodies ¶ A plain Schema parameter is a strict JSON body. Wrap it in Form[...] to read the same Schema from a form, whose values are all text: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . post ( "/import" , status = 201 ) async def import_invoice ( data : Form [ InvoiceIn ]) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . acreate ( data )) # reference=INV-1 Before validation, text is converted to the int , float and bool the Schema declares (and a lone value of a list field becomes a one-item list); Schema and JSON stay strict. A value that does not convert, or several values for a scalar, fails with the normal 422 type error. Empty text is not turned into None , and nested Schema fields are not read from form keys. An action with a Form[...] parameter and no parsers= uses FormParser (add MultiPartParser() explicitly for multipart text fields). Form[...] is valid only for the Schema body of a POST, PUT, PATCH or QUERY action, takes only form parsers (a JSON body needs a plain Schema parameter, so one cannot be coerced by mistake), and appears in OpenAPI as application/x-www-form-urlencoded . XML bodies ¶ XML[...] reads a Schema from an application/xml body: the elements under the root become the fields, text is converted to the declared int , float and bool , and the strict validation follows. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class Line ( Schema ): sku : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 40 )] qty : int class Order ( Schema ): customer : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 120 )] lines : list [ Line ] @invoices . post ( "/orders" , status = 201 ) async def receive_order ( data : XML [ Order ]) -> OrderReceipt : return OrderReceipt ( lines = len ( data . lines )) # <order><customer>Ada</customer><lines><sku>a</sku><qty>2</qty></lines></order> A repeated element is a list (a single one still fills a list field), nested elements fill nested Schema fields, and an empty element is None . Attributes are not read and namespace prefixes are dropped ( <a:x> and <b:x> are both x ). Malformed XML, a DTD, a custom entity, mixed text and child elements, a character XML 1.0 forbids (a control character other than tab, carriage return and line feed, written directly or as  ), an encoding declaration other than UTF-8, or exceeding XMLParser(max_depth=..., max_elements=...) is 400 invalid_xml . max_depth defaults to 32 and may be raised to at most 1000 ( hinoki.parsers.MAX_XML_DEPTH ); a larger value raises ValueError when the parser is created. As with Form[...] , the action takes only XMLParser (selected when parsers= is omitted), and the OpenAPI document lists application/xml . Upload files ¶ Bind a file by the multipart field name. An action that declares a file parameter and no parsers= gets MultiPartParser() automatically, with its default limits, unless the application's parsers= include one; pass parsers=[MultiPartParser(...)] to change them. UploadedFile contains the client filename, claimed content type and in-memory bytes ; it does not save files or validate their content. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /attachments" , status = 201 , parsers = [ MultiPartParser ( max_parts = 4 , max_part_bytes = 512_000 )], ) async def attach ( request : Request , invoice_id : UUID , document : UploadedFile ) -> Attached : title = request . POST . get ( "title" , "" )[: 120 ] # Validate content and choose a generated storage name before saving. return Attached ( title = title , filename = document . filename , size = document . size ) @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /scans" , status = 201 ) # MultiPartParser() selected async def attach_scans ( invoice_id : UUID , scans : list [ UploadedFile ]) -> Attached : ... UploadedFile requires exactly one part with that name. list[UploadedFile] requires at least one and keeps repeated parts in order. To make a single file optional, write file: UploadedFile | None = None . Declare the text fields next to the files as a Form[Schema] parameter; they are converted and validated like any form body (a failure is 422 with the parameter's path, such as meta.pages ). A plain JSON Schema body cannot be combined with files and is refused at registration. Use request.POST for undeclared text fields or request.FILES when names or repetitions are dynamic. class ScanMeta ( Schema ): title : str pages : int @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /scan" , status = 201 ) async def attach_scan ( invoice_id : UUID , meta : Form [ ScanMeta ], scan : UploadedFile ) -> Attached : return Attached ( title = meta . title , filename = scan . filename , size = scan . size ) Parser precedence for a file action: its own parsers= (which must then include MultiPartParser , or registration fails), then an application-wide Hinoki(parsers=[...]) that includes a MultiPartParser , then the automatic MultiPartParser() . An application parser list without multipart does not apply to file actions, and actions without file parameters keep their parsers. All declared files require multipart/form-data . A missing file is a 422 validation error; a wrong media type is 415 ; malformed multipart is 400 ; a part or complete body over its configured limit is 413 payload_too_large . A zero-byte body with no Content-Type is treated as absent input for optional files; an explicitly multipart empty body is malformed, while a valid closing-boundary-only body has no parts. The default complete-body limit is 1 MiB, and the parser buffers bytes in memory: this API is for bounded small uploads, not streaming. Warning Concurrent uploads multiply memory use. Keep limits conservative, never use the supplied filename as a filesystem path, and verify content instead of trusting the declared media type. See parsers and renderers and testing uploads . Responses ¶ Return a value matching the declared response type, or return Response ( from hinoki import Response ) when the handler must set a status, headers or body that a typed result cannot express, annotated as InvoiceOut | Response . Declare expected APIError subclasses in errors=(...) ; their status, stable code and message feed the OpenAPI document and the strict test client ( errors ). Paginated actions are described in pagination . Rate limit an action ¶ RateLimit(limit, window) admits limit requests per window seconds for one key. Its counters live in a database table that every worker and host shares, so the limit holds across workers and after a restart. A route names it with rate_limit= : # notes/apps/accounts/api.py from hinoki import RateLimit , http from .schemas import LoginIn , SessionOut @http . post ( "/auth/login" , rate_limit = RateLimit ( 3 , 3600 , headers = True ), atomic = True ) async def login ( data : LoginIn ) -> SessionOut : ... The default storage, DatabaseLimits() , uses the Database of the worker and the hinoki_rate_limits table. Hinoki never creates it at import or at startup: register the app that owns it and apply its migration once per deployment. hinoki app add ratelimit --models hinoki.ratelimit_store.models --migrations hinoki.ratelimit_store.migrations hinoki migrations apply ratelimit The algorithm is a cell rate (GCRA): a burst of limit is admitted at once, then one more request every window / limit seconds. A refused request uses up no quota. One statement counts each request, in the native core, on the async path and on the sync path alike. A route that otherwise runs on Kiso's native handler lane stays there. Argument Meaning key "client" (default, the trusted client address; an IPv6 address counts by its /64), "caller" (the authenticated caller's id; an anonymous request falls back to the client) or a plain function of the RateLimitContext returning a string scope What the quota belongs to; the method and the route template ( GET /items ) by default, so one path under two methods has two quotas. Routes that give the same scope share one quota tenant A plain function of the context returning an extra key segment, so tenants never share a bucket cost What one request spends, at most limit unknown_factor A request with no known client address shares one bucket unknown_factor times as large (default 10). Set server.trusted_proxies behind a proxy headers True adds RateLimit-Limit , RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset (whole seconds) to admitted and refused answers; the OpenAPI document lists them. Off by default on_error "closed" (default) answers 503 rate_limit_unavailable when the table is unreachable or missing; "open" admits the request, counts it as failed_open and logs once a minute storage DatabaseLimits(table=..., max_rows=..., timeout=..., sweep_every=...) or MemoryLimits(max_rows=..., sweep_every=...) , which counts in one worker's memory and forgets on restart: for development and tests only. The buckets belong to the MemoryLimits instance, so routes given the same instance and the same scope and tenant count together clock A function returning an aware datetime ; hinoki.testing.ManualClock in tests window is a whole number of seconds from 1 to 86,400. Arguments are checked when the route is declared: limit is a whole number from 1 to 4,294,967,295 and at most one request per microsecond of the window , and timeout is from 0.001 to 5 seconds; anything else is a ValueError . Keys are hashed in the native core and only the digest is stored: no address, user id or custom key reaches SQL, logs or metrics. The table holds at most max_rows buckets (default 1,000,000) and the migration indexes its state column; expired rows are deleted in small batches, oldest first, while requests are counted, and once the table is full of live rows every new key of a scope counts in one shared overflow bucket of that scope , unknown_factor times as large, until rows expire. Keys already in the table keep their own buckets; the overflow bucket adds at most one row per scope , and while it is in use the tenant segment does not separate new keys. A flood of new keys therefore spends the overflow bucket and is refused, never admitted without a count. A key part is limited to 1,024 bytes, and an oversized one is answered 503 . One check, the wait for a connection, the sweep of expired rows and the count included, is bounded by timeout seconds (default 0.5, at most 5); the sweep gets at most half of it and runs before the count, so a stale "full" mark never refuses the first new key after rows expire. Hosts stamp buckets with their own clock, so keep host clocks in sync. A refusal and the unavailable and failed-open outcomes are counted in the metrics ; an unavailable outcome also counts a key, tenant or clock function that raised. Any object with a check method is a policy too, when the application needs another store or rule: # notes/apps/accounts/api.py from hinoki import RateLimitContext , errors , http from .stores import RedisStore # your module's resource class LoginLimit : async def check ( self , context : RateLimitContext ) -> None : store = context . resource ( RedisStore ) # provided by a module, per worker if not await store . allow ( f "login: { context . client } " , limit = 5 , window = 60 ): raise errors . TooManyRequests ( retry_after = 60 ) @http . post ( "/auth/login" , rate_limit = LoginLimit (), atomic = True ) async def login ( data : LoginIn ) -> SessionOut : ... check is def or async def and returns to allow the request. It runs after the route is matched and the caller authenticated, and before the body is read, parsed or handled, so a refused request costs neither a body read nor a password hash. A sync check runs on the bounded executor, so it must use a sync client with finite timeouts (cancelling the waiter does not stop its thread); an async one runs on the event loop. RateLimitContext holds only method , route (the path template), client (the trusted client address, None when unknown; a forwarded address counts only from a configured trusted proxy), caller (the authenticated Caller , None on a public route) and resource(kind) , which returns the worker-owned resource that a module provided, such as a Redis client or the Database . It carries no headers, credentials, body or query values. The refusal is errors.TooManyRequests(retry_after) : status 429, code rate_limited , and Retry-After set to retry_after , a whole number of seconds from 1 to 86,400 (anything else is refused when the error is created). The route documents it in OpenAPI by itself, with Retry-After as a required integer header. Only that error answers 429. Any other exception from the policy or its store, including a TooManyRequests that was built without its constructor, is answered 503 rate_limit_unavailable : the request is refused rather than allowed unchecked, the answer and the log name the route and never the exception, and the application's error handlers and debug output never see it. Cancellation is not caught. Limiting failed credentials of a BearerAuth provider belongs in that provider, because authentication runs first. The policy runs after the route is matched and the caller is authenticated, so it never sees a request whose credentials were refused and cannot throttle failed authentication attempts (guessing a password or a token). To bound those, limit at the reverse proxy, or put the limit on an unauthenticated login route (as /auth/login above), where the handler checks the credentials after the policy has run. A refusal emits a RateLimited event (policy class name, route template, retry_after ; no key, caller or address) when the application has a handler for it. A handler cannot change the 429 . The response is checked against the annotation ¶ Every action's return value is checked against its return annotation, and the annotation itself is checked when the app starts. There is nothing to switch on. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} /raw" ) async def raw_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : return { "id" : invoice_id } # a dict is not an InvoiceOut: 500 internal_error At startup. An annotation that cannot be checked stops the app with a RegistrationError that names the action: no annotation, Any , object , set[...] , a plain class, or Response inside a collection. Annotate a concrete type, or declare the action with validate_response=False to skip the check for that action. At runtime. A result that does not match is a 500 internal_error , because the fault is the server's, not the client's. With the debug setting on (development only; hinoki dev does not turn it on) the answer names the action, the type it returned and the annotation it broke, for example raw_invoice returned a dict that does not match its return annotation InvoiceOut . Without debug the body is generic. The log and the answer never contain the value itself. With atomic=True the check runs inside the transaction, so a mismatch rolls the write back. What is accepted. A Schema class, list[...] , dict[str, ...] and Page[...] of these, str , int , float , bool (a bool is not an int ), bytes , datetime , date , UUID , Decimal , None , plain dict and list , Any or object as an item type, and unions of these. Annotated[...] and a PEP 695 type alias are unwrapped (a recursive alias stops the app with a RegistrationError ; with validate_response=False too when it holds a Schema , because it cannot be narrowed; an alias that cannot be resolved, such as one with a TypeVarTuple parameter, is refused the same way, naming the action). The check never coerces. Response . -> Response and InvoiceOut | Response are accepted: a returned Response carries its own status, headers and body and is not checked. The OpenAPI document describes InvoiceOut | Response by its typed arm, InvoiceOut . Actions with a bodyless status ( 204 , 304 ) are not checked. What it does not check. A Schema instance is valid by construction, so the check is about the shape of the result, not the field values. A custom renderer or a dump() override can still change the bytes afterwards. See also ¶ Errors Parsers and renderers Authentication

docs.text: This page covers what one action receives and what it returns. How to organise actions is in Function-based APIs and Class-based APIs ; how they reach the application is in Register routes . The fragments below add actions to the invoices group of the Billing app, which supplies their access policy and transactions.
docs.title: Requests and responses

docs.text: # notes/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) Use @http.get , @http.post , @http.put , @http.patch , @http.delete or @http.query ( from hinoki import http ), or the same methods on a RouteGroup . Hinoki also answers HEAD through each GET route: it runs the GET response path and returns the same status and representation headers without a body, so the GET handler runs for HEAD requests too. A 405 response's Allow header includes HEAD whenever GET is available. Option Meaning status Success status (default 200 ) access Access policy; None is public atomic True runs the action in a transaction ( transactions ); there is no transaction option pagination Page-number policy ( pagination ) parsers , renderers Body formats in and out ( codecs ) errors APIError classes the action may raise ( errors ) rate_limit A rate-limit policy ( below ) cors http.Cors(...) : this action's own CORS policy, replacing the application's ( CORS ) include_in_schema , tags , deprecated , operation_id What the OpenAPI document says about the action; include_in_schema=False leaves it out without changing how it is served or protected, and deprecated ( True or a date ) also adds a Deprecation header and a warning log ( deprecate an action ) validate_response False skips the response check Each option is checked when the route is declared or registered. The fragments below continue notes/apps/billing/api.py from function APIs . Besides its imports they use these: from typing import Annotated from hinoki import XML , Field , Form , MultiPartParser , Query , Request , UploadedFile
docs.title: Declare an action

docs.text: QUERY is the HTTP method for a read whose input does not fit a query string: it is safe and idempotent like GET , and carries a body like POST . # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceSearch ( Schema ): text : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] limit : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 100 )] = 20 @invoices . query ( "/search" ) async def search_invoices ( data : InvoiceSearch ) -> list [ InvoiceOut ]: rows = await Invoice . filter ( reference__contains = data . text ) . limit ( data . limit ) return InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows ) curl -X QUERY http://127.0.0.1:8000/billing/invoices/search -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"text": "2026"}' The body is bound, parsed and validated exactly as for POST : the same parsers, size limit and 400 / 413 / 415 / 422 answers. A QUERY action must not change state. RouteGroup(atomic=True) applies to POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE only; pass atomic=True on the action if the read needs a transaction. @http.query inside an API class works like the other methods. A 405 answer lists QUERY in Allow where it is available; HEAD is answered through GET routes only. Hinoki sends no Accept-Query or cache headers by itself. The method is recent. Granian passes it through over ASGI and WSGI (both are tested), but a proxy, gateway, firewall or HTTP client may reject it, and browsers send a CORS preflight for it. Keep a GET or POST route beside it when clients cannot send QUERY . In the OpenAPI document a QUERY operation appears under the path's query field ( x-query with openapi_version="3.1" ); see OpenAPI .
docs.title: Read with a body: @http.query

docs.text: Typed path parameters come from the path, query parameters from the query string, and a body parameter from the request body. Declare request: Request as the first parameter when you need headers, cookies or raw request data; it is injected only when that parameter is annotated. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceLabel ( Schema ): id : UUID locale : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 35 )] @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} /label" ) async def invoice_label ( request : Request , invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceLabel : locale = request . headers . get ( "accept-language" , "en" )[: 35 ] return InvoiceLabel ( id = invoice_id , locale = locale ) Request path, query and body values are validated before the handler runs; a Schema body uses Schema.validate() and reports nested field errors with its parameter prefix. Discriminated request variants belong in a wrapper Schema field ( Annotated[Cat | Dog, Field(discriminator="kind")] ); bare union body parameters are not supported. Hinoki does not coerce input values into different types, except in Query[...] , Form[...] and XML[...] . Return a Schema built from the row: InvoiceOut.from_model(row) or InvoiceOut.from_models(rows) ( model schemas ). A returned dict or Model where a Schema is declared is a 500 internal_error ( the response check ). Use a wrapper Schema for a discriminated response union too; bare union return annotations are rejected by OpenAPI generation.
docs.title: Bind request values

docs.text: Query[...] reads a whole query string into a Schema , for any method: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) class InvoiceFilter ( Schema ): paid : bool = False limit : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 100 )] = 20 @invoices . get ( "/recent" ) async def recent_invoices ( filters : Query [ InvoiceFilter ]) -> InvoiceRecent : rows = await Invoice . filter ( paid = filters . paid ) . limit ( filters . limit ) return InvoiceRecent ( items = InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows )) # ?paid=true&limit=5 Text is converted to the int , float and bool the Schema declares before the strict validation (a repeated key fills a list field, a single one still does). A value that does not convert, a repeated key for a scalar, a missing required field and an unknown key (by default) are 422 errors, reported with the parameter name as prefix. The Schema owns the whole query string, so the action takes no other query or page parameters, at most one Query[...] , and it cannot be a path parameter. OpenAPI lists one query parameter per field. A plain path or query parameter ( n: int , slug: str ) takes no constraints: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1)] on one is refused with a RegistrationError when the routes are declared, because nothing would enforce it. Any Field(...) is refused, even one with only description or examples : scalar parameters read none of its attributes, and refusing every form is simpler and more explicit than allowing a subset. The same holds for the path and query parameters of a WebSocket route. Put the constraints in a Schema and take it as Query[...] (above) or as the body; on a WebSocket, validate inside the handler.
docs.title: Query strings as a Schema

docs.text: A plain Schema parameter is a strict JSON body. Wrap it in Form[...] to read the same Schema from a form, whose values are all text: # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . post ( "/import" , status = 201 ) async def import_invoice ( data : Form [ InvoiceIn ]) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . acreate ( data )) # reference=INV-1 Before validation, text is converted to the int , float and bool the Schema declares (and a lone value of a list field becomes a one-item list); Schema and JSON stay strict. A value that does not convert, or several values for a scalar, fails with the normal 422 type error. Empty text is not turned into None , and nested Schema fields are not read from form keys. An action with a Form[...] parameter and no parsers= uses FormParser (add MultiPartParser() explicitly for multipart text fields). Form[...] is valid only for the Schema body of a POST, PUT, PATCH or QUERY action, takes only form parsers (a JSON body needs a plain Schema parameter, so one cannot be coerced by mistake), and appears in OpenAPI as application/x-www-form-urlencoded .

Any object with a check method is a policy too, when the application needs another store or rule: # notes/apps/accounts/api.py from hinoki import RateLimitContext , errors , http from .stores import RedisStore # your module's resource class LoginLimit : async def check ( self , context : RateLimitContext ) -> None : store = context . resource ( RedisStore ) # provided by a module, per worker if not await store . allow ( f "login: { context . client } " , limit = 5 , window = 60 ): raise errors . TooManyRequests ( retry_after = 60 ) @http . post ( "/auth/login" , rate_limit = LoginLimit (), atomic = True ) async def login ( data : LoginIn ) -> SessionOut : ... check is def or async def and returns to allow the request. It runs after the route is matched and the caller authenticated, and before the body is read, parsed or handled, so a refused request costs neither a body read nor a password hash. A sync check runs on the bounded executor, so it must use a sync client with finite timeouts (cancelling the waiter does not stop its thread); an async one runs on the event loop. RateLimitContext holds only method , route (the path template), client (the trusted client address, None when unknown; a forwarded address counts only from a configured trusted proxy), caller (the authenticated Caller , None on a public route) and resource(kind) , which returns the worker-owned resource that a module provided, such as a Redis client or the Database . It carries no headers, credentials, body or query values. The refusal is errors.TooManyRequests(retry_after) : status 429, code rate_limited , and Retry-After set to retry_after , a whole number of seconds from 1 to 86,400 (anything else is refused when the error is created). The route documents it in OpenAPI by itself, with Retry-After as a required integer header. Only that error answers 429. Any other exception from the policy or its store, including a TooManyRequests that was built without its constructor, is answered 503 rate_limit_unavailable : the request is refused rather than allowed unchecked, the answer and the log name the route and never the exception, and the application's error handlers and debug output never see it. Cancellation is not caught. Limiting failed credentials of a BearerAuth provider belongs in that provider, because authentication runs first. The policy runs after the route is matched and the caller is authenticated, so it never sees a request whose credentials were refused and cannot throttle failed authentication attempts (guessing a password or a token). To bound those, limit at the reverse proxy, or put the limit on an unauthenticated login route (as /auth/login above), where the handler checks the credentials after the policy has run. A refusal emits a RateLimited event (policy class name, route template, retry_after ; no key, caller or address) when the application has a handler for it. A handler cannot change the 429 .
docs.title: Rate limit an action

docs.text: Every action's return value is checked against its return annotation, and the annotation itself is checked when the app starts. There is nothing to switch on. # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} /raw" ) async def raw_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : return { "id" : invoice_id } # a dict is not an InvoiceOut: 500 internal_error At startup. An annotation that cannot be checked stops the app with a RegistrationError that names the action: no annotation, Any , object , set[...] , a plain class, or Response inside a collection. Annotate a concrete type, or declare the action with validate_response=False to skip the check for that action. At runtime. A result that does not match is a 500 internal_error , because the fault is the server's, not the client's. With the debug setting on (development only; hinoki dev does not turn it on) the answer names the action, the type it returned and the annotation it broke, for example raw_invoice returned a dict that does not match its return annotation InvoiceOut . Without debug the body is generic. The log and the answer never contain the value itself. With atomic=True the check runs inside the transaction, so a mismatch rolls the write back. What is accepted. A Schema class, list[...] , dict[str, ...] and Page[...] of these, str , int , float , bool (a bool is not an int ), bytes , datetime , date , UUID , Decimal , None , plain dict and list , Any or object as an item type, and unions of these. Annotated[...] and a PEP 695 type alias are unwrapped (a recursive alias stops the app with a RegistrationError ; with validate_response=False too when it holds a Schema , because it cannot be narrowed; an alias that cannot be resolved, such as one with a TypeVarTuple parameter, is refused the same way, naming the action). The check never coerces. Response . -> Response and InvoiceOut | Response are accepted: a returned Response carries its own status, headers and body and is not checked. The OpenAPI document describes InvoiceOut | Response by its typed arm, InvoiceOut . Actions with a bodyless status ( 204 , 304 ) are not checked. What it does not check. A Schema instance is valid by construction, so the check is about the shape of the result, not the field values. A custom renderer or a dump() override can still change the bytes afterwards.

docs.text: Errors ¶ Hinoki separates malformed requests, authentication failures and application errors. Handlers may declare the application errors they can raise so clients and generated tools can inspect the contract. Built-in HTTP errors ¶ Every public error type lives in one namespace: from hinoki import errors . It holds errors.BadRequest , errors.Unauthorized , errors.Forbidden , errors.NotFound and errors.Conflict , each derived from errors.APIError , plus the framework's own failures ( errors.RegistrationError , errors.ValidationError , errors.ObjectNotFound , errors.ErrorRegistry and the others listed in the reference ). They carry an HTTP status and a stable code . Raise them when the response is an expected part of the API: from uuid import UUID from hinoki import Schema , errors , http class TaskOutput ( Schema ): id : UUID done : bool class TaskAlreadyDone ( errors . Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." @http . post ( "/tasks/ {task_id} /complete" , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone ), atomic = True ) async def complete ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : ... The Tracker example declares the same error in errors.py and raises it from its complete action. An action may declare several errors. The runtime maps a declared APIError to its status and response body. Unexpected exceptions remain server errors; do not expose exception text to clients. Your own errors need no registration ¶ Every APIError subclass answers by itself with its status , code and message . Pick the base class whose status you want and raise it: Base class Status Use it for errors.BadRequest 400 a malformed or refused request errors.Unauthorized 401 the caller is not authenticated errors.Forbidden 403 the caller may not do this errors.NotFound 404 the resource does not exist errors.Conflict 409 the request contradicts the current state (a duplicate, already done) errors.TooManyRequests 429 a route's rate limit policy refused the request; retry_after seconds are sent as Retry-After errors.APIError the status you set anything else class PaymentDeclined ( errors . BadRequest ): # answers 400 on its own code = "payment_declined" message = "The payment was declined." class QuotaExceeded ( errors . APIError ): # any other status status = 402 code = "quota_exceeded" message = "The quota is used up." Declare them on the action with errors=(PaymentDeclined,) for the contract (OpenAPI, MCP, strict_errors ). Nothing else is needed. Exceptions you cannot change ¶ A library or the database raises its own exception, which is not an HTTP error, and the client would receive 500 internal_error . Answer it with a function on the app. The function receives the exception and returns the APIError to send; an instance can set its own status : # notes/main.py (continued) from hinoki import errors from notes.apps.billing.gateway import CardDeclined @app . error_handler ( CardDeclined ) def card_declined ( error : CardDeclined ) -> errors . APIError : return errors . APIError ( error . reason , status = 402 , code = "card_declined" ) CardDeclined stands for any exception your code or a library raises, here one the Billing app's payment gateway client defines. The most specific class wins: a handler for HardQuota is used before one for its base Quota . Application handlers are consulted before the built-in ones. A handler may be def or async def . One that fails, or does not return an APIError , counts as "not handled" and the client receives 500 internal_error without the exception text. An exception type can be registered once (a second registration raises ValueError ), and only before the app serves (afterwards RegistrationError ). The decorator returns the function unchanged. A class or a value that is not a function is refused with TypeError . app.errors.handle(Kind) is the same call without the app checks. The decorator needs the module-level app ( Register routes ); app.error_handler(Kind)(handler) registers a function defined elsewhere. Built in, with nothing to write: ObjectNotFound is answered with 404 not_found , and a database UniqueViolation with 409 unique_conflict ( errors.UniqueConflict ) without exposing the constraint name. Register your own handler to replace either. Validation and binding errors ¶ Input that does not match a path, query, header or body annotation fails before the handler runs. Schema validation is strict and reports field paths with 422 . Unsupported content types receive 415 ; malformed supported content receives a parser error. A body larger than execution.max_body_bytes , or a multipart part larger than its parser's max_part_bytes , receives 413 payload_too_large . Query strings over execution.max_query_bytes receive 414 uri_too_long ; combined headers over execution.max_header_bytes receive 431 headers_too_large . A Host outside the allowed_hosts setting receives 400 disallowed_host , and a CORS preflight from an origin outside cors.origins receives 403 cors_origin_denied ( hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). These are framework-level failures and do not need to be listed in the action's errors= . When security.redirect_https is enabled, a plain HTTP request receives 308 with an HTTPS Location before routing or body parsing. The redirect requires an explicit allowed_hosts list and preserves the request method and target. A target that is not a path, such as OPTIONS * , is not redirected. See browser security settings . ModelValidationError is raised before an ORM insert or update when a Model field constraint or custom validator refuses a value. In an HTTP request it uses the same 422 validation_error response shape as Schema validation, including field paths, codes and messages. The admin displays the field messages in its form. Keep Schema validation at the request boundary; Model checks also cover non-HTTP writes. See Model field constraints and validators . Every HTTP request receives a request ID in the configured server.request_id_header header ( x-request-id by default). Hinoki generates the ID unless server.trust_request_id=True and the request comes from a configured trusted proxy with a valid inbound ID. Built-in error bodies also include request_id . Use the ID to connect a client report with the server log entry. Unhandled exceptions are logged with the ID and returned as 500 internal_error without exposing exception text. The debug setting adds the exception type, message and traceback to that answer for development. Check the contract ¶ Use ASGIClient(..., strict_errors=True) in tests to fail if a handler returns an error that it did not declare (an error answered by an app.error_handler counts too). hinoki check can also enforce rules about access, transaction, response and schema declarations; see rules . Earlier revisions exported these names from hinoki itself and kept the HTTP errors in hinoki.httperrors ; both are gone. Use errors.<Name> ; from hinoki import NotFound raises ImportError .
