docs.text: Events ¶ An event is a class; a handler is a function registered for that class. Events let one part of an application announce that something happened without importing the parts that react. Nothing registers by import: the application lists its handler collections, and the order they run in is the order of that list. Events are typed (mypy checks the payload), they have no string names, and the moment a handler runs is part of how you register it. Events are not a message queue: delivery stays inside one worker process, with no retry and no at-least-once guarantee. A minimal example ¶ from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , events , http class NoteSaved ( Schema ): text : str class Saved ( Schema ): status : str handlers = events . Handlers ( "notes" ) @handlers . after_commit ( NoteSaved ) async def tell_search ( event : NoteSaved ) -> None : print ( "index" , event . text ) @http . post ( "/notes" , access = None ) async def save () -> Saved : await events . emit ( NoteSaved ( text = "hello" )) return Saved ( status = "saved" ) app = Hinoki ( events = [ handlers ], include = [ save ]) events= and include= are passed by hand here because the example is one file. A project lists the collection in hinoki.toml instead ( below ). The Tracker example keeps its handlers in tracker/apps/activity/events.py , and the Blog example also emits its own event from an action. Your own events can be a Schema (as above: frozen, keyword-only and validated when built) or a frozen dataclass ; registration accepts any class. A Schema costs a validation per event, and it cannot hold a model class or instance, so the built-in model events below ( subject: type[M] , instance: M ) are dataclasses and an event that carries a row should carry its identifier instead. events.emit uses the bus of the current worker. Outside a request, a startup hook or a management command it raises EventError unless you wrap the code in events.use(app.events) . Two moments, named in the registration ¶ Decorator Runs May fail the write Function kind @handlers.in_transaction(E) Inside the writer's transaction, when the event is emitted Yes: an exception rolls the transaction back async def only @handlers.after_commit(E) After the outermost transaction commits No def or async def An in_transaction handler must be quick and may only use the active transaction's connection. It is async def only because its timeout can be enforced on awaiting code only, and a synchronous call on another thread cannot join a transaction another task opened. Emitting such an event with no transaction active raises EventError . An after_commit handler is queued on the transaction and dropped if the transaction (or its savepoint) rolls back. Outside a transaction it runs at once. Its failure is logged, counted and never propagated: the write has already committed. A plain def runs on the bounded sync executor. A handler that writes to the database from after_commit must open its own transaction. Typing and subjects ¶ A handler's first parameter is annotated with the event class, and the registration is checked against it when the collection is built: a missing or mismatched annotation raises EventRegistrationError at startup, not at the first emit. An event with a subject attribute (a model class, for example) can be registered as Event[Note] to receive only that subject, or bare Event to receive every subject (annotate it Event[Any] ). Order and limits ¶ Handlers run in the order of the events= collections, then in registration order inside each collection. The limits are the events settings: Setting Default Meaning events.handler_timeout 5.0 Seconds each handler may run; EventTimeout when exceeded. events.max_handlers 16 Handlers per (event, phase); registering more raises EventRegistrationError . events.max_depth 4 How deep handlers may emit events from handlers; more raises EventError , which stops cycles. An in_transaction failure or timeout propagates to the writer, which rolls back before any HTTP error is translated. An after_commit failure is isolated: the remaining handlers still run. Declaring handlers in hinoki.toml ¶ [[apps]] name = "activity" models = "tracker.apps.activity.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.activity.migrations" routes = "tracker.apps.activity.api:routes" events = "tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers" requires = [ "tasks" , "members" ] from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki () # reads routes, events, middleware and rules from hinoki.toml Events stay per app because a handler belongs to the models and behaviour of one app and runs in dependency order, whereas middleware and rules are project-wide lists. When the manifest's project.application names the module that builds the app, Hinoki() loads events= if you did not pass it (independently of include= , middleware= and rules= ); an explicit argument (even () ) wins and skips that key. manifest_events() does the same load explicitly, for combining lists or building an app elsewhere. It imports each app's Handlers in dependency order ( requires ) and fails with a message naming the app when the target does not import or is not a Handlers . Hinoki does not generate the module: you create it yourself (for example tracker/apps/activity/events.py with handlers = events.Handlers("activity") , as in the Tracker example) and name it in the key, so there is no template to copy and a mistyped target is reported when the application is built. hinoki app add notes --models ... --events pkg.events:handlers registers an existing one; hinoki app list shows it. Testing ¶ with app . events . capture () as seen : ... # code under test emits events assert seen == [ NoteSaved ( text = "hello" )] with app . events . muted (): ... # events emitted here run no handler capture() records every event emitted in the block and still runs the handlers; muted() runs no handler ( capture() still records what is emitted). app.events.stats() returns the counters of (event, phase, outcome) , which are low-cardinality by construction. app.events.registrations lists what is registered. Seeing what is registered ¶ hinoki events lists every handler of the application without starting a server, opening a database or writing anything. It builds the application the way hinoki routes does and takes the same optional target (default: the project's application ). From examples/tracker : uv run hinoki events Created[Task] in_transaction activity async tracker.apps.activity.events.task_created Updated[Task] in_transaction activity async tracker.apps.activity.events.task_updated limits: events.handler_timeout=5.0, events.max_handlers=16, events.max_depth=4 declared in hinoki.toml: activity -> tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers Each row is the event ( Event or Event[Model] ), the phase, the name of the Handlers collection ( - when it has none), async or sync , and the handler as module.qualname , in execution order. The last line shows the events limits in force. In a project, a line declared in hinoki.toml: APP -> module:attribute follows for each app that sets events in hinoki.toml . An application with no handlers prints no event handlers registered and exits 0 . --format json prints an object with handlers ( event , phase , handler , collection , async ), limits ( handler_timeout , max_handlers , max_depth ) and apps ( app , events ). A target that cannot be loaded prints error: cannot load TARGET: ... and exits 2 . The listing shows what is registered, not whether a handler will run: that depends on the code that emits. Authentication and rate-limit events ¶ These events describe a request the application refused. They are plain frozen dataclasses ( Schema cannot hold arbitrary types, and an event emitted on every refused request should cost nothing to build). Event Payload Emitted when AuthRejected reason , route , method A route's Access policy refused the request: reason is "missing" (no credentials, 401 ), "invalid" (credentials the provider rejected, 401 ) or "forbidden" (a caller without a required permission, 403 ). Also for a WebSocket handshake ( method is WEBSOCKET ). RateLimited policy , route , method , retry_after A route's rate_limit policy refused with TooManyRequests ( 429 ), including RateLimit and the admin's shared sign-in limit. A storage failure is not a refusal and emits no event. policy is the class name of the policy; retry_after is the whole seconds sent in Retry-After . from hinoki import events from hinoki.events import AuthRejected , RateLimited security = events . Handlers ( "security" ) @security . after_commit ( AuthRejected ) async def count_rejection ( event : AuthRejected ) -> None : rejections . labels ( event . reason , event . route ) . inc () @security . after_commit ( RateLimited ) def log_limit ( event : RateLimited ) -> None : log . warning ( "rate limited %s %s ( %s s)" , event . method , event . route , event . retry_after ) No secrets, no high-cardinality values. route is the path template ( /notes/{note_id} ), never the requested path or query string. The payloads carry no credential, token, user name, caller id, address or header, so a handler can count or log them without handling personal data. Add nothing of that kind if you define similar events. They cannot change the answer. The 401 , 403 or 429 is decided before the event is emitted. Only after_commit handlers are accepted: there is no transaction, so @handlers.in_transaction(AuthRejected) raises EventRegistrationError when it is registered (an event class opts out of transactions with the class attribute has_transaction: ClassVar[bool] = False ). A failing handler is logged and counted and never reaches the response, and the whole delivery of one event, handlers included, takes at most events.handler_timeout seconds before the answer is sent. A slow handler still delays the refusal up to that limit, so keep handlers short and hand heavy work to a queue. Zero cost without a listener. The runtime builds the payload only when a handler is registered for the event (one context-variable read and one dictionary lookup). Native lane. Kiso authenticates generated CRUD and handler routes protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth in Rust and answers 401 and 403 there. When a handler is registered for AuthRejected , those routes are authenticated by Python so the event can fire ( hinoki routes --lanes reports auth_event_handlers for generated CRUD). Without such a handler nothing changes. A route with an access policy or a rate_limit also stays off the native handler lane while a handler is registered for AuthRejected or RateLimited , because the event is delivered from an asyncio task; hinoki routes shows the reason. What is not an event. A 401 , 403 or 429 raised by your own handler code or by ownership checks inside generated CRUD is not an access-policy decision and emits nothing. There is no AuthSucceeded : it would fire on every authenticated request, and Rust authenticates the fast path, so it would turn that path off for everyone who listens. Startup and shutdown. Worker lifecycle, migration and configuration-reload events are not provided: use the on_startup and on_shutdown hooks of the application. Model events ¶ Created , Updated and Deleted ( from hinoki.events import Created, Updated, Deleted ) are emitted by the model write path itself. Each carries subject , the model class, so @handlers.after_commit(Created[Note]) receives only notes and a bare Created receives every model (annotate it Created[Any] ). Event Payload Emitted by Created[M] subject , instance (the stored instance) acreate , asave of a new instance, abulk_create (one per row), generated CRUD create, admin create Updated[M] subject , instance , changed (the changed column names, read before the write) asave , aupdate_from , aupdate_within , abulk_update (one per row that changed), generated CRUD update, admin edit. Nothing is emitted when no column changed. Deleted[M] subject , count (rows one DELETE statement removed) Model.adelete , QuerySet.adelete , abulk_delete (one per chunk of keys), generated CRUD delete, admin delete. No key or row is loaded, so there is no instance; nothing is emitted when no row was deleted. from hinoki import Hinoki , db , events from hinoki.events import Created , Updated from hinoki.orm import Model , pk @db . table ( "notes" ) class Note ( Model ): id : int = pk () title : str @db . table ( "audit_lines" ) class Audit ( Model ): id : int = pk () note_id : int handlers = events . Handlers ( "notes" ) @handlers . in_transaction ( Created [ Note ]) async def audit ( event : Created [ Note ]) -> None : # Runs in the insert's transaction: raising here rolls the note back. await Audit . acreate ( id = event . instance . id , note_id = event . instance . id ) @handlers . after_commit ( Updated [ Note ]) async def reindex ( event : Updated [ Note ]) -> None : if "title" in event . changed : print ( "reindex" , event . instance . id ) app = Hinoki ( events = [ handlers ]) Any code the application runs (a request, a startup hook, a command) that calls await Note.acreate(...) or await note.asave() now emits; in a script or test wrap it in with events.use(app.events): and a database. How it runs: A write emits only when the application's bus has a handler for that event and model. With none, the write takes the path it always took: one context-variable read and one dictionary lookup, with no extra await or allocation. With an in_transaction handler the write runs in a transaction (a savepoint inside an open one), so an exception or timeout in the handler rolls the row back and reaches the caller. With only after_commit handlers no transaction is added: the handler is queued on the open transaction and dropped on rollback, or runs at once when none is open. Updated and Created are emitted after the instance holds the stored row and after the lifecycle hooks , so the instance is what a hook left. A handler that writes another model with handlers emits again, bounded by events.max_depth . Not emitted: QuerySet.aupdate , Model.aupdate , aupdate_where (one UPDATE by filter, no instances), raw SQL and migrations. Use asave or abulk_update on loaded instances when a handler must see the change. Events never reveal rows a caller cannot see: they come from the same write that applied ownership and tenant scoping. Generated CRUD update saves the instance with the scoped UPDATE (a row that left the scope is refused before any event), and the Updated instance is the row the caller was allowed to write. No delivery between services or processes, no queue, no retry, no at-least-once guarantee. For work that must survive a crash, use a job queue. docs.text: An event is a class; a handler is a function registered for that class. Events let one part of an application announce that something happened without importing the parts that react. Nothing registers by import: the application lists its handler collections, and the order they run in is the order of that list. Events are typed (mypy checks the payload), they have no string names, and the moment a handler runs is part of how you register it. Events are not a message queue: delivery stays inside one worker process, with no retry and no at-least-once guarantee.
docs.title: Events

docs.text: from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , events , http class NoteSaved ( Schema ): text : str class Saved ( Schema ): status : str handlers = events . Handlers ( "notes" ) @handlers . after_commit ( NoteSaved ) async def tell_search ( event : NoteSaved ) -> None : print ( "index" , event . text ) @http . post ( "/notes" , access = None ) async def save () -> Saved : await events . emit ( NoteSaved ( text = "hello" )) return Saved ( status = "saved" ) app = Hinoki ( events = [ handlers ], include = [ save ]) events= and include= are passed by hand here because the example is one file. A project lists the collection in hinoki.toml instead ( below ). The Tracker example keeps its handlers in tracker/apps/activity/events.py , and the Blog example also emits its own event from an action. Your own events can be a Schema (as above: frozen, keyword-only and validated when built) or a frozen dataclass ; registration accepts any class. A Schema costs a validation per event, and it cannot hold a model class or instance, so the built-in model events below ( subject: type[M] , instance: M ) are dataclasses and an event that carries a row should carry its identifier instead. events.emit uses the bus of the current worker. Outside a request, a startup hook or a management command it raises EventError unless you wrap the code in events.use(app.events) .
docs.title: A minimal example

docs.text: Decorator Runs May fail the write Function kind @handlers.in_transaction(E) Inside the writer's transaction, when the event is emitted Yes: an exception rolls the transaction back async def only @handlers.after_commit(E) After the outermost transaction commits No def or async def An in_transaction handler must be quick and may only use the active transaction's connection. It is async def only because its timeout can be enforced on awaiting code only, and a synchronous call on another thread cannot join a transaction another task opened. Emitting such an event with no transaction active raises EventError . An after_commit handler is queued on the transaction and dropped if the transaction (or its savepoint) rolls back. Outside a transaction it runs at once. Its failure is logged, counted and never propagated: the write has already committed. A plain def runs on the bounded sync executor. A handler that writes to the database from after_commit must open its own transaction.
docs.title: Two moments, named in the registration

docs.text: A handler's first parameter is annotated with the event class, and the registration is checked against it when the collection is built: a missing or mismatched annotation raises EventRegistrationError at startup, not at the first emit. An event with a subject attribute (a model class, for example) can be registered as Event[Note] to receive only that subject, or bare Event to receive every subject (annotate it Event[Any] ).
docs.title: Typing and subjects

docs.text: Handlers run in the order of the events= collections, then in registration order inside each collection. The limits are the events settings: Setting Default Meaning events.handler_timeout 5.0 Seconds each handler may run; EventTimeout when exceeded. events.max_handlers 16 Handlers per (event, phase); registering more raises EventRegistrationError . events.max_depth 4 How deep handlers may emit events from handlers; more raises EventError , which stops cycles. An in_transaction failure or timeout propagates to the writer, which rolls back before any HTTP error is translated. An after_commit failure is isolated: the remaining handlers still run.
docs.title: Order and limits

docs.text: [[apps]] name = "activity" models = "tracker.apps.activity.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.activity.migrations" routes = "tracker.apps.activity.api:routes" events = "tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers" requires = [ "tasks" , "members" ] from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki () # reads routes, events, middleware and rules from hinoki.toml Events stay per app because a handler belongs to the models and behaviour of one app and runs in dependency order, whereas middleware and rules are project-wide lists. When the manifest's project.application names the module that builds the app, Hinoki() loads events= if you did not pass it (independently of include= , middleware= and rules= ); an explicit argument (even () ) wins and skips that key. manifest_events() does the same load explicitly, for combining lists or building an app elsewhere. It imports each app's Handlers in dependency order ( requires ) and fails with a message naming the app when the target does not import or is not a Handlers . Hinoki does not generate the module: you create it yourself (for example tracker/apps/activity/events.py with handlers = events.Handlers("activity") , as in the Tracker example) and name it in the key, so there is no template to copy and a mistyped target is reported when the application is built. hinoki app add notes --models ... --events pkg.events:handlers registers an existing one; hinoki app list shows it.
docs.title: Declaring handlers in hinoki.toml

docs.text: with app . events . capture () as seen : ... # code under test emits events assert seen == [ NoteSaved ( text = "hello" )] with app . events . muted (): ... # events emitted here run no handler capture() records every event emitted in the block and still runs the handlers; muted() runs no handler ( capture() still records what is emitted). app.events.stats() returns the counters of (event, phase, outcome) , which are low-cardinality by construction. app.events.registrations lists what is registered.
docs.title: Testing

docs.text: hinoki events lists every handler of the application without starting a server, opening a database or writing anything. It builds the application the way hinoki routes does and takes the same optional target (default: the project's application ). From examples/tracker : uv run hinoki events Created[Task] in_transaction activity async tracker.apps.activity.events.task_created Updated[Task] in_transaction activity async tracker.apps.activity.events.task_updated limits: events.handler_timeout=5.0, events.max_handlers=16, events.max_depth=4 declared in hinoki.toml: activity -> tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers Each row is the event ( Event or Event[Model] ), the phase, the name of the Handlers collection ( - when it has none), async or sync , and the handler as module.qualname , in execution order. The last line shows the events limits in force. In a project, a line declared in hinoki.toml: APP -> module:attribute follows for each app that sets events in hinoki.toml . An application with no handlers prints no event handlers registered and exits 0 . --format json prints an object with handlers ( event , phase , handler , collection , async ), limits ( handler_timeout , max_handlers , max_depth ) and apps ( app , events ). A target that cannot be loaded prints error: cannot load TARGET: ... and exits 2 . The listing shows what is registered, not whether a handler will run: that depends on the code that emits.
docs.title: Seeing what is registered

docs.text: These events describe a request the application refused. They are plain frozen dataclasses ( Schema cannot hold arbitrary types, and an event emitted on every refused request should cost nothing to build). Event Payload Emitted when AuthRejected reason , route , method A route's Access policy refused the request: reason is "missing" (no credentials, 401 ), "invalid" (credentials the provider rejected, 401 ) or "forbidden" (a caller without a required permission, 403 ). Also for a WebSocket handshake ( method is WEBSOCKET ). RateLimited policy , route , method , retry_after A route's rate_limit policy refused with TooManyRequests ( 429 ), including RateLimit and the admin's shared sign-in limit. A storage failure is not a refusal and emits no event. policy is the class name of the policy; retry_after is the whole seconds sent in Retry-After . from hinoki import events from hinoki.events import AuthRejected , RateLimited security = events . Handlers ( "security" ) @security . after_commit ( AuthRejected ) async def count_rejection ( event : AuthRejected ) -> None : rejections . labels ( event . reason , event . route ) . inc () @security . after_commit ( RateLimited ) def log_limit ( event : RateLimited ) -> None : log . warning ( "rate limited %s %s ( %s s)" , event . method , event . route , event . retry_after ) No secrets, no high-cardinality values. route is the path template ( /notes/{note_id} ), never the requested path or query string. The payloads carry no credential, token, user name, caller id, address or header, so a handler can count or log them without handling personal data. Add nothing of that kind if you define similar events. They cannot change the answer. The 401 , 403 or 429 is decided before the event is emitted. Only after_commit handlers are accepted: there is no transaction, so @handlers.in_transaction(AuthRejected) raises EventRegistrationError when it is registered (an event class opts out of transactions with the class attribute has_transaction: ClassVar[bool] = False ). A failing handler is logged and counted and never reaches the response, and the whole delivery of one event, handlers included, takes at most events.handler_timeout seconds before the answer is sent. A slow handler still delays the refusal up to that limit, so keep handlers short and hand heavy work to a queue. Zero cost without a listener. The runtime builds the payload only when a handler is registered for the event (one context-variable read and one dictionary lookup). Native lane. Kiso authenticates generated CRUD and handler routes protected by an unmodified ClaimsJWTAuth in Rust and answers 401 and 403 there. When a handler is registered for AuthRejected , those routes are authenticated by Python so the event can fire ( hinoki routes --lanes reports auth_event_handlers for generated CRUD). Without such a handler nothing changes. A route with an access policy or a rate_limit also stays off the native handler lane while a handler is registered for AuthRejected or RateLimited , because the event is delivered from an asyncio task; hinoki routes shows the reason. What is not an event. A 401 , 403 or 429 raised by your own handler code or by ownership checks inside generated CRUD is not an access-policy decision and emits nothing. There is no AuthSucceeded : it would fire on every authenticated request, and Rust authenticates the fast path, so it would turn that path off for everyone who listens. Startup and shutdown. Worker lifecycle, migration and configuration-reload events are not provided: use the on_startup and on_shutdown hooks of the application.
docs.title: Authentication and rate-limit events

docs.text: Created , Updated and Deleted ( from hinoki.events import Created, Updated, Deleted ) are emitted by the model write path itself. Each carries subject , the model class, so @handlers.after_commit(Created[Note]) receives only notes and a bare Created receives every model (annotate it Created[Any] ). Event Payload Emitted by Created[M] subject , instance (the stored instance) acreate , asave of a new instance, abulk_create (one per row), generated CRUD create, admin create Updated[M] subject , instance , changed (the changed column names, read before the write) asave , aupdate_from , aupdate_within , abulk_update (one per row that changed), generated CRUD update, admin edit. Nothing is emitted when no column changed. Deleted[M] subject , count (rows one DELETE statement removed) Model.adelete , QuerySet.adelete , abulk_delete (one per chunk of keys), generated CRUD delete, admin delete. No key or row is loaded, so there is no instance; nothing is emitted when no row was deleted. from hinoki import Hinoki , db , events from hinoki.events import Created , Updated from hinoki.orm import Model , pk @db . table ( "notes" ) class Note ( Model ): id : int = pk () title : str @db . table ( "audit_lines" ) class Audit ( Model ): id : int = pk () note_id : int handlers = events . Handlers ( "notes" ) @handlers . in_transaction ( Created [ Note ]) async def audit ( event : Created [ Note ]) -> None : # Runs in the insert's transaction: raising here rolls the note back. await Audit . acreate ( id = event . instance . id , note_id = event . instance . id ) @handlers . after_commit ( Updated [ Note ]) async def reindex ( event : Updated [ Note ]) -> None : if "title" in event . changed : print ( "reindex" , event . instance . id ) app = Hinoki ( events = [ handlers ]) Any code the application runs (a request, a startup hook, a command) that calls await Note.acreate(...) or await note.asave() now emits; in a script or test wrap it in with events.use(app.events): and a database. How it runs: A write emits only when the application's bus has a handler for that event and model. With none, the write takes the path it always took: one context-variable read and one dictionary lookup, with no extra await or allocation. With an in_transaction handler the write runs in a transaction (a savepoint inside an open one), so an exception or timeout in the handler rolls the row back and reaches the caller. With only after_commit handlers no transaction is added: the handler is queued on the open transaction and dropped on rollback, or runs at once when none is open. Updated and Created are emitted after the instance holds the stored row and after the lifecycle hooks , so the instance is what a hook left. A handler that writes another model with handlers emits again, bounded by events.max_depth . Not emitted: QuerySet.aupdate , Model.aupdate , aupdate_where (one UPDATE by filter, no instances), raw SQL and migrations. Use asave or abulk_update on loaded instances when a handler must see the change. Events never reveal rows a caller cannot see: they come from the same write that applied ownership and tenant scoping. Generated CRUD update saves the instance with the scoped UPDATE (a row that left the scope is refused before any event), and the Updated instance is the row the caller was allowed to write. Native lane: Kiso runs generated create, update and delete in Rust without the model, so a model with a handler for Created , Updated or Deleted (any phase, bare or for that model) loses native eligibility for the matching action only ( create , update , delete ); it runs on the Python lane, where the event fires. hinoki routes and the plan diagnostics report the reason model_event_handlers . A hand-written async def handler that awaits acreate , abulk_create , abulk_update , adelete or abulk_delete on such a model stays off the native handler lane for the same reason. Models without handlers are unchanged.

docs.text: Function-based APIs ¶ A function-based API is a set of plain async def functions, each decorated with an HTTP method, grouped by a RouteGroup that states their shared prefix, access policy, transactions and errors once. It is the default pattern in Hinoki: use it unless a class gives you something concrete. When to use it ¶ Use functions and a RouteGroup when Use a class instead when The endpoints are ordinary reads, writes or workflows You want generated CRUD routes with hooks ( @crud ) Several actions share access= , atomic= or errors= Several resources inherit or override the same actions You want handlers a test can call as plain functions You ship a resource for other projects to include A complete example ¶ The Billing app of the Notes project serves invoices. hinoki app create billing created the app directory, its routes.py and its block in hinoki.toml ; the files below are what you write. api.py routes.py hinoki.toml models.py schemas.py # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup , errors from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: """Invoices, newest first.""" return ( await Invoice . all () . apaginate ( page )) . map ( InvoiceOut . from_model ) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} " , errors = ( errors . NotFound ,)) async def get_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . aget ( id = invoice_id )) @invoices . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) async def create_invoice ( data : InvoiceIn ) -> InvoiceOut : return InvoiceOut . from_model ( await Invoice . acreate ( data )) # notes/apps/billing/routes.py from hinoki import Includable from .api import invoices routes : list [ Includable ] = [ invoices ] # hinoki.toml (the block hinoki app create billing appended) [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [] # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" ) class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 , unique = True ) paid : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now , index = True ) # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , derive from .models import Invoice class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] @derive ( Invoice ) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): ... billing_staff is an Access policy declared once in notes/security.py ( the billing policies ). notes/main.py stays as hinoki new wrote it: the application it declares binds every routes list named in hinoki.toml ( Register routes ). The manifest prefix and the group prefix join, and a "/" path means the group prefix itself: hinoki routes --path /billing GET /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices POST /billing/invoices StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.create_invoice GET /billing/invoices/{invoice_id} StaffTokens[billing:manage] notes.apps.billing.api.get_invoice Best practices ¶ One RouteGroup per resource. State access= , atomic=True and the errors every action shares on the group. atomic=True on a group covers POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE ; reads stay outside a transaction. Keep handlers thin. Validate with a Schema , call the model or a function in operations.py , and return XOut.from_model(...) . A handler never returns a model. Write paths relative to the app. The app's prefix lives only in hinoki.toml . Never repeat /billing in code. Paginate every list : pagination= , a PageParams parameter and Page[...] . Declare what you raise. Every APIError an action can raise belongs in its errors= (or the group's). A missing row from Model.aget is answered as errors.NotFound ( 404 not_found ). List the group in routes.py . An action is served only when its group is in the list that hinoki.toml names. Group defaults and overrides ¶ An action inherits the group's options and may override them. InvoiceSummary is a Schema with one field, open: int : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/summary" , access = None ) # public on purpose async def summary () -> InvoiceSummary : return InvoiceSummary ( open = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) Option On the group On the action access= Default for every action Replaces it; access=None makes the action public atomic= Applies to POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE atomic=True / False decides for this action, any method errors= Added to every action Merged with the group's A public action must also be listed in except_ of Actions.require_access in notes/rules.py , for example except_=["notes.api.health", "notes.apps.billing.api.summary"] , or the application refuses to start ( HNK-ACC-001 ). The rule exists so that public endpoints are a written decision. Actions.require_permissions ( HNK-ACC-002 ) only checks actions that have a policy, so it needs no entry. Compose with other decorators ¶ Put the HTTP decorator outermost. The group records the function it receives when @invoices.get(...) runs, so a decorator above it would not be served. Both sync and async decorators written with functools.wraps preserve their signature and run when placed underneath @invoices.<method>(...) : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/export" ) @audited # your sync or async decorator, written with functools.wraps async def export_invoices () -> InvoiceExport : ... A wrapped function runs in an asyncio task. The native handler lane needs a plain async def . Test it ¶ A test builds its own application from the same routes list, so it needs neither the manifest nor a server. Mount the list at the manifest prefix to check the final paths, and pass the project's settings when the test sends requests: atomic=True needs the database they declare. # tests/billingroutestest.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Mount from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.apps.billing.routes import routes from notes.security import billing_staff from notes.settings import ProjectSettings def test_writes_are_staff_only_and_atomic () -> None : app = Hinoki ( include = [ Mount ( "/billing" , routes )]) found = app . resolve ( "POST" , "/billing/invoices" ) assert found is not None route , _ = found assert ( route . access , route . atomic ) == ( billing_staff , True ) async def test_anonymous_callers_are_refused () -> None : app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = [ Mount ( "/billing" , routes )]) async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : reply = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" ) assert reply . status == 401 The handlers are plain functions, so a unit test can also await get_invoice(invoice_id) inside use_database(...) . Tests that reach the database need a disposable one; see testing . Pitfalls ¶ Symptom Cause Fix The route is missing from hinoki routes The group is not in routes.py , or the app has no routes key in hinoki.toml Add it to routes: list[Includable] Paths read /billing/billing/... The prefix is in code and in hinoki.toml Keep the app prefix in hinoki.toml only ValueError on RouteGroup("/invoices/") A prefix starts with / and does not end with one RouteGroup("/invoices") TypeError: unknown action options An unknown or misspelled keyword on a group action Use the option names listed in Requests and responses RuntimeError: a RouteGroup cannot change after it is included An action is added after the group is included Declare every action at import time RegistrationError: a RouteGroup must declare at least one action An empty group in routes.py Remove it or add an action RegistrationError: a RouteGroup can be included only once The group is listed twice in one application List it once; mount the list, not each group ValueError: … already declares an HTTP route Two HTTP decorators on one function One decorator per function RegistrationError: 1 rule violation(s) naming HNK-ACC-001 A public action not listed in notes/rules.py Add it to except_ , or give it a policy

State access= , atomic=True and the errors every action shares on the group. atomic=True on a group covers POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE ; reads stay outside a transaction. Keep handlers thin. Validate with a Schema , call the model or a function in operations.py , and return XOut.from_model(...) . A handler never returns a model. Write paths relative to the app. The app's prefix lives only in hinoki.toml . Never repeat /billing in code. Paginate every list : pagination= , a PageParams parameter and Page[...] . Declare what you raise. Every APIError an action can raise belongs in its errors= (or the group's). A missing row from Model.aget is answered as errors.NotFound ( 404 not_found ). List the group in routes.py . An action is served only when its group is in the list that hinoki.toml names.
docs.title: Best practices

docs.text: An action inherits the group's options and may override them. InvoiceSummary is a Schema with one field, open: int : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/summary" , access = None ) # public on purpose async def summary () -> InvoiceSummary : return InvoiceSummary ( open = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) Option On the group On the action access= Default for every action Replaces it; access=None makes the action public atomic= Applies to POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE atomic=True / False decides for this action, any method errors= Added to every action Merged with the group's A public action must also be listed in except_ of Actions.require_access in notes/rules.py , for example except_=["notes.api.health", "notes.apps.billing.api.summary"] , or the application refuses to start ( HNK-ACC-001 ). The rule exists so that public endpoints are a written decision. Actions.require_permissions ( HNK-ACC-002 ) only checks actions that have a policy, so it needs no entry.
docs.title: Group defaults and overrides

docs.text: Put the HTTP decorator outermost. The group records the function it receives when @invoices.get(...) runs, so a decorator above it would not be served. Both sync and async decorators written with functools.wraps preserve their signature and run when placed underneath @invoices.<method>(...) : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued) @invoices . get ( "/export" ) @audited # your sync or async decorator, written with functools.wraps async def export_invoices () -> InvoiceExport : ... A wrapped function runs in an asyncio task. The native handler lane needs a plain async def .
docs.title: Compose with other decorators

docs.text: A test builds its own application from the same routes list, so it needs neither the manifest nor a server. Mount the list at the manifest prefix to check the final paths, and pass the project's settings when the test sends requests: atomic=True needs the database they declare. # tests/billingroutestest.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Mount from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.apps.billing.routes import routes from notes.security import billing_staff from notes.settings import ProjectSettings def test_writes_are_staff_only_and_atomic () -> None : app = Hinoki ( include = [ Mount ( "/billing" , routes )]) found = app . resolve ( "POST" , "/billing/invoices" ) assert found is not None route , _ = found assert ( route . access , route . atomic ) == ( billing_staff , True ) async def test_anonymous_callers_are_refused () -> None : app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , include = [ Mount ( "/billing" , routes )]) async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : reply = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" ) assert reply . status == 401 The handlers are plain functions, so a unit test can also await get_invoice(invoice_id) inside use_database(...) . Tests that reach the database need a disposable one; see testing .
docs.title: Test it

docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The route is missing from hinoki routes The group is not in routes.py , or the app has no routes key in hinoki.toml Add it to routes: list[Includable] Paths read /billing/billing/... The prefix is in code and in hinoki.toml Keep the app prefix in hinoki.toml only ValueError on RouteGroup("/invoices/") A prefix starts with / and does not end with one RouteGroup("/invoices") TypeError: unknown action options An unknown or misspelled keyword on a group action Use the option names listed in Requests and responses RuntimeError: a RouteGroup cannot change after it is included An action is added after the group is included Declare every action at import time RegistrationError: a RouteGroup must declare at least one action An empty group in routes.py Remove it or add an action RegistrationError: a RouteGroup can be included only once The group is listed twice in one application List it once; mount the list, not each group ValueError: … already declares an HTTP route Two HTTP decorators on one function One decorator per function RegistrationError: 1 rule violation(s) naming HNK-ACC-001 A public action not listed in notes/rules.py Add it to except_ , or give it a policy
docs.title: Pitfalls

docs.text: Installation ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha and installs from a source checkout. You need: Python 3.12 or newer uv 0.9 or newer a stable Rust toolchain from rustup Install from source ¶ git clone https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki cd hinoki uv sync --locked uv run hinoki version uv sync --locked builds the Rust extension and installs the development tools. The last command confirms the installation: hinoki 0.0.1 Not on PyPI yet Hinoki's package name is hinoki-api and it is not published yet. The hinoki name on PyPI belongs to an unrelated legacy package: do not install it. A project created with hinoki new points uv at this checkout in pyproject.toml ( [tool.uv.sources] ), so uv sync never fetches either package by name. Next: the Quick start creates and serves a project.

docs.text: Glossary ¶ One word, one meaning. "Schema" has four meanings in this field, so the docs keep the word for one of them. The four schemas ¶ Write Meaning Schema (code font) The Hinoki class for typed, validated request and response data: class InvoiceIn(Schema) . Always capitalised and in code font; say "a response Schema ". table state, migration state What the migration planner records about the tables ( migrations/NNNN-name.state.json ). Never "the database schema". OpenAPI document The generated /openapi.json . Its components.schemas entries are "OpenAPI schema objects". JSON Schema The standard the OpenAPI document uses to describe bodies, always by its name. Names ¶ Name Origin Hinoki 檜, the Japanese cypress of temples: fragrant, durable wood. Kiso Hinoki's Rust server, named after the Kiso Valley (Nagano, Japan), known for its hinoki forests such as Akasawa. mailer The per-worker email resource ( hinoki.mail.Mailer ): it owns the SMTP connection pool, is opened in the worker's lifespan and closed at shutdown. email template A hinoki.mail.Template : a subject, HTML and optional text in a small fixed language, checked against a context Schema and rendered in Rust. Not an admin template or an HTML page. Projects and apps ¶ Term Meaning manifest hinoki.toml : the project's application, its [project] routes map, middleware and rules, and its registered [[apps]] with their optional persistence, events and dependencies. project application The Hinoki object named by project.application ( notes.main:app ); the one a server process serves. app A package listed under [[apps]] (with optional models / migrations , events , requires , and reusable routes.py ). Not a second Hinoki object. app mount Mount("/billing", billing_routes) in the project's routes.py , deciding whether and at which prefix an app is exposed over HTTP. target module:attribute naming an app, such as notes.main:app . Commands use project.application from hinoki.toml when it is omitted. Code ¶ Term Meaning Model A class mapped to a table. Without @db.table , the name is <app>_<plural> : notes.apps.billing.models.Invoice → billing_invoices . A column reaches a client only through a Schema . action One declared endpoint ( @http.get , @invoices.post , ...): a function or an API class method. route group A RouteGroup : functions under one path prefix with shared access= , atomic= and errors= . Access The access policy of an action: an authentication provider and required permissions. Caller Who is making the request, as resolved by the provider.

docs.text: Guides ¶ One page per task. Start with data and endpoints, then add access, rules and runtime concerns as you need them. New to Hinoki? Take the tutorial or the quick start first, or read the examples in order: Notes (easy), Tracker (medium) and Blog (complete), plus the focused Mailroom (outbound email). Data ¶ Configure a database : choose the backend, set the URL or connection fields, keep credentials secret. Define models : columns, primary keys, column types, table names and write-time validators. Model options : indexes, composite uniqueness, default order, update timestamps and names, as decorators. Relations : foreign keys, one-to-one, many-to-many association models and explicit loading. Query and write rows : filters, pagination, reusable queries, creates, updates and bulk writes. Lifecycle hooks : react to a model's own writes and inspect its changed columns. Events : typed events with explicit handlers that run inside the transaction or after the commit. Migrations : plan, review, apply and check migrations for every app. Schemas : declare the data that crosses the API boundary and convert it to and from rows. Scalar field types : enums, literals, dates, decimals, bytes, addresses, secrets and paths. Collections and unions : sets, tuples, dictionaries, unions, discriminated unions, TypedDicts and dataclasses. Validate input : constraints, normalization, field and object checks, and input reshaping. Schemas from models : derive a Schema from a Model and convert rows with from_model . Time and utilities : UTC time, the application timezone, test clocks and update timestamps. Endpoints ¶ Function-based APIs : the default pattern: plain functions grouped by a RouteGroup that states access, transactions and errors once. Class-based APIs : API classes for @crud resources with hooks, inheritance and resources you ship to others. Register routes : how routes.py and hinoki.toml build the route map, with Mount , include= in tests and hinoki routes . Requests and responses : what an action receives (path, query, body, forms, XML, files) and how its result is checked. Store uploaded files : bounded memory or local-disk storage with opaque keys and streamed downloads. Generate CRUD routes : list, retrieve and write actions from a model, with access and ownership rules. Errors : malformed requests, authentication failures and declared application errors. Stream a response : Stream , EventStream and File answers sent while they are produced, on Kiso and Granian. WebSockets : @http.websocket actions with Access , typed JSON messages, limits and back-pressure, on Kiso and Granian. Compress responses : optional brotli and gzip compression of bodies, on Kiso only. Export Prometheus metrics : request counters and histograms on a dedicated listener, on Kiso only. Middleware : typed Middleware around an action or the whole app, identical on Kiso and Granian. Pagination : page-number pagination with PageNumberPagination and keyset cursors with CursorPagination . Filter, order and search a CRUD list : FilterSet with Eq , In , Range , Search and an ordering allow-list. Parsers and renderers : other body formats in and out. OpenAPI document : the OpenAPI 3.2 document (3.1 on request) generated from routes, signatures and Schema declarations. Security and checks ¶ Authentication and access : providers resolve a Caller ; Access policies check permissions. Application sessions : server-side state, cookie lifecycle, CSRF checks, session authentication and explicit stores. Hosts, CORS and HTTPS : restrict the host names an app answers to, which browser origins may read it, browser security headers, HTTPS redirects and trusted proxies. Rules : typed promises about your application, checked with a stable ID, a location and an explanation. Runtime ¶ Application modules : resources that live as long as a worker, such as a database pool. Cache values : bounded Rust memory cache or a shared database backend with explicit TTL and failure behavior. Transactions : atomic=True on actions, db.atomic in application code. Settings : typed, immutable settings from the environment, dotenv and TOML, with redacted secrets. Serve an application : hinoki dev while you work, hinoki serve in production, on Kiso (the default) or Granian. Kiso server : what Hinoki's Rust server runs natively, its limits, workers and signals, reload and reverse-proxy behaviour. Test an application : test through the whole stack with ASGIClient , against a disposable database, from the test hinoki new generates. Command line : every hinoki command, the short forms inside a project and the explicit forms outside one. Create a project : the interactive hinoki new flow, its options and what the generated project contains. Inspect an application : check rules, list routes, export the OpenAPI document, show settings and diagnose the environment. Interactive shell : an async-capable prompt with the app's settings and models. Typing : what a type checker catches in handlers, decorators and Schema construction. Integrations ¶ Add an admin : staff pages for your models, with a sign-in page, users and per-model permissions. Customize the admin : columns, hooks, bulk actions, templates and themes. Send email : SMTP, console and memory backends from a per-worker mailer, sent after a commit; no queue. Email templates : typed TOML templates rendered in Rust, checked at startup and previewed from the CLI. Expose actions over MCP : selected actions as tools for a remote MCP client. Development MCP : a server that describes your app to a coding agent; it can run requests against the app only when you enable --scenarios . Build with a coding agent : a project, rules and tools ready for an agent, the llms.txt files and Markdown mirrors of these docs, and where its authority ends. Operating ¶ Best practices : project structure, Schema contracts, Access policies, queries, Rust fast paths, testing and production operations. Sync and async code : the event loop, the bounded sync pool and which style each surface accepts. Benchmarks : retained measurements with their environment, method and limits. Changelog : every user-facing change, explorable by version and type. Native CRUD orientation run : a workload-specific measurement of generated CRUD. Concepts and project ¶ Concepts : how models, Schema classes, actions, workers and rules fit together. Request lifecycle : the order of routing, access, binding, handler, commit and response. Structure an application : layers, where each concern lives, and why. Glossary : one word, one meaning. Use other libraries : what owning Schema and Model means, and the extension points. Reference : public names, signatures and docstrings. Status : what works today and what does not yet. Documentation versions : how dev and release docs are published. Troubleshooting : common errors by their message. Toolchain and CI : local and CI commands for contributors. Release checklist : build, check and publish a release.

docs.text: Inspect an application ¶ These commands load the application, report and exit. None of them serves requests, opens a database or writes files (except openapi --output ): uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki routes Each accepts --format json for scripts. On a colour terminal the reports use ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed and – skipped; piped output, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb give plain text. Diagnose a project with doctor ¶ uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki doctor --format json With no target, doctor uses project.application from hinoki.toml . If there is no manifest or default target, it reports environment checks and marks app checks as skipped. An explicit TARGET names another app ( module:app ). Loading it imports your Python code, so module-level code may have its own side effects. Hinoki does not start app or module lifespans, run hooks, start a server, run architecture rules, connect to a database, or write files. The report covers manifest validity, Python/native extension and optional Granian availability, route registration, configured typed settings, and in-memory OpenAPI generation. An app with no settings object reports that check as skipped; a custom non- Settings object is a warning. JSON output has schema_version: 1 and stable check IDs. Settings values are not included. When the application cannot be loaded, the finding names the exception class; for a Hinoki declaration error with no chained cause (for example a missing admin secret) it also shows the message, on one line and truncated. Other exception messages are not included. Exit status is 0 when no diagnostic failed, 1 for invalid manifest or app diagnostics, and 2 when a requested target cannot be loaded. Warnings and skipped checks remain visible. Database connectivity and applied migration state are intentionally separate: use hinoki migrations status for the live ledger and hinoki migrations plan --check for model-to-file drift. Check the rules with check ¶ uv run hinoki check uv run hinoki check --phase static Option Effect Default --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE the RuleSet to run the application's own rules: Hinoki(rules=...) , else the [project] rules of hinoki.toml ( which rules run ) --package PACKAGE package for the static import checks; repeat for several the package that contains the target --phase startup\|static run one phase both --waivers PATH waiver file; must exist the app's waivers= , else hinoki-rules.toml at the project root ( which file ) --format text\|json human or versioned JSON output text --allow-effects also run checks declared effectful (files, network, database) off Exit status is 0 when no rule fails, 1 for violations and 2 when the target or the checks cannot run. An application with no rules passes with 0 rule(s) and a warning on standard error, since nothing was checked. What each rule checks, and how to read and waive a result, is in Rules . List routes with routes ¶ uv run hinoki routes From examples/tracker : GET /activity MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.activity.api.Feed.list GET /activity/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.activity.api.Feed.retrieve GET /health public tracker.routes.health GET /members/me MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.members.api.me GET /tasks MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.list POST /tasks MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.create DELETE /tasks/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.delete GET /tasks/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.retrieve POST /tasks/{item_id}/complete MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.complete Each row is method, path, access (the provider and its permissions, or public ) and handler, sorted by path. The handler is the action's rule subject, the name that except_ and waivers match: an action of an API class is named after the class it is mounted on, even when it inherits the method. --path keeps paths that start with the prefix, --method one method; no match prints no routes match and exits 1: uv run hinoki routes --path /tasks --method GET GET /tasks MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.list GET /tasks/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.retrieve --lanes adds, per route, whether Kiso runs the handler natively ( native ) or through the Python pipeline ( python ), with the reason. The access log's lane field means something narrower: a request for a native route here still logs python unless Rust runs a generated CRUD plan for it. JSON always has method , path , handler , access , status , lane and lane_reason . List event handlers with events ¶ uv run hinoki events uv run hinoki events notes.main:app --format json Prints each registered event handler in execution order (event, phase, collection, async or sync , handler), the events limits, and the events target each app declares in hinoki.toml . --format json has handlers , limits and apps . It reads the application and the manifest only; an unloadable target exits 2. Export the OpenAPI document with openapi ¶ uv run hinoki openapi --output openapi.json uv run hinoki openapi --check openapi.json uv run hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json The command builds the app without serving it or opening a database; it works even when openapi_url is disabled. With no file option it prints deterministic JSON (sorted keys, two-space indentation and a trailing newline). --output FILE writes those bytes. --check FILE compares parsed JSON, so formatting differences do not count as drift. Exit status is 0 when the file matches or is written, 1 when its JSON differs, and 2 when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or invalid JSON. --output and --check cannot be used together. --breaking-against BASELINE compares the generated document with an earlier OpenAPI JSON file (the released version) and prints one breaking: … line per change that would break an existing client. Reported: a removed operation or success response, new or newly required request input (a parameter that becomes required, a required request body where there was none), a removed response property or JSON body, a changed type (parameters included), a changed type, and a request enum that narrows or a response enum that widens. Additions are compatible and are not reported. Exit status is 0 when nothing breaks, 1 when something does, and 2 when the target cannot load or the baseline is missing or not a JSON object. It cannot be combined with --output or --check . The comparison reads the documents only; it does not check behavior that an OpenAPI document does not describe. Run --check in CI to catch an OpenAPI document that drifted from the code, and --breaking-against with the last released document before a release. See OpenAPI for what the document contains. Render llms.txt with llms ¶ uv run hinoki llms uv run hinoki llms --output llms.txt uv run hinoki llms --check llms.txt Renders the application's OpenAPI document as an llms.txt Markdown text: a title, the version, then the operations grouped by first tag with their summary, deprecation, security scheme names and request and response components. Like openapi , it builds the app without serving it or opening a database and works when openapi_url is disabled; an action with include_in_schema=False is not listed. With no file option it prints the text; --output FILE writes the same text as UTF-8 with LF line endings on every platform, and --check FILE compares it exactly, except that a CRLF line ending in the file (a Windows checkout with autocrlf ) counts as LF. Exit status is 0 when the file matches or is written, 1 when it differs, and 2 when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or unreadable, or the output cannot be written. --output and --check cannot be used together. Show settings with settings ¶ uv run hinoki settings uv run hinoki settings --format json uv run hinoki settings --example The target is an application with typed settings or a settings class ( notes.settings:ProjectSettings ). Each value is shown with where it came from; settings.Secret values are redacted. --prefix , --dotenv and --toml replace the sources the class declares. --example prints a .env.example with defaults and types, leaving required fields blank and commenting out optional values with no printable default (secrets, unset values). See Settings . Report versions with version ¶ uv run hinoki version --verbose The default prints hinoki X.Y.Z . --verbose adds the Python version, platform, native extension path and Granian version; Granian is reported as not installed when its optional package is absent. Use --format json for machine-readable output. Details the binding does not expose, including its bundled SQLite library version, are omitted rather than inferred. Errors and edge cases ¶ A target that does not import prints an error: line with the import failure ( error: cannot load TARGET: … for routes and openapi ) and exits non-zero (2 for check , routes and openapi ). Importing the target runs your module-level code; keep import-time side effects out of it. openapi options --output , --check and --breaking-against exclude each other. doctor without hinoki.toml still checks the environment and marks the application checks skipped. See also ¶ Rules OpenAPI Troubleshooting Command line
docs.title: Inspect an application

docs.text: These commands load the application, report and exit. None of them serves requests, opens a database or writes files (except openapi --output ): uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki routes Each accepts --format json for scripts. On a colour terminal the reports use ✔ ok, ▲ warning, ✘ failed and – skipped; piped output, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb give plain text.

docs.text: uv run hinoki doctor uv run hinoki doctor --format json With no target, doctor uses project.application from hinoki.toml . If there is no manifest or default target, it reports environment checks and marks app checks as skipped. An explicit TARGET names another app ( module:app ). Loading it imports your Python code, so module-level code may have its own side effects. Hinoki does not start app or module lifespans, run hooks, start a server, run architecture rules, connect to a database, or write files. The report covers manifest validity, Python/native extension and optional Granian availability, route registration, configured typed settings, and in-memory OpenAPI generation. An app with no settings object reports that check as skipped; a custom non- Settings object is a warning. JSON output has schema_version: 1 and stable check IDs. Settings values are not included. When the application cannot be loaded, the finding names the exception class; for a Hinoki declaration error with no chained cause (for example a missing admin secret) it also shows the message, on one line and truncated. Other exception messages are not included. Exit status is 0 when no diagnostic failed, 1 for invalid manifest or app diagnostics, and 2 when a requested target cannot be loaded. Warnings and skipped checks remain visible. Database connectivity and applied migration state are intentionally separate: use hinoki migrations status for the live ledger and hinoki migrations plan --check for model-to-file drift.
docs.title: Diagnose a project with doctor

docs.text: uv run hinoki check uv run hinoki check --phase static Option Effect Default --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE the RuleSet to run the application's own rules: Hinoki(rules=...) , else the [project] rules of hinoki.toml ( which rules run ) --package PACKAGE package for the static import checks; repeat for several the package that contains the target --phase startup\|static run one phase both --waivers PATH waiver file; must exist the app's waivers= , else hinoki-rules.toml at the project root ( which file ) --format text\|json human or versioned JSON output text --allow-effects also run checks declared effectful (files, network, database) off Exit status is 0 when no rule fails, 1 for violations and 2 when the target or the checks cannot run. An application with no rules passes with 0 rule(s) and a warning on standard error, since nothing was checked. What each rule checks, and how to read and waive a result, is in Rules .
docs.title: Check the rules with check

docs.text: uv run hinoki routes From examples/tracker : GET /activity MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.activity.api.Feed.list GET /activity/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.activity.api.Feed.retrieve GET /health public tracker.routes.health GET /members/me MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.members.api.me GET /tasks MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.list POST /tasks MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.create DELETE /tasks/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.delete GET /tasks/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.retrieve POST /tasks/{item_id}/complete MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.complete Each row is method, path, access (the provider and its permissions, or public ) and handler, sorted by path. The handler is the action's rule subject, the name that except_ and waivers match: an action of an API class is named after the class it is mounted on, even when it inherits the method. --path keeps paths that start with the prefix, --method one method; no match prints no routes match and exits 1: uv run hinoki routes --path /tasks --method GET GET /tasks MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.list GET /tasks/{item_id} MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.retrieve --lanes adds, per route, whether Kiso runs the handler natively ( native ) or through the Python pipeline ( python ), with the reason. The access log's lane field means something narrower: a request for a native route here still logs python unless Rust runs a generated CRUD plan for it. JSON always has method , path , handler , access , status , lane and lane_reason .

docs.text: uv run hinoki events uv run hinoki events notes.main:app --format json Prints each registered event handler in execution order (event, phase, collection, async or sync , handler), the events limits, and the events target each app declares in hinoki.toml . --format json has handlers , limits and apps . It reads the application and the manifest only; an unloadable target exits 2.

docs.text: uv run hinoki openapi --output openapi.json uv run hinoki openapi --check openapi.json uv run hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json The command builds the app without serving it or opening a database; it works even when openapi_url is disabled. With no file option it prints deterministic JSON (sorted keys, two-space indentation and a trailing newline). --output FILE writes those bytes. --check FILE compares parsed JSON, so formatting differences do not count as drift. Exit status is 0 when the file matches or is written, 1 when its JSON differs, and 2 when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or invalid JSON. --output and --check cannot be used together. --breaking-against BASELINE compares the generated document with an earlier OpenAPI JSON file (the released version) and prints one breaking: … line per change that would break an existing client. Reported: a removed operation or success response, new or newly required request input (a parameter that becomes required, a required request body where there was none), a removed response property or JSON body, a changed type (parameters included), a changed type, and a request enum that narrows or a response enum that widens. Additions are compatible and are not reported. Exit status is 0 when nothing breaks, 1 when something does, and 2 when the target cannot load or the baseline is missing or not a JSON object. It cannot be combined with --output or --check . The comparison reads the documents only; it does not check behavior that an OpenAPI document does not describe. Run --check in CI to catch an OpenAPI document that drifted from the code, and --breaking-against with the last released document before a release. See OpenAPI for what the document contains.
