docs.text: Export Prometheus metrics ¶ Kiso , Hinoki's Rust server, can count the requests it answers and serve the counts in the Prometheus text exposition format. It is off by default and it is Kiso only : hinoki serve --server granian refuses metrics.listen instead of ignoring it. The counters live in Rust and cost a few atomic additions per request; the exposition is served by a dedicated listener, never by the application's own port. # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http from hinoki.settings import AppSettings , MetricsSettings class Note ( Schema ): id : int @http . get ( "/notes/ {note_id} " ) async def note ( note_id : int ) -> Note : return Note ( id = note_id ) app = Hinoki ( settings = AppSettings ( allowed_hosts = ( "localhost" , "127.0.0.1" ), metrics = MetricsSettings ( listen = "127.0.0.1:9100" ), ), include = [ note ], ) Run hinoki serve notes.main:app --server kiso --port 8765 , request /notes/1 , /notes/2 and /nope , then scrape http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics . The lines for those requests (comments and the other families left out) are: hinoki_http_requests_total{route="/notes/{note_id}",method="GET",status="2xx",worker="0"} 2 hinoki_http_requests_total{route="",method="GET",status="4xx",worker="0"} 1 hinoki_http_requests_in_flight{worker="0"} 0 hinoki_http_response_bytes_total{route="/notes/{note_id}",worker="0"} 16 hinoki_http_response_bytes_total{route="",worker="0"} 69 The application's own port answers /metrics like any other unknown path ( 404 ). What is exported ¶ Every sample carries a worker label: the number of the process that counted it. Metric Type Labels Meaning hinoki_http_requests_total counter route , method , status Requests answered. status is the class: 1xx to 5xx hinoki_http_request_duration_seconds histogram route , method Time from the request head to the answer's head hinoki_http_requests_in_flight gauge none Requests the backend has not answered yet hinoki_http_response_bytes_total counter route Body bytes handed to the connection, after compression hinoki_http_errors_total counter route , kind invalid_response : the backend's answer could not be sent as given and became a 500 . stream_aborted : a stream failed after its head hinoki_events_total counter event , phase , outcome Event handler runs. outcome is ok , error or timeout hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds histogram event , phase Time a handler ran, whatever its outcome hinoki_email_messages_total counter backend , outcome Email sends. outcome is sent or the error kind ( invalid_address , invalid_header , invalid_message , limit_exceeded , closed , busy , connect , timeout , tls , auth , rejected , temporary , protocol , template ). template counts a Template.message that could not be rendered while a mailer is current ( Template.render alone counts nothing, it is not a send); startup and compile failures are not sends and are not counted hinoki_email_send_duration_seconds histogram backend Time of a send , whatever its outcome hinoki_email_retries_total counter backend Delivery attempts made again after a transient failure hinoki_rate_limit_decisions_total counter decision Rate limit decisions. decision is allowed , refused , unavailable (storage could not answer, or the key, tenant or clock function failed) or failed_open (storage could not answer and the route admitted the request). A route's own policy is counted too, as allowed , refused or unavailable ; a key, route or address is never a label hinoki_build_info gauge version , server Always 1 hinoki_worker_start_time_seconds gauge none Start of the worker, in Unix seconds hinoki_metrics_snapshot_errors_total counter none Snapshots of other workers that were unreadable, too large or not valid UTF-8 route is the route's pattern ( /notes/{note_id} ), never the path of the request, so the number of series is bounded by the number of routes. An answer no route produced (an unknown path, a refused host, the documentation pages) has route="" . method is GET , HEAD , POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE , OPTIONS , QUERY or OTHER . The duration is measured when the answer's head is ready, as the access log does. The time a stream takes to send its body is not in it, and a request is in flight only until the backend has answered, not until a stream ends. Bytes are counted as the pieces are handed to the connection: a stream's pieces one by one, a File as it is read, a compressed body at its compressed size. A HEAD counts none. The exposition itself is never compressed and never counted. The duration buckets are 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10 seconds. Set metrics.buckets to change them. Event handlers ¶ The two event families exist only when the application registers event handlers . Their series are created at startup, one per registered (event, phase) pair ( Created[Note] , after_commit ), in a fixed table in Rust; Python records each run with one call that adds to a counter and a histogram bucket, so nothing grows with traffic and no label comes from a payload. The histogram uses the same buckets as the request duration. A series with no run yet is not printed. Handler runs of events emitted inside a request, a startup hook or a command are all counted by the worker that ran them, under the same worker label; the table is built from the handlers of the Hinoki application served by the ASGI path of Kiso; Kiso's WSGI mode records none. Example from a real run (three emits of an event with an ok , a failing and a timed-out handler, events.handler_timeout=0.05 ): hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="ok",worker="0"} 3 hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="error",worker="0"} 3 hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="timeout",worker="0"} 3 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_bucket{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",le="0.05",worker="0"} 6 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_bucket{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",le="0.1",worker="0"} 9 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_sum{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 0.153349 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_count{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 9 Measured cost of recording on one Apple-silicon laptop (an after_commit handler that returns at once, 200,000 emits per sample, 15 interleaved samples per variant, medians over three runs): about 3.3 µs per emit with metrics off and 3.4 to 3.5 µs with them on, that is roughly 50 to 110 ns (about 2 %) more; the extension was a debug build. A handler that does real work makes the share smaller. Email ¶ The three email families exist only when the application has an email module (an email: settings.EmailSettings field). The backend label is smtp , console or memory and every outcome series is created at startup, so no recipient, subject, host or error text becomes a label; a series with no send yet is not printed, except the retries counter. The send duration uses the same buckets as the request duration. Example from a real run of one send with the memory backend: hinoki_email_messages_total{backend="memory",outcome="sent",worker="0"} 1 hinoki_email_send_duration_seconds_count{backend="memory",worker="0"} 1 hinoki_email_retries_total{backend="memory",worker="0"} 0 Without metrics, or under Granian, Mailer.stats() still counts sent and failed messages, retries and connections per worker. Settings ¶ Field Default Meaning listen unset host:port of the metrics listener (an IPv6 host in brackets). Unset keeps metrics off path /metrics The only path the listener serves allow empty Addresses or CIDRs of the peers that may scrape (the TCP peer, not X-Forwarded-For ); empty allows every peer token unset A Secret bearer token a scrape must send as Authorization: Bearer ... buckets see above 1 to 32 positive, finite, strictly increasing upper bounds in seconds snapshot_interval 1.0 0.1 to 60 seconds; how often each worker writes its snapshot when there are several A listen address off the loopback needs allow or token , so the metrics are never open to everyone by accident. The listener answers GET and HEAD only ( 405 otherwise), 404 for another path, 403 for a peer outside allow and 401 with www-authenticate: Bearer for a missing or wrong token (compared in constant time). It takes at most 64 connections, waits 5 seconds for a request head and reads at most 8 KiB of headers. Access policies do not apply to it: it does not pass through application code. Several workers ¶ hinoki serve --workers N opens the metrics listener once, like the main one, and every worker accepts scrapes on it. Counters are not added up: each worker writes a snapshot of its own numbers to a private directory (created by the supervisor, readable only by its user, removed when it exits) every snapshot_interval , and the worker that receives a scrape answers with its live numbers and the fresh snapshots of the others. Each process keeps its own series, told apart by worker , so Prometheus can sum without (worker) them and handles a restarted worker's counter reset as usual. A peer's numbers are at most one interval old (and a snapshot older than five intervals, from a worker that is gone, is ignored); the answering worker's own are live. A snapshot that is unreadable, too large or not valid UTF-8 is skipped and counted in hinoki_metrics_snapshot_errors_total . With one worker nothing is written to disk when server.sighup is "stop" : the worker binds listen itself and answers from memory. Otherwise (the default) the supervisor owns the listener and the directory even for one worker, because a reload on SIGHUP runs the old and the new worker side by side. A replacement worker takes the next free worker number (a reload of worker="0" continues as worker="1" ), starts its counters at zero, and the snapshot of the worker it replaces is removed when that one has stopped. Under hinoki dev the supervisor owns the listener, so it stays open while the worker reloads, and the counters restart with the worker. What it does not cover ¶ A worker's snapshot is limited to 4 MiB, which is roughly 2000 active route and method pairs with the default buckets and roughly 800 with 32 buckets (approximate figures). A worker whose snapshot would be larger keeps its previous file, logs the problem once to stderr, and its series leave the other workers' scrapes once that file is older than five intervals; its own scrape still shows live numbers. Pool and executor gauges, process metrics ( process_* ) and tracing are not exported. Metrics are not available under Granian or another ASGI server; wrap the ASGI application there as described in serving .

The histogram uses the same buckets as the request duration. A series with no run yet is not printed. Handler runs of events emitted inside a request, a startup hook or a command are all counted by the worker that ran them, under the same worker label; the table is built from the handlers of the Hinoki application served by the ASGI path of Kiso; Kiso's WSGI mode records none. Example from a real run (three emits of an event with an ok , a failing and a timed-out handler, events.handler_timeout=0.05 ): hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="ok",worker="0"} 3 hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="error",worker="0"} 3 hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="timeout",worker="0"} 3 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_bucket{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",le="0.05",worker="0"} 6 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_bucket{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",le="0.1",worker="0"} 9 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_sum{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 0.153349 hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_count{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 9 Measured cost of recording on one Apple-silicon laptop (an after_commit handler that returns at once, 200,000 emits per sample, 15 interleaved samples per variant, medians over three runs): about 3.3 µs per emit with metrics off and 3.4 to 3.5 µs with them on, that is roughly 50 to 110 ns (about 2 %) more; the extension was a debug build. A handler that does real work makes the share smaller.
docs.title: Event handlers

docs.text: The three email families exist only when the application has an email module (an email: settings.EmailSettings field). The backend label is smtp , console or memory and every outcome series is created at startup, so no recipient, subject, host or error text becomes a label; a series with no send yet is not printed, except the retries counter. The send duration uses the same buckets as the request duration. Example from a real run of one send with the memory backend: hinoki_email_messages_total{backend="memory",outcome="sent",worker="0"} 1 hinoki_email_send_duration_seconds_count{backend="memory",worker="0"} 1 hinoki_email_retries_total{backend="memory",worker="0"} 0 Without metrics, or under Granian, Mailer.stats() still counts sent and failed messages, retries and connections per worker.
docs.title: Email

docs.text: Field Default Meaning listen unset host:port of the metrics listener (an IPv6 host in brackets). Unset keeps metrics off path /metrics The only path the listener serves allow empty Addresses or CIDRs of the peers that may scrape (the TCP peer, not X-Forwarded-For ); empty allows every peer token unset A Secret bearer token a scrape must send as Authorization: Bearer ... buckets see above 1 to 32 positive, finite, strictly increasing upper bounds in seconds snapshot_interval 1.0 0.1 to 60 seconds; how often each worker writes its snapshot when there are several A listen address off the loopback needs allow or token , so the metrics are never open to everyone by accident. The listener answers GET and HEAD only ( 405 otherwise), 404 for another path, 403 for a peer outside allow and 401 with www-authenticate: Bearer for a missing or wrong token (compared in constant time). It takes at most 64 connections, waits 5 seconds for a request head and reads at most 8 KiB of headers. Access policies do not apply to it: it does not pass through application code.
docs.title: Settings

docs.text: hinoki serve --workers N opens the metrics listener once, like the main one, and every worker accepts scrapes on it. Counters are not added up: each worker writes a snapshot of its own numbers to a private directory (created by the supervisor, readable only by its user, removed when it exits) every snapshot_interval , and the worker that receives a scrape answers with its live numbers and the fresh snapshots of the others. Each process keeps its own series, told apart by worker , so Prometheus can sum without (worker) them and handles a restarted worker's counter reset as usual. A peer's numbers are at most one interval old (and a snapshot older than five intervals, from a worker that is gone, is ignored); the answering worker's own are live. A snapshot that is unreadable, too large or not valid UTF-8 is skipped and counted in hinoki_metrics_snapshot_errors_total . With one worker nothing is written to disk when server.sighup is "stop" : the worker binds listen itself and answers from memory. Otherwise (the default) the supervisor owns the listener and the directory even for one worker, because a reload on SIGHUP runs the old and the new worker side by side. A replacement worker takes the next free worker number (a reload of worker="0" continues as worker="1" ), starts its counters at zero, and the snapshot of the worker it replaces is removed when that one has stopped. Under hinoki dev the supervisor owns the listener, so it stays open while the worker reloads, and the counters restart with the worker.
docs.title: Several workers

docs.text: A worker's snapshot is limited to 4 MiB, which is roughly 2000 active route and method pairs with the default buckets and roughly 800 with 32 buckets (approximate figures). A worker whose snapshot would be larger keeps its previous file, logs the problem once to stderr, and its series leave the other workers' scrapes once that file is older than five intervals; its own scrape still shows live numbers. Pool and executor gauges, process metrics ( process_* ) and tracing are not exported. Metrics are not available under Granian or another ASGI server; wrap the ASGI application there as described in serving .
docs.title: What it does not cover

docs.text: Add middleware ¶ A middleware runs around an action. It is Hinoki's own typed interface, so it behaves the same on Kiso and on Granian: you do not wrap the ASGI application, and an application served by Kiso can use it. # notes/middleware.py from hinoki.http import Middleware , MiddlewareRequest , Next , Response class Tenant ( Middleware ): async def __call__ ( self , request : MiddlewareRequest , call_next : Next ) -> Response : if "x-tenant" not in request . headers : return Response ( 400 , "missing x-tenant" , content_type = "text/plain" ) response = await call_next () return response . with_header ( "x-served-by" , "tenant" ) Declare it on an action, or for the whole application. middleware= on Hinoki(...) is the explicit form; a project lists it in hinoki.toml instead ( below ): # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http from .middleware import Tenant class Pong ( Schema ): ok : bool @http . get ( "/ping" ) async def ping () -> Pong : return Pong ( ok = True ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ ping ], middleware = [ Tenant ()]) RouteGroup actions take the same option. The application's middleware runs first, then the action's, in the order listed; each one returns what the next one returned unless it answers itself. Declaring middleware in hinoki.toml ¶ The [project] table can list middleware for the whole application. Hinoki does not generate the module: you create it yourself, and you edit the list by hand (there is no command for it). The Tracker example does this with one middleware that adds a version header ( middleware.py , listed on line 4 of its hinoki.toml ). # shop/middleware.py tenant = Tenant () timing = [ Timing (), Audit ()] # a list or tuple is flattened [project] application = "shop.main:app" middleware = [ "shop.middleware:tenant" , "shop.middleware:timing" ] from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki () # reads routes, events, middleware and rules from hinoki.toml Each entry is module:attribute and resolves to one object with an async def __call__ or a list or tuple of them. The listed order is the execution order: the first one listed runs outermost. There is no dependency ordering. When the manifest's project.application names the module that builds the app, Hinoki() loads the list if you did not pass middleware= ; an explicit middleware= (even () ) wins and skips the manifest. manifest_middleware() is the explicit form, to combine lists. The result is the application's own middleware: it runs before an action's and obeys the order below . project.middleware that is not a list of module:attribute strings is rejected when the manifest loads, and a target that does not import or does not hold middleware raises a ProjectError naming the entry. What a middleware sees ¶ MiddlewareRequest is the head of the request: method , path , the matched route template in route (for example /items/{item_id} , safe to use as a metrics label), lower-case headers , the raw query string, client , scheme and request_id . It has no body and cannot change the request: headers is a read-only mapping, so authentication and the action see the headers the client sent. class Forge ( Middleware ): async def __call__ ( self , request : MiddlewareRequest , call_next : Next ) -> Response : request . headers [ "authorization" ] = "Bearer x" # TypeError: a 500 return await call_next () A middleware that needs to pass data on should answer itself or add response headers instead. The Response a middleware returns is checked like one a handler returns, also when it is built with Response.raw(status, body, headers) from encoded parts: a framing or server header ( content-length , transfer-encoding , connection , x-request-id ), an invalid name or a line break in a value is a ValueError , so the request answers 500 instead of a corrupt response. call_next() returns a Response with the action's answer. An error the action raised is already an HTTP answer, and an atomic=True transaction is already rolled back, so a middleware that reads the database after call_next() sees the state after the rollback. Call call_next() at most once (a second call is a 500 ). A middleware that raises is translated like an action error; one that returns anything but a Response is a 500 . For an action that returns Stream , EventStream or File , call_next() returns that object with an empty body : a middleware never sees the pieces, and with_header keeps the class and the source. A middleware that answers with another Response instead of the stream does not serve it, and Hinoki closes its source. See stream a response . Security, CORS and request-id headers are added after the middleware returns. Order and what stays outside ¶ Hinoki answers what needs no action first: the ready check, request size limits, host, CORS preflight and HTTPS redirect policies, the startup probe and the documentation pages. The route is chosen. An unknown path ( 404 ) or method ( 405 ) never reaches a middleware. The application's middleware, then the action's. Authentication, rate limit, negotiation, body binding, the transaction and the handler. execution.request_timeout applies to the whole of it: when it expires the 504 is produced outside the middleware, which only sees the cancellation. Cost ¶ An action with middleware is served by Python for the whole request, so it leaves the native lane : hinoki routes --lanes shows lane_reason middleware . A deprecated action ( deprecate an action ) leaves the lane the same way, with lane_reason deprecated . Actions without middleware keep their lane. A middleware that only needs to observe requests can use the access log instead, which does not change the lane. Errors and edge cases ¶ A middleware must have async def __call__ ; any other object is a TypeError when the application or the action is declared. Keep a middleware free of request state kept in globals: use the MiddlewareRequest it receives. See also ¶ Request lifecycle Serve an application Transactions

docs.text: Migrations ¶ Hinoki compares each app's models with the migration state recorded in its migration package and writes SQL files you review and commit. Nothing changes a database until you run apply ; an application never migrates at startup. hinoki migrations plan billing hinoki migrations apply Commands run from the project, where hinoki.toml registers each app's models and migrations ( hinoki new , hinoki app create ). Prefix them with uv run or activate .venv . Plan a migration ¶ hinoki migrations plan # a project with one app hinoki migrations plan billing # one app of several hinoki migrations plan billing --name add-invoice-index plan writes two files into the app's migration package: 0001-create-table-billing-invoices.sql and its .state.json . The number is automatic; the slug comes from the first change ( create table billing_invoices ) unless --name replaces it. In a project with several apps, plan needs the app name; --check and --dry-run without one cover every app. Plan for the backend you deploy The SQL uses the dialect of the selected database : usually the application's own database setting. Point it at the production backend (a disposable database of the same kind) before planning. The state file is backend-neutral. Review before applying ¶ Read both files. Changes that can lose data are destructive and are not written unless you pass --allow-destructive : dropping a table or column, changing a type or constraint, adding a non-null column; a changed derived table name (renaming the class or moving its module), which is planned as a drop and a create. Pin the name with @db.table(...) ( table names ). hinoki migrations plan billing --dry-run hinoki migrations plan billing --allow-destructive --dry-run prints the plan, destructive operations included, and writes nothing. Changing a constraint on an existing column may need a hand-written migration. Apply and inspect ¶ hinoki migrations status hinoki migrations sql 0001 -create-table-billing-invoices hinoki migrations apply hinoki migrations apply billing Command Effect status [APP] lists applied and pending migrations (nothing when there are none); writes nothing (connecting still creates a missing SQLite file): a database without the ledger has none applied, and apply creates it sql NAME prints one migration's SQL; add --app APP only when the name is ambiguous apply [APP] applies pending migrations of every app, or of APP and its prerequisites, in dependency order Which database ¶ plan , status and apply use the first of: --database URL ; the HINOKI_DATABASE_URL environment variable; the project's application ( project.application in hinoki.toml ): a DatabaseModule it passes in modules= or installs with app.install(...) , otherwise its database setting, read from its settings sources as the server reads them, for example NOTES_DATABASE__URL or .env ; local SQLite, sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 . The application is imported from the project root to read its settings, so .env and other relative settings files are the ones beside hinoki.toml , even from a subdirectory. Anything it prints while importing goes to standard error. No connection opens until the command needs one, and nothing is started. The command never falls back to another database: it stops with exit 2 when the application cannot be imported (the message names the missing module or attribute) or its settings cannot be loaded; it installs a database module of its own whose URL Hinoki cannot read; the application's database is in-memory SQLite ( sqlite://:memory: ), where nothing it migrates would survive. A --database sqlite://:memory: URL is refused with exit 1 instead, because SQLite needs a file URL there. Fix the application, or choose the database with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL , which skip step 3 and never import the application. An application without a database still migrates the local SQLite default, but the server has none to use: declare database: settings.DatabaseSettings ( configure a database ). Outside a project ( --models / --dir ), step 3 is skipped. plan , status and apply print the chosen database and its source on standard error. Everything before the host (user and password) and the URL options are masked, and a URL that does not parse is not echoed: $ NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) A relative SQLite path from the settings or the default is anchored beside hinoki.toml , so migrations run from a subdirectory use the same file; a relative SQLite URL given with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL stays relative to the current directory. The server and hinoki settings do not anchor: they resolve the path, and read .env , from the directory they start in, so start them from the project root. A connection failure prints error: database: … and exits 1 . A --database URL is visible in the process list and shell history: do not put a password in it. An older scaffold's root app keeps unprefixed ledger keys; apps from hinoki app create use namespaced keys, so accounts/0001-initial.sql and billing/0001-initial.sql are distinct records. Run apply once per deployment, from one process, never from every worker's startup ( settings ). Concurrent runs are serialized: each file runs in one transaction under a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a MySQL/MariaDB migration lock or SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE , and reads the ledger inside it. On SQLite a second runner waits at most the busy timeout (5 seconds), then fails as locked. Check migration drift ¶ hinoki migrations plan --check Exits 1 when any app has model changes without a migration file, destructive ones included, 0 otherwise, and 2 when the database whose dialect it plans for cannot be resolved ( which database ). It covers every app in dependency order ( plan billing --check : that app and its prerequisites), writes nothing and opens no connection. It imports every registered model and migration module and, unless --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL names the database, the project's application to read its database, so those imports must be safe in CI: HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = postgresql://ci@localhost/notes hinoki migrations plan --check status compares files with a live database instead. Apps and dependencies ¶ An app that references another app's models declares it in requires : # hinoki.toml [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [ "accounts" ] hinoki app create billing asks for requires ; hinoki app add NAME --models MODULE registers an existing package. Hinoki ships two such apps whose tables are optional: admin ( hinoki.admin.users.models , see the admin ) and ratelimit ( hinoki.ratelimit_store.models , the hinoki_rate_limits table of RateLimit ). Neither is applied unless you register it. Each app's tables belong only to its own migration state. The Tracker example has three such apps ( hinoki.toml lines 14-27 ): tasks requires members , and activity requires both, so apply runs them in that order. Cross-app migration safety ¶ Before planning billing , the referenced table and primary key must already be recorded in accounts ' migration state with a compatible type; plan and review accounts first. It does not need to be applied yet. A parent table or referenced column is never dropped while another app's recorded state still refers to it, in plan , --dry-run and --check ; --allow-destructive does not override this, and an all-app command fails without partial output. Remove and apply the child reference first, then plan the parent teardown in a separate deployment. --dry-run without an app previews every app, possibly against a prerequisite's not-yet-planned models: do not apply in that order. It cannot take --name . Backend behaviour ¶ Backend Behaviour SQLite rebuilds a table when ALTER TABLE cannot express the change safely; holds the pool, suspends foreign-key enforcement on reserved connections, runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check before commit and rolls back on invalid references PostgreSQL each migration runs in a transaction MySQL DDL commits implicitly: a failed migration may be partially applied (Hinoki says so). Check the schema and status before retrying; keep a backup MariaDB separate backend on the MySQL wire protocol; JSON is a text alias decoded by typed fields MySQL and MariaDB foreign keys are table-level constraints. For databases migrated by an older Hinoki, check SHOW CREATE TABLE : MySQL ignores inline REFERENCES , and MariaDB varies by version. Add a missing constraint with a reviewed manual migration; applied migrations are never rewritten. Automatic removal of a foreign-key column is refused on these backends. State files record logical types; files from older versions that recorded SQLite or MySQL type names are normalized, so switching the planner's backend is not reported as a type change. Migration compatibility ¶ For the planned 0.1.x line, Hinoki keeps migration files generated by 0.1.0 readable and applicable across patch releases. New state sidecars carry "format_version": 1 ; recognized legacy sidecars created before that marker are treated as version 1, including the historical omission of the indexes list. Hinoki rejects malformed state and unknown format versions before writing a plan. Restore damaged files from version control; Hinoki does not rewrite them automatically. Once a SQL migration has been applied, keep its exact contents unchanged. The database ledger records a SHA-256 checksum of the SQL file, and status and apply report an error if an applied file has changed or disappeared. The checksum does not cover the state sidecar and is not a signature. apply checks and executes SQL files; it does not read state sidecars. plan reads and validates sidecars. Files that do not match Hinoki's numbered migration name pattern are not treated as migrations. Review and back up both files, test migrations against disposable data, and apply them explicitly. SQL transaction and rollback behavior depends on the backend; MySQL and MariaDB may leave DDL partially applied after a failure. Hinoki may make documented Python, CLI, settings, runtime or migration-format breaks in a later 0.y.0 while it is pre-1.0. Such changes must appear in release notes; if a later format stops reading version 1, the release must document an upgrade path. No fixed deprecation period or support for old framework versions is promised. Bridge tables of many-to-many relations ¶ A many_to_many field adds its bridge model to the models module, right after its owner, so plan creates the bridge table in the same migration as the owner: the two foreign keys with ON DELETE rules, a unique pair and an index on the target column. Renaming the owner with @db.table before its first migration names the generated bridge <owner table>_<field> too. The planner does not plan table renames: changing the table of an already migrated owner drops the old bridge table and creates a new one (a destructive change plan refuses unless allowed), so move the data with a reviewed manual migration. An adopted bridge ( bridge="NoteLabel" ) is an ordinary model and migrates like one. Nothing runs against the database until you apply the migration. Without a manifest ¶ A project without hinoki.toml passes the models module and directory: hinoki migrations --dir app/migrations plan --models app.models These options cannot be combined with a manifest. Prefer adding one: the root app keeps its ledger keys, so existing history is not replayed. See also ¶ Configure a database CLI reference Define models

An application without a database still migrates the local SQLite default, but the server has none to use: declare database: settings.DatabaseSettings ( configure a database ). Outside a project ( --models / --dir ), step 3 is skipped. plan , status and apply print the chosen database and its source on standard error. Everything before the host (user and password) and the URL options are masked, and a URL that does not parse is not echoed: $ NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database) A relative SQLite path from the settings or the default is anchored beside hinoki.toml , so migrations run from a subdirectory use the same file; a relative SQLite URL given with --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL stays relative to the current directory. The server and hinoki settings do not anchor: they resolve the path, and read .env , from the directory they start in, so start them from the project root. A connection failure prints error: database: … and exits 1 . A --database URL is visible in the process list and shell history: do not put a password in it. An older scaffold's root app keeps unprefixed ledger keys; apps from hinoki app create use namespaced keys, so accounts/0001-initial.sql and billing/0001-initial.sql are distinct records. Run apply once per deployment, from one process, never from every worker's startup ( settings ). Concurrent runs are serialized: each file runs in one transaction under a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a MySQL/MariaDB migration lock or SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE , and reads the ledger inside it. On SQLite a second runner waits at most the busy timeout (5 seconds), then fails as locked.
docs.title: Which database

docs.text: hinoki migrations plan --check Exits 1 when any app has model changes without a migration file, destructive ones included, 0 otherwise, and 2 when the database whose dialect it plans for cannot be resolved ( which database ). It covers every app in dependency order ( plan billing --check : that app and its prerequisites), writes nothing and opens no connection. It imports every registered model and migration module and, unless --database or HINOKI_DATABASE_URL names the database, the project's application to read its database, so those imports must be safe in CI: HINOKI_DATABASE_URL = postgresql://ci@localhost/notes hinoki migrations plan --check status compares files with a live database instead.
docs.title: Check migration drift

docs.text: An app that references another app's models declares it in requires : # hinoki.toml [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [ "accounts" ] hinoki app create billing asks for requires ; hinoki app add NAME --models MODULE registers an existing package. Hinoki ships two such apps whose tables are optional: admin ( hinoki.admin.users.models , see the admin ) and ratelimit ( hinoki.ratelimit_store.models , the hinoki_rate_limits table of RateLimit ). Neither is applied unless you register it. Each app's tables belong only to its own migration state. The Tracker example has three such apps ( hinoki.toml lines 14-27 ): tasks requires members , and activity requires both, so apply runs them in that order.
docs.title: Apps and dependencies

docs.text: Before planning billing , the referenced table and primary key must already be recorded in accounts ' migration state with a compatible type; plan and review accounts first. It does not need to be applied yet. A parent table or referenced column is never dropped while another app's recorded state still refers to it, in plan , --dry-run and --check ; --allow-destructive does not override this, and an all-app command fails without partial output. Remove and apply the child reference first, then plan the parent teardown in a separate deployment. --dry-run without an app previews every app, possibly against a prerequisite's not-yet-planned models: do not apply in that order. It cannot take --name .
docs.title: Cross-app migration safety

docs.text: Backend Behaviour SQLite rebuilds a table when ALTER TABLE cannot express the change safely; holds the pool, suspends foreign-key enforcement on reserved connections, runs PRAGMA foreign_key_check before commit and rolls back on invalid references PostgreSQL each migration runs in a transaction MySQL DDL commits implicitly: a failed migration may be partially applied (Hinoki says so). Check the schema and status before retrying; keep a backup MariaDB separate backend on the MySQL wire protocol; JSON is a text alias decoded by typed fields MySQL and MariaDB foreign keys are table-level constraints. For databases migrated by an older Hinoki, check SHOW CREATE TABLE : MySQL ignores inline REFERENCES , and MariaDB varies by version. Add a missing constraint with a reviewed manual migration; applied migrations are never rewritten. Automatic removal of a foreign-key column is refused on these backends. State files record logical types; files from older versions that recorded SQLite or MySQL type names are normalized, so switching the planner's backend is not reported as a type change.
docs.title: Backend behaviour

docs.text: For the planned 0.1.x line, Hinoki keeps migration files generated by 0.1.0 readable and applicable across patch releases. New state sidecars carry "format_version": 1 ; recognized legacy sidecars created before that marker are treated as version 1, including the historical omission of the indexes list. Hinoki rejects malformed state and unknown format versions before writing a plan. Restore damaged files from version control; Hinoki does not rewrite them automatically. Once a SQL migration has been applied, keep its exact contents unchanged. The database ledger records a SHA-256 checksum of the SQL file, and status and apply report an error if an applied file has changed or disappeared. The checksum does not cover the state sidecar and is not a signature. apply checks and executes SQL files; it does not read state sidecars. plan reads and validates sidecars. Files that do not match Hinoki's numbered migration name pattern are not treated as migrations. Review and back up both files, test migrations against disposable data, and apply them explicitly. SQL transaction and rollback behavior depends on the backend; MySQL and MariaDB may leave DDL partially applied after a failure. Hinoki may make documented Python, CLI, settings, runtime or migration-format breaks in a later 0.y.0 while it is pre-1.0. Such changes must appear in release notes; if a later format stops reading version 1, the release must document an upgrade path. No fixed deprecation period or support for old framework versions is promised.
docs.title: Migration compatibility

docs.text: A many_to_many field adds its bridge model to the models module, right after its owner, so plan creates the bridge table in the same migration as the owner: the two foreign keys with ON DELETE rules, a unique pair and an index on the target column. Renaming the owner with @db.table before its first migration names the generated bridge <owner table>_<field> too. The planner does not plan table renames: changing the table of an already migrated owner drops the old bridge table and creates a new one (a destructive change plan refuses unless allowed), so move the data with a reviewed manual migration. An adopted bridge ( bridge="NoteLabel" ) is an ordinary model and migrates like one. Nothing runs against the database until you apply the migration.
docs.title: Bridge tables of many-to-many relations

docs.text: A project without hinoki.toml passes the models module and directory: hinoki migrations --dir app/migrations plan --models app.models These options cannot be combined with a manifest. Prefer adding one: the root app keeps its ledger keys, so existing history is not replayed.

docs.text: Lifecycle hooks ¶ A model can react to its own writes with before_save , before_create , after_create and after_save . Each is an ordinary method, def or async def , taking only self . A model without hooks pays nothing. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) import logging log = logging . getLogger ( __name__ ) class Invoice ( Model ): ... # fields as in Define models def before_save ( self ) -> None : if self . was_changed ( "reference" ): self . reference = self . reference . strip () . upper () async def after_create ( self ) -> None : self . after_commit ( lambda : log . info ( "invoice %s created" , self . id )) Order ¶ Write Hooks insert ( acreate , insert , asave of a new instance) before_save , before_create , write, after_create , after_save update ( asave of a loaded instance, aupdate_from ) before_save , write, after_save before_* hooks may change the values about to be written. after_* hooks see the stored row (generated keys, database defaults, @db.timestamps() ). An update with no changed column after before_save writes nothing and skips after_save . To extend an inherited hook, call super() . Instance state ¶ Member Meaning is_new True until the row is written or loaded; still True inside the hooks of an insert is_dirty True for a new instance or when a column differs from the stored row changes {column: Change(old, new)} ; a new instance lists every column with old=UNSET was_changed("reference") whether one column differs; an unknown name raises FieldError Stored values are refreshed after the after_* hooks, so changes still shows this write's changes while they run. Transactions and after_commit ¶ With any hook defined, the write runs in a transaction (a savepoint inside an open one): an exception in a hook rolls the write back and reaches the caller. A hook that opens its own db.atomic() fails with DatabaseError ( nested atomic scopes (savepoints) must be opened by the task that owns the transaction ) when a sync write runs inside a sync handler's with db.atomic(): ; from async code it nests as a savepoint. after_* hooks run before the commit. Work that must happen only after it goes through self.after_commit(callback) , a sync or async callable without arguments. Callbacks run in order after the outermost commit; a rollback drops them; an exception in one is logged and does not undo the commit. See transactions . Limits ¶ Hooks belong to instances: QuerySet.aupdate , adelete , Model.aupdate , aupdate_where and raw SQL do not run them. Events complete hooks for code that is not the model: Created , Updated and Deleted model events fire from the same writes (and from adelete ), with handlers registered per application instead of overridden on the class. after_commit on a model and db.after_commit keep working unchanged. Sync hooks run inline on the event loop: keep them short and use async def for I/O. is_new , is_dirty , changes , was_changed , after_commit and the four hook names are reserved field names. From a helper task of a transaction (the sync model methods of a sync handler), a hooked write joins that transaction; an error still rolls the whole transaction back. A hook assigned to the class after creation is used from the next write. Generated CRUD and the admin's create and edit forms save through the same methods, so hooks run there too; deletes run none ( CRUD ). See also ¶ Query and write rows Transactions

docs.text: Model options ¶ Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators, read top to bottom like action decorators. There is no nested class Meta ; only names stay class keywords. # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now # Customer is the model declared earlier in this file (see Models). @db . unique ( "customer_id" , "reference" ) @db . indexed ( "customer_id" , "created_at" ) @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) @db . timestamps () class Quote ( Model , label = "Quote" , plural = "Quotes" ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) customer_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Customer , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "quotes" ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) Option Form Effect single-column index field(index=True) CREATE INDEX on one column composite or foreign-key index @db.indexed("a", "b") CREATE INDEX on the columns, in order composite uniqueness @db.unique("a", "b", name=None) UNIQUE (a, b) , named with name= ; one column uses field(unique=True) default order @db.ordered_by("-created_at", "id") order of queries without order_by ; - is descending update timestamp @db.timestamps() refreshes updated_at on every ORM update soft delete @db.soft_delete("deleted_at") marks a nullable datetime column; delete() sets it and queries skip those rows ( soft delete ) status change time @db.track_status("status", changed_at="status_changed_at") records when the status column changes; decorators stack ( lifecycle utilities ) table name @db.table("quotes") (optional) replaces the derived <app>_<models> name app part of the name app="sales" (class keyword, optional) replaces <app> ; ignored with an explicit table display names label= , plural= (class keywords, optional) replace the derived singular and plural Every option decorator is reached through from hinoki import db . The same objects are also importable from hinoki.orm , which keeps older imports such as from hinoki.orm import unique, timestamps working. Composite uniqueness ¶ @db.unique("a", "b") adds UNIQUE (a, b) to the table; it needs two or more distinct columns. A single column uses field(unique=True) . @db . unique ( "customer_id" , "reference" , name = "uq_quotes_customer_reference" ) class Quote ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) customer_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Customer , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 ) Without name= the backend names the constraint. With it, the migration renders CONSTRAINT "uq_quotes_customer_reference" UNIQUE (...) on PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB, so the constraint keeps a stable, chosen name in the database. A name is a letter or underscore followed by up to 62 letters, digits or underscores, compared without case (as MySQL and MariaDB do). Planning refuses a name already used by another constraint, a table, or an index or foreign key that Hinoki names, among the planned models and, in a project with hinoki.toml , in every app. Only a table model can name a constraint: on an abstract model name= raises RegistrationError , because every table inheriting it would repeat the name. Unnamed constraints are inherited as usual. Changing the constraints or their names on an existing table is not planned on PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB (write that migration by hand). SQLite rebuilds the table; a rename alone is not destructive, while changed columns are reported as destructive because existing rows may violate them. Indexes ¶ Use field(index=True) for one ordinary column and @db.indexed(...) for a composite index. A foreign_key has no index= option: index it with @db.indexed("customer_id") , or with a composite index that starts with it. The optional HNK-DB-002 rule ( Models.require_foreign_key_index ) checks this. index= takes True or False ; a primary key or unique column is already indexed and refuses index=True . field(index=True) and @db.indexed("column") on the same column produce one index. Names are ix_<table>_<columns>_<digest> , cut to the backend limit (63 bytes on PostgreSQL, 64 on MySQL and MariaDB); the digest keeps indexed("a_b") and indexed("a", "b") apart. Adding or removing an index is a non-destructive migration. Default order ¶ @db.ordered_by(...) orders every query that has no order_by , lists and pages included. An explicit order_by replaces it; counts and bulk updates ignore it. End with a unique column ( "-id" ) so pages are stable. Update timestamps ¶ @db.timestamps() sets a declared, non-nullable updated_at: datetime on every ORM update statement, including asave and abulk_update . @db.timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) names another column or injects a clock. The parentheses are required: a bare @db.timestamps raises RegistrationError . See utilities . Names ¶ Leave the table name derived for new models. Pin it with @db.table(...) when the model has migration history and its class or module may change: a changed derived name is planned as a guarded drop and create, never a rename. Naming the table twice with different names ( @db.table twice, or with table= ) is an error naming both. Use label= / plural= for irregular or localized nouns. See table and display names . Rules for all options ¶ Column names are checked when the decorator runs; a typo fails at import with the model and the unknown names. Apply options before the model is used: the migration planner, the query layer and the admin read them from the class. Options of abstract bases are inherited; a decorator on the subclass replaces that kind of option. A table model does not pass its options to a subclass. Not yet Partial and expression indexes are not available. See also ¶ Define models Migrations

docs.text: Schemas from models ¶ A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model with @derive(Model, ...) . Response handlers convert rows explicitly with from_model . # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from hinoki import Schema , derive from .models import Invoice @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" ,)) class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): ... @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "id" , "reference" , "paid" )) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): ... @derive ( Invoice , exclude = ( "customer_id" ,)) class InvoiceDetail ( Schema ): customer_name : str @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" , "paid" ), partial = True ) class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): ... Option Effect @derive(Invoice) every column only=("a", "b") exactly these columns exclude=("a",) every column except these partial=True every selected field optional ( UNSET when absent) partial=("a",) only the named fields optional Column types, maximum lengths, defaults and nullability carry over. Annotations in the class body add or override fields; methods and checks are kept. Relations are not derived: declare nested shapes explicitly. Derivation takes every column by default, so use only or exclude when a column is private. These fail when the class is declared, with RegistrationError : unknown columns, a non-model, only together with exclude , an empty only=() , partial names outside the selection, a class that is not a Schema , and a second @derive . ( exclude=() selects every column.) Inherit from a derived schema ¶ A subclass inherits its base's fields; only and exclude cannot remove them. A derivation that would leave out a column the base declares fails closed: @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" ,)) # RegistrationError: inherited field 'id' class ReferenceOnly ( InvoiceOut ): ... Derive the narrower schema from Schema instead. A selection that keeps or widens the inherited columns is allowed. Convert rows ¶ Return a Schema , never a Model : # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup , errors from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceDetail , InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff ) def to_detail ( invoice : Invoice ) -> InvoiceDetail : return InvoiceDetail . from_model ( invoice , customer_name = invoice . customer . name ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceDetail ]: rows = await Invoice . all () . select_related ( "customer" ) . apaginate ( page ) return rows . map ( to_detail ) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} " , errors = ( errors . NotFound ,)) async def get_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceDetail : invoice = await Invoice . filter ( id = invoice_id ) . select_related ( "customer" ) . aget () return to_detail ( invoice ) from_model(row, **extra) reads the attributes the schema needs; extra fills fields the model lacks, such as customer_name . A missing attribute raises AttributeError . from_models(rows, **extra) converts a list; extra is shared by every row. For a page, Page.map(InvoiceOut.from_model) . Relations must be loaded first ( select_related ); nothing is fetched lazily. An invalid stored value (longer than the schema allows) is the server's fault: it becomes 500 internal_error , logged with the ValidationError , never a client 422. Returning a model A handler annotated with a Schema must return an instance of that Schema (converted explicitly with from_model(...) or an ORM projection). Returning a Model , a list or page of models, or a plain dict fails the response check with 500 internal_error (rolling back atomic=True transactions before sending the response), unless the action sets validate_response=False . A subclass instance is sent as the declared type: see Subclass instances below. See the response check . Subclass instances ¶ A response sends the type its annotation declares. An instance of a subclass ( Private(Public) ) shows the fields and @computed_field values of the declared class, never the fields the subclass added, in the JSON, XML and dump() outputs alike. An exact instance is sent unchanged. Narrowed, wherever the annotation names a Schema S : the top level and a Schema field: S , S | None , a union of S with other types, list[S] , list[S | None] , list[list[S]] , tuple[S, ...] , tuple[S, T] , dict[str, S] , Page[S] and CursorPage[S] (the top level only for the two pages), and the T field of a generic Envelope[S] ; the top level also takes a TypedDict of these and any combination of them; top-level dict , tuple and TypedDict shapes are narrowed too, with validate_response=False where the check refuses the annotation; the abstract forms Sequence[S] , MutableSequence[S] , Collection[S] , Iterable[S] (a returned list , tuple , set or frozenset ), set[S] , frozenset[S] , Set[S] , MutableSet[S] (a set holding a subclass instance is written as a list, in JSON and XML alike, in the set's iteration order—not deterministic for subclass members; the response check refuses a set annotation, so these take validate_response=False ), Mapping[str, S] and MutableMapping[str, S] (a returned dict ), and a PEP 695 type alias of any of these ( type Items = list[S] ; a generic one with its arguments substituted, type Box[T] = list[T] as Box[S] , type Ident[T] = T , type Pair[A, B] = dict[B, A] ). A @computed_field whose return annotation does not resolve fails closed with a RegistrationError at the first compile of the class ( validate , body decoding, dump , or OpenAPI generation; not at Hinoki(include=...) or hinoki check ); a tuple returned where list[S] is declared (with validate_response=False : the response check, on by default, answers 500 for it), and a lazy projection ( aget_as , aproject ) held anywhere above; the reply= of a WebSocket route, for send_json . A recursive TypedDict that holds a Schema at a position that requires response narrowing raises RegistrationError when the route is registered, including with validate_response=False . For example, this return declaration requires narrowing the item field at every depth: from __future__ import annotations from typing import TypedDict from hinoki import Schema class Item ( Schema ): id : int class Tree ( TypedDict ): item : Item children : list [ Tree ] Use a Schema for the recursive structure. A recursive TypedDict whose fields only hold plain values can still be registered. Written whole, because no declared schema decides them: a position typed Any or object ; a dataclass, and a Page inside another container ( dict[str, Page[S]] ); a declared class that overrides dump() : the declared class's own dump() runs on the instance restricted to the declared fields (a subclass's own dump() no longer decides); a value that is not a list , tuple , set , frozenset or dict where a collection is declared (a generator or iterator returned for Iterable[S] , a mapping that is not a dict ) is not walked, and the JSON and XML encoders refuse it: return the declared container; a list that a lazy projection already holds, changed afterwards with list.append(projection, subclass_instance) : the JSON encoder drops the appended item and the XML encoder writes the list storage as it is. A narrowed value keeps the wire names (aliases) of an exact one. Custom renderers that take objects ( consumes_objects = True , or a JSONRenderer subclass overriding prepare ) always receive a Narrowed view of the declared class—never the raw instance, even when the returned object is an exact instance of the declared class—so nested subclass instances in its fields cannot leak. docs.text: A Schema can take its fields and constraints from a Model with @derive(Model, ...) . Response handlers convert rows explicitly with from_model . # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from hinoki import Schema , derive from .models import Invoice @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" ,)) class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): ... @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "id" , "reference" , "paid" )) class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): ... @derive ( Invoice , exclude = ( "customer_id" ,)) class InvoiceDetail ( Schema ): customer_name : str @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" , "paid" ), partial = True ) class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): ... Option Effect @derive(Invoice) every column only=("a", "b") exactly these columns exclude=("a",) every column except these partial=True every selected field optional ( UNSET when absent) partial=("a",) only the named fields optional Column types, maximum lengths, defaults and nullability carry over. Annotations in the class body add or override fields; methods and checks are kept. Relations are not derived: declare nested shapes explicitly. Derivation takes every column by default, so use only or exclude when a column is private. These fail when the class is declared, with RegistrationError : unknown columns, a non-model, only together with exclude , an empty only=() , partial names outside the selection, a class that is not a Schema , and a second @derive . ( exclude=() selects every column.)

docs.text: A subclass inherits its base's fields; only and exclude cannot remove them. A derivation that would leave out a column the base declares fails closed: @derive ( Invoice , only = ( "reference" ,)) # RegistrationError: inherited field 'id' class ReferenceOnly ( InvoiceOut ): ... Derive the narrower schema from Schema instead. A selection that keeps or widens the inherited columns is allowed.

docs.text: Return a Schema , never a Model : # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup , errors from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceDetail , InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff ) def to_detail ( invoice : Invoice ) -> InvoiceDetail : return InvoiceDetail . from_model ( invoice , customer_name = invoice . customer . name ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceDetail ]: rows = await Invoice . all () . select_related ( "customer" ) . apaginate ( page ) return rows . map ( to_detail ) @invoices . get ( "/ {invoice_id} " , errors = ( errors . NotFound ,)) async def get_invoice ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> InvoiceDetail : invoice = await Invoice . filter ( id = invoice_id ) . select_related ( "customer" ) . aget () return to_detail ( invoice ) from_model(row, **extra) reads the attributes the schema needs; extra fills fields the model lacks, such as customer_name . A missing attribute raises AttributeError . from_models(rows, **extra) converts a list; extra is shared by every row. For a page, Page.map(InvoiceOut.from_model) . Relations must be loaded first ( select_related ); nothing is fetched lazily. An invalid stored value (longer than the schema allows) is the server's fault: it becomes 500 internal_error , logged with the ValidationError , never a client 422. Returning a model A handler annotated with a Schema must return an instance of that Schema (converted explicitly with from_model(...) or an ORM projection). Returning a Model , a list or page of models, or a plain dict fails the response check with 500 internal_error (rolling back atomic=True transactions before sending the response), unless the action sets validate_response=False . A subclass instance is sent as the declared type: see Subclass instances below. See the response check .

docs.text: Define models ¶ A Model maps a Python class to one table. Annotated fields are the columns; indexes, ordering and other options are decorators . A model never opens a connection on import and never loads a relation implicitly. # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Customer ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) email : str = field ( max_length = 254 , unique = True ) @db . indexed ( "customer_id" , "created_at" ) @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) customer_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Customer , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "invoices" ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 , unique = True ) paid : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) The tables are billing_customers and billing_invoices . Changing a model never changes the database: create the tables with hinoki migrations plan billing and hinoki migrations apply ( migrations ). Declare columns ¶ Declaration Column name: str required, not null note: str \| None = None nullable, optional in the constructor paid: bool = False default value id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4) the primary key email: str = field(max_length=254, unique=True) bounded text, unique created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now, index=True) factory default, single-column index customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(Customer, on_delete=...) a reference ( relations ) field() takes unique , index , max_length , default , default_factory , constraints and validators . The annotation gives the type and nullability. One primary key. pk() declares it; pass default or default_factory when the constructor may omit it. A nullable key ( int | None ) raises RegistrationError when the class is defined. Keyword-only constructor. Invoice(reference="INV-1", customer_id=c.id) . Indexes. field(index=True) indexes one column; it cannot be combined with unique=True or pk() , which are already indexed. A foreign_key has no index= option: index it with @db.indexed(...) , or a composite index that starts with it, as Invoice does ( model options ). Composite uniqueness is @db.unique("a", "b") ; there is no nested class Meta . Column types ¶ Python type Stored as Read back as str , int , float , bool the backend's text, integer, float and boolean types the same type UUID , datetime native on PostgreSQL; text on SQLite UUID , datetime dict[...] , list[...] JSON (JSON text on SQLite, text alias on MariaDB) decoded by the annotation bytes BYTEA on PostgreSQL, blob on SQLite bytes date , time ISO text ( time with microseconds, no timezone) date , time timedelta whole microseconds, bigint timedelta Enum subclass its value: bigint when every value is an integer, else text the member IPv4Address , IPv6Address , IPv4Network , IPv6Network text the ipaddress object; writes accept only that class Decimal exact, per backend (below) Decimal A stored value that does not read back as its annotation raises FieldError . date and timedelta compare and order by value. A column type without a SQL type (a set, tuple, Literal , Path , Secret , Any , object , or a union of several types such as int | str ) raises RegistrationError when the class is defined. Annotated[str, Field(max_length=32)] sizes the column like field(max_length=32) . SQLite's contains folds ASCII case only. Decimal columns ¶ Backend Column Filters and ordering PostgreSQL numeric = , ne , in , isnull , gt , gte , lt , lte , order_by MySQL, MariaDB decimal(65,30) the same; read back with scale 30 ( Decimal("1.5") returns as Decimal("1.500…0") , equal in value) SQLite text (its exact spelling) = , ne , in , isnull only; 12.3 and 12.30 differ; range filters and order_by raise FieldError # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) from decimal import Decimal class Price ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) amount : Decimal # inside an async operation # every backend cheap = await Price . filter ( amount = Decimal ( "9.99" )) # not SQLite ordered = await Price . filter ( amount__gte = Decimal ( "5" )) . order_by ( "amount" ) A filter value is a Decimal , an int or a numeric string; a float , a bool , NaN , an infinity or contains raises FieldError . decimal(65,30) bounds MySQL and MariaDB to 35 digits before the point; PostgreSQL numeric is unbounded. A table that already stores a Decimal as text on PostgreSQL or MySQL needs a reviewed migration that changes the column type. A generated CRUD list whose @db.ordered_by names a Decimal column takes the Python path on SQLite, where that ordering is refused. Table and display names ¶ Hinoki derives the table name <app>_<models> and display names from the class. Model Module Table Labels Invoice notes.apps.billing.models billing_invoices Invoice / Invoices LineItem notes.apps.billing.models billing_line_items Line item / Line items Note notes.models or notes.models.note notes_notes Note / Notes APIKey notes.models notes_api_keys API key / API keys The app is the package that holds the models module; a module without a models segment uses its own last name. The plural is a small English rule: consonant + y → ies ; s , x , z , ch , sh → es ; otherwise s . It does not know irregular nouns ( Person → persons ). Override Form app part of the name class Invoice(Model, app="accounts") whole table name (never prefixed) @db.table("invoices") display names class Person(Model, label="Person", plural="People") Pin the table name with @db.table(...) when a model already has migration history and you rename the class or move its module: a changed derived name is planned as a drop and a create, which the destructive-migration guard stops; it is never a rename. The optional HNK-DB-001 rule ( Models.require_explicit_table ) requires every matching model to pin it. Names must be portable ASCII of at most 63 characters. A derived name that is rejected ( sqlite_… , hinoki_migrations , non-ASCII such as class Café ) does not stop the class from being defined: @db.table("cafes") can still name it. Without one, the error is raised when the model is first used (query, write, migration plan, project or admin registration, or a foreign key to it). Model field constraints and validators ¶ field() can also check values before every ORM write. Use constraints=Field(...) for built-in checks and validators=(...) for synchronous application rules: # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) from hinoki import Field def no_padding ( value : str ) -> None : if value != value . strip (): raise ValueError ( "surrounding whitespace is not allowed" ) class Product ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) sku : str = field ( max_length = 32 , constraints = Field ( min_length = 3 , pattern = r "[A-Z0-9-]+" ) ) weight_kg : float = field ( constraints = Field ( gt = 0 )) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 , validators = ( no_padding ,)) When. Immediately before inserts and ORM updates, filtered bulk updates included; never on construction, assignment or reads. Invalid declarations fail when the class is created. Checks. String and list lengths, patterns, membership, numeric bounds on int , float and Decimal (a NaN or infinite Decimal is refused), and multiple_of on int and Decimal . strip , lower and upper normalize a str before the other checks, and the normalized text is what is written (an instance being saved gets it too). A JSON column ( dict[...] , list[dict[...]] ) takes no built-in checks; validators still run on it. Failure. ModelValidationError , before any SQL, with details holding each field's path , code and message . In a request it becomes the standard 422 response; the admin shows the messages. Validators are synchronous, raise ValueError to refuse, perform no I/O and do not change the value. Rules about other rows, permissions or current state belong in an operation. These checks protect CLI, admin and direct ORM writes; a Schema still validates HTTP input first ( validate input ). Database constraints remain authoritative. Share fields: abstract models and mixins ¶ An abstract model has no table: it is not migrated, cannot be queried and only exists to be subclassed. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) class Keyed ( Model , abstract = True ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) @db . timestamps () @db . ordered_by ( "-updated_at" ) class Tracked ( Model , abstract = True ): created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now , index = True ) class Article ( Keyed , Tracked ): title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) Article has created_at , updated_at , id and title , is ordered by -updated_at , indexes updated_at and refreshes it on every update. Tracked.all() raises ModelError . abstract=True is not inherited; an abstract model needs no primary key, a table model needs exactly one, its own or inherited. Options from abstract bases are inherited: all @db.unique and @db.indexed , the order and timestamp column of the first base that sets one, a soft-delete option, and status tracks. A decorator on the subclass replaces that kind of option. A field(index=True) index belongs to its column and is dropped when a subclass redeclares the column without it. Constraint names are not inherited: an abstract model cannot use @db.unique(..., name=...) . Plain mixins (non-model classes) contribute annotated fields and methods; ClassVar annotations are not fields. Type checkers do not see mixin fields as constructor arguments: prefer an abstract model. Conflicting types. Two bases giving one field different types are refused unless the class redeclares the field. Subclassing a table model copies its columns into a separate, unrelated table; no join, no shared rows, no inherited options. Column order follows dataclass rules: model bases (last listed first), then mixins, then the class's own fields. A foreign key in an abstract model needs a per-subclass reverse name; see relations . Lifecycle utilities ¶ UUIDModel , TimestampedModel and SoftDeleteModel are composable abstract bases. Their columns remain ordinary typed fields and are included in table_state() and migration plans. UUIDModel supplies a UUIDv4 primary key ( id: UUID = uuid_pk() ); TimestampedModel supplies created_at and updated_at ; SoftDeleteModel supplies an indexed nullable deleted_at column. For configurable UUID primary keys, use uuid_pk() : it defaults to UUIDv4, accepts version=7 (time-ordered RFC 9562 UUIDv7 generated in Rust, also available as hinoki.orm.uuid7 / hinoki.utils.uuid7 ), or any custom default_factory . For opaque URL-safe identifiers or share codes, use urlsafe_token(nbytes=32, unique=True) — values are generated by Rust's CSPRNG ( hinoki.core.make_token ) and validated against ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$ . For authentication secrets (password reset tokens, API keys, sessions), store a hash instead of a raw token column. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import ( Model , SoftDeleteModel , TimestampedModel , UUIDModel , field , urlsafe_token , uuid_pk , ) from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Document ( UUIDModel , TimestampedModel , SoftDeleteModel ): title : str share_token : str = urlsafe_token () @db . track_status ( "status" , changed_at = "status_changed_at" ) class Order ( Model ): id : UUID = uuid_pk ( version = 7 ) status : str = "draft" status_changed_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) @db.soft_delete(column="archived_at", clock=...) and @db.track_status(field="state", changed_at="state_changed_at", clock=...) can use custom declared columns. Decorators validate columns and types when the model is registered; tracked status decorators can be stacked. The supplied clock is used for managed timestamps, otherwise the model's @db.timestamps(clock=...) clock is used. On a soft-delete model, all() , filter() and model lookups see live rows only. with_deleted() includes every row and only_deleted() selects deleted rows. Instance asoft_delete() / soft_delete() and arestore() / restore() run normal save hooks. is_deleted reports the instance state. These methods are idempotent; unsaved instances are refused. previous(name) returns the stored value (or UNSET on a new instance), and changed_fields lists fields that differ from the last snapshot. Status tracking updates its timestamp only when an instance save actually changes the tracked value; an explicit timestamp value is preserved. A bulk QuerySet.aupdate() is a single SQL statement and cannot compare old values, so it updates the timestamp whenever the tracked field is included in values , even when the supplied status equals the current value. Soft deletion is an UPDATE ; database ON DELETE CASCADE and RESTRICT actions apply only to physical ahard_delete() calls. Ordinary unique=True and @db.unique(...) constraints continue to include soft-deleted rows. A partial unique index for live rows needs a custom SQL migration. Relate models through a link table ¶ many_to_many(...) is a class attribute, not a column: the model keeps its own columns and Hinoki generates (or adopts) a bridge model that holds the links. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) class Label ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 40 ) class Memo ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) labels : ClassVar [ ManyToMany [ Label ]] = many_to_many ( Label , related_name = "memos" ) Memo.__bridges__ lists the generated bridge model, MemoLabels on the table <memo table>_labels ; @db.table on Memo names the bridge after the new table (set it before the first migration: later table changes are not planned as renames, see migrations ). Declaration, link writes, scopes and limits are in relations . See also ¶ Model options Query and write rows Relations Migrations

docs.text: Hinoki derives the table name <app>_<models> and display names from the class. Model Module Table Labels Invoice notes.apps.billing.models billing_invoices Invoice / Invoices LineItem notes.apps.billing.models billing_line_items Line item / Line items Note notes.models or notes.models.note notes_notes Note / Notes APIKey notes.models notes_api_keys API key / API keys The app is the package that holds the models module; a module without a models segment uses its own last name. The plural is a small English rule: consonant + y → ies ; s , x , z , ch , sh → es ; otherwise s . It does not know irregular nouns ( Person → persons ). Override Form app part of the name class Invoice(Model, app="accounts") whole table name (never prefixed) @db.table("invoices") display names class Person(Model, label="Person", plural="People") Pin the table name with @db.table(...) when a model already has migration history and you rename the class or move its module: a changed derived name is planned as a drop and a create, which the destructive-migration guard stops; it is never a rename. The optional HNK-DB-001 rule ( Models.require_explicit_table ) requires every matching model to pin it. Names must be portable ASCII of at most 63 characters. A derived name that is rejected ( sqlite_… , hinoki_migrations , non-ASCII such as class Café ) does not stop the class from being defined: @db.table("cafes") can still name it. Without one, the error is raised when the model is first used (query, write, migration plan, project or admin registration, or a foreign key to it).
