docs.text: field() can also check values before every ORM write. Use constraints=Field(...) for built-in checks and validators=(...) for synchronous application rules: # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) from hinoki import Field def no_padding ( value : str ) -> None : if value != value . strip (): raise ValueError ( "surrounding whitespace is not allowed" ) class Product ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) sku : str = field ( max_length = 32 , constraints = Field ( min_length = 3 , pattern = r "[A-Z0-9-]+" ) ) weight_kg : float = field ( constraints = Field ( gt = 0 )) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 , validators = ( no_padding ,)) When. Immediately before inserts and ORM updates, filtered bulk updates included; never on construction, assignment or reads. Invalid declarations fail when the class is created. Checks. String and list lengths, patterns, membership, numeric bounds on int , float and Decimal (a NaN or infinite Decimal is refused), and multiple_of on int and Decimal . strip , lower and upper normalize a str before the other checks, and the normalized text is what is written (an instance being saved gets it too). A JSON column ( dict[...] , list[dict[...]] ) takes no built-in checks; validators still run on it. Failure. ModelValidationError , before any SQL, with details holding each field's path , code and message . In a request it becomes the standard 422 response; the admin shows the messages. Validators are synchronous, raise ValueError to refuse, perform no I/O and do not change the value. Rules about other rows, permissions or current state belong in an operation. These checks protect CLI, admin and direct ORM writes; a Schema still validates HTTP input first ( validate input ). Database constraints remain authoritative.
docs.title: Model field constraints and validators

docs.text: An abstract model has no table: it is not migrated, cannot be queried and only exists to be subclassed. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) class Keyed ( Model , abstract = True ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) @db . timestamps () @db . ordered_by ( "-updated_at" ) class Tracked ( Model , abstract = True ): created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now , index = True ) class Article ( Keyed , Tracked ): title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) Article has created_at , updated_at , id and title , is ordered by -updated_at , indexes updated_at and refreshes it on every update. Tracked.all() raises ModelError . abstract=True is not inherited; an abstract model needs no primary key, a table model needs exactly one, its own or inherited. Options from abstract bases are inherited: all @db.unique and @db.indexed , the order and timestamp column of the first base that sets one, a soft-delete option, and status tracks. A decorator on the subclass replaces that kind of option. A field(index=True) index belongs to its column and is dropped when a subclass redeclares the column without it. Constraint names are not inherited: an abstract model cannot use @db.unique(..., name=...) . Plain mixins (non-model classes) contribute annotated fields and methods; ClassVar annotations are not fields. Type checkers do not see mixin fields as constructor arguments: prefer an abstract model. Conflicting types. Two bases giving one field different types are refused unless the class redeclares the field. Subclassing a table model copies its columns into a separate, unrelated table; no join, no shared rows, no inherited options. Column order follows dataclass rules: model bases (last listed first), then mixins, then the class's own fields. A foreign key in an abstract model needs a per-subclass reverse name; see relations .
docs.title: Share fields: abstract models and mixins

docs.text: UUIDModel , TimestampedModel and SoftDeleteModel are composable abstract bases. Their columns remain ordinary typed fields and are included in table_state() and migration plans. UUIDModel supplies a UUIDv4 primary key ( id: UUID = uuid_pk() ); TimestampedModel supplies created_at and updated_at ; SoftDeleteModel supplies an indexed nullable deleted_at column. For configurable UUID primary keys, use uuid_pk() : it defaults to UUIDv4, accepts version=7 (time-ordered RFC 9562 UUIDv7 generated in Rust, also available as hinoki.orm.uuid7 / hinoki.utils.uuid7 ), or any custom default_factory . For opaque URL-safe identifiers or share codes, use urlsafe_token(nbytes=32, unique=True) — values are generated by Rust's CSPRNG ( hinoki.core.make_token ) and validated against ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$ . For authentication secrets (password reset tokens, API keys, sessions), store a hash instead of a raw token column. from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import ( Model , SoftDeleteModel , TimestampedModel , UUIDModel , field , urlsafe_token , uuid_pk , ) from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Document ( UUIDModel , TimestampedModel , SoftDeleteModel ): title : str share_token : str = urlsafe_token () @db . track_status ( "status" , changed_at = "status_changed_at" ) class Order ( Model ): id : UUID = uuid_pk ( version = 7 ) status : str = "draft" status_changed_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) @db.soft_delete(column="archived_at", clock=...) and @db.track_status(field="state", changed_at="state_changed_at", clock=...) can use custom declared columns. Decorators validate columns and types when the model is registered; tracked status decorators can be stacked. The supplied clock is used for managed timestamps, otherwise the model's @db.timestamps(clock=...) clock is used. On a soft-delete model, all() , filter() and model lookups see live rows only. with_deleted() includes every row and only_deleted() selects deleted rows. Instance asoft_delete() / soft_delete() and arestore() / restore() run normal save hooks. is_deleted reports the instance state. These methods are idempotent; unsaved instances are refused. previous(name) returns the stored value (or UNSET on a new instance), and changed_fields lists fields that differ from the last snapshot. Status tracking updates its timestamp only when an instance save actually changes the tracked value; an explicit timestamp value is preserved. A bulk QuerySet.aupdate() is a single SQL statement and cannot compare old values, so it updates the timestamp whenever the tracked field is included in values , even when the supplied status equals the current value. Soft deletion is an UPDATE ; database ON DELETE CASCADE and RESTRICT actions apply only to physical ahard_delete() calls. Ordinary unique=True and @db.unique(...) constraints continue to include soft-deleted rows. A partial unique index for live rows needs a custom SQL migration.
docs.title: Lifecycle utilities

docs.text: many_to_many(...) is a class attribute, not a column: the model keeps its own columns and Hinoki generates (or adopts) a bridge model that holds the links. # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) class Label ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 40 ) class Memo ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) labels : ClassVar [ ManyToMany [ Label ]] = many_to_many ( Label , related_name = "memos" ) Memo.__bridges__ lists the generated bridge model, MemoLabels on the table <memo table>_labels ; @db.table on Memo names the bridge after the new table (set it before the first migration: later table changes are not planned as renames, see migrations ). Declaration, link writes, scopes and limits are in relations .

docs.text: Own resources with modules ¶ A module owns something that lives as long as a worker or a command run: a connection pool, a client, a thread pool. It opens the resource at startup, provides it to the rest of the application and closes it when the run ends. Nothing is opened at import time. # notes/passwords.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from hinoki import Module , ModuleContext from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher class Passwords ( Module ): name = "passwords" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( self , ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ]: hasher = PasswordHasher () ctx . provide ( PasswordHasher , hasher ) try : yield finally : hasher . close () Install it on the application. The rules come from hinoki.toml , so the call names only what is specific to this app: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from notes.passwords import Passwords from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , title = "Notes" , modules = [ Passwords ()], ) Each worker runs lifespan up to yield before it answers requests, and the finally block when it stops, even if a later module fails to start. Use what a module provides ¶ ctx.provide(Type, value) registers a value under its type; ctx.get(Type) returns it (or raises LookupError ) and ctx.find(Type) returns None instead. The value is reachable from: Where How Another module's lifespan ctx.get(PasswordHasher) , with requires = (Passwords,) A startup or shutdown hook ctx.get(PasswordHasher) A management command context.get(PasswordHasher) , with requires = (Passwords,) A rate-limit policy context.resource(PasswordHasher) # notes/commands.py from argparse import ArgumentParser , Namespace from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher from hinoki.management import Command , CommandContext from notes.passwords import Passwords class HashPassword ( Command ): name = "hash-password" help = "print the Argon2id hash of a password" requires = ( Passwords ,) def add_arguments ( self , parser : ArgumentParser ) -> None : parser . add_argument ( "password" ) async def handle ( self , context : CommandContext , args : Namespace ) -> None : print ( await context . get ( PasswordHasher ) . hash ( args . password )) With commands=[HashPassword] on the application, hinoki manage hash-password s3cret starts only Passwords (and what it requires), runs the command and closes it. Request handlers can receive a module-provided value as a parameter when its type inherits Resource . Model methods also find the worker's Database through the ORM context. Ordinary module values remain available through ModuleContext in lifespans, hooks and commands, and through the policy context where supported. Inject a worker resource into a handler ¶ Declare a concrete Resource type, provide its instance from a module, then use that type as a handler parameter. Hinoki resolves the annotation when routes are registered and injects the worker's instance for each request: from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from hinoki import Hinoki , Module , ModuleContext , Resource , http class Mailer ( Resource ): async def send ( self , address : str , subject : str ) -> None : ... class MailerModule ( Module ): name = "mailer" @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan ( self , ctx : ModuleContext ) -> AsyncIterator [ None ]: mailer = Mailer () ctx . provide ( Mailer , mailer ) yield @http . post ( "/welcome" ) async def welcome ( email : str , mailer : Mailer ) -> dict [ str , str ]: await mailer . send ( email , "Welcome" ) return { "status" : "sent" } app = Hinoki ( include = [ welcome ], modules = [ MailerModule ()]) The same annotation works on function handlers, synchronous def handlers and methods on an API class. A resource parameter does not cause Hinoki to build a Request ; declare request: Request only when the handler needs request data. Resource parameters are not client inputs, so they do not appear in the OpenAPI document or MCP tool schema. Kiso also leaves them out of the Rust route input list; a route can keep its native route specification when its other inputs and handler behavior meet the native-path requirements. Resources are mandatory worker contracts. A default value, a name that collides with a {path} parameter, or two parameters requesting the same resource type raises RegistrationError during registration. After all modules start and before startup hooks run, Hinoki checks every required type with ModuleContext.get . A missing provider fails startup with the route and type in the error; the worker does not become ready. The database module ¶ A database: settings.DatabaseSettings field on your settings class is enough: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule (from hinoki.db ) before any declared module, so a module with requires = (DatabaseModule,) can call ctx.get(Database) in its lifespan. Declaring DatabaseModule , or a subclass of it, in modules= replaces the automatic one; modules that require DatabaseModule still start after it. See database connection ownership . The email module ¶ An email: settings.EmailSettings field installs EmailModule (from hinoki.mail ) the same way: one Mailer per worker, opened in the lifespan and closed at shutdown, available as ctx.get(Mailer) , to mail.send(...) in handlers and hooks, and to commands that declare requires = (EmailModule,) . Declaring EmailModule in modules= replaces the automatic one. See send email . Declare modules ¶ modules= accepts instances and classes. An instance is the plain choice; a class is built with its from_settings(settings) classmethod, which you override to read your settings (the default raises TypeError and says so). requires decides the order: dependencies start first and stop last. An empty or duplicate name , a missing requirement, a cycle, or a type provided twice fails startup with ModuleGraphError . A module whose class extends a required class satisfies that requirement. Keep lifespan bounded (it shares lifecycle.startup_timeout ), fail fast when a required service is unavailable, and close what you own in finally . Startup and shutdown hooks ¶ For an action at the edge of a worker's life that owns no resource, such as warming a cache, logging the build or flushing a counter, list functions on the application instead of writing a module ( ProjectSettings here declares a database field, so the database module is installed): # notes/main.py import logging from hinoki import Hinoki , ModuleContext from hinoki.db import Database from notes.settings import ProjectSettings log = logging . getLogger ( "notes" ) async def warm_cache ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : await ctx . get ( Database ) . fetch ( "SELECT 1" ) def say_goodbye ( ctx : ModuleContext ) -> None : log . info ( "worker stopping" ) app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , on_startup = [ warm_cache ], on_shutdown = [ say_goodbye ] ) A hook takes the worker's ModuleContext ( ctx.settings , ctx.get(Type) , ctx.tasks ). It is async def , or a plain def that runs on the bounded sync executor like a sync handler. Model methods reach the worker's database inside a hook as they do inside a request. Pass hooks as a list or tuple when constructing Hinoki ; the app's on_startup and on_shutdown tuples are read-only. Hooks must be callables, not async generators, and must return None . A plain def may instead return an awaitable, which Hinoki awaits; use async def when the hook needs to await work directly. Startup hooks Shutdown hooks Run Once per worker, after every module has started, in the listed order Once per worker, before background tasks, the sync executor and the modules are closed, in the listed order Time limit Share lifecycle.startup_timeout with the modules Each has its own lifecycle.shutdown_timeout Requests Answered 503 not_ready until the last hook returns Answered 503 not_ready from the moment shutdown begins A hook fails or times out Startup fails: later hooks do not run, no shutdown hook runs, the modules already started are closed, and the server is told that startup failed. The log has the traceback; the message names the hook ( startup hook 'warm_cache' failed to start: TimeoutError ) It is logged and reported as a shutdown error; the remaining hooks and the module cleanup still run Shutdown hooks run only after a startup that completed, and a shutdown hook is not the finally of a startup hook. Use this rule to choose: a resource you own is a module (its lifespan closes it even when a later step of startup fails); an action is a hook . A plain def hook that is still running when its time limit passes cannot be interrupted; it keeps its executor thread until it returns. Hooks run where the application serves requests: under hinoki dev / serve and any ASGI server, on the first request of each WSGI worker, and in the test clients . hinoki manage commands, check , routes and migrations do not run them. Scripts outside the server ¶ For app maintenance tasks, declare a management command and list its required module classes in Command.requires . Hinoki starts only those modules and their dependencies for one command run, so a database module is opened and closed without starting the HTTP server or unrelated modules. Standalone scripts outside Hinoki's server or management-command runner have no module lifespan. Open their own Database and close it explicitly; do not import a module-global pool. The blog seed script demonstrates this pattern. Errors and edge cases ¶ ctx.get for a type nobody provided raises LookupError: <Type> was not provided ; declare the providing module in requires . A module class without from_settings in modules= fails at construction: pass an instance instead. hinoki check , routes and migrations do not start modules or run hooks. See also ¶ Settings : where a module reads its configuration. Command line : running management commands. Sync and async : where sync hooks run.

docs.text: Create a project ¶ hinoki new creates a working project: an application with a health route, typed settings, architecture rules, a test and instructions for AI agents. From the Hinoki checkout: uv run hinoki new Answer the questions ¶ In a terminal, hinoki new asks for everything the command line leaves out: Question Answers Default Project name lower-case letters and digits, single underscores between words, starting with a letter none Parent directory any path . (here) Database none ; sqlite (local file in .hinoki/ ); postgresql (also writes .env.example ) none Server kiso (Hinoki's own Rust server: native handler lane, access log); granian (general-purpose ASGI server: runs any ASGI app) kiso Agent instructions and MCP config? yes / no yes Agent skills? yes / no no Initialize a git repository? yes / no yes Install dependencies (uv sync)? yes / no yes Create an app now? yes / no yes App name (only after yes) the same rule as the project name; an invalid name is asked again core Each answer collapses into a summary line. When the files are written, the command lists the key ones, creates the app you named with the same code as hinoki app create (and registers it in hinoki.toml ), runs git init and uv sync with a timer, and ends with the next commands to type. When no app was created, the summary says how to add one. Nothing is written until the last answer, so Ctrl-C, Esc or end of input cancels cleanly (exit 130). Create a project without questions ¶ Every question has a flag. --no-input never asks and uses the defaults for what is missing, which suits scripts and CI (without a terminal no question is asked either): uv run hinoki new notes --no-input --database sqlite --git --install Option Effect NAME the package name; required with --no-input --dir PATH parent directory; the project is PATH/NAME --database none\|sqlite\|postgresql see Choose a database --server kiso\|granian see Choose a server --agent-files / --no-agent-files write AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json --skills / --no-skills also write the agent skills under .claude/skills --git / --no-git run git init ; no commit is made. Without a prompt: off --install / --no-install run uv sync . Without a prompt: off --app NAME also create this app and register it, without asking. The name is checked before anything is written --no-app create no app and do not ask about one; the two flags exclude each other --hinoki SOURCE where the project installs Hinoki from; see below What you get ¶ notes/ ├── hinoki.toml project registry: application, routes, apps ├── hinoki-rules.toml rule waivers (an example, commented out) ├── pyproject.toml dependencies, pytest, Ruff ├── README.md ├── AGENTS.md agent instructions (with CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json) ├── notes/ │ ├── main.py the application │ ├── api.py the health endpoint │ ├── routes.py the routes hinoki.toml points to │ ├── settings.py typed settings (NOTES_ variables and .env) │ └── rules.py architecture rules └── tests/ └── healthtest.py one test, no database needed hinoki.toml names the application, so project commands find it on their own. notes/main.py creates Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...) and automatically loads [project] routes ( notes/routes.py ), where you mount exposed apps with Mount("/<name>", ...) . The rules list in the same table is how the application gets notes/rules.py (see which rules run ). # hinoki.toml [project] application = "notes.main:app" routes = "notes.routes:routes" rules = [ "notes.rules:project_rules" ] The project package holds no models and registers no app. Models live in apps: The last question of hinoki new (or --app billing ) creates the first one; uv run hinoki app create billing adds more later. Either way it writes notes/apps/billing/ and adds the [[apps]] entry for it ( hinoki app create ). Run it ¶ cd notes uv run pytest uv run hinoki dev Run uv sync first if you answered no to installing. The application answers on http://127.0.0.1:8000/health , with its documentation at /docs . Choose a database ¶ sqlite and postgresql add one field to notes/settings.py : class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings Its value comes from NOTES_DATABASE__<FIELD> variables (two underscores between the group and the field) in the environment or in .env ; keep .env out of git. With no value set it is the SQLite file .hinoki/local.sqlite3 . postgresql also writes .env.example with a placeholder URL; copy it to .env and fill it in: # .env.example NOTES_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/notes none declares no field, and a request that queries a model fails with no database is active . Add the field above when you add models. Configure a database lists the URL forms and the connection fields. No database is created or contacted. Create the tables with hinoki migrations apply once you have models. Choose a server ¶ kiso needs no configuration. granian writes settings.toml with [server] server = "granian" , which the settings class reads. Either way, NOTES_SERVER__SERVER and --server on dev and serve override the choice. Serve an application compares the two. Where Hinoki comes from ¶ This repository's pre-alpha Hinoki framework (package hinoki-api ) is not published on PyPI yet; the hinoki name belongs to an unrelated legacy package. The generated pyproject.toml therefore names this repository as the source under [tool.uv.sources] : Given Source written --hinoki /path/to/checkout that checkout, editable --hinoki https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki@REV (or git+https://... ) that repository, pinned to REV when given nothing, running from a source checkout the checkout you ran it from nothing, any other installation the public repository, default branch Checkout paths and Git source values are escaped as TOML strings. How it looks in a terminal ¶ On a colour, UTF-8 terminal (macOS and Linux) the prompts sit on a guide rail and answer to keys: type a name (backspace edits, Ctrl-U clears), move through the database and server lists with ↑/↓ or pick one by number, and switch yes/no with ←/→ or y / n ; Enter confirms. Each answered prompt collapses into one summary line. The run then lists the key files it created, times git init and uv sync (with a spinner while they run) and ends with the next commands. Every colour terminal shows the same banner: a branch ( ╭─ , │ , ╰─ ) titled Hinoki with the tagline and the version, then the Python version and the documentation and source addresses; hinoki app create shows the same banner. Elsewhere the prompts are numbered lists and [Y/n] questions answered with Enter. Output that is piped, NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb give plain ASCII with no escape sequences. HINOKI_ANIMATE=0 (or CI ) turns off the tagline animation and the spinner. When the terminal reports a light background through COLORFGBG , darker shades of the same colours are used. Ctrl-C or Esc cancels before anything is written (exit status 130); so does the end of input. Errors and edge cases ¶ The name must be lower-case letters and digits, with single underscores between words ( my_shop , api_v1 ), starting with a letter, and not hinoki , a Python keyword or a standard-library module such as json , which would shadow imports in the project. A refused name is asked again; with --no-input the command exits 2. An app name follows the same rule. A refused name is asked again; --app with a bad name exits 2 before anything is written. If the project is written but the app cannot be created, the error is printed, the project stays and the exit status is 2. PATH/NAME must not exist or must be empty; nothing is overwritten. git or uv missing or failing prints a warning and keeps the project. Nothing else is installed or run. See also ¶ Installation Quick start Command line Test an application

docs.text: hinoki new creates a working project: an application with a health route, typed settings, architecture rules, a test and instructions for AI agents. From the Hinoki checkout: uv run hinoki new
docs.title: Create a project

docs.text: In a terminal, hinoki new asks for everything the command line leaves out: Question Answers Default Project name lower-case letters and digits, single underscores between words, starting with a letter none Parent directory any path . (here) Database none ; sqlite (local file in .hinoki/ ); postgresql (also writes .env.example ) none Server kiso (Hinoki's own Rust server: native handler lane, access log); granian (general-purpose ASGI server: runs any ASGI app) kiso Agent instructions and MCP config? yes / no yes Agent skills? yes / no no Initialize a git repository? yes / no yes Install dependencies (uv sync)? yes / no yes Create an app now? yes / no yes App name (only after yes) the same rule as the project name; an invalid name is asked again core Each answer collapses into a summary line. When the files are written, the command lists the key ones, creates the app you named with the same code as hinoki app create (and registers it in hinoki.toml ), runs git init and uv sync with a timer, and ends with the next commands to type. When no app was created, the summary says how to add one. Nothing is written until the last answer, so Ctrl-C, Esc or end of input cancels cleanly (exit 130).

docs.text: Every question has a flag. --no-input never asks and uses the defaults for what is missing, which suits scripts and CI (without a terminal no question is asked either): uv run hinoki new notes --no-input --database sqlite --git --install Option Effect NAME the package name; required with --no-input --dir PATH parent directory; the project is PATH/NAME --database none\|sqlite\|postgresql see Choose a database --server kiso\|granian see Choose a server --agent-files / --no-agent-files write AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json --skills / --no-skills also write the agent skills under .claude/skills --git / --no-git run git init ; no commit is made. Without a prompt: off --install / --no-install run uv sync . Without a prompt: off --app NAME also create this app and register it, without asking. The name is checked before anything is written --no-app create no app and do not ask about one; the two flags exclude each other --hinoki SOURCE where the project installs Hinoki from; see below

Either way it writes notes/apps/billing/ and adds the [[apps]] entry for it ( hinoki app create ).

docs.text: OpenAPI document ¶ Hinoki.openapi() builds an OpenAPI 3.2 document from the routes registered with the app (3.1 on request, see the document version ). Paths, parameters, request bodies, response schemas, declared errors and supported authentication schemes come from the action declarations and type annotations. Generate the document from the application without starting a server: hinoki openapi --output openapi.json hinoki openapi --check openapi.json hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json --output writes stable, sorted JSON. --check compares parsed JSON with a committed file, so whitespace-only changes do not report drift. --breaking-against compares with an earlier document (the released one) and prints one breaking: … line per change that would break an existing client. The three options are exclusive. The command opens no database and works even when openapi_url is disabled. See inspect an application for output and exit status. Serve the document and viewers ¶ All three URLs are disabled by default. Set openapi_url to serve JSON; add docs_url for the bundled Swagger UI or redoc_url for ReDoc. A project created with hinoki new already sets the first two: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , redoc_url = "/redoc" , ) The corresponding docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url and docs.redoc_url settings provide the same defaults. A viewer requires openapi_url . llms_url does not: see describe the API for agents . Hinoki(...) arguments override settings; passing None disables a page. The packaged viewers (Swagger UI 5.35.1 and ReDoc 3.2.0, which read OpenAPI 3.2 and list QUERY operations) work without a CDN; ReDoc 3 is loaded as a JavaScript module with its usage reporting turned off. The generated OpenAPI document, Swagger UI, ReDoc and their assets answer HEAD with the same status and representation headers as GET , without a response body. Each request still has its own request ID in the configured response header ( x-request-id by default). Describe the API for agents ( llms.txt ) ¶ The same document can be rendered as an llms.txt Markdown text for a coding agent or an LLM client: the title and version, then the operations grouped by their first tag, each with its method, path, operation ID, summary and a few facts ( deprecated , the security scheme names, the request and success response components). Untagged operations are listed under Operations . hinoki llms hinoki llms --output llms.txt hinoki llms --check llms.txt The command opens no database and works when openapi_url is disabled. --check exits 1 when the committed file differs from the generated text. See inspect an application for output and exit status. Serving it is opt-in. Set llms_url , or docs.llms_url , and the text is answered at that path; the default None serves nothing: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki ( llms_url = "/llms.txt" ) The Hinoki(...) argument overrides the setting and None disables the page. Unlike the viewers it does not need openapi_url : the text is rendered from Hinoki.openapi() once at startup. It answers GET and HEAD as text/markdown; charset=utf-8 (the media type of Markdown, RFC 7763) with Cache-Control: no-cache , and it is not listed in the OpenAPI document. llms_url cannot equal openapi_url , docs_url or redoc_url , and a route on the same path stops startup. hinoki new does not enable it. The page is public, like the OpenAPI document when that is served. It is built only from the document, so it leaves out what the document leaves out: include_in_schema=False actions and the admin's pages. Leaving an action out neither hides it nor authorizes anything. The text names security schemes, never credentials. The renderer, hinoki.ai.llms.render_llms , is Python: it reads the dictionary that the Python OpenAPI builder produces and does no I/O. The finished page is handed to Kiso as a prebuilt static answer, like the document and the viewers. Hinoki's own documentation for agents is a separate set of files. The document version ¶ The openapi field is 3.2.0 by default. Hinoki(openapi_version="3.1") or the docs.openapi_version setting ( "3.1" or "3.2" ) writes a 3.1.0 document instead; any other value raises ValueError . hinoki openapi and the served document follow the application's choice. The version changes one thing: where a QUERY action is written. Every other operation, schema and component is the same in both. from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki ( openapi_version = "3.1" ) # keep a 3.1 document for a 3.1-only consumer OpenAPI 3.2.0 was checked against the bundled and current readers; use "3.1" for a consumer that only reads 3.1. @apidevtools/swagger-parser 13.1.0, for one, rejects every 3.2.0 document, and openapi-typescript 7.13.0 reads a 3.2 document but leaves its query operations out. QUERY operations ¶ An action declared with @http.query is written under the path item's query field in a 3.2 document (Path Item Object, OpenAPI 3.2.0 section 4.9 ), with the same operation object as any other method: operation ID, parameters, request body, responses and security. { "paths" : { "/search" : { "get" : { "operationId" : "search_page" }, "query" : { "operationId" : "search" }}}} With openapi_version="3.1" there is no such field, so the same operation object is written under the x-query extension instead and the document stays valid 3.1. A 3.1 document with a query field would be invalid, and a 3.2 document never carries both, because the two entries would repeat the operationId . Readers of a 3.1 document that look only at the standard method fields do not see x-query operations. The application MCP, explain_action and hinoki openapi --breaking-against read both fields, so a baseline written as 3.1 compares correctly with a 3.2 document. What is generated ¶ A unique operationId is derived from the handler's qualified name. If names collide, Hinoki appends a numeric suffix. A paginated response's envelope component is named after its items ( Page_Book , Page_integer , Page_string ). Two different security schemes, page envelopes or a page envelope and a Schema (a class named Page_Book beside Page[Book] ) that would share a name get a numeric suffix ( KeyAuth_2 , Page_array_2 , Page_Book_2 ) instead of overwriting each other; two different Schema classes with the same name are still a registration error. The first line of the handler docstring becomes summary ; the remaining lines become description . Path, query and pagination parameters come from the bound handler signature. A list with filters= documents one typed query parameter per filter: boolean , integer , number or string schemas (with format for dates, instants, UUIDs and decimals, and an enum for a Literal ), name.from and name.to for a Range , name.null for a nullable field, a comma-separated array ( style: form , explode: false , maxItems ) for In , search with its length limit, and ordering as an array whose enum is each declared key and its - form. The same parameters appear in 3.1 and 3.2 documents. Body fields and successful response fields come from Schema annotations. Parser and renderer media types supply the content types. Typed UploadedFile parameters generate a multipart/form-data request body with binary file properties. Repeated files use an array of binary items; optional single-file bindings are not required in the body or property list. A Form[Schema] body next to files is documented as one object holding the schema's fields and the file properties, with the schema's additionalProperties and both lists of required names. Text keys read dynamically through request.POST are not inferred or listed. A declared errors=(...) adds response entries for those APIError classes. Request binding and schema validation errors are documented as 422 where the action has request inputs. access=... adds a security requirement when its authentication provider supplies an OpenAPI scheme. Authentication responses are included in the operation. Admin HTML routes marked hide_from_docs are omitted. A dict[str, X] field becomes type: object with additionalProperties (the value schema), propertyNames (the key schema) and minProperties / maxProperties from its declared entry limits. The framework bounds on client input (1000 entries, 256-character keys) are not part of the document because components describe responses too; see dictionary fields . date , time and timedelta fields become type: string with format: date , time and duration . A Decimal field becomes type: string , format: decimal and a pattern for its text form, with ge / le / gt / lt as the string extensions x-minimum / x-maximum / x-exclusiveMinimum / x-exclusiveMaximum (JSON Schema's numeric keywords do not apply to a string, and a string keeps the exact value); examples and defaults are written as decimal text; max_digits and decimal_places are not written, nor is a Decimal field's multiple_of . An int field's multiple_of becomes multipleOf . IP address and network fields become type: string with format: ipv4 , ipv6 , ipv4network or ipv6network . A Path field becomes type: string with format: path , and a Secret field type: string with format: password and writeOnly: true . A bytes field becomes type: string , format: byte and contentEncoding: base64 , and its decoded-size limits are not written either, since they count bytes rather than characters. See dates, durations, decimals and bytes . An Enum or Literal field becomes type: string or type: integer with an enum list of the values (the member values, never the names), inline in the property; a nullable one is wrapped in anyOf with null . See enums and literals . A set[X] or frozenset[X] field becomes an array with uniqueItems: true , tuple[X, ...] an array of X , and a fixed tuple[X, Y] an array with prefixItems , items: false and equal minItems / maxItems . See sets and tuples . A many-to-many ids field such as tag_ids (declared with ids_name="tag_ids" ) is an array of string items with format: uuid (or the target key's type), uniqueItems: true and maxItems from its declared limit, in request and response schemas alike. A plain union such as int | str becomes anyOf of its variants, and Any or object an unconstrained schema ( {} ). See plain unions and Any . Discriminated unions declared as Schema fields become OpenAPI oneOf schemas with a discriminator and explicit tag-to-component mapping. Variant tag fields appear as required string enums; the runtime uses the same tags to select exactly one branch. List items, nested fields and nullable unions retain that structure. For route input and response documentation, put the union inside a wrapper Schema ; bare union return annotations are rejected instead of producing an incomplete schema. The return value is also checked against the annotation at runtime ( details ). oneOf : - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Cat" - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Dog" discriminator : propertyName : type mapping : cat : "#/components/schemas/Cat" dog : "#/components/schemas/Dog" See Collections and unions: discriminated unions for the Python declarations and validation behavior. For file binding syntax, limits and the in-memory boundary, see upload files . An action annotated -> Stream or -> File documents its 200 response as application/octet-stream with {"type": "string", "format": "binary"} , and -> EventStream as text/event-stream with {"type": "string"} . The media type a Stream sends is chosen by the handler at run time, so the document does not list it. An annotation such as -> Stream | NoteOut also documents the plain arm, under the media types of the route's renderers, next to the streamed one. See stream a response . Add a useful docstring to each handler because it is the source for operation text: @http . get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : """Read one task. Returns the task visible to the authenticated caller. """ ... Per-action controls ¶ include_in_schema , tags , deprecated and operation_id are options of @http.get , post , put , patch , delete and query : from hinoki import Access , Hinoki , Schema , http from notes.security import staff_auth # any authentication provider admin_only = Access ( auth = staff_auth , permissions = [ "ops:run" ]) class Started ( Schema ): status : str class Totals ( Schema ): tasks : int @http . get ( "/ops/reindex" , access = admin_only , include_in_schema = False ) async def reindex () -> Started : return Started ( status = "started" ) @http . get ( "/v1/totals" , tags = [ "tasks" ], deprecated = True , operation_id = "totalsV1" ) async def totals () -> Totals : return Totals ( tasks = 0 ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ reindex , totals ]) include_in_schema=False leaves the action out of Hinoki.openapi() , hinoki openapi and /openapi.json . The action is still registered, served and protected by its Access exactly as before: leaving it out neither hides it from a caller who knows the path nor authorizes anything. A path whose actions are all left out is not listed, and a Schema or security scheme used only by left-out actions does not appear under components . tags lists non-empty names, in order and without repeats, written to the operation's tags . deprecated=True writes deprecated: true . A deprecated action also tells its callers at run time: each response carries a Deprecation header and the call is logged as a warning, see deprecate an action . operation_id replaces the generated operation ID. It must be a non-empty string, and two documented actions with the same value stop include with a RegistrationError ; a generated ID never takes a value that an action declared. A left-out action does not take part in that check. RouteGroup(prefix, include_in_schema=..., tags=...) sets defaults for its actions: an action's own include_in_schema wins, and its tags follow the group's. crud(...) takes include_in_schema as one flag for the whole resource or a mapping by action ( {"delete": False} ; unknown names are refused), plus tags and deprecated for every generated action. It has no operation_id , because one value cannot name several actions. An MCP tool is built from the OpenAPI document, so expose_as_mcp refuses an action left out with include_in_schema=False instead of exposing it. The admin's HTML pages are always left out of the document and are not affected by these options. Deprecate an action ¶ from datetime import date from hinoki import Schema , http class Totals ( Schema ): tasks : int @http . get ( "/v1/totals" , deprecated = date ( 2026 , 11 , 22 )) async def totals_v1 () -> Totals : return Totals ( tasks = 0 ) deprecated takes True , False or the datetime.date the action was deprecated on (a datetime is refused). It does three things: The document marks the operation deprecated: true . Every response, success or error, carries a Deprecation header: @<unix seconds> for a date (the form of RFC 9745, midnight UTC), true when no date is given. The hinoki.deprecated logger warns deprecated action called: GET /v1/totals (N call(s) since the last report) . An action is reported at most once per minute, with the calls it stayed quiet about, so a busy action does not flood the log; the state is one entry per deprecated action. Nothing is logged at startup. The header and the warning are produced by the Python pipeline, so a deprecated action leaves the native lane ( hinoki routes --lanes shows lane_reason deprecated ) and, for generated CRUD, the native CRUD plan. The response and the access check do not change. There is no Sunset header. Current limits ¶ operation_id is per action only, and deprecated is per action or set for every action generated by one crud(...) ; a RouteGroup sets tags and include_in_schema but has no group-wide deprecated or operation_id . There is no tag metadata (descriptions) in the document's top-level tags . Response bodies are generated from annotations; every action's return value is checked against its annotation at runtime, and an annotation that cannot be checked stops the app at startup ( details ). See project status for other API boundaries.

The renderer, hinoki.ai.llms.render_llms , is Python: it reads the dictionary that the Python OpenAPI builder produces and does no I/O. The finished page is handed to Kiso as a prebuilt static answer, like the document and the viewers. Hinoki's own documentation for agents is a separate set of files.
docs.title: Describe the API for agents (llms.txt)

docs.text: The openapi field is 3.2.0 by default. Hinoki(openapi_version="3.1") or the docs.openapi_version setting ( "3.1" or "3.2" ) writes a 3.1.0 document instead; any other value raises ValueError . hinoki openapi and the served document follow the application's choice. The version changes one thing: where a QUERY action is written. Every other operation, schema and component is the same in both. from hinoki import Hinoki app = Hinoki ( openapi_version = "3.1" ) # keep a 3.1 document for a 3.1-only consumer OpenAPI 3.2.0 was checked against the bundled and current readers; use "3.1" for a consumer that only reads 3.1. @apidevtools/swagger-parser 13.1.0, for one, rejects every 3.2.0 document, and openapi-typescript 7.13.0 reads a 3.2 document but leaves its query operations out.
docs.title: The document version

docs.text: An action declared with @http.query is written under the path item's query field in a 3.2 document (Path Item Object, OpenAPI 3.2.0 section 4.9 ), with the same operation object as any other method: operation ID, parameters, request body, responses and security. { "paths" : { "/search" : { "get" : { "operationId" : "search_page" }, "query" : { "operationId" : "search" }}}} With openapi_version="3.1" there is no such field, so the same operation object is written under the x-query extension instead and the document stays valid 3.1. A 3.1 document with a query field would be invalid, and a 3.2 document never carries both, because the two entries would repeat the operationId . Readers of a 3.1 document that look only at the standard method fields do not see x-query operations. The application MCP, explain_action and hinoki openapi --breaking-against read both fields, so a baseline written as 3.1 compares correctly with a 3.2 document.
docs.title: QUERY operations

docs.text: A unique operationId is derived from the handler's qualified name. If names collide, Hinoki appends a numeric suffix. A paginated response's envelope component is named after its items ( Page_Book , Page_integer , Page_string ). Two different security schemes, page envelopes or a page envelope and a Schema (a class named Page_Book beside Page[Book] ) that would share a name get a numeric suffix ( KeyAuth_2 , Page_array_2 , Page_Book_2 ) instead of overwriting each other; two different Schema classes with the same name are still a registration error. The first line of the handler docstring becomes summary ; the remaining lines become description . Path, query and pagination parameters come from the bound handler signature. A list with filters= documents one typed query parameter per filter: boolean , integer , number or string schemas (with format for dates, instants, UUIDs and decimals, and an enum for a Literal ), name.from and name.to for a Range , name.null for a nullable field, a comma-separated array ( style: form , explode: false , maxItems ) for In , search with its length limit, and ordering as an array whose enum is each declared key and its - form. The same parameters appear in 3.1 and 3.2 documents. Body fields and successful response fields come from Schema annotations. Parser and renderer media types supply the content types. Typed UploadedFile parameters generate a multipart/form-data request body with binary file properties. Repeated files use an array of binary items; optional single-file bindings are not required in the body or property list. A Form[Schema] body next to files is documented as one object holding the schema's fields and the file properties, with the schema's additionalProperties and both lists of required names. Text keys read dynamically through request.POST are not inferred or listed. A declared errors=(...) adds response entries for those APIError classes. Request binding and schema validation errors are documented as 422 where the action has request inputs. access=... adds a security requirement when its authentication provider supplies an OpenAPI scheme. Authentication responses are included in the operation. Admin HTML routes marked hide_from_docs are omitted. A dict[str, X] field becomes type: object with additionalProperties (the value schema), propertyNames (the key schema) and minProperties / maxProperties from its declared entry limits. The framework bounds on client input (1000 entries, 256-character keys) are not part of the document because components describe responses too; see dictionary fields . date , time and timedelta fields become type: string with format: date , time and duration . A Decimal field becomes type: string , format: decimal and a pattern for its text form, with ge / le / gt / lt as the string extensions x-minimum / x-maximum / x-exclusiveMinimum / x-exclusiveMaximum (JSON Schema's numeric keywords do not apply to a string, and a string keeps the exact value); examples and defaults are written as decimal text; max_digits and decimal_places are not written, nor is a Decimal field's multiple_of . An int field's multiple_of becomes multipleOf . IP address and network fields become type: string with format: ipv4 , ipv6 , ipv4network or ipv6network . A Path field becomes type: string with format: path , and a Secret field type: string with format: password and writeOnly: true . A bytes field becomes type: string , format: byte and contentEncoding: base64 , and its decoded-size limits are not written either, since they count bytes rather than characters. See dates, durations, decimals and bytes . An Enum or Literal field becomes type: string or type: integer with an enum list of the values (the member values, never the names), inline in the property; a nullable one is wrapped in anyOf with null . See enums and literals . A set[X] or frozenset[X] field becomes an array with uniqueItems: true , tuple[X, ...] an array of X , and a fixed tuple[X, Y] an array with prefixItems , items: false and equal minItems / maxItems . See sets and tuples . A many-to-many ids field such as tag_ids (declared with ids_name="tag_ids" ) is an array of string items with format: uuid (or the target key's type), uniqueItems: true and maxItems from its declared limit, in request and response schemas alike. A plain union such as int | str becomes anyOf of its variants, and Any or object an unconstrained schema ( {} ). See plain unions and Any . Discriminated unions declared as Schema fields become OpenAPI oneOf schemas with a discriminator and explicit tag-to-component mapping. Variant tag fields appear as required string enums; the runtime uses the same tags to select exactly one branch. List items, nested fields and nullable unions retain that structure. For route input and response documentation, put the union inside a wrapper Schema ; bare union return annotations are rejected instead of producing an incomplete schema. The return value is also checked against the annotation at runtime ( details ). oneOf : - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Cat" - $ref : "#/components/schemas/Dog" discriminator : propertyName : type mapping : cat : "#/components/schemas/Cat" dog : "#/components/schemas/Dog" See Collections and unions: discriminated unions for the Python declarations and validation behavior. For file binding syntax, limits and the in-memory boundary, see upload files . An action annotated -> Stream or -> File documents its 200 response as application/octet-stream with {"type": "string", "format": "binary"} , and -> EventStream as text/event-stream with {"type": "string"} . The media type a Stream sends is chosen by the handler at run time, so the document does not list it. An annotation such as -> Stream | NoteOut also documents the plain arm, under the media types of the route's renderers, next to the streamed one. See stream a response . Add a useful docstring to each handler because it is the source for operation text: @http . get ( "/tasks/ {task_id} " ) async def get_task ( task_id : UUID ) -> TaskOutput : """Read one task. Returns the task visible to the authenticated caller. """ ...
docs.title: What is generated

docs.text: include_in_schema , tags , deprecated and operation_id are options of @http.get , post , put , patch , delete and query : from hinoki import Access , Hinoki , Schema , http from notes.security import staff_auth # any authentication provider admin_only = Access ( auth = staff_auth , permissions = [ "ops:run" ]) class Started ( Schema ): status : str class Totals ( Schema ): tasks : int @http . get ( "/ops/reindex" , access = admin_only , include_in_schema = False ) async def reindex () -> Started : return Started ( status = "started" ) @http . get ( "/v1/totals" , tags = [ "tasks" ], deprecated = True , operation_id = "totalsV1" ) async def totals () -> Totals : return Totals ( tasks = 0 ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ reindex , totals ]) include_in_schema=False leaves the action out of Hinoki.openapi() , hinoki openapi and /openapi.json . The action is still registered, served and protected by its Access exactly as before: leaving it out neither hides it from a caller who knows the path nor authorizes anything. A path whose actions are all left out is not listed, and a Schema or security scheme used only by left-out actions does not appear under components . tags lists non-empty names, in order and without repeats, written to the operation's tags . deprecated=True writes deprecated: true . A deprecated action also tells its callers at run time: each response carries a Deprecation header and the call is logged as a warning, see deprecate an action . operation_id replaces the generated operation ID. It must be a non-empty string, and two documented actions with the same value stop include with a RegistrationError ; a generated ID never takes a value that an action declared. A left-out action does not take part in that check. RouteGroup(prefix, include_in_schema=..., tags=...) sets defaults for its actions: an action's own include_in_schema wins, and its tags follow the group's. crud(...) takes include_in_schema as one flag for the whole resource or a mapping by action ( {"delete": False} ; unknown names are refused), plus tags and deprecated for every generated action. It has no operation_id , because one value cannot name several actions. An MCP tool is built from the OpenAPI document, so expose_as_mcp refuses an action left out with include_in_schema=False instead of exposing it. The admin's HTML pages are always left out of the document and are not affected by these options.
docs.title: Per-action controls

docs.text: from datetime import date from hinoki import Schema , http class Totals ( Schema ): tasks : int @http . get ( "/v1/totals" , deprecated = date ( 2026 , 11 , 22 )) async def totals_v1 () -> Totals : return Totals ( tasks = 0 ) deprecated takes True , False or the datetime.date the action was deprecated on (a datetime is refused). It does three things: The document marks the operation deprecated: true . Every response, success or error, carries a Deprecation header: @<unix seconds> for a date (the form of RFC 9745, midnight UTC), true when no date is given. The hinoki.deprecated logger warns deprecated action called: GET /v1/totals (N call(s) since the last report) . An action is reported at most once per minute, with the calls it stayed quiet about, so a busy action does not flood the log; the state is one entry per deprecated action. Nothing is logged at startup. The header and the warning are produced by the Python pipeline, so a deprecated action leaves the native lane ( hinoki routes --lanes shows lane_reason deprecated ) and, for generated CRUD, the native CRUD plan. The response and the access check do not change. There is no Sunset header.
docs.title: Deprecate an action

docs.text: operation_id is per action only, and deprecated is per action or set for every action generated by one crud(...) ; a RouteGroup sets tags and include_in_schema but has no group-wide deprecated or operation_id . There is no tag metadata (descriptions) in the document's top-level tags . Response bodies are generated from annotations; every action's return value is checked against its annotation at runtime, and an annotation that cannot be checked stops the app at startup ( details ). See project status for other API boundaries.
docs.title: Current limits

docs.text: Pagination ¶ An action opts into page-number pagination with pagination=PageNumberPagination() , or into cursor pagination with pagination=CursorPagination() . A size you leave out comes from the application's pagination settings group; without settings the defaults are page_size=20 and max_page_size=100 . The framework parses and validates page and page_size , injects a PageParams value, and documents both query parameters in OpenAPI. The Billing app lists invoices a page at a time. The handler asks the model for one page, and Page.map() turns its rows into Schema instances: # notes/apps/billing/api.py from hinoki import RouteGroup from hinoki.pagination import Page , PageNumberPagination , PageParams from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import Invoice from .schemas import InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True ) @invoices . get ( "/" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: return ( await Invoice . all () . apaginate ( page )) . map ( InvoiceOut . from_model ) Pages are one-based. page_size defaults to the strategy's configured size and cannot exceed its maximum. Invalid values produce a validation response before the handler runs; page is limited to 1 000 000 000, and longer or larger values answer 422 with the code le . Page contains items , page , page_size , total and the computed pages . Empty result sets have zero pages; a page beyond the end has an empty items list. Page.map() converts each item while preserving the counts and requested page. Defaults for the whole application ¶ settings.AppSettings has a pagination group, set in code, in the environment or in TOML. With the project's settings class: # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" ): pass export NOTES_PAGINATION__PAGE_SIZE = 25 export NOTES_PAGINATION__MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 200 The application in notes/main.py reads them through Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...) . Precedence, from strongest to weakest: a size set on the action's PageNumberPagination(...) , the application's pagination settings, then 20 and 100. Each size is resolved separately, so PageNumberPagination(page_size=10) keeps its 10 and takes its maximum from the settings. The result must satisfy 1 <= page_size <= max_page_size : invalid settings fail when they load, and an action whose own size does not fit the resolved other one (for example PageNumberPagination(max_page_size=10) under a settings page_size of 25) fails when it is included, naming the action. The generated OpenAPI parameters show the resolved values. Use the queryset's apaginate / paginate methods for database rows. They append the primary key as the last sort key (after any order_by ), so rows with equal sort values keep one position across pages. Page.of(rows, params) slices an in-memory sequence and counts that sequence; it is not a substitute for database pagination on large tables. Concurrent count and rows ¶ Pass concurrent=True to run the COUNT(*) and page-row queries together on PostgreSQL or MySQL pools with max_size >= 2 : @invoices . get ( "/fast" , pagination = PageNumberPagination (), atomic = False ) async def list_invoices_fast ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: return ( await Invoice . all () . apaginate ( page , concurrent = True )) . map ( InvoiceOut . from_model ) Because the two queries check out separate pool connections, they may observe slightly different snapshots under concurrent writes (the same trade-off as any non-transactional read). Inside an active transaction ( atomic=True or async with db.atomic(): ), on SQLite, or when the pool has max_size < 2 , apaginate(..., concurrent=True) automatically runs the count and row queries sequentially on one connection so transactions preserve read-your-writes and single-connection pools never deadlock. Direct schema projection ¶ Use apaginate_as (or paginate_as in sync handlers) to project rows directly to a Schema in Rust without constructing intermediate Python Model or Schema objects on the response path: @invoices . get ( "/projected" , pagination = PageNumberPagination ()) async def list_invoices_projected ( page : PageParams ) -> Page [ InvoiceOut ]: return await Invoice . all () . apaginate_as ( InvoiceOut , page , concurrent = True ) The returned Page[InvoiceOut] carries the pre-encoded JSON bytes and owned rows. Returning it from a handler emits the exact same JSON as (await Invoice.all().apaginate(page)).map(InvoiceOut.from_model) and passes validate_response=True checks. Accessing .items , calling .map() , or inspecting elements materializes the InvoiceOut instances from the owned rows without issuing a second database query. Scalar fields, select_related , and 1-level prefetch_related (reverse foreign keys and many-to-many) are encoded directly in Rust; schemas with computed fields, hooks, validators, custom dump() , or scoped prefetches fall back to normal Python hydration transparently. Cursor (keyset) pagination ¶ pagination=CursorPagination(...) pages by position instead of by offset. A response carries next and previous cursors that clients should treat as opaque; the database starts each page at the cursor's row through the sort index, so a page costs the same at any depth, and no COUNT runs. Use it for long, growing lists or feeds; keep page numbers when users jump to page n or need a total. # notes/apps/billing/api.py from hinoki.pagination import CursorPage , CursorPagination , CursorParams @invoices . get ( "/feed" , pagination = CursorPagination ( page_size = 20 )) async def feed ( page : CursorParams ) -> CursorPage [ InvoiceOut ]: return ( await Invoice . all () . apaginate_cursor ( page )) . map ( InvoiceOut . from_model ) export NOTES_PAGINATION__CURSOR_SECRET = " $( openssl rand -hex 32 ) " GET /invoices/feed?limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "next": "<cursor>", "previous": null, "page_size": 20} . Pass next as cursor to read forward and previous to read back. next is null on the last page; previous is null on the first. Generated lists switch with crud(..., pagination=CursorPagination()) and return the same envelope. Ordering. The page follows the query's order_by (or the model's ordered_by ), with the primary key appended as the final tie-break, so rows with equal sort values are never skipped or repeated. Sort columns must be non-null int , str , uuid , datetime or float columns; anything else raises a FieldError , and a crud(...) whose model ordering is invalid fails at registration with a RegistrationError naming the model and column (an ordering added by a custom get_queryset is checked on each request). A str sort value is bounded: at most 1024 bytes per value, and a whole cursor at most 4096 characters, the same limit for issuing and reading. A page whose boundary row exceeds it, and whose link is needed, answers 422 with the field cursor and the code unencodable (it never answers 500 ); order by a shorter column when values can be long. The queryset's own limit and offset are ignored. Filters and scope. The cursor holds a position. get_queryset , ownership and tenant policies are applied to every page exactly as for the first one, so a cursor cannot reach rows its holder could not list. On a generated list with client filters , the cursor is also bound to the filters and the ordering that the client sent: a cursor used with different ones answers 422 with the code invalid . A list without client filters keeps its cursors valid as before. The ordering columns of the FilterSet must be non-null int , str , uuid , datetime or float columns, checked when the routes are declared. Signing. Cursors are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in Rust and bound to the table and the ordering they were issued for, so they are tamper-proof. They are not encrypted: a cursor is base64 and readable, and it contains the sort-key values of the boundary row. Do not order a cursor list by a column whose value must stay private, even when the read Schema hides it. The secret comes from CursorPagination(secret=...) or pagination.cursor_secret and must have at least 32 bytes; without one, including the action fails with a RegistrationError . Changing the secret invalidates outstanding cursors. Expiry. cursor_ttl_seconds (setting) or CursorPagination(ttl=...) makes a cursor expire; the default never does. Errors. A tampered, malformed, foreign or differently ordered cursor answers 422 with the field cursor and the code invalid ; an expired one answers 422 with expired ; an unencodable boundary value answers 422 with unencodable . limit follows the same bounds as page_size . Rust path. The keyset WHERE , the signature, the direction handling and, for a generated plain list, the JSON page are produced in Rust. Indexes. Index the sort columns in the sort order (for example (rank DESC, id) ) to get the constant-time pages; without one the database sorts the table for every page. Admin. The admin lists keep page-number pagination. The pagination settings group also takes cursor_secret and cursor_ttl_seconds ; sizes resolve as described above, and page_size / max_page_size apply to limit . The measurements are in benchmarks/README.md ( cursorbench.py ).

docs.text: Structure an application ¶ Opinionated, with reasons. Each practice below is enforced by the framework, checkable with an optional rule , or a convention left to review. The Tracker example shows them together: api → operations → models , row permission in the statements, the direction enforced by Imports.forbid , operations tested without HTTP. 1. Three layers, one direction ¶ HTTP layer actions (functions or API classes) shapes, status codes, access, atomic=True │ ▼ Operations plain async functions one business operation each; no HTTP types │ ▼ Persistence Model / QuerySet tables, relations, explicit loading HTTP layer turns a request into typed values ( Schema , path and query parameters, Caller ) and an operation's result into a response Schema . No business rules, no SQL. Operations hold the rules ("an editor may publish only their own draft"). They take plain arguments ( principal , a Schema , IDs), so an action, a CLI command, a test, an admin hook or an MCP tool can call them. An action that reads cookies or headers cannot be reused; an operation can. Persistence never imports the HTTP layer. Rule: Imports.forbid(source="notes.apps.billing.models", target="notes.apps.billing.api") , and the same for operations → api. Small apps may skip the middle layer. Add it when an action holds a rule another entry point needs. 2. Where each concern lives ¶ Actions are functions by default, grouped in a RouteGroup that states shared options once; an API class earns its place for crud(...) resources with hooks or inherited actions. Concern Put it Why Routes Each app's routes.py ; prefixes only in hinoki.toml ( register routes ). Convention One place to read the map; one source per path segment Authentication A provider ( BearerAuth , JWTAuth , …) returning a Caller One path for HTTP, admin and MCP Coarse permission access= on the action, or once on its RouteGroup . Public is the default : protect on purpose. Rule: Actions.require_access A forgotten policy is the most common hole Row permission (owner, tenant) The statement : scope aupdate / adelete by owner so check and write are one operation No check-then-write race; hidden rows look missing ( 404 ). If the API promises a distinct 403 , make the conditional write and its fallback explicit, and document what it reveals Input validation The Schema (types, constraints, patterns) Strict, no coercion, validated in Rust before your code runs Business rules Operations Testable without HTTP Transactions atomic=True on every write. Rule: Transactions.require_atomic Commit after the response is encoded; rollback before the error becomes HTTP Errors Raise APIError subclasses and declare them: errors=(InvoiceAlreadyPaid,) . Translate exceptions you cannot change once with @app.error_handler(...) The declaration feeds OpenAPI, MCP and ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) . A database UniqueViolation is already 409 unique_conflict . A returned Response commits the transaction Secrets Settings and the environment, never defaults Nothing to leak from the repository 3. Schema classes and models ¶ Models describe tables; Schema classes describe the API. Never return a model : respond with InvoiceOut.from_model(row) . Name classes by role: InvoiceIn (what a client may set), InvoicePatch (every field UNSET by default), InvoiceOut (what a client may see, often @derive(Invoice) ). Rules: Actions.forbid_model_responses() refuses a Model return type, also inside list , Page and unions; Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", …) keeps columns out of responses through nesting and subclasses. Create from a Schema and add what only the server knows: await Post.acreate(data, author_id=principal.user.id) ; server values win. Update with await row.aupdate_from(patch) , which writes only what was sent. A server-assigned field does not exist in the input Schema at all; the keyword override is a second line of defence. Constraints and patterns belong on the Schema , in the Rust pattern syntax (whole value, no look-around). 4. Relations and queries ¶ Relations are never lazy. Load what the response shows ( select_related for single values, prefetch_related for collections) in the function that builds the response, so the cost is visible in one place. Paginate every list ( pagination= + PageParams + Page[...] ). Never return an unbounded list; never load a whole table to count or aggregate (use acount() , filters or SQL). Rule: Actions.require_pagination . Filter and order only by names you choose; never pass client-supplied column names to filter or order_by . For a generated list, declare them once in a hinoki.filters.FilterSet ( done: Eq[bool] , search = Search("title") , ordering = (...) ) and pass filters=TaskFilters to crud(...) , as Tracker does. 5. Sync and async ¶ Prefer async handlers. A sync handler runs on a bounded pool and uses the sync model methods; it must not block for long, and a full queue answers 503 overloaded . Password hashing has its own bounded pool. Never call blocking code from an async handler. See sync and async code . 6. Modules ¶ An application is a set of modules with explicit dependencies and a lifespan ( DatabaseModule , your own Module ). Importing a module registers and opens nothing. Resources are created once per worker, in its lifespan. Migrations are a deploy step, never run at startup or from every worker. A standalone script owns and closes its own short-lived connection. 7. Migrations ¶ hinoki migrations plan billing hinoki migrations apply plan writes reviewable SQL and a state file; destructive operations are flagged and need --allow-destructive , and a new NOT NULL column without a default is flagged. Review the SQL like code and apply it to a disposable database first. See migrations . 8. Testing ¶ Run database tests against disposable servers for each backend you support: HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL (PostgreSQL), HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL , HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL . Without a URL those tests are skipped: read the skip summary; one backend's green run is not conformance for another. Drive HTTP behaviour through the ASGI client (no sockets); test operations directly. For security code, use independent test vectors and inject the clock ( JWTAuth.now ). 9. Security defaults to keep ¶ HTTPS terminates somewhere you control ( Admin(secure_cookies=True) behind a proxy); access= on everything that is not public on purpose; CSRF on every cookie-authenticated form (the admin does it); a strict CSP; Argon2id passwords; JWT keys with a fixed algorithm and a kid ; no token, password or hash in logs or error bodies; uploads within the 1 MiB body limit; no real personal data in tests or fixtures. 10. Rules to turn on from day one ¶ hinoki new enables eight rules ( HNK-ACC-001 , HNK-ACC-002 , HNK-API-001 , HNK-API-002 , HNK-API-003 , HNK-TXN-001 , HNK-SCH-001 , HNK-SCH-002 ) and leaves the model rules HNK-DB-001 and HNK-DB-002 commented out until the first model exists. Turn those on then, and add Imports.forbid ( HNK-IMP-001 ) for the direction in section 1 . List the rule modules in the manifest, [project] rules = ["tracker.rules:policy", "tracker.rules:layers"] , and Hinoki() loads them; project-wide middleware is listed the same way (see rules and middleware ). Waivers live in hinoki-rules.toml , are the owner's decision, carry a reason and a bounded target, and are never edited by tools or agents to pass a check. 11. Anti-patterns ¶ Returning a Model , or a dict built from one. A business rule inside an action that another entry point also needs. Response(4xx) from an atomic=True action: it commits. Client-supplied column names reaching filter or order_by . Applying migrations at startup; creating a pool at import. A broad waiver ( * ), or editing waivers to silence a rule. Catching Exception in an action to "keep going": let the framework translate it and roll back. app.include(...) in a project with hinoki.toml : list the routes in routes.py . 12. More than one service ¶ Split a system only for a reason you can name (independent deploys, different scaling, a team boundary); every split costs something the framework cannot hide. No joins, no shared transaction. A foreign key never crosses a service. Store the other service's ID as a plain value and treat its answers as snapshots. A write across two services is a sequence of calls that can half-fail: make each step idempotent and decide what a retry does before writing the code. Each service owns its tables. Others call its API, never its database. Its migrations belong to it and are applied by its deploy step ( section 7 ). The caller is a Caller too. Service-to-service calls authenticate like any client (a JWT with a service identity and narrow permissions); do not forward the end user's token unless the callee must act as that user. Wrap every remote call in an operation ( section 1 ) with a timeout and a failure you chose ( 502 or 503 ), never a client library's exception. Share contracts, not models. Publish the response Schema classes or the OpenAPI document; keep models private. A runnable two-service example and a client helper do not exist yet.

docs.text: Opinionated, with reasons. Each practice below is enforced by the framework, checkable with an optional rule , or a convention left to review. Add it when an action holds a rule another entry point needs.
