docs.text: Check architecture with rules ¶ Rules are typed promises about your application: "every private action names a policy", "writes are atomic", "no response leaks password_hash ". Each one is a Python object with a stable ID, deterministic behaviour and an exact fix line. They are optional, and a project created with hinoki new starts with them on: # notes/rules.py """The project's rules. Weaken them only with the owner's decision (see hinoki-rules.toml).""" from hinoki import rules project_rules = rules . RuleSet ( # Anything not public on purpose names an access policy, and the policy names permissions. rules . Actions . require_access ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" ]), rules . Actions . require_permissions ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" ]), # Responses are concrete Schema types and lists are paginated. rules . Actions . forbid_model_responses ( match = "notes.*" ), rules . Actions . require_return_type ( match = "notes.*" ), rules . Actions . require_pagination ( match = "notes.*" ), # Writes run in a transaction that rolls back before errors become HTTP. rules . Transactions . require_atomic (), # Secrets never reach a client, and request text is bounded. rules . Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "password_hash" , "password" , "token" ), rules . Schemas . require_string_limits (), # Turn these on with your first model (a model rule that matches no model # fails the check): tables are pinned and foreign keys are indexed. # rules.Models.require_explicit_table(match="notes.*"), # rules.Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="notes.*"), ) hinoki.toml lists the set under [project] , and Hinoki() loads it (see which rules run ): [project] application = "notes.main:app" rules = [ "notes.rules:project_rules" ] Check it at any time: hinoki check The twelve rules ¶ ID Rule Phase Checks HNK-ACC-001 rules.Actions.require_access(match="*", except_=()) startup every matching action names an Access policy (public by default is the common hole) HNK-ACC-002 rules.Actions.require_permissions(match="*", except_=()) startup an action with an Access policy names at least one permission, so "any authenticated caller" is never implicit HNK-API-001 rules.Actions.forbid_model_responses(match="*", except_=()) startup no action returns a Model (or a list or page of them): responses are Schema classes HNK-API-002 rules.Actions.require_return_type(match="*", except_=()) startup every action annotates a concrete return type (not missing, Any or object ; None is fine for a 204 ) HNK-API-003 rules.Actions.require_pagination(match="*", except_=()) startup a GET action never returns a plain list[...] (alone or in a union): it returns a Page HNK-TXN-001 rules.Transactions.require_atomic(methods=("POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"), match="*", except_=()) startup state-changing actions declare atomic=True , on the action or its RouteGroup HNK-SCH-001 rules.Schemas.forbid_exposure(*fields) startup the named fields never appear in a response Schema : nested, in a subclass, in a union variant, as a field, an alias or a computed field; an action returning a dict is reported as unverifiable HNK-SCH-002 rules.Schemas.require_string_limits() startup every text field a client sends (nested, in containers, dict values and union variants included) has max_length or one_of ; Enum and Literal fields pass HNK-DB-001 rules.Models.require_explicit_table(match="*") startup matching models pin their table with @db.table(...) or table= , so renaming the class cannot rename the table HNK-DB-002 rules.Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="*") startup every foreign-key column leads an index, a primary key or a unique constraint HNK-MAIL-001 EmailTemplatesMatch() static every registered email template loads and matches its context Schema (opt-in, see below ) HNK-IMP-001 rules.Imports.forbid(source, target) static modules under source never import target , read from the source files; dynamic imports are reported, not ignored Every built-in rule has severity error . HNK-API-002 matters most for actions with validate_response=False : any other action with an unusable return annotation already stops the app. HNK-TXN-001 does not check the admin's own routes, which open their own short transactions. An opt-in rule: email templates ¶ EmailTemplatesMatch() ( HNK-MAIL-001 , phase static ) is listed in the table but runs only when you put it in your RuleSet . It reads every registered email template (the files included) and checks it against its context Schema , reporting one diagnostic per template that is refused. Because it reads files it declares the effect files , so hinoki check reports it as unverifiable unless you pass --allow-effects : from hinoki.rules import EmailTemplatesMatch , RuleSet rules = RuleSet ( EmailTemplatesMatch ()) hinoki check --rules myproject.rules:rules --allow-effects Choose what a rule covers ¶ Action rules match fnmatch patterns against an action's qualified name: module.function for a function, module.Class.method for an API class (named after the class it is mounted on), and module.<Model>Crud.<action> for a crud(...) value, where module is the one that calls crud(...) . A bare health matches nothing; write notes.api.health or *.health . except_ takes the same patterns and is how you say "public on purpose". The Blog example names its exceptions once: # examples/blog/blog/rules.py from hinoki import rules PUBLIC = [ "blog.apps.blog.api.health" , "blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.listing" , "blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.one" , "blog.apps.blog.accounts.*.login" , # public on purpose: it is how you sign in ] SIGNED_IN = [ "blog.apps.blog.accounts.*.me" ] # any signed-in user, no permission blog_rules = rules . RuleSet ( rules . Actions . require_access ( match = "blog.*" , except_ = PUBLIC ), rules . Actions . require_permissions ( match = "blog.*" , except_ = [ * PUBLIC , * SIGNED_IN ]), rules . Transactions . require_atomic ( except_ = [ "hinoki.ai.mcpapp.*" ]), rules . Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token_hash" , "password_hash" ), rules . Imports . forbid ( source = "blog.apps.blog.models" , target = "blog.apps.blog.api" ), # ... and the other six rules, see the file ) Blog passes blog_rules and its waiver file to Hinoki(...) by hand. Tracker lists two sets in its manifest instead, rules = ["tracker.rules:policy", "tracker.rules:layers"] , and its Hinoki(...) call names no rules. The model rules match the model's module ( blog.* ) and report unverifiable when no model matches, even with * . In a project with hinoki.toml , hinoki check first imports the models of every [[apps]] entry, so they are found without importing them from the application module. require_access and require_atomic report unverifiable when a pattern other than * matches no action. Neither passes silently. Which rules run ¶ The application's rules are, in this order of precedence: Hinoki(rules=...) , when you pass it. An explicit argument wins, even an empty RuleSet() , and the manifest is not read for rules. The [project] rules list of hinoki.toml , when rules= is omitted and the manifest's project.application names the module that builds the app. Otherwise none. rules is a list of module:attribute entries, each a RuleSet . The sets are merged in the order listed into one RuleSet , so the report keeps that order. The same rule (same id and summary) listed by two entries is a ProjectError naming both entries, never a silent override; rules that share an id but differ in their arguments, such as two rules.Imports.forbid(...) , are different rules. An entry that does not import, is not a RuleSet , or a list of anything else is rejected the same way. You edit the list by hand; no command writes it. manifest_rules() (from hinoki.project ) is the explicit form, for Hinoki(rules=manifest_rules()) or a test. hinoki check and hinoki mcp run --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE when you give it and otherwise the app's own rules, which are the two sources above. When rules run ¶ Where Rules Waivers On failure Application startup ( hinoki dev , hinoki serve , any ASGI server, the test clients) startup rules of the application's rules the waiver file startup fails with RegistrationError listing every failing diagnostic hinoki check both phases (or --phase ) the waiver file, or --waivers exit code 1 hinoki mcp both phases the waiver file, or --waivers reported to the agent Startup enforcement means a broken promise never serves traffic. During a migration you can pass enforce_rules=False to Hinoki(...) : violations are then logged as a warning instead. Read the results ¶ hinoki check prints one line per finding, with its location and a fix: hint. This output comes from a deliberately broken project in Hinoki's own tests, checked from a clone of the repository: hinoki check tests.projects.rulesapp:create_app --rules tests.projects.rulesapp:rules tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose) tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] POST /items (create) declares no access policy fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose) tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare atomic=True fix: add atomic=True to the action (or declare it on a RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) group) 2 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived Each status means one thing: violated (demonstrated), unverifiable (the check could not decide: a dynamic import, a pattern that matched nothing, a return type that does not name its schema, or a rule that crashed), waived and warning (a notice about the waiver file itself). Unverifiable fails like a violation; it is never a pass. A warning never fails. The fix line each rule prints: ID fix: HNK-ACC-002 name at least one permission in the Access policy of the action HNK-API-001 return a Schema (for example PostOut.from_model(row)) instead of the Model HNK-API-002 annotate the action's return type (a Schema, or None for status 204) HNK-API-003 return Page[Item] or CursorPage[Item] and paginate the action HNK-SCH-001 remove the field from the response Schema, or return a Schema that does not carry it HNK-SCH-002 bound the field: Annotated[str, Field(max_length=...)] or one_of=... HNK-DB-001 name the table with @db.table(...) or table=... on the model HNK-DB-002 index the column: @db.indexed(" ") on the model, or an index or unique group that starts with it HNK-IMP-001 move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between hinoki check --format json prints the same diagnostics as versioned data ( schema_version , rules , summary , and per diagnostic rule , severity , phase , status , message , location , explanation , subject , waiver , fix ) for CI, editors and agents. summary counts each status ( violated , unverifiable , waived , warning ) and adds failing , the number that sets the exit code. schema_version is 2 : version 1 reported waiver notices as violated and had no warning count. Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 failing, 2 the check could not run. The other options are on Inspect an application . Accept an exception with a waiver ¶ Prefer except_ for things that are public or special by design . A waiver is for a known violation the owner accepts for a while. It lives in hinoki-rules.toml at the project root, which hinoki new creates: # hinoki-rules.toml [[waiver]] rule = "HNK-ACC-001" target = "tests.projects.rulesapp.health" reason = "liveness probe is public by design" owner = "platform-team" expires = 2027-01-31 rule , target , reason and owner are required. target is an fnmatch pattern on the diagnostic's subject and must be bounded: a literal prefix of at least five characters containing a dot ( shop.api.* , never * ). expires is optional and must be a TOML date, written without quotes; the waiver applies through that day and expires once the current UTC date is later. The waived diagnostic keeps its line and gains the decision: tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [waived] GET /health (health) declares no access policy fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose) waived: liveness probe is public by design (platform-team, until 2027-01-31) An expired waiver stops applying and reports HNK-WVR-002 ; one that matches nothing reports HNK-WVR-001 . Both have status warning : they print as [warning] , count under warning(s) in the summary ( summary.warning in JSON) and never change the exit code. A diagnostic that means "the rule could not do its job" cannot be waived. An invalid or unreadable file makes hinoki check exit with 2 . Which waiver file ¶ hinoki check , hinoki mcp and application startup read the same file: The file named by Hinoki(waivers=...) , or by --waivers on check and mcp . A named file must exist. Otherwise hinoki-rules.toml at the project root: the directory of the nearest hinoki.toml , searched from the working directory upwards. Running from a subdirectory of the project finds the same file. Without a hinoki.toml , hinoki-rules.toml in the working directory. app = Hinoki ( rules = rules , waivers = "config/hinoki-rules.toml" ) A missing default file means no waivers. A directory or a broken symbolic link with that name is an error, not an absent file. hinoki mcp --waivers PATH also applies PATH to the app that run_scenario starts. Waivers at startup ¶ Application startup applies the waiver file the same way as hinoki check . This app requires access on every action, yet it starts and serves /health because the owner waived it. It passes rules= by hand, the explicit form, to keep the example in one file: # shop/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http , rules class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) app = Hinoki ( rules = rules . RuleSet ( rules . Actions . require_access ()), include = [ health ]) # hinoki-rules.toml [[waiver]] rule = "HNK-ACC-001" target = "shop.main.health" reason = "liveness probe is public by design" owner = "platform-team" Without the waiver, hinoki serve fails at startup with RegistrationError: 1 rule violation(s) . At startup: An absent default file means no waivers. An invalid or unreadable file, or a missing file named with waivers= , fails startup with RegistrationError ("invalid waivers: .../hinoki-rules.toml: waiver #1: missing target"), even with enforce_rules=False . An expired waiver does not apply: the violation fails startup and the RegistrationError also lists the HNK-WVR-002 notice. Without a remaining violation the notice is logged as a warning. HNK-WVR-001 (unused waiver) is reported only by hinoki check and hinoki mcp : startup runs only the startup rules, so a waiver for a static rule such as HNK-IMP-001 is expected to match nothing there. Waivers are the owner's decision: tools read the file and never write it. Put it under CODEOWNERS; the generated AGENTS.md tells agents the same. Your own rules ¶ Subclass hinoki.rules.Rule with a stable id , an explanation , an optional fix and a check that yields diagnostics. phase defaults to Phase.STARTUP and severity to Severity.ERROR . # notes/rules.py from collections.abc import Iterator from hinoki.rules import Diagnostic , Project , Rule , qualified , where class NoDelete ( Rule ): id = "NOTES-API-001" explanation = "This project archives rows instead of deleting them." fix = "use PATCH to set archived=true" def check ( self , project : Project ) -> Iterator [ Diagnostic ]: for route in project . app . routes : if route . method == "DELETE" : yield self . diagnostic ( f "DELETE { route . path } removes a row" , where ( route . handler ), subject = qualified ( route ), ) Add NoDelete() to the RuleSet . where(obj) gives a file:line location; qualified(route) gives the subject that waivers match (without a subject the location is used; an empty subject cannot be waived). A rule that needs side effects (running code, files, network, a database) lists them in effects and only runs under hinoki check --allow-effects ; at startup it is refused and reported as unverifiable. RuleSet raises ValueError for an empty ID or the same ID twice. Errors and edge cases ¶ A rule that raises is reported as unverifiable with "the rule failed to run", never skipped. HNK-IMP-001 runs only in hinoki check and hinoki mcp ; it needs the source files of the checked packages ( --package , default: the target's top-level package). The model rules in a project without models are unverifiable, which is why the scaffold keeps them commented out. See also ¶ Inspect an application : every hinoki check option. Authentication and access : what HNK-ACC-001/002 ask for. Build with a coding agent : the same diagnostics for agents through hinoki mcp .
docs.title: Rules

docs.text: Rules are typed promises about your application: "every private action names a policy", "writes are atomic", "no response leaks password_hash ". Each one is a Python object with a stable ID, deterministic behaviour and an exact fix line. They are optional, and a project created with hinoki new starts with them on: # notes/rules.py """The project's rules. Weaken them only with the owner's decision (see hinoki-rules.toml).""" from hinoki import rules project_rules = rules . RuleSet ( # Anything not public on purpose names an access policy, and the policy names permissions. rules . Actions . require_access ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" ]), rules . Actions . require_permissions ( match = "notes.*" , except_ = [ "notes.api.health" ]), # Responses are concrete Schema types and lists are paginated. rules . Actions . forbid_model_responses ( match = "notes.*" ), rules . Actions . require_return_type ( match = "notes.*" ), rules . Actions . require_pagination ( match = "notes.*" ), # Writes run in a transaction that rolls back before errors become HTTP. rules . Transactions . require_atomic (), # Secrets never reach a client, and request text is bounded. rules . Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "password_hash" , "password" , "token" ), rules . Schemas . require_string_limits (), # Turn these on with your first model (a model rule that matches no model # fails the check): tables are pinned and foreign keys are indexed. # rules.Models.require_explicit_table(match="notes.*"), # rules.Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="notes.*"), ) hinoki.toml lists the set under [project] , and Hinoki() loads it (see which rules run ): [project] application = "notes.main:app" rules = [ "notes.rules:project_rules" ] Check it at any time: hinoki check
docs.title: Check architecture with rules

docs.text: ID Rule Phase Checks HNK-ACC-001 rules.Actions.require_access(match="*", except_=()) startup every matching action names an Access policy (public by default is the common hole) HNK-ACC-002 rules.Actions.require_permissions(match="*", except_=()) startup an action with an Access policy names at least one permission, so "any authenticated caller" is never implicit HNK-API-001 rules.Actions.forbid_model_responses(match="*", except_=()) startup no action returns a Model (or a list or page of them): responses are Schema classes HNK-API-002 rules.Actions.require_return_type(match="*", except_=()) startup every action annotates a concrete return type (not missing, Any or object ; None is fine for a 204 ) HNK-API-003 rules.Actions.require_pagination(match="*", except_=()) startup a GET action never returns a plain list[...] (alone or in a union): it returns a Page HNK-TXN-001 rules.Transactions.require_atomic(methods=("POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"), match="*", except_=()) startup state-changing actions declare atomic=True , on the action or its RouteGroup HNK-SCH-001 rules.Schemas.forbid_exposure(*fields) startup the named fields never appear in a response Schema : nested, in a subclass, in a union variant, as a field, an alias or a computed field; an action returning a dict is reported as unverifiable HNK-SCH-002 rules.Schemas.require_string_limits() startup every text field a client sends (nested, in containers, dict values and union variants included) has max_length or one_of ; Enum and Literal fields pass HNK-DB-001 rules.Models.require_explicit_table(match="*") startup matching models pin their table with @db.table(...) or table= , so renaming the class cannot rename the table HNK-DB-002 rules.Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="*") startup every foreign-key column leads an index, a primary key or a unique constraint HNK-MAIL-001 EmailTemplatesMatch() static every registered email template loads and matches its context Schema (opt-in, see below ) HNK-IMP-001 rules.Imports.forbid(source, target) static modules under source never import target , read from the source files; dynamic imports are reported, not ignored Every built-in rule has severity error . HNK-API-002 matters most for actions with validate_response=False : any other action with an unusable return annotation already stops the app. HNK-TXN-001 does not check the admin's own routes, which open their own short transactions.
docs.title: The twelve rules

docs.text: EmailTemplatesMatch() ( HNK-MAIL-001 , phase static ) is listed in the table but runs only when you put it in your RuleSet . It reads every registered email template (the files included) and checks it against its context Schema , reporting one diagnostic per template that is refused. Because it reads files it declares the effect files , so hinoki check reports it as unverifiable unless you pass --allow-effects : from hinoki.rules import EmailTemplatesMatch , RuleSet rules = RuleSet ( EmailTemplatesMatch ()) hinoki check --rules myproject.rules:rules --allow-effects
docs.title: An opt-in rule: email templates

docs.text: Action rules match fnmatch patterns against an action's qualified name: module.function for a function, module.Class.method for an API class (named after the class it is mounted on), and module.<Model>Crud.<action> for a crud(...) value, where module is the one that calls crud(...) . A bare health matches nothing; write notes.api.health or *.health . except_ takes the same patterns and is how you say "public on purpose". The Blog example names its exceptions once: # examples/blog/blog/rules.py from hinoki import rules PUBLIC = [ "blog.apps.blog.api.health" , "blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.listing" , "blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.one" , "blog.apps.blog.accounts.*.login" , # public on purpose: it is how you sign in ] SIGNED_IN = [ "blog.apps.blog.accounts.*.me" ] # any signed-in user, no permission blog_rules = rules . RuleSet ( rules . Actions . require_access ( match = "blog.*" , except_ = PUBLIC ), rules . Actions . require_permissions ( match = "blog.*" , except_ = [ * PUBLIC , * SIGNED_IN ]), rules . Transactions . require_atomic ( except_ = [ "hinoki.ai.mcpapp.*" ]), rules . Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token_hash" , "password_hash" ), rules . Imports . forbid ( source = "blog.apps.blog.models" , target = "blog.apps.blog.api" ), # ... and the other six rules, see the file ) Blog passes blog_rules and its waiver file to Hinoki(...) by hand. Tracker lists two sets in its manifest instead, rules = ["tracker.rules:policy", "tracker.rules:layers"] , and its Hinoki(...) call names no rules. The model rules match the model's module ( blog.* ) and report unverifiable when no model matches, even with * . In a project with hinoki.toml , hinoki check first imports the models of every [[apps]] entry, so they are found without importing them from the application module. require_access and require_atomic report unverifiable when a pattern other than * matches no action. Neither passes silently.
docs.title: Choose what a rule covers

docs.text: The application's rules are, in this order of precedence: Hinoki(rules=...) , when you pass it. An explicit argument wins, even an empty RuleSet() , and the manifest is not read for rules. The [project] rules list of hinoki.toml , when rules= is omitted and the manifest's project.application names the module that builds the app. Otherwise none. rules is a list of module:attribute entries, each a RuleSet . The sets are merged in the order listed into one RuleSet , so the report keeps that order. The same rule (same id and summary) listed by two entries is a ProjectError naming both entries, never a silent override; rules that share an id but differ in their arguments, such as two rules.Imports.forbid(...) , are different rules. An entry that does not import, is not a RuleSet , or a list of anything else is rejected the same way. You edit the list by hand; no command writes it. manifest_rules() (from hinoki.project ) is the explicit form, for Hinoki(rules=manifest_rules()) or a test. hinoki check and hinoki mcp run --rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE when you give it and otherwise the app's own rules, which are the two sources above.
docs.title: Which rules run

docs.text: Where Rules Waivers On failure Application startup ( hinoki dev , hinoki serve , any ASGI server, the test clients) startup rules of the application's rules the waiver file startup fails with RegistrationError listing every failing diagnostic hinoki check both phases (or --phase ) the waiver file, or --waivers exit code 1 hinoki mcp both phases the waiver file, or --waivers reported to the agent Startup enforcement means a broken promise never serves traffic. During a migration you can pass enforce_rules=False to Hinoki(...) : violations are then logged as a warning instead.
docs.title: When rules run

docs.text: hinoki check prints one line per finding, with its location and a fix: hint. This output comes from a deliberately broken project in Hinoki's own tests, checked from a clone of the repository: hinoki check tests.projects.rulesapp:create_app --rules tests.projects.rulesapp:rules tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose) tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] POST /items (create) declares no access policy fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose) tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare atomic=True fix: add atomic=True to the action (or declare it on a RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) group) 2 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived Each status means one thing: violated (demonstrated), unverifiable (the check could not decide: a dynamic import, a pattern that matched nothing, a return type that does not name its schema, or a rule that crashed), waived and warning (a notice about the waiver file itself). Unverifiable fails like a violation; it is never a pass. A warning never fails. The fix line each rule prints: ID fix: HNK-ACC-002 name at least one permission in the Access policy of the action HNK-API-001 return a Schema (for example PostOut.from_model(row)) instead of the Model HNK-API-002 annotate the action's return type (a Schema, or None for status 204) HNK-API-003 return Page[Item] or CursorPage[Item] and paginate the action HNK-SCH-001 remove the field from the response Schema, or return a Schema that does not carry it HNK-SCH-002 bound the field: Annotated[str, Field(max_length=...)] or one_of=... HNK-DB-001 name the table with @db.table(...) or table=... on the model HNK-DB-002 index the column: @db.indexed(" ") on the model, or an index or unique group that starts with it HNK-IMP-001 move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between hinoki check --format json prints the same diagnostics as versioned data ( schema_version , rules , summary , and per diagnostic rule , severity , phase , status , message , location , explanation , subject , waiver , fix ) for CI, editors and agents. summary counts each status ( violated , unverifiable , waived , warning ) and adds failing , the number that sets the exit code. schema_version is 2 : version 1 reported waiver notices as violated and had no warning count. Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 failing, 2 the check could not run. The other options are on Inspect an application .
docs.title: Read the results

docs.text: Prefer except_ for things that are public or special by design . A waiver is for a known violation the owner accepts for a while. It lives in hinoki-rules.toml at the project root, which hinoki new creates: # hinoki-rules.toml [[waiver]] rule = "HNK-ACC-001" target = "tests.projects.rulesapp.health" reason = "liveness probe is public by design" owner = "platform-team" expires = 2027-01-31 rule , target , reason and owner are required. target is an fnmatch pattern on the diagnostic's subject and must be bounded: a literal prefix of at least five characters containing a dot ( shop.api.* , never * ). expires is optional and must be a TOML date, written without quotes; the waiver applies through that day and expires once the current UTC date is later. The waived diagnostic keeps its line and gains the decision: tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [waived] GET /health (health) declares no access policy fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose) waived: liveness probe is public by design (platform-team, until 2027-01-31) An expired waiver stops applying and reports HNK-WVR-002 ; one that matches nothing reports HNK-WVR-001 . Both have status warning : they print as [warning] , count under warning(s) in the summary ( summary.warning in JSON) and never change the exit code. A diagnostic that means "the rule could not do its job" cannot be waived. An invalid or unreadable file makes hinoki check exit with 2 .
docs.title: Accept an exception with a waiver

docs.text: hinoki check , hinoki mcp and application startup read the same file: The file named by Hinoki(waivers=...) , or by --waivers on check and mcp . A named file must exist. Otherwise hinoki-rules.toml at the project root: the directory of the nearest hinoki.toml , searched from the working directory upwards. Running from a subdirectory of the project finds the same file. Without a hinoki.toml , hinoki-rules.toml in the working directory. app = Hinoki ( rules = rules , waivers = "config/hinoki-rules.toml" ) A missing default file means no waivers. A directory or a broken symbolic link with that name is an error, not an absent file. hinoki mcp --waivers PATH also applies PATH to the app that run_scenario starts.
docs.title: Which waiver file

docs.text: Application startup applies the waiver file the same way as hinoki check . This app requires access on every action, yet it starts and serves /health because the owner waived it. It passes rules= by hand, the explicit form, to keep the example in one file: # shop/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , http , rules class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) app = Hinoki ( rules = rules . RuleSet ( rules . Actions . require_access ()), include = [ health ]) # hinoki-rules.toml [[waiver]] rule = "HNK-ACC-001" target = "shop.main.health" reason = "liveness probe is public by design" owner = "platform-team" Without the waiver, hinoki serve fails at startup with RegistrationError: 1 rule violation(s) . At startup: An absent default file means no waivers. An invalid or unreadable file, or a missing file named with waivers= , fails startup with RegistrationError ("invalid waivers: .../hinoki-rules.toml: waiver #1: missing target"), even with enforce_rules=False . An expired waiver does not apply: the violation fails startup and the RegistrationError also lists the HNK-WVR-002 notice. Without a remaining violation the notice is logged as a warning. HNK-WVR-001 (unused waiver) is reported only by hinoki check and hinoki mcp : startup runs only the startup rules, so a waiver for a static rule such as HNK-IMP-001 is expected to match nothing there. Waivers are the owner's decision: tools read the file and never write it. Put it under CODEOWNERS; the generated AGENTS.md tells agents the same.

docs.text: Native CRUD phase 1: end-to-end orientation run ¶ This is one host-specific orientation measurement, not a performance claim or a framework ranking. The primary table reports five alternating pairs of Hinoki's automatically selected Rust generated CRUD path (declared with the since-removed CrudAPI class when measured; crud(...) now generates the same routes) and a manually implemented equivalent Django Bolt endpoint. Both apps use the same PostgreSQL table and deterministic 10,000-row seed. Their list, detail, create and update responses were verified against the database before timing. Run started: 2026-11-18T03:09:11.864738+00:00. Host: Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-10300H CPU @ 2.50GHz (8 logical CPUs), Linux-7.2.11-arch1-1-x86_64-with-glibc2.44; Python 3.13.18; PostgreSQL postgres (PostgreSQL) 17.12 (Debian 17.12-1.pgdg13+1); Rust rustc 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09); Oha oha 1.17.0. Hinoki 0.0.1 uses Kiso and tokio-postgres; Django Bolt 0.13.0 uses Django 6.1.3 with psycopg 3.3.9 and its Actix server. Each starts 4 processes with a pool of 10 database connections per process. Scenarios: list page sizes 20 and 100, detail, create and PATCH update. Each sample has 10 s warm-up, then 20 s measured with 64 concurrent connections. Server CPUs: 0-3; load generator CPUs: 6-7; response compression disabled. Each sample's one-minute host load is checked before its server starts and must be at most 1.0. Across the samples, scenario start loads ranged from 0.81 to 1.00. SQL calls are read from pg_stat_statements after each timed request window; the table reports the median calls per successful HTTP request. Scenario Hinoki median req/s (range, CV) Django Bolt median req/s (range, CV) Paired median ratio SQL calls/request (Hinoki / Bolt) Median p50 ms (Hinoki / Bolt) Median p99 ms (Hinoki / Bolt) list_20 4444.4 (4340.9-4492.7, 1.3%) 2342.2 (2289.1-2347.0, 1.0%) 1.90x 2.00 / 2.00 13.62 / 27.18 34.91 / 43.04 list_100 3860.4 (3843.6-5415.4, 19.1%) 2151.1 (1864.7-2160.4, 7.8%) 2.06x 2.00 / 2.00 14.51 / 28.58 35.67 / 58.00 detail 36700.3 (36062.4-36868.6, 0.9%) 6940.5 (6798.4-6953.3, 1.1%) 5.30x 1.00 / 1.00 1.61 / 8.86 4.35 / 17.92 create 6221.5 (5908.0-6468.7, 3.8%) 2561.0 (2412.8-2629.9, 3.3%) 2.45x 2.00 / 1.00 8.71 / 21.65 23.87 / 58.14 update 327.6 (267.9-357.5, 11.8%) 332.4 (191.5-375.0, 23.5%) 1.07x 3.04 / 2.02 168.48 / 155.92 647.31 / 362.09 The paired ratio is a descriptive ratio of the five pairwise throughput values. The samples are not a universal ranking and do not establish production performance. Host, OS, Python, server, ORM, driver, database, warm-cache state, and workload all affect these results. CV above 15% marks that scenario as unstable for interpretation; no sample is dropped. Raw oha JSON, per-sample start-load metadata and SQL stats, server logs, environment metadata, verifier output, request bodies, and the machine-readable summary are retained in benchmarks/comparative/results/2026-11-18/crud-phase1/ . Reproduction: build the native extension in release mode, start an isolated PostgreSQL 17 container, then run phase1_orientation.py as documented in benchmarks/README.md . The script refuses to time a sample whose starting load is above 1.0. Supplemental samples ¶ Because the initial list_100 Hinoki CV exceeded 15%, five additional alternating pairs (6-10) were collected separately. This block is not pooled into the primary table: Scenario Hinoki median req/s (range, CV) Django Bolt median req/s (range, CV) list_100, pairs 6-10 5088.4 (5073.4-5128.2, 0.4%) 2080.8 (2066.3-2085.8, 0.4%) The supplemental block is internally stable, while the initial Hinoki list_100 series remains unstable and shows a change in throughput regime. Treat both blocks as host-specific orientation data; the stable follow-up does not erase the initial variance. The supplemental update series stopped at Hinoki pair 7 after unsuccessful responses (status distribution: 200 = 3,554, 500 = 20). Its server log reports database connection acquisition timeouts. The failed sample and log are retained and excluded from throughput summaries; the initial update series remains volatile (Hinoki CV 11.8%, Django Bolt CV 23.5%).

docs.text: Collections and unions ¶ A field can hold list[X] , set[X] , frozenset[X] , tuple[X, ...] , tuple[X, Y] , dict[str, X] , a nested Schema , a TypedDict , a dataclass, a plain union, a discriminated union or Any . X is any supported type, so list[dict[str, int]] works. Error paths add [index] for items and .key for entries: rows[1][0].x , points.gate.x . Sets and tuples ¶ from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class Place ( Schema ): tags : Annotated [ set [ str ], Field ( max_length = 5 )] point : tuple [ float , float ] path : tuple [ int , ... ] = () place = Place . validate ({ "tags" : [ "a" , "b" , "a" ], "point" : [ 1.5 , 2 ]}) assert place . tags == { "a" , "b" } and place . point == ( 1.5 , 2.0 ) assert place . dump () == { "tags" : [ "a" , "b" ], "point" : [ 1.5 , 2.0 ], "path" : []} They travel as JSON arrays. Set duplicates collapse; length limits count the array as sent. A fixed tuple's length comes from its type and refuses Field(...) . Set items must be hashable (scalars, enums, tuples and frozensets of those). Bare set , tuple[()] and a misplaced ... raise RegistrationError . Construction takes exactly the declared container; to_dict() keeps it, dump() writes arrays (sets sorted when comparable). No model column type: store a list[X] (JSON) and build sets in the Schema . Served by the Python lane. OpenAPI: uniqueItems for sets; prefixItems , minItems , maxItems for fixed tuples. docs.text: Scalar field types ¶ A Schema field can be str , int , float , bool , UUID , datetime , date , time , timedelta , Decimal , bytes , an Enum class, a Literal , an ipaddress type, Email , Url , Slug , Secret or Path ; optionally | None (accepts null ) or | Unset , and wrapped in Annotated[..., Field(...)] . Containers, unions and nested types are in collections and unions . Anything else raises RegistrationError when the class is created. Numbers ¶ JSON input is strict: a float is never an integer, and bool is never a number. A float field always holds a float : JSON 1 becomes 1.0 , and Reading(value=1).value is 1.0 , also inside lists, sets, tuples and dict[str, float] . A float variant of a plain union keeps the value it was given. Multiples ¶ Field(multiple_of=step) requires an int or Decimal to be an exact whole multiple of a positive step. It runs after the bounds and fails with multiple_of . A float field refuses multiple_of (float multiples are inexact): use Decimal . from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class Order ( Schema ): quantity : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 0 , multiple_of = 5 )] price : Annotated [ Decimal , Field ( multiple_of = Decimal ( "0.05" ), max_digits = 8 )] Order . validate ({ "quantity" : 10 , "price" : "9.95" }) # accepted Order . validate ({ "quantity" : 12 , "price" : "9.97" }) # two multiple_of errors Enums and literals ¶ An Enum , StrEnum or IntEnum class, or a Literal of strings or of integers, accepts only its values. The wire carries the value; validation returns the member. import enum from typing import Literal from hinoki import Schema class Status ( enum . StrEnum ): DRAFT = "draft" SENT = "sent" class Priority ( enum . IntEnum ): LOW = 1 HIGH = 3 class Ticket ( Schema ): channel : Literal [ "web" , "email" ] status : Status = Status . DRAFT priority : Priority = Priority . LOW ticket = Ticket . validate ({ "channel" : "web" , "status" : "sent" , "priority" : 3 }) assert ticket . status is Status . SENT and ticket . priority is Priority . HIGH assert ticket . dump () == { "channel" : "web" , "status" : "sent" , "priority" : 3 } Strict values. "3" , 3.0 and True are not 3 . A wrong type answers type ; a value outside the list answers one_of , and the message lists the accepted values, never member names. One kind. All values are str or all int (64-bit). A mixed enum or Literal , None inside a Literal (write Literal["a"] | None ), a Flag , an empty enum, an enum member inside a Literal and other value types raise RegistrationError . Field(...) constraints are refused: the type is the list. Construction takes members for an enum field and the listed values for a Literal ; dump() writes values, to_dict() keeps members. Text sources read an IntEnum or int Literal like an int . Models. An Enum column stores the value; a Literal column has no SQL type: use an enum or str / int in the model and the Literal in the Schema . OpenAPI: type string or integer with an inline enum list. Dates, durations, decimals and bytes ¶ These travel as JSON strings and validate identically on both lanes. import datetime as dt from decimal import Decimal from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema class Booking ( Schema ): day : dt . date opens : dt . time length : dt . timedelta price : Annotated [ Decimal , Field ( ge = 0 , max_digits = 8 , decimal_places = 2 )] receipt : Annotated [ bytes , Field ( max_length = 1024 )] booking = Booking . validate ( { "day" : "2026-03-14" , "opens" : "09:30:00+01:00" , "length" : "PT1H30M" , "price" : "19.90" , "receipt" : "aGVsbG8=" , } ) assert booking . length == dt . timedelta ( hours = 1 , minutes = 30 ) assert booking . dump ()[ "price" ] == "19.90" Type Accepted input Output Error code date YYYY-MM-DD , a real date in years 0001–9999 same text date time HH:MM:SS[.f…] (1–6 fraction digits) with Z or ±HH:MM isoformat() time ; time_tz without offset timedelta ISO 8601 [-]P[nD][T[nH][nM][n[.f…]S]] ; no years, months or weeks PT1H30M , -PT0.5S duration ; duration_range Decimal string -?(0\|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.[0-9]+)? or integer; no floats, booleans, exponents, NaN , infinities fixed-point string keeping the scale ( "0.10" ) decimal bytes standard padded base64, no whitespace, not URL-safe padded base64 bytes Times need an offset on the wire, like a datetime ; from_model() accepts naive values. A date field refuses a datetime . Decimal is exact. ge , le , gt , lt take an int or Decimal . max_digits (default 64, at most 1000) counts all digits, decimal_places those after the point; checked in the order max_digits , decimal_places , max_whole_digits , bounds, multiple_of . bytes size. Lengths count decoded bytes. Without max_length , client input is capped at 65 536 bytes ( hinoki.fieldtypes.MAX_BYTES_LENGTH ); model-derived fields are not capped. pattern matches the decoded bytes read as Latin-1. Output. The JSON and XML encoders write these values in their wire form anywhere, including in a plain dict or at the top level; a JSONRenderer with a default hook passes them to the hook first outside a Schema . OpenAPI: format date , time , duration , decimal (with a pattern ) and byte ( contentEncoding: base64 ). Internet addresses, Email , Url and Slug ¶ from ipaddress import IPv4Address , IPv4Network from hinoki import Email , Schema , Url class Allowlist ( Schema ): owner : Email homepage : Url | None = None source : IPv4Address subnet : IPv4Network | None = None rule = Allowlist . validate ( { "owner" : "ops@example.com" , "source" : "10.0.0.7" , "subnet" : "10.0.0.0/24" } ) assert rule . source == IPv4Address ( "10.0.0.7" ) IPv4Address , IPv6Address , IPv4Network , IPv6Network read strict ASCII text and become the object (codes ipv4 , ipv6 , ipv4network , ipv6network ). IPv4 refuses leading zeros, IPv6 refuses zone ids, networks refuse host bits ( 10.0.0.7/24 ). Field(...) is refused. A union such as IPv4Address | IPv6Address takes either. Email , Url and Slug are Annotated[str, Field(format=...)] shortcuts; Email checks syntax, not deliverability. They work as model columns. Models store addresses as text and check the class before a write. Secret and Path ¶ from pathlib import Path from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , Secret class Account ( Schema ): password : Annotated [ Secret , Field ( min_length = 8 )] home : Path account = Account . validate ({ "password" : "correct horse" , "home" : "/srv/ann" }) assert account . password . reveal () == "correct horse" assert account . dump () == { "password" : "**********" , "home" : "/srv/ann" } Secret shows ********** in str , dump() and responses (its repr is Secret('**********') ); only reveal() returns the text, and errors never repeat it. Construction takes a str only; two secrets compare in constant time. It is the same type as settings.Secret , and JWTKey(key=...) and SessionSettings(csrf_secret=...) accept it. Path reads a non-empty string without NUL (at most 4096 characters without max_length ) and never touches the file system; code path . Both are served by the Python lane by design and have no model column type. OpenAPI: format: path ; a secret is format: password , writeOnly . See also ¶ Collections and unions Validate input OpenAPI

docs.text: Validate input ¶ A Schema validates in three stages: Rust checks types and Field(...) constraints, then @field_normalize canonicalizes values, then @field_check and @object_check reject what the rules forbid. All failures are returned together in errors.ValidationError.details , and a request answers 422. Built-in and custom validation ¶ # notes/apps/accounts/schemas.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Invalid , Schema , field_check , field_normalize , object_check Username = Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 , pattern = r "[a-z0-9_]+" )] class Registration ( Schema ): username : Username email : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "email" , max_length = 254 )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 , max_length = 128 )] confirmation : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 128 )] @field_normalize ( "email" ) def lowercase_email ( self , value : str ) -> str : return value . lower () @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "password_mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" ) Tool Runs Use for Field(...) first, in Rust lengths, pattern , numeric bounds, one_of , format ( email , url , slug , hex_color ) Field(strip=, lower=, upper=) before every other check trimming and case folding of str @field_normalize("f") after structural validation typed canonical form; the result is checked against the same constraints @field_check("f") after normalization rejecting one value @object_check after field checks rules across fields Checks raise Invalid(code, message, path=...) and return None ; a non- None return or an async method is a programming error. Normalizers are typed synchronous methods returning str ; they cannot reject input or rescue a value that failed structural validation. All three run for Schema.validate(...) , Schema(...) and from_model() . They never run on a Model : model writes have their own constraints and validators . No I/O and no side effects. Rules that depend on current data belong in an operation. Normalize text ¶ class Signup ( Schema ): handle : Annotated [ str , Field ( strip = True , lower = True , min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 )] Signup . validate ({ "handle" : " AbC " }) . handle # "abc" strip removes what str.strip() removes; lower and upper follow str.lower() / str.upper() . Constraints see the normalized text, and a custom normalizer receives it. Only str fields accept these options; lower and upper together, or a one_of value the normalization would change, raise RegistrationError . Results are the same on both lanes and for direct construction. The OpenAPI document describes the constraints, not the normalization. The result, the exceptions and dump(exclude_unset=True) are the same as on the Python path. Anything the plan does not vouch for (positional arguments, a value of a subclass type, an unknown or missing argument, a class that overrides _validate_instance , a validate of its own, or a graph with checks, normalizers or @before_validate ) runs the ordinary Python code. A default_factory whose result is rejected may be called a second time by that fallback. Consequences: field values are not in vars(instance) . A class can combine only one base that declares fields with slots; declare the others with slots=False : class Audited ( Schema , slots = False ): created_by : str class Ticket ( Audited ): title : str Without it, two field-bearing bases raise a RegistrationError that names slots=False . Rules that depend on current data belong in an operation.

docs.text: Schemas ¶ A Schema describes data that crosses the API boundary and validates it strictly. Models describe tables; a column reaches a client only when a Schema names it. # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py from datetime import datetime from typing import Annotated from uuid import UUID from hinoki import UNSET , Field , Schema , Unset class InvoiceIn ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] class InvoicePatch ( Schema ): reference : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 40 )] | Unset = UNSET paid : bool | Unset = UNSET class InvoiceOut ( Schema ): id : UUID reference : str paid : bool created_at : datetime Validation, construction and JSON serialization run in Rust. Validate input ¶ data = InvoiceIn . validate ({ "reference" : "INV-1" }) No coercion. "1" is not 1 . Text sources are the explicit exception: Schema.validate_text() , Form[...] , Query[...] and XML[...] first convert text to the int , float and bool the fields declare. Unknown keys are refused unless the class ignores them . Every problem is reported with its path, up to 50, in errors.ValidationError.details ; a request answers 422. Constraints, normalization and custom checks are in validate input . Supported field types are in scalar field types and collections and unions . Partial updates ¶ Declare a field X | Unset = UNSET . A field the client did not send stays UNSET and is left out of dump() and to_dict() , so await invoice.aupdate_from(patch) writes only what was sent. Convert to and from rows ¶ # inside an async operation invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data , customer_id = customer . id ) await invoice . aupdate_from ( patch ) out = InvoiceOut . from_model ( invoice ) outs = InvoiceOut . from_models ( rows ) Server keywords win over client values, and a Schema never carries the primary key. from_model(row, **extra) reads the expected attributes; relations must already be loaded. from_models(rows) converts a synchronous iterable to a list. See schemas from models . to_dict() returns Python values (UUID and datetime stay objects); dump() returns the JSON-compatible form. Both skip UNSET . Construct, change and project ¶ Schema(...) takes Python values ( UUID , aware datetime , nested Schema instances) and validates them immediately. Schema.validate(data) is the wire path: JSON-compatible input, aliases resolved, errors with wire names. from_model() validates too, but accepts the naive datetimes some drivers return. An instance is frozen. replace(**changes) returns a validated copy; an unknown name raises TypeError : card = InvoiceOut . validate ( payload ) paid = card . replace ( paid = True ) dump() projects to JSON-compatible data: out . dump ( exclude_unset = True ) out . dump ( include = { "id" , "reference" }) out . dump ( by_alias = False ) include and exclude take Python field names, top level only; exclusion wins. exclude_unset=True omits fields filled by defaults that the caller did not supply; explicit "" , None , 0 or False are kept. A custom __init__ makes it raise TypeError . With no options dump() honours custom dump() overrides; recursive options refuse a custom-dumped nested value. An override using the new options must accept the same keyword-only signature. A nested Schema is written as the type its field declares: a subclass instance held in a field inner: Public (or Public | None , list[Public] , dict[str, Public] , tuple[Public, ...] ) shows Public 's fields and computed values, never the fields its subclass added. An exact instance is written unchanged. A field typed Any or object has no declared schema and writes the value whole, and a declared class that overrides dump() decides its own shape. A @computed_field is narrowed by its return annotation. dump_for_storage (the cache) narrows the same way. The OpenAPI document already describes the declared type. Which positions are narrowed . Filtering a dump is not authorization and does not change the OpenAPI document: declare a Schema with only the fields the caller may see. dump and replace are reserved method names; a field with either name raises RegistrationError . Wire aliases ¶ # notes/apps/billing/schemas.py (continued) class CustomerOut ( Schema ): display_name : Annotated [ str , Field ( alias = "displayName" )] person = CustomerOut . validate ({ "displayName" : "Aki" }) assert person . dump () == { "displayName" : "Aki" } assert person . to_dict () == { "display_name" : "Aki" } The alias is the only accepted input key; sending both names is an error. dump() , validation errors and the OpenAPI document use wire names; a check's default path is translated, an explicit Invalid(path=...) is already a wire path. name: str = Field(alias="...") works too. Aliases are unique and cannot contain . , [ or ] . Models take no aliases. Document a field ¶ class TagOut ( Schema ): name : Annotated [ str , Field ( max_length = 40 , description = "Tag label." , examples = ( "priority" ,)) ] legacy : Annotated [ str | None , Field ( deprecated = True )] = None description , examples and deprecated appear in the OpenAPI document next to the property and change nothing about validation. Many-to-many ids fields ¶ derive(Post, only=("title", "tag_ids")) adds the ids field of a many_to_many relation when only= names it ( tag_ids here comes from ids_name="tag_ids" ; the default is tags_ids : a set of the target's keys with Field(max_length=max_items) ); derive(Post) and exclude= take columns only, so a derived Schema never carries the field unless it is asked for. The field holds keys only: Hinoki never loads related rows while a Schema is serialized, so a read needs prefetch_related first (generated CRUD does it, and from_model reads the loaded keys). See many-to-many fields . Computed fields ¶ from hinoki import computed_field class CustomerCard ( Schema ): first : str last : str @computed_field ( alias = "displayName" , description = "First and last name" ) def full_name ( self ) -> str : return f " { self . first } { self . last } " CustomerCard(first="Ada", last="Lovelace").dump() includes "displayName": "Ada Lovelace" . Computed values are output only: they follow the declared fields in dump() and responses (both lanes), are readOnly in OpenAPI, are left out of to_dict() , and a client that sends one gets an unknown-field error. The method takes only self and needs a return annotation; a name clash with a field is a RegistrationError . computed_fields() returns them; subclasses inherit them. Class configuration ¶ from hinoki import SchemaConfig , SchemaExtra class VendorEvent ( Schema , config = SchemaConfig ( extra = SchemaExtra . IGNORE )): event_id : str revision : int SchemaExtra.IGNORE discards unknown keys in decoded input and request bodies; declared fields stay strict, and ignored values are never stored or dumped. Constructor keywords and from_model(..., **extra) keep their strict signatures; each nested Schema uses its own configuration. The OpenAPI document marks the schema additionalProperties: true . Generic schemas ¶ from hinoki import http from notes.security import reader # an `Access` policy class Envelope [ T ]( Schema ): data : T count : int = 0 @http . get ( "/me" , access = reader ) async def me () -> Envelope [ CustomerOut ]: return Envelope [ CustomerOut ]( data = CustomerOut ( display_name = "Ada" )) Envelope[CustomerOut] is a cached Schema subclass with its own OpenAPI component ( Envelope_CustomerOut_ ). The bare Envelope cannot validate or be a field; self-referencing generics and generic subclasses of generic schemas raise RegistrationError . Scope and non-goals ¶ Schema is designed for typed data at the HTTP/JSON and ORM boundary. The following are intentionally out of scope: Arbitrary Python types. Every field type has a defined wire representation and OpenAPI schema object. Application-only objects stay outside the wire Schema . Implicit lossy coercion. JSON input is validated strictly ( "1" is not 1 ). Only explicit text sources ( validate_text() , Form[...] , Query[...] , XML[...] ) convert text to typed fields; reshape legacy input with @before_validate . Mutable instances. Instances are frozen; call replace(...) for a validated copy. Stateful or I/O-performing validation and serialization. Checks, normalizers, @before_validate and @computed_field are synchronous and perform no I/O. Rules that depend on stored data belong in an operation. A validator plugin system. Extend validation with @before_validate , @field_normalize , @field_check and @object_check on the Schema . docs.text: Serve an application ¶ From the project directory: hinoki dev hinoki serve hinoki dev reloads on every change while you work; hinoki serve runs without reload, with the workers your settings ask for. Both read the application from project.application in hinoki.toml . To run another application, pass its target: module:app , such as hinoki dev notes.main:app . A function callable without arguments that returns an application (a factory) is also accepted. On Kiso, when the application sets docs_url , hinoki dev prints the address of the documentation page under the listening on line, for example docs: http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs , with the address in the brand colour on a terminal that takes colour (plain text in a pipe, in CI or with NO_COLOR set); nothing is printed when docs_url is unset. hinoki serve prints it too when it runs a supervisor (more than one worker), but not with a single worker, which runs in the command's own process. Each worker imports the target, then opens what the application owns (database pool, modules) in its lifespan and closes it on shutdown. Importing your code never opens a connection. See database connection ownership . The adapter drives the same ASGI callable on a background event loop that it owns, so routing, binding, access, errors, limits and the OpenAPI document behave as under ASGI. Specifics: Startup is lazy under Granian (Kiso starts them with the worker). Modules (including the database pool) start on the first request of each worker process, so a pre-forking server can import the file in its master process. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop. Bodies are buffered. Request bodies are read up to max_body_bytes plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers 413 . A percent-encoded slash ( %2F ) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad Content-Length answers 400 . One protocol per process. Apply migrations once per deployment, from one process, not from every worker's startup. Set workers and the connection limits for the machine, and check GET /health after the rollout. Build the application at import time instead, as in wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter(create_app()) . A Kiso-only setting under --server granian exits with status 2 and names the setting. A server that kills workers without exiting normally skips it, as it would any atexit hook. Async handlers run on the adapter's loop and sync handlers on the bounded executor, as under ASGI. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop. Bodies are buffered. Request bodies are read up to max_body_bytes plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers 413 . On Kiso the bytes of the bodies being read are bounded by what the threads and the queue could hold ( (threads + queue) * max_body_bytes ); a request that would pass it answers 503 before its body is read. Responses are complete before they are sent: an application with an action that returns Stream , EventStream or File is refused when the adapter starts ( WSGIStartupError naming the actions; serve it with ASGI or Kiso, see streaming ), and a client disconnect is not reported to the handler. Paths. The server decodes the path once and the adapter passes it on without decoding again, so a client's %2520 reaches the handler as %20 , as under ASGI. A percent-encoded slash ( %2F ) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad Content-Length answers 400 . One protocol per process. Do not serve the same application object over ASGI and WSGI in one process; the adapter owns its own loop and module lifespan. Run two processes if you need both. The path is checked against Kiso and Granian ( --interface wsgi , with one and two workers) by a parity test, not against every WSGI server.
docs.title: WSGI on Kiso

docs.text: Before the first deployment: Run uv run hinoki check and uv run pytest ; both must pass. Set debug off and narrow allowed_hosts to your host names. Serve over HTTPS, with the TLS files or a proxy listed in trusted_proxies . Give secrets ( Secret settings, cursor_secret ) through the environment, never the repository. Apply migrations once per deployment, from one process, not from every worker's startup. Set workers and the connection limits for the machine, and check GET /health after the rollout.

docs.text: Application sessions ¶ Application sessions keep small JSON state on the server and identify it with a random cookie token. The raw token is sent to the client; the store keeps only its SHA-256 digest. This is separate from the optional admin's session table and cookie. Configure a store explicitly. The CSRF key must be at least 32 bytes; keep it in a secret setting or environment variable, and configure the same value on every worker: from collections.abc import Mapping from hinoki import Access , Caller , Hinoki , http from hinoki.sessions import ( DatabaseSessionStore , Session , SessionAuth , SessionModule , SessionSettings , ) session_settings = SessionSettings ( csrf_secret = secret_from_environment ) @http . post ( "/login" ) async def login ( session : Session ) -> dict [ str , str ]: user = await verify_credentials () await session . rotate () # issue a fresh token after authentication session [ "user_id" ] = str ( user . id ) session . subject = str ( user . id ) return { "status" : "signed_in" } def resolve_user ( data : Mapping [ str , object ]) -> Caller [ User ] | None : user_id = data . get ( "user_id" ) return load_caller ( user_id ) if isinstance ( user_id , str ) else None session_auth = SessionAuth ( resolve_user ) @http . get ( "/me" , access = Access ( auth = session_auth )) async def me ( caller : Caller [ User ]) -> UserSchema : return UserSchema . from_user ( caller . user ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ login , me ], modules = [ SessionModule ( DatabaseSessionStore (), session_settings )], ) csrf_secret takes bytes , text or a settings.Secret (encoded as UTF-8) of at least 32 bytes; it is left out of the settings' repr and comparisons, and settings.csrf_key() returns the bytes. SessionAuth resolves a Caller from the read-only session data and works with Access and Caller[T] . It documents the configured cookie name as an OpenAPI cookie security scheme. If SessionSettings.cookie_name is customized, pass the same name to SessionAuth(cookie_name=...) . SessionModule(store, settings) requires its SessionSettings . A custom Auth that composes SessionAuth (for example, one that tries a bearer token and then the session) is detected automatically: Hinoki loads the session and applies the CSRF rules below. Set uses_session = True on an Auth class that reads the session in another way. SessionAuth also works on @http.websocket routes. The session is loaded read-only during the handshake, and an unknown or expired cookie refuses the connection. The handshake Origin is checked by the websocket origin rules. State and response lifecycle ¶ Session is request-scoped. It provides get , item lookup and assignment, del session[key] , clear , rotate , invalidate , csrf_token , is_new , modified and subject . Values must be JSON serializable; the default encoded payload limit is 16 KiB. None is a normal value inside the mapping. Nested values returned by reads are copies; assign the updated value back through session[key] to persist a nested change. Hinoki loads a session when a route declares session: Session or uses SessionAuth . Mutations are saved and Set-Cookie is added only after the handler returns successfully (that is, without raising an exception) and after any atomic=True SQL transaction has committed, so a session store failure does not roll back an already-committed SQL transaction. A returned Response with an error status is still a successful handler return. If the handler raises, pending changes and cookie changes are discarded. rotate() issues a fresh token and revokes the old one on successful response; use it on login and privilege changes to prevent fixation. invalidate() revokes the current token and sends a clearing cookie. Revocations are retained until the session's absolute expiry, so an already-running request cannot restore a revoked token with a stale write. MemorySessionStore drops a revoked session's data immediately and keeps only a bounded record of revoked tokens. The cookie defaults to HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , Secure , and Path=/ . cookie_secure=False is available for local HTTP development. The absolute timeout defaults to 14 days and the idle timeout to one day. A successful request refreshes the idle expiry after the 60-second touch interval. Missing, malformed and expired cookies start as an anonymous session; they do not emit a cookie unless the handler changes the session. CSRF ¶ Unsafe methods ( POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE , QUERY ) on a route that uses a session or SessionAuth require a valid X-CSRF-Token when the request carries an existing session cookie. The token is an HMAC-SHA256 value bound to that session; session.csrf_token() returns it for a frontend to place in the header. When Origin is present it must match the request origin, and an explicit Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site or none is rejected. GET , HEAD and OPTIONS are safe methods. For example, a page or JSON bootstrap action can return session.csrf_token() ; the browser then sends that value in X-CSRF-Token for writes. A missing or invalid token receives 403 csrf_rejected . Store failures fail closed with 503 session_unavailable ; a session is never silently treated as anonymous when the store is down. The bootstrap action must establish a token before asking for the CSRF value: @http . get ( "/csrf" ) async def csrf_bootstrap ( session : Session ) -> dict [ str , str ]: if session . is_new : await session . rotate () return { "csrf_token" : session . csrf_token ()} The successful response persists the session and sends its cookie; subsequent unsafe requests can send the returned CSRF token with that cookie. Stores, migrations and limits ¶ Store Visibility and ownership Capacity and cleanup MemorySessionStore(max_sessions=10_000) Per worker process; workers do not share sessions Bounded by session count; it removes expired sessions and returns 503 when full of live or revoked sessions DatabaseSessionStore() Shared by workers through the application's Database No configured row cap; call purge_expired() from a scheduled maintenance task DatabaseSessionStore depends on DatabaseModule when it is not given a database directly. It expects the hinoki_sessions table. Apply the SQL at migrations_path() / "0001-initial.sql" through an explicit project migration and review/apply that migration before starting the application. Importing the module and starting the worker do not create or alter tables. purge_expired() deletes rows past their absolute expiry, including revoked token tombstones; revoked rows remain until that expiry. The database store keeps JSON session data as plain text, so do not put secrets in session values unless the application encrypts them before storage or the database's at-rest protections meet its policy. Sessions identify a subject for revocation with delete_by_subject ; they do not implement user ownership or authorization by themselves. The application still owns account checks and permission policy. Database cleanup is explicit; Hinoki does not start a background purge task. SessionTooLarge is a 413 response. A malformed store row or database failure is reported as SessionUnavailable (503) without exposing the token, SQL or stored data. Session migrations and revocation are distinct from file storage and cache migrations.
