docs.text: Configure an application with settings ¶ Settings are typed, immutable classes. You declare the fields your application needs; Hinoki adds the groups every application has, reads values from the environment, .env and TOML once, and refuses to start when something is wrong. # notes/settings.py from typing import Literal from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings support_email : str = "support@example.com" stripe_key : settings . Secret | None = None theme : Literal [ "light" , "dark" ] = "light" notes/main.py passes the class with Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) , which loads it while building the application. Your fields are then on app.settings , and modules read them as ctx.settings . Declare fields ¶ A field without a default is required. Use plain types ( str , int , bool , tuple[str, ...] , Literal[...] , X | None ), settings.Secret for anything confidential, and a settings.Settings subclass for a group of your own. Settings types live in the hinoki.settings namespace ( settings.AppSettings , settings.DatabaseSettings , settings.Secret , settings.Settings , settings.SettingsError ); name your loaded value app_settings so the namespace is not shadowed. settings.AppSettings brings the built-in groups: execution , lifecycle , logging , docs , server , pagination , cors , compression , metrics , security , events and admin , plus timezone , debug and allowed_hosts (see Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url , docs.redoc_url and docs.llms_url default to None ; the generated main.py passes openapi_url and docs_url as Hinoki(...) arguments, which win over settings; the other two stay off. llms_url must start with / . Built-in fields and defaults ¶ Group Field Default Constraint or effect execution sync_workers 8 1 to 1024 worker threads execution sync_queue 64 0 or greater queued calls execution request_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive; request expiry returns 504 execution max_body_bytes 1048576 (1 MiB) 1 to 1073741824 bytes; larger request bodies return 413 execution max_query_bytes 8192 (8 KiB) 1 to 1048576 raw query-string bytes; larger queries return 414 execution max_header_bytes 32768 (32 KiB) 1 to 1048576 combined header bytes; larger headers return 431 execution max_streams 64 1 or greater; streams open at once per worker, more answer 503 with Retry-After: 1 before the handler runs execution stream_idle_timeout None (uses request_timeout ) Must be positive; seconds a Stream may stay silent before it is cut execution sse_keepalive 15.0 seconds Must be positive; quiet seconds before an EventStream sends a comment ( keepalive=None on the stream turns it off) execution max_websockets 1000 1 or greater; open WebSocket connections per worker (Kiso), more are refused with 503 before the upgrade execution ws_max_message_bytes 1048576 (1 MiB) 1 to 1073741824 ; a larger WebSocket message closes the connection with 1009 execution ws_queue 64 1 or greater; messages queued in each direction of a WebSocket (Kiso) execution ws_ping_interval 20.0 seconds Must be positive, or None to send no pings (Kiso) execution ws_pong_timeout 20.0 seconds Must be positive; a peer that does not answer a ping in time is dropped (Kiso) execution ws_close_timeout 5.0 seconds Must be positive; how long a WebSocket close handshake may take (Kiso) lifecycle startup_timeout 30.0 seconds Must be positive lifecycle shutdown_timeout 10.0 seconds Must be positive logging level info debug , info , warning , error or critical logging format text text or json logging config unset module:attribute of a logging.config.dictConfig mapping (or a function returning one) for your own loggers, handlers and formatters logging include_request_id false Add the active request ID to Hinoki log records for request correlation docs title Hinoki API OpenAPI info title docs version 0.1.0 OpenAPI info version docs openapi_url None JSON document route; disabled when None docs docs_url None Swagger UI route; requires openapi_url docs redoc_url None ReDoc route; requires openapi_url docs llms_url None llms.txt route; does not need openapi_url docs openapi_version 3.2 3.2 or 3.1 : the document's openapi version; Hinoki(openapi_version=...) overrides it. See the document version server server kiso granian or kiso ; --server overrides it. See Kiso server server interface asgi asgi or wsgi : what hinoki serve calls (a Hinoki application or a WSGI callable); --interface overrides it. See WSGI pagination page_size 20 Page size an action's PageNumberPagination() leaves out; 1 to max_page_size . See Pagination pagination max_page_size 100 Largest page_size a client may ask for pagination cursor_secret , cursor_ttl_seconds unset settings.Secret of at least 32 bytes that signs cursors, and an optional lifetime in seconds; see Pagination events handler_timeout 5.0 seconds Must be positive; seconds each handler may run. See Events events max_handlers 16 1 or greater; handlers per event and phase events max_depth 4 1 or greater; how deep handlers may emit events server host 127.0.0.1 Bind address used by hinoki dev/serve server port 8000 1 to 65535 server workers 1 1 to 256 ; dev uses one worker for reload server runtime_threads 1 Must be positive server backlog 1024 Must be positive server access_log unset One line per request on either server. Unset logs in hinoki dev only (or whenever access_log_format is set); true or false decides for dev and serve server access_log_skip unset Kiso only: paths the log leaves out, exact or a * prefix; failures are still logged server server_timing unset Kiso only: add a Server-Timing header with the time taken and the serving lane; unset means hinoki dev only, so browser developer tools show it server sighup unset Kiso only, hinoki serve : "reload" (also what unset means) replaces the workers one at a time on SIGHUP , "stop" stops the server instead; see reload on SIGHUP server reuse_port unset Kiso only: on Linux, multi-worker hinoki serve on a non-zero port gives each worker its own SO_REUSEPORT socket; false forces one shared listening descriptor everywhere; refused under Granian server recent_requests unset Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line for hinoki mcp 's recent_requests tool; works with the access log off server access_log_slow_ms unset Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow (ms); failures are still logged server access_log_format unset Kiso only (Granian refuses it): pretty , plain , json or logger (route to the hinoki.access Python logger). Unset is pretty on a colour terminal and plain otherwise server max_connections unset (10000) Kiso only: open-connection limit, 1 to 1000000 ; refused under Granian server header_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: time to receive request headers, and the keep-alive idle limit; refused under Granian server body_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: silence allowed while a body is read (at most half of execution.request_timeout ); refused under Granian server write_timeout unset (30 seconds) Kiso only: how long a response write may make no progress before the connection is closed; above 0 and at most 3600; refused under Granian server native_dispatch unset (on) Kiso only: run the async def handlers it can prove safe without an asyncio task (see the native handler lane ); false keeps every handler in an asyncio task; refused under Granian server tls_cert_file , tls_key_file unset PEM certificate chain and private key; both or neither, and both must exist. Serves HTTPS on either server; Kiso reads them once at start server http2 false Serve HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN h2 , with http/1.1 as fallback); needs tls_cert_file and tls_key_file , otherwise refused when settings load. No cleartext HTTP/2; on either server server trusted_proxies empty IP addresses or CIDRs allowed to supply forwarded client/protocol metadata; an IPv6 zone id ( fe80::1%lo0 ) is refused when settings load, whichever server runs server request_id_header x-request-id HTTP header used for generated request IDs; other framework-owned names are refused server trust_request_id false Accept a validated inbound ID only from a peer in trusted_proxies cors origins empty Allowed browser origins ( scheme://host[:port] ), or the single entry * ; empty disables CORS cors methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, QUERY Methods a preflight allows cors headers authorization, content-type Request headers a preflight allows cors expose_headers empty Response headers a browser script may read cors credentials false Allow cookies and HTTP authentication; refused together with * cors max_age 600 seconds 0 to 86400 ; how long a browser may cache a preflight compression enabled false Compress responses with brotli or gzip; Kiso only ( serve --server granian refuses it). The other compression fields are in compress responses metrics listen unset host:port of the Prometheus metrics listener; Kiso only ( serve --server granian refuses it). The other metrics fields are in export Prometheus metrics admin secret unset The server secret (32+ bytes, from the environment or *_FILE ) that keys the admin's CSRF tokens; an admin without its own secret= needs it admin session_hours 12 1 to 720 ; a signed-in admin session ends this long after sign-in, whatever else happens admin idle_minutes 120 1 to session_hours * 60 ; ... or this long after its last request admin min_password_length 12 8 to 128 ; the shortest password the admin's own users may have admin theme unset A built-in admin theme name ( studio , console , paper , bento ) used by an Admin without its own theme= ; an unknown name is refused when the settings load security redirect_https false Send known HTTP requests to HTTPS with 308 ; requires explicit allowed_hosts security hsts_seconds 0 0 to 63072000 ; emit HSTS only when the effective scheme is HTTPS security hsts_include_subdomains false Add includeSubDomains ; requires nonzero hsts_seconds security hsts_preload false Add preload ; requires subdomains and at least one year of HSTS security frame_options sameorigin settings.FrameOptions.DENY or .SAMEORIGIN security referrer_policy same-origin A supported settings.ReferrerPolicy enum value (top level) timezone UTC IANA timezone name used by app.now() (top level) debug false Adds exception details to 500 answers; development only (top level) allowed_hosts * Host names, .domain or * ; other Host values receive 400 ; * with debug off refuses to start an app that includes the admin or a WebSocket route; with debug on, such an app accepts loopback hosts only ( localhost , *.localhost , 127.0.0.0/8 , [::1] ) settings.DatabaseSettings is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a settings.AppSettings group. Its url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; max_size defaults to 10 connections per worker and must be at least 1 . settings.EmailSettings is optional in the same way: an email: settings.EmailSettings field installs the email module . Its backend ( smtp , console or memory ) is required and has no default; password is a Secret ( NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD or NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD_FILE ). Every field, its default and its range are in send email . Where values come from ¶ load is the only place configuration is read; Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) calls it for you. Highest first: Source Example overrides= in code (tests) ProjectSettings.load(overrides={"theme": "dark"}) the process environment NOTES_THEME=dark a *_FILE variable (container secrets) NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe the .env file the class names NOTES_THEME=dark in .env the TOML file the class names theme = "dark" in settings.toml the default in the class theme: ... = "light" Name a TOML file on the class with toml="settings.toml" (a project created with --server granian already does). Tables map to groups: [database] with max_size = 12 sets database.max_size . TOML cannot hold settings.Secret values or the database URL; keep those in the environment or *_FILE files. load(prefix=..., dotenv=..., toml=...) overrides what the class declared. A TOML file named on the class or passed to load must exist and parse (an empty file is fine); a missing .env is skipped. Relative .env and TOML paths resolve from the current directory, so start the server from the project root. Load the class yourself when module code needs a typed value before the application exists: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from notes.settings import ProjectSettings settings = ProjectSettings . load () app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , title = f "Notes ( { settings . theme } )" ) Routes, events, middleware and rules come from hinoki.toml , so Hinoki(...) needs no include= , events= or rules= here. Variable names ¶ The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a double underscore. Field Variable support_email NOTES_SUPPORT_EMAIL stripe_key NOTES_STRIPE_KEY database.url NOTES_DATABASE__URL execution.sync_workers NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS logging.format NOTES_LOGGING__FORMAT Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no 1_000 , no 0x10 ), booleans are true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 , lists are comma separated (use tuple[str, ...] to keep them immutable), Literal[...] takes one of its choices, and an empty value for X | None means None . Mistakes fail at startup, all at once ¶ A variable that starts with your prefix and looks like one of your settings but names no field is an error (a typo guard; strict=False turns it off). It looks like a setting when its first word starts a field's variable ( NOTES_DATABASE_URL , NOTES_SERVER__PROT ) or when it is spelt close to one ( NOTES_THEMES ). Other variables that only share the prefix belong to another program and are ignored: systemd's JOURNAL_STREAM does not break a project whose prefix is JOURNAL_ . A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and every problem is listed together , with variable names and reasons but never values: invalid settings: NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer NOTES_DATABASE__MAX_SIZE: must be an integer NOTES_THEMES: unknown setting Keep secrets secret ¶ Declare them as settings.Secret (or settings.Secret | None ). A settings.Secret (the same type as hinoki.Secret ) prints as ********** in repr , str , logs and error messages, and as *** in describe() and the settings command; you get the real text only with secret.reveal() , at the one place that needs it (where the payment client is built: app_settings.stripe_key.reveal() ). Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or files : with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe ; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error. A .env file is for development; never commit it. Pickling or serialising a settings object stores its secrets in plain text, so don't. A validate() method you add to a group shows its message in errors, so never put a field's value in it. See what is in effect ¶ hinoki settings NOTES_DATABASE__URL environment *** NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS default 8 NOTES_STRIPE_KEY file *** NOTES_THEME .env dark The second column is where each value came from: override , environment , .env , toml , file or default . The command reads the prefix, .env and TOML file the class declares; --prefix , --dotenv and --toml override them. --format json prints the same for tools, and --example writes a ready .env.example : every variable with its default and type, required values blank to fill in, and the optional ones with no printable default (secrets such as the database URL, values that default to unset) commented out, so a copied file keeps their defaults: hinoki settings --example > .env.example Logging and your own loggers ¶ Declare loggers, handlers and formatters with a standard logging.config.dictConfig mapping, and point logging.config at it: # notes/logs.py LOGGING = { "version" : 1 , "formatters" : { "short" : { "format" : " %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s " }}, "handlers" : { "console" : { "class" : "logging.StreamHandler" , "formatter" : "short" }}, "loggers" : { "orders" : { "handlers" : [ "console" ], "level" : "INFO" }}, } NOTES_LOGGING__CONFIG = notes.logs:LOGGING The value may also name a function that returns the mapping. It is applied when each worker starts, right after Hinoki's own hinoki logger setup, with disable_existing_loggers off unless your mapping sets it. A mapping that configures the hinoki logger replaces Hinoki's handler on it. A target that cannot be imported or is not a mapping raises during startup. Kiso's access log is written by Kiso; set server.access_log_format = "logger" to route it through the hinoki.access logger. Database connection ownership ¶ A database: settings.DatabaseSettings field is all it takes: Hinoki installs DatabaseModule for it (a module declared in modules= replaces it). With nothing configured, the URL is the local SQLite file sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 , and the module creates its hidden directory and file when it starts. Configure a database covers the URL, the connection fields, TLS and each backend. The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if the database is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. Nothing connects when modules or models are imported. Each worker owns its own pool, so budget replicas × workers × max_size against the server database's connection limit. One-off scripts have a different lifecycle: they open a short-lived Database themselves ( use the database from a script ). examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/seed.py does so, applies migrations, inserts synthetic rows and closes the pool in finally . It is a one-time seed for a fresh disposable database, not a repeatable reset: cd examples/blog export BLOG_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://app:password@localhost/blog uv run python -m blog.apps.blog.seed Use a disposable database for the example. The seed command is not a production migration mechanism and is not run at app startup. Errors and edge cases ¶ Setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error; only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read. A variable with your prefix that looks like a setting (same first word, or a close spelling) but names no field is an error; other variables that only share the prefix, such as JOURNAL_STREAM , are ignored. Pass strict=False to load to turn the check off. The server group is applied by hinoki dev and hinoki serve , not by other ASGI servers ( Serving ). See also ¶ Hosts, CORS and HTTPS Own resources with modules Configure a database
docs.title: Settings

docs.text: Settings are typed, immutable classes. You declare the fields your application needs; Hinoki adds the groups every application has, reads values from the environment, .env and TOML once, and refuses to start when something is wrong. # notes/settings.py from typing import Literal from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings support_email : str = "support@example.com" stripe_key : settings . Secret | None = None theme : Literal [ "light" , "dark" ] = "light" notes/main.py passes the class with Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) , which loads it while building the application. Your fields are then on app.settings , and modules read them as ctx.settings .
docs.title: Configure an application with settings

docs.text: A field without a default is required. Use plain types ( str , int , bool , tuple[str, ...] , Literal[...] , X | None ), settings.Secret for anything confidential, and a settings.Settings subclass for a group of your own. Settings types live in the hinoki.settings namespace ( settings.AppSettings , settings.DatabaseSettings , settings.Secret , settings.Settings , settings.SettingsError ); name your loaded value app_settings so the namespace is not shadowed. settings.AppSettings brings the built-in groups: execution , lifecycle , logging , docs , server , pagination , cors , compression , metrics , security , events and admin , plus timezone , debug and allowed_hosts (see Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). docs.openapi_url , docs.docs_url , docs.redoc_url and docs.llms_url default to None ; the generated main.py passes openapi_url and docs_url as Hinoki(...) arguments, which win over settings; the other two stay off. llms_url must start with / .

seconds a Stream may stay silent before it is cut execution sse_keepalive 15.0 seconds Must be positive; quiet seconds before an EventStream sends a comment ( keepalive=None on the stream turns it off) execution max_websockets 1000 1 or greater; Unset is pretty on a colour terminal and plain otherwise server max_connections unset (10000) Kiso only: open-connection limit, 1 to 1000000 ; refused under Granian server header_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: time to receive request headers, and the keep-alive idle limit; refused under Granian server body_read_timeout unset (10 seconds) Kiso only: silence allowed while a body is read (at most half of execution.request_timeout ); refused under Granian server write_timeout unset (30 seconds) Kiso only: how long a response write may make no progress before the connection is closed; above 0 and at most 3600; refused under Granian server native_dispatch unset (on) Kiso only: run the async def handlers it can prove safe without an asyncio task (see the native handler lane ); false keeps every handler in an asyncio task; refused under Granian server tls_cert_file , tls_key_file unset PEM certificate chain and private key; both or neither, and both must exist. Serves HTTPS on either server; Kiso reads them once at start server http2 false Serve HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN h2 , with http/1.1 as fallback); needs tls_cert_file and tls_key_file , otherwise refused when settings load. No cleartext HTTP/2; on either server server trusted_proxies empty IP addresses or CIDRs allowed to supply forwarded client/protocol metadata; an IPv6 zone id ( fe80::1%lo0 ) is refused when settings load, whichever server runs server request_id_header x-request-id HTTP header used for generated request IDs; other framework-owned names are refused server trust_request_id false Accept a validated inbound ID only from a peer in trusted_proxies cors origins empty Allowed browser origins ( scheme://host[:port] ), or the single entry * ; empty disables CORS cors methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, QUERY Methods a preflight allows cors headers authorization, content-type Request headers a preflight allows cors expose_headers empty Response headers a browser script may read cors credentials false Allow cookies and HTTP authentication; refused together with * cors max_age 600 seconds 0 to 86400 ; how long a browser may cache a preflight compression enabled false Compress responses with brotli or gzip; Kiso only ( serve --server granian refuses it). The other compression fields are in compress responses metrics listen unset host:port of the Prometheus metrics listener; Kiso only ( serve --server granian refuses it). The other metrics fields are in export Prometheus metrics admin secret unset The server secret (32+ bytes, from the environment or *_FILE ) that keys the admin's CSRF tokens; an admin without its own secret= needs it admin session_hours 12 1 to 720 ; a signed-in admin session ends this long after sign-in, whatever else happens admin idle_minutes 120 1 to session_hours * 60 ; ... or this long after its last request admin min_password_length 12 8 to 128 ; the shortest password the admin's own users may have admin theme unset A built-in admin theme name ( studio , console , paper , bento ) used by an Admin without its own theme= ; an unknown name is refused when the settings load security redirect_https false Send known HTTP requests to HTTPS with 308 ; requires explicit allowed_hosts security hsts_seconds 0 0 to 63072000 ; emit HSTS only when the effective scheme is HTTPS security hsts_include_subdomains false Add includeSubDomains ; requires nonzero hsts_seconds security hsts_preload false Add preload ; requires subdomains and at least one year of HSTS security frame_options sameorigin settings.FrameOptions.DENY or .SAMEORIGIN security referrer_policy same-origin A supported settings.ReferrerPolicy enum value (top level) timezone UTC IANA timezone name used by app.now() (top level) debug false Adds exception details to 500 answers; development only (top level) allowed_hosts * Host names, .domain or * ; other Host values receive 400 ; * with debug off refuses to start an app that includes the admin or a WebSocket route; with debug on, such an app accepts loopback hosts only ( localhost , *.localhost , 127.0.0.0/8 , [::1] ) settings.DatabaseSettings is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a settings.AppSettings group. Its url defaults to sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3 ; max_size defaults to 10 connections per worker and must be at least 1 . settings.EmailSettings is optional in the same way: an email: settings.EmailSettings field installs the email module . Its backend ( smtp , console or memory ) is required and has no default; password is a Secret ( NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD or NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD_FILE ). Every field, its default and its range are in send email .

docs.text: load is the only place configuration is read; Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings) calls it for you. Highest first: Source Example overrides= in code (tests) ProjectSettings.load(overrides={"theme": "dark"}) the process environment NOTES_THEME=dark a *_FILE variable (container secrets) NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe the .env file the class names NOTES_THEME=dark in .env the TOML file the class names theme = "dark" in settings.toml the default in the class theme: ... = "light" Name a TOML file on the class with toml="settings.toml" (a project created with --server granian already does). Tables map to groups: [database] with max_size = 12 sets database.max_size . TOML cannot hold settings.Secret values or the database URL; keep those in the environment or *_FILE files. load(prefix=..., dotenv=..., toml=...) overrides what the class declared. A TOML file named on the class or passed to load must exist and parse (an empty file is fine); a missing .env is skipped. Relative .env and TOML paths resolve from the current directory, so start the server from the project root. Load the class yourself when module code needs a typed value before the application exists: # notes/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from notes.settings import ProjectSettings settings = ProjectSettings . load () app = Hinoki ( settings = settings , title = f "Notes ( { settings . theme } )" ) Routes, events, middleware and rules come from hinoki.toml , so Hinoki(...) needs no include= , events= or rules= here.

docs.text: The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a double underscore. Field Variable support_email NOTES_SUPPORT_EMAIL stripe_key NOTES_STRIPE_KEY database.url NOTES_DATABASE__URL execution.sync_workers NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS logging.format NOTES_LOGGING__FORMAT Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no 1_000 , no 0x10 ), booleans are true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0 , lists are comma separated (use tuple[str, ...] to keep them immutable), Literal[...] takes one of its choices, and an empty value for X | None means None .

docs.text: A variable that starts with your prefix and looks like one of your settings but names no field is an error (a typo guard; strict=False turns it off). It looks like a setting when its first word starts a field's variable ( NOTES_DATABASE_URL , NOTES_SERVER__PROT ) or when it is spelt close to one ( NOTES_THEMES ). Other variables that only share the prefix belong to another program and are ignored: systemd's JOURNAL_STREAM does not break a project whose prefix is JOURNAL_ . A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and every problem is listed together , with variable names and reasons but never values: invalid settings: NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer NOTES_DATABASE__MAX_SIZE: must be an integer NOTES_THEMES: unknown setting

docs.text: Declare them as settings.Secret (or settings.Secret | None ). A settings.Secret (the same type as hinoki.Secret ) prints as ********** in repr , str , logs and error messages, and as *** in describe() and the settings command; you get the real text only with secret.reveal() , at the one place that needs it (where the payment client is built: app_settings.stripe_key.reveal() ). Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or files : with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe ; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both NOTES_STRIPE_KEY and NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE is an error. A .env file is for development; never commit it. docs.text: Explore an application in the shell ¶ hinoki shell opens Python with your application loaded and its database connected, so you can try queries against real data: uv run hinoki shell >>> await Note . filter ( body = "" ) . acount () 3 >>> [ note . title for note in await Note . all ()] ['Ship it', 'Ship the docs', 'Ship the tests'] >>> settings . database . url Secret('***') What is in the namespace ¶ Name Value app the application from hinoki.toml ( [project] application ) settings its validated settings model classes every concrete model of every registered app, by class name ( Note , …) Two models with the same class name in different apps stop the shell before the prompt; select the modules you need with --models . A model may not be called app or settings . Await at the prompt ¶ The shell keeps one event loop for the session, so top-level await and multiline statements work. Use the async ORM methods ( acount() , aget() , awaiting a query): the synchronous ones are meant for def handlers and cannot block the shell's loop. Choose the application and models ¶ uv run hinoki shell --models notes.apps.notes.models uv run hinoki shell notes.main:app In a project the target defaults to project.application , and every registered app's models are loaded; repeat --models to load only some. Outside a project, pass a target ( module:app ); --models is then optional. What starts and what does not ¶ Each module the application installs, the database first, starts in dependency order and closes when the session ends. The application's on_startup and on_shutdown hooks do not run, so nothing sends mail or seeds data behind your back, and migrations are never applied: run hinoki migrations apply yourself. Unmanaged asyncio tasks are cancelled on exit. Each task gets up to two waits of lifecycle.shutdown_timeout (10 seconds by default); a task still running after the second cancellation is abandoned. Startup is bounded too: if a module suppresses cancellation while opening, the shell stops the loop and cannot guarantee that the module released what it had opened. Real data, your privileges Code at the prompt runs with your user's privileges against the configured database and can change it. Point the settings at a development database. How it looks ¶ On a colour terminal the shell opens with the Hinoki banner, which lists the application title, the settings class, the loaded models and the Python version, and a hinoki ❯ prompt. NO_COLOR , TERM=dumb and HINOKI_ANIMATE=0 behave as for hinoki new ; without colour the shell prints Hinoki interactive shell; use Ctrl-D or Ctrl-C to exit. and Python's >>> / ... prompts. Errors and edge cases ¶ Without a terminal the shell exits 2: " hinoki shell requires an interactive terminal". Ctrl-D exits, Ctrl-C at the prompt exits, Ctrl-C during a cell interrupts that cell. exit() , quit() or raise SystemExit in a cell also end the session and close the app modules; the shell exits 0 whatever code is passed. A model module that does not import stops the shell with cannot load model module '…' ; a duplicate class name with model name 'Note' occurs in both '…' and '…' . Both exit 2. Outside a project without a target: pass TARGET outside a project with hinoki.toml . See also ¶ Models Own resources with modules Command line

docs.text: Project status ¶ Hinoki is pre-alpha and not released. In the planned 0.1.x line, documented Python, CLI, settings and runtime contracts, plus migration files, stay compatible across patch releases: patches do not intentionally remove or change a documented contract. Additions and fixes for incorrect behavior remain possible and will be described in the changelog. Breaking changes may arrive in a later 0.y.0 and will be called out in release notes. No fixed deprecation period, support window for older framework versions or compatibility promise for undocumented internals is offered. Migration sidecars use a versioned format; known legacy unversioned state, including the earlier shape without index metadata, is read as version 1. Review migration SQL and state, back them up, test against disposable data and apply changes explicitly. Hinoki does not guarantee rollback of partially applied MySQL or MariaDB DDL. See migration compatibility for format details. This repository is not published on PyPI yet (its package name will be hinoki-api ). The hinoki project name currently belongs to an unrelated legacy package. Use this repository's source checkout for evaluation. The documentation site separates current development docs from release-tagged versions. Until the first release, the site root points to the dev docs. Implemented and exercised ¶ The repository includes typed function and class endpoints, routes registered per app in routes.py , project-wide middleware and rules lists in hinoki.toml , optional model-backed CRUD route generation, request binding and strict schemas, built-in and custom Schema validation, bounded typed multipart uploads, opt-in Model write constraints and validators, access policies and declared errors, optional architecture rules, settings and worker modules, SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB ORM backends with relations, querysets and file-based migrations, sync and async handlers, atomic writes ( atomic=True on actions, db.atomic as a block or decorator, sync and async), model lifecycle hooks with instance state and after-commit callbacks, composable TimestampedModel and SoftDeleteModel bases, soft-delete scopes and restore/hard-delete APIs, stackable status-change tracking and field snapshot helpers, typed events with explicit handlers ( in_transaction and after_commit , declared per app in hinoki.toml ; Created , Updated and Deleted model events from the model write path, and a model with handlers for one leaves the native lane for the matching generated action), AuthRejected and RateLimited events for refused requests ( after_commit only, no credentials or paths in the payload; the hinoki events command lists the registered handlers), bulk_create / bulk_update / bulk_delete and their abulk_* forms (one transaction each), a runtime check of every response against its return annotation (startup errors for annotations that cannot be checked), route-level rate limits (the built-in RateLimit or a policy the application supplies), OpenAPI, parsers, renderers, development and application MCP, and an optional admin with four styles, its own users, sign-in page, per-model permissions and shared sign-in limits, and hinoki admin commands. The examples are the best way to see the pieces together, in three levels plus a focused one: Notes (easy) is one app with generated CRUD; Tracker (medium) has several apps with explicit dependencies, access policies, transactions, a filtered list, events, and project-wide middleware and rules; Blog (complete) adds a tenant, login, the admin, application MCP, a streamed export, an audit trail from events, a rule waiver and optional metrics. Mailroom sends templated email behind an API key. Each is a self-contained project with its own hinoki.toml , tests and README. Current boundaries ¶ SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB are supported ORM databases; SQLite is the local-development default. MySQL and MariaDB have separate real-server integration coverage in CI. SQL Server and Oracle are not supported. See the database guide for backend-specific TLS, migration and feature limits, including MariaDB JSON behavior. Hinoki does not open database connections at import or apply migrations automatically. Rate limits: RateLimit counts in a shared database table (or in memory for development), counted in the Rust core on both the async and sync paths ( rate limit an action ); a route can still name any other policy. The admin's sign-in uses a per-worker window by default and DatabaseLoginWindow for a limit shared by every worker ( limit sign-in attempts ). There is no tracing integration or health route; Kiso's Prometheus metrics are in export Prometheus metrics . The ASGI adapter and application handler calls run in Python, except for the Kiso native paths described below. The Rust extension provides path matching, selected query/header/cookie parsing, schema validation/serialization, cryptography and SQL ORM compilation/execution, and drives eligible generated CRUD writes and eligible async def ORM handlers. Built-in security settings add browser response headers, HSTS on effective HTTPS requests, and an opt-in 308 HTTPS redirect that requires explicit allowed hosts. Generated typing for some keyword-based ORM calls is less precise than model construction; see typing . Many-to-many relations are declared with many_to_many(...) on one model (a generated or adopted bridge table, bounded link sets, within= scopes, generated CRUD <field>_ids ); an association model with extra columns is still written by hand. Through-model columns on the generated bridge, nested writes of related rows and many-to-many filters on admin lists are not available, and generated CRUD reads related rows only as ids. Routes with an ids field run natively when the targets are scoped with all_rows(...) or own_rows(...) , and a custom scope callable, a hook or a Linked / Unlinked handler keeps them on the Python lane. End-to-end performance claims are not made without comparable retained measurements; see the benchmark report and its limits. The default server is Kiso, Hinoki's Rust HTTP server (Granian stays available with --server granian , and any other ASGI server can run the app). It serves serve and dev : HTTP/1.1, optional TLS and, with server.http2 over TLS, HTTP/2 (no h2c or server push; WebSocket upgrades only for @http.websocket actions, over HTTP/1.1), an access log (pretty, plain or JSON, with path exclusions and a slow floor), a startup banner naming Kiso, most request-pipeline work still runs in Python and so do handlers, except that an async def handler provably limited to ORM reads and stock writes ( atomic=True , guarded and body routes included) is driven from Rust without an asyncio task ( native handler lane ), and eligible public generated create , update and delete actions run their transaction in Rust ( generated CRUD ); no performance figure is claimed. Kiso applies host, CORS preflight and HTTPS-redirect policies natively before its optional startup_url probe; the probe reports startup completion, not general application or database health. See Kiso . The server adapter is ASGI. hinoki.wsgi.WSGIAdapter wraps an application for WSGI servers (buffered bodies; an application with a streamed action is refused at start); verified with Granian only, see serving . Actions can stream: Stream , EventStream (server-sent events) and File are sent while they are produced, on Kiso and on Granian, with a bounded buffer, an idle timeout, keep-alive comments and a disconnect check; the stream count, the file lookup, the length check and the SSE frames are Rust on both servers; see stream a response for what runs in Rust and what stays in Python. Streamed actions are not available through WSGIAdapter , atomic=True , MCP or the native lane. WebSockets ( @http.websocket , see WebSockets ) run on Kiso, with framing and limits in Rust, and on Granian through the ASGI websocket scope, where only the Origin check and the message size are enforced by Hinoki; they are not available through WSGIAdapter or over HTTP/2. Kiso can export Prometheus metrics from a dedicated listener ( metrics.listen , off by default; Kiso only, and hinoki serve --server granian refuses it). The registry, the exposition and the cross-worker merge are Rust; only the settings are Python. Event handler runs are recorded into the same registry ( hinoki_events_total , hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds ). See export Prometheus metrics . No overhead figure is claimed for requests; the cost per event handler run is measured in that page . Outbound email is SMTP only ( smtp , plus console and memory for development and tests), sent from a per-worker Mailer on the same worker loop; the message render, the SMTP conversation, TLS, the pool and retries are Rust. There is no queue, no guaranteed delivery ( possibly_sent marks the ambiguous case), no SMTPUTF8, XOAUTH2, DKIM or inline images, no HTTP providers, and the admin sends no email in 0.1.0. Email templates are a small fixed language (values, if , for ) rendered in Rust with typed contexts checked at worker startup, and hinoki mail check and hinoki mail preview run them from the CLI. See send email and email templates . Kiso can compress response bodies with brotli or gzip ( compression.enabled , off by default; Kiso only, and hinoki serve --server granian refuses it): negotiation of accept-encoding , Vary , size and content-type rules, no-transform , streams, event streams and files, a flush whenever a stream pauses, and a bound on concurrent compressions are Rust; only the settings are Python. See compress responses . No compression ratio or throughput claim is made beyond the measurement stated there. CORS is an application-wide policy in the cors settings group, and an action, a RouteGroup or crud(...) can replace it with cors=http.Cors(...) ( per-route CORS ). Application MCP has its own allowed-origin check. Pagination uses page numbers by default, and cursor (keyset) pagination is available for generated and handwritten lists. Generated crud(...) lists accept client filters, ordering and search declared in a FilterSet ( filters= ): Eq , In , Range , .null , Search and an ordering allow-list, parsed and compiled to predicates in Rust, applied on top of get_queryset , with typed OpenAPI parameters and cursors bound to the filters. On Kiso, offset-paginated filtered lists without custom get_queryset / filter_queryset hooks run on the native generated-CRUD lane; CursorPagination and custom hooks stay on the Python lane. Operators beyond those, filters across relations and filters on the admin lists are not provided. See CRUD . OpenAPI generation writes an OpenAPI 3.2 document (3.1 with docs.openapi_version ), creates operation IDs and reads summary/description from handler docstrings; an action can set tags , deprecated , operation_id and include_in_schema ( per-action controls ). QUERY actions are the query operation in 3.2 and x-query in 3.1 ( the document version ). Top-level tag descriptions are not available. There is no maintained Docker image or deployment recipe. hinoki serve runs the app on Kiso by default, or on Granian with --server granian ; container packaging and process orchestration are application deployment choices. See the roadmap for project direction and contributing for local checks.

docs.text: Hinoki is pre-alpha and not released. In the planned 0.1.x line, documented Python, CLI, settings and runtime contracts, plus migration files, stay compatible across patch releases: patches do not intentionally remove or change a documented contract. Additions and fixes for incorrect behavior remain possible and will be described in the changelog. Breaking changes may arrive in a later 0.y.0 and will be called out in release notes. No fixed deprecation period, support window for older framework versions or compatibility promise for undocumented internals is offered. Migration sidecars use a versioned format; known legacy unversioned state, including the earlier shape without index metadata, is read as version 1. Review migration SQL and state, back them up, test against disposable data and apply changes explicitly. Hinoki does not guarantee rollback of partially applied MySQL or MariaDB DDL. See migration compatibility for format details. This repository is not published on PyPI yet (its package name will be hinoki-api ). The hinoki project name currently belongs to an unrelated legacy package. Use this repository's source checkout for evaluation. The documentation site separates current development docs from release-tagged versions. Until the first release, the site root points to the dev docs.

docs.text: Store uploaded files ¶ FileStorage stores bounded byte values behind opaque keys. Install a FileStorageModule and request FileStorage in a handler: from pathlib import Path from hinoki import Hinoki , Schema , UploadedFile , http from hinoki.http.response import Response from hinoki.storage import FileStorage , FileStorageModule , LocalFileStorage class UploadResult ( Schema ): key : str size : int sha256 : str @http . post ( "/documents" , status = 201 ) async def upload ( document : UploadedFile , storage : FileStorage ) -> UploadResult : saved = await storage . save ( document ) return UploadResult ( key = saved . key , size = saved . size , sha256 = saved . sha256 ) @http . get ( "/documents" ) async def download ( key : str , storage : FileStorage ) -> Response : return await storage . open_response ( key ) app = Hinoki ( include = [ upload , download ], modules = [ FileStorageModule ( LocalFileStorage ( Path ( "var/uploads" )))], ) FileStorage can also be used from a synchronous def handler with save_sync , read_sync , exists_sync and delete_sync . The async API is save , read , exists , delete and open_response . save accepts an UploadedFile or bytes and returns StoredFile(key, size, content_type, sha256, filename) . Empty files are allowed. Pass the opaque key as the key query parameter. Generated keys contain / for filesystem sharding, so they do not fit a single {key} path segment. Choose a backend ¶ Backend Ownership and visibility Bounds and I/O MemoryFileStorage Owned by the worker process; workers do not share values Per-file and total byte limits; async methods perform in-memory work LocalFileStorage(root) Files on the configured filesystem; workers on one host can share a volume; separate hosts need a shared volume Per-file limit and a local quota counter; async filesystem operations use a bounded per-worker thread pool Both backends default to a 10 MiB per-file limit. MemoryFileStorage defaults to a 64 MiB total limit. LocalFileStorage(max_total_bytes=...) checks the filesystem size when the worker starts and tracks its own writes and deletes. That counter is per worker process; concurrent workers can each accept a write before seeing the other's counter, so it is not a global quota. No background cleanup or cross-host coordination is provided. open_response() returns a Response for either backend. The memory backend buffers its bounded value in that response; the local backend returns a streamed File (a Response subtype), sent by the server without copying its body into a Python response buffer. Pass filename= and content_type= to open_response() to set the download name and media type. Without them both backends behave alike: the stored content type is used unless it is application/octet-stream , otherwise the type is guessed from the file name, and a file with no name is sent as a plain attachment . The storage key is never offered as a file name. disposition="inline" is honored only for passive media types: image/png , image/jpeg , image/gif , image/webp , image/avif , application/pdf and text/plain . Any other type, such as text/html , image/svg+xml or text/javascript , is sent as attachment so an uploaded file cannot run script in the application's origin. An unknown disposition raises ValueError . LocalFileStorage creates its root during worker startup, checks that it is a writable directory, uses unique generated keys and atomically replaces a temporary file. Directories use mode 0700 and files use 0600 . The uploaded filename is metadata and is never used as a filesystem path. Errors and access control ¶ The public errors are FileTooLarge (413), StorageQuotaExceeded (507), InvalidStorageKey (400), StoredFileNotFound (404) and StorageUnavailable (503). A malformed key or filesystem failure does not include a raw path in its public message. A missing FileStorageModule fails startup before a route that requests FileStorage becomes available. Storage checks whether a key is valid; it does not decide who owns that key. Routes must apply their own Access policy and verify the record's tenant or user ownership before reading or deleting a key. A successful database transaction does not make the filesystem write transactional: an application that saves a blob and later rolls back must delete or reconcile that blob itself. Uploaded parts are first parsed into bounded in-memory UploadedFile values; storage does not stream request uploads directly to disk.

docs.text: Stream a response ¶ An action can answer with a body that is sent while it is produced: Stream for bytes or text, EventStream for server-sent events and File for a file on disk. The handler returns the object; the status, the headers and the source of the body are fixed at that point, so access, validation, rate limits, errors and the request timeout all happen before the first byte. # notes/exports.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from hinoki import http from hinoki.http import Stream from notes.security import reader # an `Access` policy @http . get ( "/export.csv" , access = reader ) async def export () -> Stream : async def rows () -> AsyncIterator [ str ]: yield "id,title \n " for note_id in range ( 1 , 4 ): yield f " { note_id } ,note { note_id } \n " return Stream ( rows (), content_type = "text/csv; charset=utf-8" , headers = { "content-disposition" : 'attachment; filename="notes.csv"' }, ) The return annotation can name -> Stream , -> EventStream or -> File , alone or in a union ( -> Stream | NoteOut ). The base annotation -> Response also allows these streamed response subtypes. That is how Hinoki knows at startup which actions may stream. An action that returns one of them without an annotation that allows it answers 500 , and the stream is closed. Stream ¶ Stream(body, *, status=200, headers=(), content_type=None, length=None) . body is an async iterable or a plain iterable of bytes or str (a str is sent as UTF-8). A plain iterable, including a sync generator, is advanced on the bounded sync executor, so a handler declared with def can stream. The default content-type is application/octet-stream . Without length the body is sent with chunked framing on HTTP/1.1. With length the answer carries that content-length , and a body that does not match it is cut off instead of ending as complete, on Kiso and under an ASGI server alike: a body that is too long is cut at the length, and one that is too short is aborted. A piece that is neither bytes nor str ends the stream like an exception. An async generator cannot be the handler itself: write return Stream(rows()) instead. Hinoki refuses the declaration when the application is created. EventStream and Event ¶ # notes/events.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from hinoki import Request , http from hinoki.http import Event , EventStream from notes.security import reader @http . get ( "/notes/events" , access = reader ) async def note_events ( request : Request ) -> EventStream : after = request . headers . get ( "last-event-id" ) async def events () -> AsyncIterator [ Event ]: yield Event ({ "after" : after }, event = "hello" , id = "1" ) yield Event ( "done" ) return EventStream ( events (), retry = 3000 ) EventStream(events, *, status=200, headers=(), keepalive=..., retry=None) takes an iterable of Event or str (a str is the data of one event). The answer has content-type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8 , cache-control: no-store and x-accel-buffering: no . retry is the reconnection delay in milliseconds, sent before the first event. Event(data=None, *, event=None, id=None, retry=None, comment=None) : data that is not a str (a Schema , a dict , a list or a scalar) is sent as JSON; a line break in a str becomes one data: line per line. event and id that contain CR, LF or NUL raise ValueError when the Event is created, so a value from a client cannot add a field. retry is a non-negative number of milliseconds. While the source is quiet, a comment ( : ) is sent every keepalive seconds so proxies do not close the connection; the default is execution.sse_keepalive (15 seconds) and keepalive=None turns it off. A client that reconnects sends Last-Event-ID ; read it from request.headers as above. File ¶ # notes/downloads.py from pathlib import Path from hinoki import http from hinoki.http import File from notes.security import reader REPORTS = Path ( "/srv/notes/reports" ) @http . get ( "/reports/q3.pdf" , access = reader ) async def report () -> File : return File ( "q3.pdf" , root = REPORTS , filename = "q3-report.pdf" ) File(path, *, root=None, filename=None, content_type=None, status=200, headers=()) . A relative path is taken from root . With root , the file must be inside it once symbolic links are resolved; a missing file, a directory or a path that leaves root answers 404 . A symbolic link inside root that points outside it is refused the same way. filename adds content-disposition: attachment , with an ASCII fallback and the exact UTF-8 name when they differ. A name with / or a control character raises ValueError . The content-type is guessed from the name unless you give it, and the answer has the file size as content-length and accept-ranges: none . When the server does not send the file itself, no more than that size is read, so a file that grows meanwhile is cut at the size the head declared. Range requests are not supported. Resolve and check the path from trusted data; a root is what keeps a client-supplied name inside a directory. Registration rules ¶ Hinoki refuses these when the application is created ( RegistrationError naming the action): Declaration Why atomic=True on an action that streams The transaction would stay open for the whole body Status 204 or 304 with a stream These answers have no body An async def or def generator as the handler Return Stream(...) or EventStream(...) built from it WSGIAdapter refuses to start an application that has such an action ( serving ); the application's MCP endpoint refuses to expose it; the OpenAPI document describes Stream and File as application/octet-stream ( string , binary ) and EventStream as text/event-stream ( string ); the arms of a union that are not streamed are documented next to them. Errors and what the client sees ¶ Situation Result Access, rate limit, validation, 404 or an exception before the handler returns The normal JSON error; nothing was sent yet execution.request_timeout expires before the handler returns 504 timeout execution.max_streams streams already open on the worker 503 with Retry-After: 1 ; the handler does not run The source raises after the head The error is logged by hinoki.runtime with the request id and the response is cut: the client never sees it end as complete A Stream is silent for execution.stream_idle_timeout The response is cut and the source is closed The client goes away The source is closed ( aclose() of an async iterator, close() of a plain one). A plain iterator whose next() is blocked on a worker thread cannot be interrupted: the stream keeps its max_streams place until that call returns, and the source is closed then Server shutdown Open event streams end normally; other streams are cut when the shutdown timeout ends stream_idle_timeout defaults to request_timeout ; it applies to Stream only, because an event stream is covered by the keep-alive. The status of the head is the one the access log records, even if the body is cut later. max_streams counts the streams in a worker (default 64 ) from the time the handler is about to run until the body ends. A File on Kiso is sent by the server alone, so it holds its place only until the head is decided. A HEAD request to a GET action that streams gets the headers only, and the source is closed without being read. Middleware ¶ call_next() returns the Stream , EventStream or File itself, with an empty body ; a middleware never sees the pieces. response.with_header(...) keeps the class and the source. A middleware that returns a different Response instead of the stream does not serve it: Hinoki closes its source. An action that streams is always served by Python and never takes the native lane : hinoki routes --lanes shows lane_reason streamed response . What runs where ¶ Rust does what is a computation or a timer on its own; Python does what has to call the application's code or live in the event loop. Kiso. The application's iterator runs in Python and every piece it produces crosses to Rust as a Python bytes . From there, framing, the bounded queue (a slow client slows the iterator down), the idle timeout, the keep-alive comments, the declared-length check and the disconnect check run in the server. SSE framing is done by core.sse_frame . A File is opened and sent by the server: the bytes of the file never enter Python. Granian (ASGI). Each piece is an ASGI http.response.body message built in Python, so this path has no native part for the body. The idle timeout, the keep-alive and the disconnect watcher run in Python, and a client that leaves is noticed through receive() . A File is sent with the ASGI http.response.pathsend extension when the server offers it, and read in chunks on the sync executor otherwise. Both paths, in Rust. The count behind execution.max_streams ( core.StreamLimit : an atomic counter whose places give themselves back when released or dropped), the file lookup of a File ( core.locate_file : real path, root check, regular file and size, on a blocking thread and not in the sync executor; at most 32 lookups run at once in the process and one more answers 503 with Retry-After: 1 instead of queueing), the declared-length arithmetic of the ASGI pump ( core.Tally ), the content-disposition value ( core.content_disposition ) and the SSE frames. A WSGI stream's idle timeout is the connection's own timer, as on Kiso. Neither path is called native: the application's iterator is Python on both. What stays in Python, and why: The source. The iterator is user code, and a plain one has to run on a worker thread; Rust cannot call it from a runtime thread without moving a Python object there. Taking the place and the 503 . The place is taken in the pipeline right before the handler runs, because the answer to a full worker is a normal Hinoki error ( Retry-After: 1 , the application's error format, middleware) that is built in Python. The count itself is Rust. The ASGI timers and the watcher. The idle timeout and the keep-alive wrap an await on the application's iterator and the watcher is a task on receive() ; both are asyncio objects of the server's loop. A Rust state machine would only compute a deadline that Python must still schedule, so they stay as they are. Registration rules, the annotation check, middleware and HEAD . They inspect Python annotations and Response objects. The content-type of a File . It is guessed from the name with the standard library's mimetypes ; Hinoki does not carry a second table. Measured behavior ¶ These were checked with a running server (see tests/kisostreamingtest.py and tests/runtime/granianstreamtest.py ): Pieces reach the client before the body ends, on Kiso and on Granian. On Kiso, a client that does not read stops the producer: after a pause the number of produced pieces stops growing, bounded by the queue of 8 pieces and the socket buffers. On Kiso, a client that leaves a stream that keeps writing closes the source at once. A client that leaves a stream that is silent is noticed at the next write: the next keep-alive of an event stream, the idle timeout of a Stream , or the next piece. A silent Stream with a long idle timeout keeps its iterator, its max_streams place and its source open until then. On Granian, a client that leaves an endless stream closes the source, and an event stream carries keep-alive comments. Closing the server with an open event stream ends the stream normally on Kiso. This was not measured on Granian. Range requests are not provided. Kiso can compress these bodies when asked; see compress responses . Test a stream ¶ ASGIClient.stream() gives the head and the pieces as they are sent, and leaving the block simulates a disconnect: async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : async with client . stream ( "GET" , "/notes/events" , token = "t" ) as reply : first = await anext ( reply . chunks ()) client.get() still collects the whole body; on a stream that never ends it stops with BodyTooLarge after max_bytes (10 MiB by default). See testing . See also ¶ Endpoints Kiso server Middleware Settings

docs.text: An action can answer with a body that is sent while it is produced: Stream for bytes or text, EventStream for server-sent events and File for a file on disk. The handler returns the object; the status, the headers and the source of the body are fixed at that point, so access, validation, rate limits, errors and the request timeout all happen before the first byte. # notes/exports.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from hinoki import http from hinoki.http import Stream from notes.security import reader # an `Access` policy @http . get ( "/export.csv" , access = reader ) async def export () -> Stream : async def rows () -> AsyncIterator [ str ]: yield "id,title \n " for note_id in range ( 1 , 4 ): yield f " { note_id } ,note { note_id } \n " return Stream ( rows (), content_type = "text/csv; charset=utf-8" , headers = { "content-disposition" : 'attachment; filename="notes.csv"' }, ) The return annotation can name -> Stream , -> EventStream or -> File , alone or in a union ( -> Stream | NoteOut ). The base annotation -> Response also allows these streamed response subtypes. That is how Hinoki knows at startup which actions may stream. An action that returns one of them without an annotation that allows it answers 500 , and the stream is closed.
docs.title: Stream a response

docs.text: Stream(body, *, status=200, headers=(), content_type=None, length=None) . body is an async iterable or a plain iterable of bytes or str (a str is sent as UTF-8). A plain iterable, including a sync generator, is advanced on the bounded sync executor, so a handler declared with def can stream. The default content-type is application/octet-stream . Without length the body is sent with chunked framing on HTTP/1.1. With length the answer carries that content-length , and a body that does not match it is cut off instead of ending as complete, on Kiso and under an ASGI server alike: a body that is too long is cut at the length, and one that is too short is aborted. A piece that is neither bytes nor str ends the stream like an exception. An async generator cannot be the handler itself: write return Stream(rows()) instead. Hinoki refuses the declaration when the application is created.

The answer has content-type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8 , cache-control: no-store and x-accel-buffering: no . retry is the reconnection delay in milliseconds, sent before the first event. While the source is quiet, a comment ( : ) is sent every keepalive seconds so proxies do not close the connection; the default is execution.sse_keepalive (15 seconds) and keepalive=None turns it off. A client that reconnects sends Last-Event-ID ; read it from request.headers as above.

docs.text: Sync and async code ¶ Each worker runs one event loop. async def is the native style; a plain def handler or hook is fully supported and runs on a bounded thread pool, with the request's context and blocking ORM twins that never block the loop. Two actions added to the invoices group of function endpoints , answering with a one-field Schema : # notes/apps/billing/api.py (in the invoices group's module) from hinoki import Schema class UnpaidCount ( Schema ): count : int @invoices . get ( "/unpaid/count" ) async def count_unpaid () -> UnpaidCount : # async: await the a... method return UnpaidCount ( count = await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . acount ()) @invoices . get ( "/unpaid/count-sync" ) def count_unpaid_sync () -> UnpaidCount : # sync: the twin without the "a" return UnpaidCount ( count = Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . count ()) The group carries the access policy and atomic=True for both. A name with the a prefix awaits the database ( aget , acreate , acount ); the same name without it is the blocking twin. A queryset is lazy until evaluated: await queryset is the async form of queryset.list() . Choose a style ¶ Prefer async def . Use def for code that is naturally blocking: a library without async support, or CPU work measured to be short. Never call blocking code from an async def . From a def , use the sync twin instead of calling an a... coroutine. CPU-heavy work belongs in a separate process, not in either pool. A sync ORM call made on the event loop raises, naming the a... method to use. What runs where ¶ Surface Async Sync Notes Action handlers async def def Sync runs on the executor CRUD hooks ( get_queryset , written_queryset , to_schema , store , change , remove ) async def def Same executor as handlers Auth providers ( authenticate , resolve , resolve_token , JWT resolve_claims ) async def def Sync hooks run on the executor Model writes and lookups acreate , aget , aget_or_none , aget_as , aget_or_none_as , aupdate , aupdate_where , adelete , asave , aupdate_from , abulk_create , abulk_update , abulk_delete The same names without a Sync calls work only inside a sync handler or hook served by Hinoki; both take returning=False ( queries ) QuerySet reads await qs , afirst , aget , aget_as , aget_or_none_as , acount , aexists , aproject , apaginate , apaginate_as list , first , get , get_as , get_or_none_as , count , exists , project , paginate , paginate_as QuerySet writes aupdate , adelete update , delete Relations select_related , prefetch_related same Never lazy in either style Raw SQL ( Database.fetch , fetch_one , execute ) async none Async-only escape hatch Transactions atomic=True same The runtime owns it Atomic blocks async with db.atomic(): , @db.atomic on async def with db.atomic(): , @db.atomic on def Sync forms raise RuntimeError on the loop ( transactions ) Schema , Request , Response , parsers, renderers plain code same No I/O Password hashing await hasher.hash/verify hash_sync , verify_sync Async calls use their own bounded pool Error handlers ( app.error_handler ) async def def Run on the loop: no blocking calls Module lifespans async context manager none Resources belong to the worker's loop Startup and shutdown hooks async def hook(ctx) def hook(ctx) Hinoki(on_startup=..., on_shutdown=...) ; sync runs on the executor Admin hooks ( stats , check , save , remove ) async def none The admin runs on the loop Tests ASGIClient SyncClient Same behaviour Size the pool ¶ execution.sync_workers (default 8 ) threads serve sync handlers and hooks; execution.sync_queue (default 64 ) requests may wait for one. A full queue answers 503 overloaded with Retry-After . See settings . Errors and edge cases ¶ Sync hooks share the pool with sync handlers. A flood of bad credentials or slow hooks can fill the queue and turn legitimate sync work into 503 . Keep sync hooks short, reject malformed credentials before touching the database, and prefer async hooks. A sync auth hook runs before the action's transaction opens , so it is never part of it. Sync model calls work only inside the app's sync handlers and hooks. In a test body, use the async API (an async fixture) or your own connection, also with SyncClient . Async only: module lifespans, admin hooks, background tasks ( ctx.tasks.start_soon takes coroutines) and raw Database SQL. A sync error handler runs on the loop and must not call the ORM; its failure is treated as unhandled. SyncClient works only inside its with block and raises a timeout error after timeout seconds (default 60). The test suite exercises sync and async handlers, sync authentication hooks, ORM calls through both clients, mixed traffic and cancellation against a disposable database. See also ¶ Request lifecycle Transactions Settings
