docs.text: Test an application ¶ A project created with hinoki new already has a test that runs a request through the whole stack, without a network socket: # tests/healthtest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import app async def test_health_answers_through_the_whole_stack () -> None : async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : reply = await client . get ( "/health" ) assert ( reply . status , reply . body ) == ( 200 , { "status" : "ok" }) Run it with uv run pytest . The generated pyproject.toml sets asyncio_mode = "auto" and collects files named *test.py . ASGIClient runs the application's startup (modules, database pool, startup hooks and rules ) when the block opens and its shutdown when it closes. A reply has status , headers , body (decoded JSON, or text) and raw bytes. Test protected actions ¶ token= sends Authorization: Bearer <token> , so a test exercises the real provider and policy: # tests/billingtest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import app async def test_invoices_need_a_staff_token () -> None : async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : anonymous = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" ) unknown = await client . get ( "/billing/invoices" , token = "not-a-token" ) assert anonymous . status == 401 assert unknown . status == 401 Use a disposable database ¶ The application reads its settings when its module is imported, so point the prefix variable at a throwaway database first. A conftest.py at the project root is imported before any test module: # conftest.py import os os . environ [ "NOTES_DATABASE__URL" ] = "sqlite://./.hinoki/test.sqlite3" This applies when the settings declare database: settings.DatabaseSettings . Create the tables once, with the same variable: NOTES_DATABASE__URL = sqlite://./.hinoki/test.sqlite3 uv run hinoki migrations apply When settings.toml sets engine and its connection fields, a URL conflicts with them ( set either url or engine with its fields, not both ). Override the fields instead, and clear the server-only ones SQLite refuses: # conftest.py import os os . environ . update ( NOTES_DATABASE__ENGINE = "sqlite" , NOTES_DATABASE__NAME = ".hinoki/test.sqlite3" , NOTES_DATABASE__HOST = "" , NOTES_DATABASE__USER = "" , ) Apply the migrations with the same variables, and pass the same keys under "database" to overrides= in the example below. When one test needs other settings, build a second application from the same code instead of changing the shared one. Give main.py a create_app(settings) factory, as examples/notes/notes/main.py does ( create_app , line 12). The factory lives in the module hinoki.toml names as project.application , so Hinoki(...) fills routes, events, middleware and rules from the manifest. This example only calls /health , so its new database needs no tables; to give a test migrated tables, copy them as below : # tests/settingstest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import create_app from notes.settings import ProjectSettings async def test_health_with_its_own_database () -> None : settings = ProjectSettings . load ( overrides = { "database" : { "url" : "sqlite://./.hinoki/other.sqlite3" }} ) async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( settings )) as client : assert ( await client . get ( "/health" )) . status == 200 A Hinoki(...) built in any other module (a test, a script) does not read the manifest; pass what you want explicitly (or use manifest_routes() , manifest_events() , manifest_middleware() and manifest_rules() from hinoki.project ). Use synthetic rows and credentials, and never point test settings at production data. Give each test its own database ¶ The tests above share one file, so rows one test writes are still there in the next. To start every test from empty, migrated tables, migrate a database in the test's temporary directory with the app's own migrations and build the application on it, as examples/notes/notes_tests/conftest.py does: # tests/conftest.py from collections.abc import AsyncIterator from pathlib import Path import pytest from hinoki.db import Database from hinoki.orm import migrator from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import create_app from notes.settings import ProjectSettings MIGRATIONS = Path ( __file__ ) . parents [ 1 ] / "notes" / "apps" / "notes" / "migrations" @pytest . fixture async def client ( tmp_path : Path ) -> AsyncIterator [ ASGIClient ]: url = f "sqlite:// { tmp_path / 'test.sqlite3' } " database = await Database . connect ( url , max_size = 1 ) await migrator . apply ( database , MIGRATIONS ) database . close () settings = ProjectSettings . load ( overrides = { "database" : { "url" : url }}) async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( settings )) as client : yield client A test takes client as an argument; whatever it writes is gone in the next test. The migrations come from the app's own directory, so a new migration is picked up without extra steps. In a project with several apps, apply each app's migration directory in dependency order. The fixture builds SQLite files only. Test email ¶ With email: settings.EmailSettings set to backend=EmailBackend.MEMORY , every sent message is kept in the worker's mailer.outbox and nothing leaves the process; outbox entries carry the Message and the rendered bytes. A sample test is in send email . For SMTP behaviour use a fake server on 127.0.0.1 and synthetic example.com addresses. To test a template without sending, call template.render(context) (it returns the three parts) or run hinoki mail preview ; see email templates . Catch undeclared errors ¶ ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) fails the test when an action answers an HTTP error that is missing from its errors= declaration, so the OpenAPI document cannot drift from what the action really does. ASGIClient and SyncClient (for synchronous tests, below ) both have get , post , put , patch , delete , head , options and query (the HTTP QUERY method; its body goes in json= or body= , while the query= option of every call is the query string), plus request(method, path, ...) for any other method. The path is only the path: a ? or # in it raises ValueError instead of being routed as part of the path (which would answer a 404 for the wrong reason). Send the query string with query= : reply = await client . get ( "/items" , query = "limit=10&offset=20" ) Test file uploads ¶ ASGIClient and SyncClient accept data= and files= and build the multipart boundary and Content-Type header for you. Use a sequence of file tuples to send repeated field names in order: # tests/uploadtest.py async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : response = await client . post ( "/documents" , data = { "title" : "Report" }, files = [( "document" , "report.txt" , b "contents" , "text/plain" )], ) assert response . status == 201 Each file tuple is (field_name, filename, content_bytes, content_type) . Form data may be a mapping or an ordered sequence of (name, text) pairs; sequences retain repeated names. Do not pass json= or raw body= together with data= / files= ; the helper owns the multipart content type and boundary. The application enforces its configured complete-body and per-part limits. This helper sends complete in-memory bodies and does not model streaming uploads. For streamed responses see test streams . Headers and hosts ¶ headers= accepts a mapping or a sequence of (name, value) pairs. Use pairs to send a repeated header; Hinoki's request header mapping joins repeated values with ", " . A client can add a default Host header to each request: # tests/headerstest.py async with ASGIClient ( app , host = "api.example.com" ) as client : response = await client . get ( "/health" , headers = [( "X-Trace" , "first" ), ( "X-Trace" , "second" )] ) The default remains no Host header. Set headers={"host": "other.example.com"} on a call to override the client's host. Because the clients run in-process, they do not log the startup warning about the default allowed_hosts = * that a served worker logs ( Hosts, CORS and HTTPS ). Test streams ¶ client.get() waits for the end of a streamed response and returns the whole body. To see the head and the pieces as they are sent, use client.stream() ; leaving the block tells the application that the client disconnected, so the source of the stream is closed: # tests/eventstest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import app async def test_events_arrive_one_by_one () -> None : async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : async with client . stream ( "GET" , "/notes/events" , token = "t" ) as reply : assert reply . status == 200 assert reply . headers [ "content-type" ] . startswith ( "text/event-stream" ) first = await anext ( reply . chunks ()) reply.chunks() yields each piece as the application sent it, and raises the error that cut the response, if one did. reply.read() collects the rest. SyncClient.stream() is the same with with and a plain iterator. A stream that never ends makes client.get() fail with BodyTooLarge once the body passes max_bytes (10 MiB; pass max_bytes= to change it), so a test cannot hang on it. The in-process client runs the ASGI pump, not Kiso's: it shows what the client receives and when the source is closed, not the server's queue, timeouts or keep-alive. Synchronous tests and time ¶ SyncClient is available for synchronous test functions. It runs the app's lifespan and refuses unsafe nested use from a running event loop. For deterministic time, ManualClock is a thread-safe callable clock. It accepts and returns timezone-aware instants normalized to UTC; advance(seconds=...) and set(datetime) control its value. A naive datetime raises ValueError . Pass it to app.now(clock) or other code that accepts a Clock . Test the layers separately ¶ Keep business operations independent of Request and HTTP response types when practical. Test ownership and state transitions against a disposable database, then test route binding, access, status codes and error declarations through ASGIClient . Repository checks ¶ From the checkout, the documented gates are: uv run --locked ruff check . uv run --locked ruff format --check . uv run --locked mypy uv run --locked complexipy . --failed uv run --locked pytest --cov cargo fmt --all --check cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings cargo test --workspace uv run --locked --group docs mkdocs build --strict PostgreSQL-dependent Python and Rust tests require HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; without it those tests are skipped. Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also require HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL , respectively. CI provides disposable real-server services. See toolchain and CI for the Rust complexity check, the pre-commit hooks and the packaging checks. See also ¶ Create a project : what the generated tests and settings contain. docs.text: A project created with hinoki new already has a test that runs a request through the whole stack, without a network socket: # tests/healthtest.py from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient from notes.main import app async def test_health_answers_through_the_whole_stack () -> None : async with ASGIClient ( app ) as client : reply = await client . get ( "/health" ) assert ( reply . status , reply . body ) == ( 200 , { "status" : "ok" }) Run it with uv run pytest . The generated pyproject.toml sets asyncio_mode = "auto" and collects files named *test.py . ASGIClient runs the application's startup (modules, database pool, startup hooks and rules ) when the block opens and its shutdown when it closes. A reply has status , headers , body (decoded JSON, or text) and raw bytes.

docs.text: Toolchain and CI ¶ All Python commands run through uv with the lock enforced; Rust through Cargo . CI runs the same commands. Setup ¶ uv sync --locked # creates .venv, builds the Rust extension (maturin), installs dev groups uv run --locked pre-commit install Requires: uv ≥ 0.9, a stable Rust toolchain (rustup) with rustfmt and clippy . The PyO3 extension build backend requires maturin ≥ 1.16.0 ( [build-system] in pyproject.toml ); uv selects it from the isolated build-system requirement. Gates ¶ Gate Command Lock is current uv lock --check Lint (+ autofix) uv run --locked ruff check --fix . Format uv run --locked ruff format . Types + typing fixtures uv run --locked mypy (checks python/hinoki , tests and examples ) Python cognitive complexity uv run --locked complexipy . --failed Rust cognitive complexity Install rust-code-analysis-cli 0.0.25, then run mkdir -p /tmp/hinoki-rust-complexity && rust-code-analysis-cli -m -p crates -O json --pr -o /tmp/hinoki-rust-complexity && python scripts/check_rust_complexity.py /tmp/hinoki-rust-complexity Python tests + coverage uv run --locked pytest --cov (runs tests and the tests of examples/notes , examples/tracker , examples/blog and examples/mailroom ) Only the real-server tests uv run --locked pytest -m runtime Rust format / lints / tests cargo fmt --all --check · cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings · cargo test --workspace (see PyO3 setup below) All hooks uv run --locked pre-commit run --all-files Measuring coverage ¶ Coverage also measures child processes ( patch = ["subprocess"] with parallel and sigterm in [tool.coverage.run] ), so the supervisor, worker and hinoki serve tests count. CI runs two phases and merges them: the main suite with pytest -n 4 --cov , then the isolated server and process suites ( tests/runtime , tests/kisoservertest.py , tests/kisoclitest.py , tests/wsgitest.py , tests/ratelimitservertest.py , tests/kisometricstest.py , tests/kisoreloadtest.py , tests/ratelimitsharedtest.py and tests/adminsharedlimittest.py ) with --cov --cov-append . Locally: uv run --locked pytest -n 4 --cov --cov-report = term-missing uv run --locked coverage report --precision = 2 --skip-covered -m Without the database URLs below, the database-backed tests (most of the admin, parts of the ORM and the migrator) are skipped and their lines show as uncovered. A few unreachable guards carry # pragma: no cover with the reason next to it. Database tests ¶ The binding tests embed Python. Select the interpreter explicitly and add its shared-library directory when running the workspace suite locally: PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace CI sets these variables for the Rust job using its uv-managed Python 3.13. PostgreSQL-dependent tests in tests/dbtest.py , tests/transactiontest.py and crates/orm/tests/postgres.rs need a disposable server and run only when HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is set; otherwise pytest reports them as skipped and Cargo prints SKIPPED . Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL ; test each supported backend separately and read the skip summary. A run without the PostgreSQL URL does not verify PostgreSQL behavior. Locally: docker run -d --name hinoki-test-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD = hinoki -e POSTGRES_DB = hinoki \ -p 127 .0.0.1:54399:5432 --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17-alpine export HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL = postgres://postgres:hinoki@127.0.0.1:54399/hinoki uv run --locked pytest PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace docker rm -f hinoki-test-pg CI provides the same database as a service container. Never point the variable at a database with real data: tests create and drop tables. The Python and Rust suites include ORM/model tests. PostgreSQL-dependent tests run only with a disposable HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL . CI provides disposable real-server services. The native CRUD differential test build enables the private sql-trace Cargo feature so it can compare SQL text, parameters and order for both request lanes; ordinary wheels are built without that feature. Build it into the environment with uv run --no-sync --with "maturin>=1.9.4,<2" maturin develop --manifest-path crates/bindings/Cargo.toml --features sql-trace . Without it those tests skip; set HINOKI_REQUIRE_SQL_TRACE=1 (CI does) to make a missing trace build fail them instead. The CI Rust job also runs cargo clippy -p hinoki-bindings --all-targets --features sql-trace -- -D warnings . Generated OpenAPI is validated with openapi-spec-validator inside the Python tests. The retained benchmark report has reproducible end-to-end measurements, but benchmark runs are separate from the default CI test gate. Decisions ¶ Python ≥ 3.12 , dev interpreter 3.13 ( .python-version ), CI 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, abi3 wheels (smoke-tested in a clean 3.12 environment by the wheel CI job). Ruff is the only linter/formatter ( ruff check with --fix , then ruff format ), version pinned in pyproject.toml ( lint group) and in .pre-commit-config.yaml ; keep them equal when bumping. mypy --strict is the separate type check. No overlapping tools (no black, isort, flake8, pylint). maturin is the build backend ( python-source = "python" , extension hinoki.core ); uv rebuilds when Rust sources change ( tool.uv.cache-keys ). Cognitive complexity is capped at 15 for every Python function and Rust function/closure. CI runs pinned complexipy and rust-code-analysis-cli ; test and development code are included. Refactor over-budget functions instead of suppressing analyzer findings. Unsafe Rust is gated. kiso , hinoki-orm , hinoki-mail and hinoki-ratelimit have #![forbid(unsafe_code)] ; hinoki-bindings has #![deny(unsafe_code)] , so a new unsafe block fails the build until its function carries a narrow #[allow(unsafe_code)] and a SAFETY: comment stating why it is sound. Today there are three categories: the inherited-listener descriptor in kiso.rs ( OwnedFd::from_raw_fd ), the CPython FFI calls of the typed decoder, and two typed-decoder functions ( string and number ) that use str::from_utf8_unchecked on bytes checked to be ASCII. Dependency groups: lint , typecheck , test , aggregated by dev . Granian is both the optional runtime server extra and a test dependency for server integration coverage. Two environments, two responsibilities ¶ uv owns the project: .venv , uv.lock , the dependency groups and every tool declared in them ( ruff , mypy , pytest , pre-commit itself). Run them with uv run --locked ... . pre-commit builds its own isolated environments for the hooks it fetches (e.g. ruff-pre-commit ); these are not the project .venv and are not managed by uv. That is why the Ruff revision in .pre-commit-config.yaml must equal the ruff== pin in pyproject.toml ( uv.lock ). Hooks never rewrite sources/ -style historical snapshots (excluded globally). CI never applies fixes: it fails if a hook would change a file. pre-commit install is a manual step in a Git checkout, never triggered by importing the framework. CI workflow hygiene ¶ Third-party actions in .github/workflows/ are pinned to a full commit SHA with the released tag in a trailing comment. To update one, resolve the new tag to its commit ( gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/ref/tags/TAG ), replace the SHA and the comment together, and let the PR's CI run prove it. Each Python X job sets UV_PYTHON to its matrix version and asserts the interpreter before testing. Without it uv run follows .python-version and every job would test 3.13. Locally, run another version with uv run --locked --python 3.14 pytest (use UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT to keep its environment apart). ci.yml checks out with persist-credentials: false : no CI job pushes. deploy-docs.yml keeps the token because it pushes to gh-pages . The audit job checks Cargo.lock ( cargo audit , cargo deny check ) and uv.lock ( uv export of every group and extra, then pip-audit --require-hashes --disable-pip ). Locally: uv export --locked --all-groups --all-extras --no-emit-project --format requirements-txt -o /tmp/requirements.txt && uvx pip-audit==2.10.1 --require-hashes --disable-pip -r /tmp/requirements.txt . A pull request that only changes docs/ , theme/ , assets/ , mkdocs.yml , LICENSE or Markdown files in the repository root skips the work of the Python X , rust , wheel and audit jobs: the changes job lists the files through the API and, on any doubt, runs everything. The skipped jobs still report success, so the required checks need no change. pre-commit checks only the files of such a pull request and docs always runs. CodeQL and SonarCloud do not start for such a pull request. Native extension: editable install, rebuild, wheel ¶ Task Command Notes Editable install (first time) uv sync --locked maturin builds a debug extension into the project Rebuild after changing Rust uv sync --locked (or any uv run ) tool.uv.cache-keys watches crates/**/*.rs and Cargo.toml ; uv reinstalls when they change. docs.text: Coverage also measures child processes ( patch = ["subprocess"] with parallel and sigterm in [tool.coverage.run] ), so the supervisor, worker and hinoki serve tests count. CI runs two phases and merges them: the main suite with pytest -n 4 --cov , then the isolated server and process suites ( tests/runtime , tests/kisoservertest.py , tests/kisoclitest.py , tests/wsgitest.py , tests/ratelimitservertest.py , tests/kisometricstest.py , tests/kisoreloadtest.py , tests/ratelimitsharedtest.py and tests/adminsharedlimittest.py ) with --cov --cov-append . Locally: uv run --locked pytest -n 4 --cov --cov-report = term-missing uv run --locked coverage report --precision = 2 --skip-covered -m Without the database URLs below, the database-backed tests (most of the admin, parts of the ORM and the migrator) are skipped and their lines show as uncovered. A few unreachable guards carry # pragma: no cover with the reason next to it.
docs.title: Measuring coverage

docs.text: The binding tests embed Python. Select the interpreter explicitly and add its shared-library directory when running the workspace suite locally: PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace CI sets these variables for the Rust job using its uv-managed Python 3.13. PostgreSQL-dependent tests in tests/dbtest.py , tests/transactiontest.py and crates/orm/tests/postgres.rs need a disposable server and run only when HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL is set; otherwise pytest reports them as skipped and Cargo prints SKIPPED . Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL ; test each supported backend separately and read the skip summary. A run without the PostgreSQL URL does not verify PostgreSQL behavior. Locally: docker run -d --name hinoki-test-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD = hinoki -e POSTGRES_DB = hinoki \ -p 127 .0.0.1:54399:5432 --tmpfs /var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17-alpine export HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL = postgres://postgres:hinoki@127.0.0.1:54399/hinoki uv run --locked pytest PYTHON = " $( uv run --locked python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)' ) " PYTHON_LIBDIR = " $( " $PYTHON " -c 'import sysconfig; print(sysconfig.get_config_var("LIBDIR"))' ) " PYO3_PYTHON = " $PYTHON " \ LD_LIBRARY_PATH = " $PYTHON_LIBDIR ${ LD_LIBRARY_PATH :+: $LD_LIBRARY_PATH } " \ cargo test --workspace docker rm -f hinoki-test-pg CI provides the same database as a service container. Never point the variable at a database with real data: tests create and drop tables. The Python and Rust suites include ORM/model tests. PostgreSQL-dependent tests run only with a disposable HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL ; migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also use HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL and HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL . CI provides disposable real-server services. The native CRUD differential test build enables the private sql-trace Cargo feature so it can compare SQL text, parameters and order for both request lanes; ordinary wheels are built without that feature. Build it into the environment with uv run --no-sync --with "maturin>=1.9.4,<2" maturin develop --manifest-path crates/bindings/Cargo.toml --features sql-trace . Without it those tests skip; set HINOKI_REQUIRE_SQL_TRACE=1 (CI does) to make a missing trace build fail them instead. The CI Rust job also runs cargo clippy -p hinoki-bindings --all-targets --features sql-trace -- -D warnings . Generated OpenAPI is validated with openapi-spec-validator inside the Python tests. The retained benchmark report has reproducible end-to-end measurements, but benchmark runs are separate from the default CI test gate.

docs.text: Python ≥ 3.12 , dev interpreter 3.13 ( .python-version ), CI 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14, abi3 wheels (smoke-tested in a clean 3.12 environment by the wheel CI job). Ruff is the only linter/formatter ( ruff check with --fix , then ruff format ), version pinned in pyproject.toml ( lint group) and in .pre-commit-config.yaml ; keep them equal when bumping. mypy --strict is the separate type check. No overlapping tools (no black, isort, flake8, pylint). maturin is the build backend ( python-source = "python" , extension hinoki.core ); uv rebuilds when Rust sources change ( tool.uv.cache-keys ). Cognitive complexity is capped at 15 for every Python function and Rust function/closure. CI runs pinned complexipy and rust-code-analysis-cli ; test and development code are included. Refactor over-budget functions instead of suppressing analyzer findings. Unsafe Rust is gated. kiso , hinoki-orm , hinoki-mail and hinoki-ratelimit have #![forbid(unsafe_code)] ; hinoki-bindings has #![deny(unsafe_code)] , so a new unsafe block fails the build until its function carries a narrow #[allow(unsafe_code)] and a SAFETY: comment stating why it is sound. Today there are three categories: the inherited-listener descriptor in kiso.rs ( OwnedFd::from_raw_fd ), the CPython FFI calls of the typed decoder, and two typed-decoder functions ( string and number ) that use str::from_utf8_unchecked on bytes checked to be ASCII. Dependency groups: lint , typecheck , test , aggregated by dev . Granian is both the optional runtime server extra and a test dependency for server integration coverage.
docs.title: Decisions

docs.text: uv owns the project: .venv , uv.lock , the dependency groups and every tool declared in them ( ruff , mypy , pytest , pre-commit itself). Run them with uv run --locked ... . pre-commit builds its own isolated environments for the hooks it fetches (e.g. ruff-pre-commit ); these are not the project .venv and are not managed by uv. That is why the Ruff revision in .pre-commit-config.yaml must equal the ruff== pin in pyproject.toml ( uv.lock ). Hooks never rewrite sources/ -style historical snapshots (excluded globally). CI never applies fixes: it fails if a hook would change a file. pre-commit install is a manual step in a Git checkout, never triggered by importing the framework.
docs.title: Two environments, two responsibilities

docs.text: Third-party actions in .github/workflows/ are pinned to a full commit SHA with the released tag in a trailing comment. To update one, resolve the new tag to its commit ( gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/git/ref/tags/TAG ), replace the SHA and the comment together, and let the PR's CI run prove it. Each Python X job sets UV_PYTHON to its matrix version and asserts the interpreter before testing. Without it uv run follows .python-version and every job would test 3.13. Locally, run another version with uv run --locked --python 3.14 pytest (use UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT to keep its environment apart). ci.yml checks out with persist-credentials: false : no CI job pushes. deploy-docs.yml keeps the token because it pushes to gh-pages . The audit job checks Cargo.lock ( cargo audit , cargo deny check ) and uv.lock ( uv export of every group and extra, then pip-audit --require-hashes --disable-pip ). Locally: uv export --locked --all-groups --all-extras --no-emit-project --format requirements-txt -o /tmp/requirements.txt && uvx pip-audit==2.10.1 --require-hashes --disable-pip -r /tmp/requirements.txt . A pull request that only changes docs/ , theme/ , assets/ , mkdocs.yml , LICENSE or Markdown files in the repository root skips the work of the Python X , rust , wheel and audit jobs: the changes job lists the files through the API and, on any doubt, runs everything. The skipped jobs still report success, so the required checks need no change. pre-commit checks only the files of such a pull request and docs always runs. CodeQL and SonarCloud do not start for such a pull request.

docs.text: Run writes in transactions ¶ An action opts into a database transaction with atomic=True . The transaction opens for the request and commits only after the handler returns and the response body is encoded and rendered. Set it once on a RouteGroup and every write method of the group is atomic: # notes/apps/billing/api.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import RouteGroup from notes.security import billing_staff from .models import AuditEvent , Invoice # AuditEvent: any model of yours from .schemas import InvoiceIn , InvoiceOut invoices = RouteGroup ( "/invoices" , access = billing_staff , atomic = True ) @invoices . post ( "/" , status = 201 ) # atomic: a write method in an atomic group async def create_invoice ( data : InvoiceIn ) -> InvoiceOut : invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data ) await AuditEvent . acreate ( subject = invoice . reference , action = "created" ) return InvoiceOut . from_model ( invoice ) @invoices . post ( "/ {invoice_id} /remind" , status = 204 , atomic = False ) # writes nothing async def remind ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> None : ... On a single action, write @http.post("/invoices", atomic=True) . Hinoki checks the returned value against the response annotation before encoding it (see the response check ). What rolls back ¶ If the handler raises, response encoding/rendering fails, the request times out, or the task is cancelled, the transaction rolls back before the error response is translated. A value that does not match the response annotation is rejected as a 500 , and the transaction rolled back, unless the action opts out with validate_response=False . Returning a streamed response ( Stream , EventStream , or File ) from an atomic=True action annotated -> http.Response is rejected as a 500 inside the transaction and rolls back as well, whereas returning a plain non-stream http.Response with a 4xx status (such as 409 ) is a normal return and commits; raise an APIError when a rejected operation should roll back. Session persistence ( Session.commit() ) runs after the handler and its atomic=True SQL transaction have committed, so a session store write failure happens in a separate boundary after the SQL commit. Do not send email, write local files, or perform another irreversible side effect inside the transaction; arrange it after the transaction commits, or use an outbox owned by the application. RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) makes POST , PUT , PATCH and DELETE atomic by default; GET actions are not. An action opts out with atomic=False . A project created with hinoki new enforces rules.Transactions.require_atomic() ( HNK-TXN-001 ), so a write that opts out stops hinoki check and startup until you record the decision. List the action in except_ in notes/rules.py : # notes/rules.py, listed in `rules` of hinoki.toml from hinoki import rules project_rules = rules . RuleSet ( # ... the other rules rules . Transactions . require_atomic ( except_ = [ "notes.apps.billing.api.remind" ]), ) A temporary exception goes in hinoki-rules.toml instead ( waivers ). Atomic blocks and functions in application code ¶ db.atomic ( from hinoki import db ) opens the same kind of scope in your own code, on the database that is current for the task: the one a request makes active, or the one set with hinoki.orm.use_database(...) . Use it as a block: # notes/apps/billing/operations.py from hinoki import db from .models import AuditEvent , Invoice async def mark_paid ( invoice : Invoice ) -> None : async with db . atomic (): invoice . paid = True await invoice . asave () await AuditEvent . acreate ( subject = invoice . reference , action = "paid" ) or as a decorator on an async def , with or without parentheses: # notes/apps/billing/operations.py @db . atomic async def settle_all () -> int : return await Invoice . filter ( paid = False ) . aupdate ({ "paid" : True }, returning = False ) @db . atomic () async def reopen ( invoice_id : UUID ) -> None : await Invoice . aupdate ( id = invoice_id , paid = False ) Each call of a decorated function opens its own scope: returning commits, an exception rolls back and propagates. The wrapper keeps the function's name, docstring, signature and annotations ( functools.wraps ). In a sync handler, hook or helper, use the same API without await : with db.atomic(): as a block, or @db.atomic on a plain def . The sync model methods ( create , update , bulk_create , ...) inside it run in the same transaction: # notes/apps/billing/operations.py @db . atomic def settle_all_sync () -> int : return Invoice . update_where ({ "paid" : False }, { "paid" : True }, returning = False ) def mark_paid_sync ( invoice : Invoice ) -> None : with db . atomic (): invoice . paid = True invoice . save () The sync forms only work on a worker thread served by Hinoki, as the sync model methods do; on the event loop they raise RuntimeError (use async with there). A nested sync scope is a savepoint, like the async one. Raw Database.execute and fetch remain async-only (see sync and async ). db.atomic() is current_database().atomic() resolved when the block is entered or the function is called. When you hold a Database yourself (a script, a module lifespan, ctx.get(Database) ), call database.atomic() directly; it behaves the same. Database.migration() is the separate, exclusive scope used for migrations. Nesting and savepoints ¶ A scope opened while another scope of the same task is already open becomes a savepoint, whether it comes from atomic=True , async with , or a decorated function. An exception inside the inner scope rolls back only that savepoint; the outer transaction continues and commits when it ends. A decorated function called from an atomic=True action therefore joins the request's transaction as a savepoint rather than committing on its own. # notes/apps/billing/operations.py async def create_with_discount ( data : InvoiceIn , coupon_id : UUID ) -> Invoice : async with db . atomic (): invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data ) try : async with db . atomic (): # SAVEPOINT await Coupon . aupdate ( id = coupon_id , used = True ) raise CouponExpired () except CouponExpired : pass # only the coupon update is undone return invoice # the invoice committed when the outer block ended A child task cannot share its parent's active transaction: opening a nested scope from another task raises DatabaseError . Decorated functions and routes ¶ A function decorated with @db.atomic can also be a route handler (put the HTTP decorator outermost). Binding, OpenAPI and the native server see the original signature, and the handler runs inside its own atomic scope. That scope covers the handler call only: it commits when the handler returns, before the response is encoded. atomic=True on the action is the declaration that also covers response encoding, and it is what HNK-TXN-001 ( rules.Transactions.require_atomic ) reads: the rule does not inspect decorators, so an action that is only decorated with @db.atomic is still reported. Prefer atomic=True on actions and keep db.atomic for application code that the action calls. On the native server lane, a handler is still Python code: Rust calls the Python function, so a @db.atomic function behaves exactly as on the Python pipeline, including the rollback when it raises. After-commit callbacks ¶ Database.after_commit(callback) (for example current_database().after_commit(...) ) registers a sync or async callable without arguments to run after the outermost transaction commits, which is where email, queue publishing and cache invalidation belong. Callbacks run in registration order; a rollback of the transaction, or of the savepoint scope that registered them, drops them, and an exception in one is logged without undoing the commit. Calling it outside a transaction raises DatabaseError . Model hooks register through self.after_commit(callback) ; see lifecycle hooks . # notes/apps/billing/operations.py from hinoki.orm import current_database async def issue ( data : InvoiceIn ) -> Invoice : async with db . atomic (): invoice = await Invoice . acreate ( data ) current_database () . after_commit ( lambda : publish ( "invoice.issued" , invoice . id )) return invoice A send that fails after the commit is logged and does not undo the commit; the callback is not retried. For an email, current_database().after_commit(lambda: mail.send(message)) sends only once the data is durable and never on rollback; see send email . Errors and edge cases ¶ after_commit outside a transaction, or a nested scope opened from a child task, raises DatabaseError . The sync forms raise RuntimeError on the event loop. An action that is only decorated with @db.atomic is still reported by HNK-TXN-001 ; declare atomic=True . See also ¶ Rules : rules.Transactions.require_atomic makes atomic writes a checked promise. Lifecycle hooks : self.after_commit in model hooks. Sync and async

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Each section starts with the message or symptom you see. error: cannot load notes.main:app ¶ Run the command from the project directory (the one with hinoki.toml ) and check the module path and the attribute after the colon. Hinoki adds the current directory to the import path, but the module must still import cleanly: the text after the colon is the original exception. Settings report a missing or unknown variable ¶ Check the settings class's prefix= and the nested names: groups are joined with __ , as in NOTES_DATABASE__URL . Print every expected name with: hinoki settings --example settings.Secret values are shown redacted on purpose. The database connection fails at startup ¶ Each worker opens its pool during startup. Check the backend URL, network reachability and the server from the same environment as the worker, and the backend notes in configure a database . While debugging, use one worker and a small pool: total connections are replicas × workers × pool size. server.<name> is not supported by the granian server ¶ hinoki serve refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, and exits with status 2. Unset it or run on Kiso, the default. See settings that apply to one server only . cannot listen on HOST:PORT ¶ The address is in use, or the host or port is invalid. Stop the other process or pass another --port ; the command exits with status 2. Every request answers 400 disallowed_host or 503 not_ready ¶ 400 disallowed_host : the Host header is not in allowed_hosts . 503 not_ready : the worker has not finished starting, or has begun shutting down ( startup probe ). RelationNotLoaded ¶ Relations are never loaded lazily. Name the relation in the query that needs it: select_related("author") for a single row, prefetch_related("posts") for a collection. See relations . hinoki check reports unverifiable ¶ The rule could not establish its promise. Read the explanation and any fix: line. Some rules inspect only declarations; checks with side effects run only with hinoki check --allow-effects . Sync handlers answer 503 overloaded ¶ Sync handlers and sync hooks share a bounded pool and queue. Move database and network calls to async handlers, keep sync hooks short, or size the pool; see sync and async code . A migration is marked destructive ¶ Read the generated SQL and the data it removes, and test it against a disposable copy before passing --allow-destructive . See migrations . Report a problem ¶ Collect the environment without reading settings or opening a database: hinoki version --verbose --format json hinoki doctor hinoki doctor imports the project application but does not start it, run rules, connect to a database or write files. Include the Hinoki version, the command or route, the complete diagnostic and a minimal example; remove credentials and personal data first.

docs.text: Type checking Hinoki applications ¶ Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. The repository is checked with mypy in strict mode; other checkers and IDEs have not been evaluated systematically. Run the project's check from its checkout: uv run --locked mypy In a project created by hinoki new , mypy is part of the dev dependency group: uv run mypy notes Typed surfaces ¶ Contract Result HTTP decorators Preserve a handler's parameter and return types. http.* and RouteGroup methods share the same typed keyword options, so atomic="yes" or a misspelled keyword such as stauts=201 is a type error. Schema classes Generated constructors check required, unknown and mistyped fields; Field(default_factory=...) preserves the value type. @derive(...) synthesizes fields at runtime, so declare explicit fields when you need static attribute checking on a public schema. Application and route groups Hinoki.include , API classes and RouteGroup provide typed declarations. Unknown include items fail at app construction. Authentication context Annotate a parameter as Caller[User] to receive the typed caller and application user. Decorator composition User decorators should preserve signatures with functools.wraps , ParamSpec and TypeVar . For standalone handlers the final decorated function is dispatched. With RouteGroup , put the HTTP decorator outermost so it captures the final sync or async wrapped handler. Hinoki separates three checks: a preserved handler signature for the type checker, statically known fields on explicitly annotated Schema classes, and registration-time validation of the route contract when Hinoki builds its routes. ORM method signatures ¶ Model construction and common instance operations are typed. Some ORM methods that accept arbitrary model field names still have broad keyword signatures, so a checker may not catch a misspelled field passed to these methods: task = Task ( title = "Write docs" ) # constructor fields and values are checked await task . asave () Fields inherited from an abstract model are part of the checked constructor. Fields that come from a plain (non-model) mixin exist at run time but are not constructor arguments for a type checker; use an abstract model when you need them checked. Model.acreate(**values) and some filter/update keyword calls cannot currently verify each field name against the model class. Use the constructor plus asave() when you want field-level checking on insertion. This limitation does not affect runtime validation of model fields or database constraints. The return types of the write methods are checked: aupdate returns the model, aupdate_where and QuerySet.aupdate a list of it, and with a literal returning=False each returns int ( writes that do not read the row back ). A returning value that is a plain bool gives the union of both. acreate and insert return the model either way. Unpacking a dictionary into aupdate(**values) or update(**values) gives Any , because the dictionary could hold returning ; pass returning=True explicitly to keep the model type. The Python package includes typing metadata, and the compiled hinoki.core module has a matching stub. See the API reference for the public signatures.

docs.text: Time and utilities ¶ Hinoki ships a few helpers where the framework defines the behaviour. Use the standard library for everything else. UTC time ¶ utc_now() returns a timezone-aware datetime in UTC; use it for field factories and application code. # notes/apps/billing/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now class Event ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) A clock is any callable returning an aware datetime ( hinoki.utils.Clock ). Code that depends on time accepts a clock; tests pass a fixed one. No process-wide patching is needed. utc_today(clock=utc_now) returns the date in UTC, independent of the machine's timezone: 2026-01-02 00:30+02:00 is 2026-01-01 . Test clocks ¶ # tests/clocktest.py from datetime import UTC , datetime from hinoki.testing import ManualClock def test_clock_moves () -> None : clock = ManualClock ( datetime ( 2026 , 1 , 1 , tzinfo = UTC )) first = clock () clock . advance ( seconds = 60 ) assert ( clock () - first ) . total_seconds () == 60 ManualClock stores UTC instants, accepts only aware values and works with app.now(clock) , utc_today(clock) and @db.timestamps(clock=...) . Application timezone ¶ # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" ): timezone : str = "Europe/Rome" app.now() returns an aware datetime in the settings' IANA timezone (default UTC ); an invalid name fails while settings load. Apps in one process can use different timezones; there is no Hinoki(timezone=...) . app.now(clock) takes a clock for tests. Model update timestamps ¶ # notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued) @db . timestamps () class Statement ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) updated_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) @db.timestamps() sets the non-nullable updated_at: datetime column on every ORM update: Model.aupdate , aupdate_where , asave , aupdate_from , abulk_update , QuerySet.aupdate and their sync forms. One statement gives every row the same time; a value supplied for the column is replaced. @db.timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock) names another column or injects a clock; clock values must be aware and are stored in UTC. Creation uses the field factories. Raw SQL bypasses the decorator: use a database trigger if independent writers need database-authoritative times. Both columns are ordinary fields, visible to type checkers and migrations. Other common needs ¶ Need Use UUID identifiers uuid.uuid4() secret tokens secrets , or hinoki.crypto.random_token() for Hinoki authentication file system paths pathlib.Path configuration settings requests in tests hinoki.testing clients ( testing ) Hinoki has no slug, retry or environment helpers: their rules belong to the application. See also ¶ Model options Testing

docs.text: Restrict hosts, origins and HTTPS ¶ A new application answers any Host , sends no CORS headers, never redirects to HTTPS and trusts no proxy. That keeps development friction-free; before a deployment, name what it serves. The built-in groups ( cors , security , server ) are set from the environment, .env or a TOML file the class names; a value assigned to such a group in the class body is not read. # notes/settings.py from hinoki import settings class ProjectSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "NOTES_" , dotenv = ".env" , toml = "settings.toml" ): pass # settings.toml allowed_hosts = [ "api.example.com" ] [cors] origins = [ "https://app.example.com" ] [security] redirect_https = true hsts_seconds = 31_536_000 [server] trusted_proxies = [ "10.20.0.0/16" ] Every field can also come from the environment, which is usually where a deployment sets them and which wins over the TOML file: NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS = api.example.com,.example.org NOTES_CORS__ORIGINS = https://app.example.com,http://localhost:5173 NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS = true Debug, allowed hosts and CORS ¶ These three are off or permissive by default, so an application behaves the same until you set them. debug ¶ With debug on, the 500 internal_error answer for an unhandled exception also carries a debug object: { "error" : "internal_error" , "request_id" : "5f0c…" , "debug" : { "exception" : "builtins.RuntimeError" , "message" : "the cache is cold" , "traceback" : [ "Traceback (most recent call last):\n" , "…" ] } } Declared errors, validation errors and the other framework answers are unchanged, and the exception is logged either way. Exception messages can contain data you would not publish, so keep debug off in a deployment; each worker logs a warning at startup while it is on. debug changes nothing else: it does not enable documentation pages, relax authentication or skip the host check (with an admin or a WebSocket route and allowed_hosts at * it narrows the hosts to loopback, see below), and hinoki dev does not set it. allowed_hosts ¶ The Host header of every request must match one entry: Entry Matches * (the default) Any host; nothing is checked api.example.com That host, on any port .example.org example.org and every subdomain 127.0.0.1 , ::1 That address ( [::1]:8000 in the header) Matching ignores case, the port and a trailing dot. The header must be exactly one host with an optional port; a request for another host, with two Host headers or without a usable one, receives 400 disallowed_host before routing, authentication and body reading; documentation routes are covered too. Entries are names: a scheme, port, path, non-ASCII text (write an international name in its ASCII IDNA form, xn--... ) or a partial wildcard such as *.example.com fails at load, and * cannot be mixed with other entries. A dot entry is as wide as it reads: .com allows every .com host. Set the list in a deployment that is reachable under more names than it should answer to. While allowed_hosts is * (the default, and the case for an app built without settings) and debug is off, each worker logs a warning at startup (logger hinoki.runtime , shown with the default logging settings): every Host header is accepted, so links, redirects and cache keys built from it, such as a password-reset link, can name a host the client chose (Host header injection). Name the hosts the deployment serves to silence it, for example allowed_hosts=("app.example.com",) , or (".example.com",) for a domain and its subdomains ( NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com ). It is only a warning for a plain API, so the default keeps working in development. An app that includes the admin or registers a WebSocket route is refused at startup instead (the lifespan fails with a message naming allowed_hosts , and hinoki serve logs the error and exits with status 1; the server may already have logged that it is listening, but it answers no request): the admin's CSRF check and the WebSocket same-origin check compare the Origin header with the Host header, so with * a DNS-rebinding page ( Host: evil.example , Origin: https://evil.example ) would pass both. Name the served hosts. debug lifts the refusal for local development only, and then the app accepts loopback hosts only: with debug on and allowed_hosts at * , an app that serves an admin or a WebSocket route accepts only the Host names localhost , *.localhost , any 127.0.0.0/8 address and [::1] (with or without a port, in any case, with or without a trailing dot) for the whole app, and any other Host receives 400 , so a DNS-rebinding page cannot reach a development server; set allowed_hosts to serve other names (an explicit list is always used as given). An app without an admin or a WebSocket route still accepts any Host under debug . Each worker logs a startup warning while the loopback-only rule applies. With debug on the any-host warning is not logged, and the in-process test clients ( ASGIClient , SyncClient ) and the MCP run_scenario tool, which receive no network Host header, do not log it either. The in-process test clients send no Host header, so a test of an application with a restrictive list passes one: await client.get("/x", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) . cors ¶ CORS is off while cors.origins is empty: no header is added and OPTIONS requests receive 405 . With origins configured: A request whose Origin is listed receives access-control-allow-origin with that origin and vary: origin , on every answer including errors, so a browser client can read a 401 or 422 body. credentials = true adds access-control-allow-credentials: true ; expose_headers is sent as access-control-expose-headers . A request from any other origin, or without an Origin , is served normally without the permission headers and still carries vary: origin , so a shared cache never hands one origin's answer to another; the browser refuses to hand the response to the page. CORS tells browsers what to allow. It is not authentication and does not stop a non-browser client. A preflight ( OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method ) is answered with 204 , the configured methods , headers and max_age , without reaching a route or its access policy. A preflight from an origin that is not listed receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Origins are compared exactly, in lower case as browsers send them: https://app.example.com and https://app.example.com:8443 are different origins, and a trailing slash or path is refused at load. Browsers leave a default port out of Origin , so list https://app.example.com , not https://app.example.com:443 . The single entry * answers every origin with access-control-allow-origin: * ; it cannot be combined with credentials , and browsers will not send cookies or HTTP authentication to it. The application policy applies to every route that does not declare its own, including the ASGI and WSGI adapters (see per-route CORS below). An answer that already sets access-control-allow-origin itself (a Response with that header) is sent as it is, without the policy's headers. Per-route CORS ¶ An action can carry its own policy with cors=http.Cors(...) , for a public feed, a partner endpoint or a route that must not be readable from the origins the rest of the application allows. http.Cors takes the fields of settings.CorsSettings ( origins , methods , headers , expose_headers , credentials , max_age ) and requires at least one origin: # notes/apps/feed/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http from notes.security import reader # an `Access` policy partner = http . Cors ( origins = ( "https://partner.example" ,), credentials = True ) class Feed ( Schema ): feed : str @http . get ( "/feed/partner" , access = reader , cors = partner ) async def partner_feed () -> Feed : return Feed ( feed = "partner" ) Precedence. The route's policy replaces the application's for that route; nothing is merged, so the application's origins do not apply to it. An action without cors= keeps the application policy, and a route with cors= works even while the application's cors.origins is empty. Preflight. A preflight is answered for the route the browser asks about: Access-Control-Request-Method names the method, the request path names the route. A route with its own policy answers with its own methods , headers , max_age and origin check ( 403 cors_origin_denied for an origin it does not list). A method that no route has on that path is answered by the application policy. A preflight never runs the route's access policy, a transaction or the handler. Answers. Every answer from a matched route, errors from access or validation included, carries that route's headers and vary: origin . Answers before a route is known ( 404 , 405 ) carry the application's. Groups and generated CRUD. RouteGroup("/feed", cors=http.Cors(...)) is the default of its actions ( cors=None on an action returns it to the application policy), and crud(..., cors=http.Cors(...)) gives all generated actions the policy. Kiso decides these natively; the ASGI and WSGI adapters apply the same rules in Python. Security headers and HTTPS ¶ Every HTTP response gets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff , the configured X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy , including errors, OpenAPI/docs and admin responses. Defaults are SAMEORIGIN and same-origin , preserving the admin's existing referrer privacy default. These fields are owned by the app security policy: configured values replace same-named headers returned by a route. The choices are enums rather than arbitrary strings, and environment/TOML values must match the listed wire values exactly. FrameOptions provides deny and sameorigin . ReferrerPolicy provides no-referrer , no-referrer-when-downgrade , same-origin , origin , strict-origin , origin-when-cross-origin , strict-origin-when-cross-origin and unsafe-url . unsafe-url can disclose the full referring URL to another origin; use it only when that is intended. # settings.toml [security] redirect_https = true hsts_seconds = 31_536_000 hsts_include_subdomains = true frame_options = "deny" referrer_policy = "strict-origin" For configuration loaded from the environment, set NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com and NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true . A wildcard host policy cannot be combined with the redirect: Hinoki requires an explicit host allowlist before constructing an absolute Location , which avoids redirecting an attacker supplied Host value. The redirect is 308 , preserves the method and raw path/query, and runs before route lookup, authentication and body reading. A configured CORS preflight is answered before redirecting so browser preflight requests remain usable. HSTS defaults off. Hinoki emits it only when the request's effective scheme is HTTPS. Behind TLS termination, configure the exact proxy addresses in server.trusted_proxies ; an untrusted X-Forwarded-Proto does not enable HSTS or suppress the redirect. hsts_preload also requires hsts_include_subdomains and a max-age of at least one year. Use HSTS only after confirming that HTTPS is available for every covered host: browsers retain the policy after the response. Reverse proxies and request IDs ¶ Forwarded metadata is ignored unless the immediate socket peer matches server.trusted_proxies . Configure only the addresses or CIDRs of proxies that remove client-supplied forwarding headers and write their own values. For example: # settings.toml # The private address used by this deployment's ingress, not every private network. [server] trusted_proxies = [ "10.20.0.0/16" ] request_id_header = "x-correlation-id" trust_request_id = true From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single X-Forwarded-Proto value of http or https and walks a bounded X-Forwarded-For chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. Request.scheme and Request.client use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. X-Forwarded-Host is never used: Host , allowed_hosts and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header. On a listener bound to :: , an IPv4 peer can appear as ::ffff:a.b.c.d , which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see behind a reverse proxy . Request IDs are generated by default. With trust_request_id=True , one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in Request.request_id , built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private. Set logging.include_request_id=true to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append request_id=<id> and JSON logs include a request_id field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers. Errors and edge cases ¶ An invalid allowed_hosts entry, a * mixed with names, or a CORS origin with a path fails when settings load, before any worker starts. A served app with the admin or a WebSocket route, allowed_hosts at * and debug off does not start; with debug on it answers 400 to every Host that is not loopback ( localhost , *.localhost , 127.0.0.0/8 , [::1] ). The in-process test clients are exempt. redirect_https=True with allowed_hosts left at * is refused at load: the redirect needs a host it can trust. A request for an unlisted host receives 400 disallowed_host ; a preflight from an unlisted origin receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Tests with a restrictive host list pass the header: await client.get("/health", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) . See also ¶ Settings : how values are loaded, named and inspected. Kiso server : addresses behind a proxy on Kiso. Errors : the JSON bodies of these answers.

docs.text: With debug on, the 500 internal_error answer for an unhandled exception also carries a debug object: { "error" : "internal_error" , "request_id" : "5f0c…" , "debug" : { "exception" : "builtins.RuntimeError" , "message" : "the cache is cold" , "traceback" : [ "Traceback (most recent call last):\n" , "…" ] } } Declared errors, validation errors and the other framework answers are unchanged, and the exception is logged either way. Exception messages can contain data you would not publish, so keep debug off in a deployment; each worker logs a warning at startup while it is on. debug changes nothing else: it does not enable documentation pages, relax authentication or skip the host check (with an admin or a WebSocket route and allowed_hosts at * it narrows the hosts to loopback, see below), and hinoki dev does not set it.
docs.title: debug

docs.text: The Host header of every request must match one entry: Entry Matches * (the default) Any host; nothing is checked api.example.com That host, on any port .example.org example.org and every subdomain 127.0.0.1 , ::1 That address ( [::1]:8000 in the header) Matching ignores case, the port and a trailing dot. The header must be exactly one host with an optional port; a request for another host, with two Host headers or without a usable one, receives 400 disallowed_host before routing, authentication and body reading; documentation routes are covered too. Entries are names: a scheme, port, path, non-ASCII text (write an international name in its ASCII IDNA form, xn--... ) or a partial wildcard such as *.example.com fails at load, and * cannot be mixed with other entries. A dot entry is as wide as it reads: .com allows every .com host. Set the list in a deployment that is reachable under more names than it should answer to. While allowed_hosts is * (the default, and the case for an app built without settings) and debug is off, each worker logs a warning at startup (logger hinoki.runtime , shown with the default logging settings): every Host header is accepted, so links, redirects and cache keys built from it, such as a password-reset link, can name a host the client chose (Host header injection). Name the hosts the deployment serves to silence it, for example allowed_hosts=("app.example.com",) , or (".example.com",) for a domain and its subdomains ( NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com ). It is only a warning for a plain API, so the default keeps working in development. An app that includes the admin or registers a WebSocket route is refused at startup instead (the lifespan fails with a message naming allowed_hosts , and hinoki serve logs the error and exits with status 1; the server may already have logged that it is listening, but it answers no request): the admin's CSRF check and the WebSocket same-origin check compare the Origin header with the Host header, so with * a DNS-rebinding page ( Host: evil.example , Origin: https://evil.example ) would pass both. Name the served hosts. debug lifts the refusal for local development only, and then the app accepts loopback hosts only: with debug on and allowed_hosts at * , an app that serves an admin or a WebSocket route accepts only the Host names localhost , *.localhost , any 127.0.0.0/8 address and [::1] (with or without a port, in any case, with or without a trailing dot) for the whole app, and any other Host receives 400 , so a DNS-rebinding page cannot reach a development server; set allowed_hosts to serve other names (an explicit list is always used as given). An app without an admin or a WebSocket route still accepts any Host under debug . Each worker logs a startup warning while the loopback-only rule applies. With debug on the any-host warning is not logged, and the in-process test clients ( ASGIClient , SyncClient ) and the MCP run_scenario tool, which receive no network Host header, do not log it either. The in-process test clients send no Host header, so a test of an application with a restrictive list passes one: await client.get("/x", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) .
docs.title: allowed_hosts

docs.text: CORS is off while cors.origins is empty: no header is added and OPTIONS requests receive 405 . With origins configured: A request whose Origin is listed receives access-control-allow-origin with that origin and vary: origin , on every answer including errors, so a browser client can read a 401 or 422 body. credentials = true adds access-control-allow-credentials: true ; expose_headers is sent as access-control-expose-headers . A request from any other origin, or without an Origin , is served normally without the permission headers and still carries vary: origin , so a shared cache never hands one origin's answer to another; the browser refuses to hand the response to the page. CORS tells browsers what to allow. It is not authentication and does not stop a non-browser client. A preflight ( OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method ) is answered with 204 , the configured methods , headers and max_age , without reaching a route or its access policy. A preflight from an origin that is not listed receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Origins are compared exactly, in lower case as browsers send them: https://app.example.com and https://app.example.com:8443 are different origins, and a trailing slash or path is refused at load. Browsers leave a default port out of Origin , so list https://app.example.com , not https://app.example.com:443 . The single entry * answers every origin with access-control-allow-origin: * ; it cannot be combined with credentials , and browsers will not send cookies or HTTP authentication to it. The application policy applies to every route that does not declare its own, including the ASGI and WSGI adapters (see per-route CORS below). An answer that already sets access-control-allow-origin itself (a Response with that header) is sent as it is, without the policy's headers.
docs.title: cors

docs.text: An action can carry its own policy with cors=http.Cors(...) , for a public feed, a partner endpoint or a route that must not be readable from the origins the rest of the application allows. http.Cors takes the fields of settings.CorsSettings ( origins , methods , headers , expose_headers , credentials , max_age ) and requires at least one origin: # notes/apps/feed/api.py from hinoki import Schema , http from notes.security import reader # an `Access` policy partner = http . Cors ( origins = ( "https://partner.example" ,), credentials = True ) class Feed ( Schema ): feed : str @http . get ( "/feed/partner" , access = reader , cors = partner ) async def partner_feed () -> Feed : return Feed ( feed = "partner" ) Precedence. The route's policy replaces the application's for that route; nothing is merged, so the application's origins do not apply to it. An action without cors= keeps the application policy, and a route with cors= works even while the application's cors.origins is empty. Preflight. A preflight is answered for the route the browser asks about: Access-Control-Request-Method names the method, the request path names the route. A route with its own policy answers with its own methods , headers , max_age and origin check ( 403 cors_origin_denied for an origin it does not list). A method that no route has on that path is answered by the application policy. A preflight never runs the route's access policy, a transaction or the handler. Answers. Every answer from a matched route, errors from access or validation included, carries that route's headers and vary: origin . Answers before a route is known ( 404 , 405 ) carry the application's. Groups and generated CRUD. RouteGroup("/feed", cors=http.Cors(...)) is the default of its actions ( cors=None on an action returns it to the application policy), and crud(..., cors=http.Cors(...)) gives all generated actions the policy. Kiso decides these natively; the ASGI and WSGI adapters apply the same rules in Python.
docs.title: Per-route CORS

docs.text: Every HTTP response gets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff , the configured X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy , including errors, OpenAPI/docs and admin responses. Defaults are SAMEORIGIN and same-origin , preserving the admin's existing referrer privacy default. These fields are owned by the app security policy: configured values replace same-named headers returned by a route. The choices are enums rather than arbitrary strings, and environment/TOML values must match the listed wire values exactly. FrameOptions provides deny and sameorigin . ReferrerPolicy provides no-referrer , no-referrer-when-downgrade , same-origin , origin , strict-origin , origin-when-cross-origin , strict-origin-when-cross-origin and unsafe-url . unsafe-url can disclose the full referring URL to another origin; use it only when that is intended. # settings.toml [security] redirect_https = true hsts_seconds = 31_536_000 hsts_include_subdomains = true frame_options = "deny" referrer_policy = "strict-origin" For configuration loaded from the environment, set NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com and NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true . A wildcard host policy cannot be combined with the redirect: Hinoki requires an explicit host allowlist before constructing an absolute Location , which avoids redirecting an attacker supplied Host value. The redirect is 308 , preserves the method and raw path/query, and runs before route lookup, authentication and body reading. A configured CORS preflight is answered before redirecting so browser preflight requests remain usable. HSTS defaults off. Hinoki emits it only when the request's effective scheme is HTTPS. Behind TLS termination, configure the exact proxy addresses in server.trusted_proxies ; an untrusted X-Forwarded-Proto does not enable HSTS or suppress the redirect. hsts_preload also requires hsts_include_subdomains and a max-age of at least one year. Use HSTS only after confirming that HTTPS is available for every covered host: browsers retain the policy after the response.
docs.title: Security headers and HTTPS

docs.text: Forwarded metadata is ignored unless the immediate socket peer matches server.trusted_proxies . Configure only the addresses or CIDRs of proxies that remove client-supplied forwarding headers and write their own values. For example: # settings.toml # The private address used by this deployment's ingress, not every private network. [server] trusted_proxies = [ "10.20.0.0/16" ] request_id_header = "x-correlation-id" trust_request_id = true From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single X-Forwarded-Proto value of http or https and walks a bounded X-Forwarded-For chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. Request.scheme and Request.client use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. X-Forwarded-Host is never used: Host , allowed_hosts and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header. On a listener bound to :: , an IPv4 peer can appear as ::ffff:a.b.c.d , which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see behind a reverse proxy . Request IDs are generated by default. With trust_request_id=True , one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in Request.request_id , built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private. Set logging.include_request_id=true to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append request_id=<id> and JSON logs include a request_id field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers.
docs.title: Reverse proxies and request IDs

docs.text: An invalid allowed_hosts entry, a * mixed with names, or a CORS origin with a path fails when settings load, before any worker starts. A served app with the admin or a WebSocket route, allowed_hosts at * and debug off does not start; with debug on it answers 400 to every Host that is not loopback ( localhost , *.localhost , 127.0.0.0/8 , [::1] ). The in-process test clients are exempt. redirect_https=True with allowed_hosts left at * is refused at load: the redirect needs a host it can trust. A request for an unlisted host receives 400 disallowed_host ; a preflight from an unlisted origin receives 403 cors_origin_denied . Tests with a restrictive host list pass the header: await client.get("/health", headers={"host": "api.example.com"}) .
docs.title: Errors and edge cases
