It keeps the class and, for a streamed answer, the source of the body. hinoki.http.response.set_cookie ¶ set_cookie ( name : str , value : str , * , path : str = "/" , max_age : int | None = None , http_only : bool = True , secure : bool = True , same_site : str = "Lax" , ) -> tuple [ str , str ] A ("set-cookie", ...) header for Response(headers=[...]) . The name must be a token and the value cookie-safe (no space, quote, comma, semicolon or backslash); encode richer data yourself. hinoki.http.Stream ¶ Stream ( body : Source , * , status : int = 200 , headers : ResponseHeaders = (), content_type : str | None = None , length : int | None = None , ) Bases: Sourced A body of bytes or str pieces (a str is sent as UTF-8). body is an iterable or an async iterable; a plain iterable is advanced in the bounded sync executor. length declares the exact size when it is known, which gives the answer a content-length ; without it the body is sent with chunked framing (HTTP/1.1) or until the stream ends (HTTP/2). hinoki.http.EventStream ¶ EventStream ( events : AsyncIterable [ Event | str ] | Iterable [ Event | str ], * , status : int = 200 , headers : ResponseHeaders = (), keepalive : float | EllipsisType | None = ... , retry : int | None = None , ) Bases: Sourced Server-sent events ( text/event-stream ) from an iterable of Event or str (a str is the data of one event). retry is the reconnection delay in milliseconds sent to the client first. keepalive is the seconds of silence after which a comment is sent: the default is execution.sse_keepalive , None turns it off. The answer has cache-control: no-store and x-accel-buffering: no . retry_frame instance-attribute ¶ retry_frame = ( None if retry is None else Event ( retry = retry ) . wire ) keepalive instance-attribute ¶ keepalive = keepalive preamble property ¶ preamble : bytes encode ¶ encode ( piece : object ) -> bytes hinoki.http.Event ¶ Event ( data : object = None , * , event : str | None = None , id : str | None = None , retry : int | None = None , comment : str | None = None , ) One server-sent event. data that is not a str (a Schema , a dict , a list or a scalar) is sent as JSON; None sends no data field. Line breaks in data and comment become separate lines; event and id with CR, LF or NUL raise ValueError here. wire instance-attribute ¶ wire : bytes = core . sse_frame ( text , event , id , retry , comment ) hinoki.http.File ¶ File ( path : str | PathLike [ str ], * , root : str | PathLike [ str ] | None = None , filename : str | None = None , content_type : str | None = None , status : int = 200 , headers : ResponseHeaders = (), ) Bases: Streamed A file sent by the server: File("reports/q3.pdf", root=REPORTS) . A relative path is taken from root . With root the file must be inside it once symbolic links are resolved; a missing file, a directory or a path that leaves root answers 404 . filename adds a content-disposition: attachment header. The content-type is guessed from the name unless given. The whole file is sent with its size as content-length (ranges are not supported: accept-ranges: none ). path instance-attribute ¶ path = os . fspath ( path ) root instance-attribute ¶ root = None if root is None else os . fspath ( root ) same_body ¶ same_body ( other : Streamed ) -> bool hinoki.access.Access dataclass ¶ Access ( auth : BaseAuth [ Any ], permissions : Iterable [ str ] = () ) Which provider authenticates an action and which permissions it requires. Access(auth=tokens, permissions=["posts:write"]) . Declaring an Access does not protect anything by itself: only actions that name it are protected. Enforcement belongs to the request pipeline. auth instance-attribute ¶ auth : BaseAuth [ Any ] permissions class-attribute instance-attribute ¶ permissions : frozenset [ str ] = field ( default_factory = frozenset ) hinoki.errors.APIError ¶ APIError ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: Exception An error with a public HTTP representation. Subclasses set status , code and message ; an instance may override them, which is how a handler answers with a status of its own: APIError("Card declined", status=402, code="card_declined") . details is public data, never internal state. hinoki.errors.BadRequest ¶ BadRequest ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: APIError hinoki.errors.Unauthorized ¶ Unauthorized ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: APIError hinoki.errors.Forbidden ¶ Forbidden ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: APIError hinoki.errors.NotFound ¶ NotFound ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: APIError hinoki.errors.Conflict ¶ Conflict ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: APIError hinoki.errors.TooManyRequests ¶ TooManyRequests ( retry_after : int , message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , ) Bases: APIError The one error a rate_limit policy may raise to refuse a request. retry_after is a whole number of seconds from 1 to 86,400, sent as Retry-After ; anything else is refused when the error is created. hinoki.errors.UniqueConflict ¶ UniqueConflict ( message : str | None = None , * , code : str | None = None , status : int | None = None , details : list [ dict [ str , Any ]] | None = None , headers : dict [ str , str ] | None = None , ) Bases: Conflict A unique value is already in use: the answer to a UniqueViolation . hinoki.errors.ObjectNotFound ¶ Bases: ModelError A query that must return one row returned none. Each model has its own subclass as Model.NotFound ; HTTP maps it to 404. hinoki.errors.ErrorRegistry ¶ ErrorRegistry () Maps exception classes to handlers; the most specific class wins. is_builtin ¶ is_builtin ( exc : Exception ) -> bool Whether only synchronous built-in translations can answer exc : no application handler matches it. translate_builtin ¶ translate_builtin ( exc : Exception ) -> APIError | None translate for an exception is_builtin accepted, without a coroutine. translate async ¶ translate ( exc : Exception ) -> APIError | None The public error for exc , or None if nothing handles it. A handler that fails or returns something else is treated as unhandled. Middleware ¶ A project-wide middleware subclasses Middleware ; see the middleware guide . List it in middleware of [project] in hinoki.toml or pass middleware=[...] to Hinoki . hinoki.http.Middleware ¶ Base class for a middleware; any object with this async call works. hinoki.http.MiddlewareRequest dataclass ¶ MiddlewareRequest ( method : str , path : str , route : str , headers : Mapping [ str , str ], query : str , client : tuple [ str , int ] | None , scheme : str , request_id : str , ) The head of the request: no body, nothing to change. method instance-attribute ¶ method : str path instance-attribute ¶ path : str route instance-attribute ¶ route : str headers instance-attribute ¶ headers : Mapping [ str , str ] query instance-attribute ¶ query : str client instance-attribute ¶ client : tuple [ str , int ] | None scheme instance-attribute ¶ scheme : str request_id instance-attribute ¶ request_id : str hinoki.http.Next module-attribute ¶ Next = Callable [[], Awaitable [ Response ]] hinoki.http.cors.Cors dataclass ¶ Cors () Bases: CorsSettings The browser origins that may read this action's answers. It takes the fields of settings.CorsSettings and replaces the application's policy for the action: nothing is merged. origins is required; an action with no cors= keeps the application's policy. validate ¶ validate () -> None WebSockets ¶ The WebSockets guide explains the handler, access policies, origins and limits. hinoki.http.websocket ¶ websocket ( path : str , * , access : Access | Unset | None = UNSET , message : type [ Schema ] | None = None , reply : type [ Schema ] | None = None , subprotocols : Sequence [ str ] | Mapping [ str , Access | None ] = (), origins : Sequence [ str ] = (), max_message_bytes : int | None = None , idle_timeout : float | None = None , ) -> Callable [ [ Callable [ P , Coroutine [ Any , Any , R ]]], Callable [ P , Coroutine [ Any , Any , R ]], ] Declare a WebSocket action on path ( /rooms/{room} ), on a function or on a method of an API class (whose prefix it then takes). access authenticates the handshake; a refusal is the usual HTTP answer. message and reply are the Schema of the JSON the client sends and receives. subprotocols names the ones the action speaks (the client must offer one); a mapping gives each its own Access . origins adds allowed browser origins to the same-origin and application CORS ones. max_message_bytes and idle_timeout override the execution.ws_* settings; idle_timeout (seconds without a message from the client) is off by default. The handler's annotations are read when the application includes it, so they may name classes defined later. hinoki.http.WebSocket ¶ WebSocket ( transport : Transport , * , path : str , subprotocol : str | None = None , message : type [ Schema ] | None = None , reply : type [ Schema ] | None = None , ) One open WebSocket, as the handler sees it. receive_* wait for the next message and raise WebSocketClosed once the connection is over; send_* wait for room in the bounded outgoing queue. async for message in socket ends when the connection does. transport instance-attribute ¶ transport = transport path instance-attribute ¶ path = path subprotocol instance-attribute ¶ subprotocol = subprotocol message instance-attribute ¶ message = message reply instance-attribute ¶ reply = reply closed property ¶ closed : tuple [ int , str ] | None (code, reason) once the connection is over, else None . receive_text async ¶ receive_text () -> str The next message, which must be text; a binary one closes with 1003. receive_bytes async ¶ receive_bytes () -> bytes The next message, which must be binary; a text one closes with 1003. receive_json async ¶ receive_json () -> Any receive_json ( schema : type [ S ]) -> S receive_json ( schema : type [ Schema ] | None = None ) -> Any The next text message parsed as JSON and, with a Schema (the argument, else the route's message ), validated. Text that is not JSON closes with 1007; JSON that does not validate closes with 1008. send_text async ¶ send_text ( text : str ) -> None send_bytes async ¶ send_bytes ( data : bytes ) -> None send_json async ¶ send_json ( value : object ) -> None Send value as a JSON text message. With reply= on the route a dict is validated into that Schema first, and an instance of a subclass of it is sent with the fields of reply only. close async ¶ close ( code : int = CloseCode . NORMAL , reason : str = "" ) -> None Close after the messages already queued. ValueError for a code that a peer may not send ( 1005 , 1006 , 1015 and anything outside 1000 to 4999); closing a closed connection does nothing. hinoki.http.WebSocketClosed ¶ WebSocketClosed ( code : int = ABNORMAL , reason : str = '' ) Bases: Exception The connection is closed: the peer closed it, the server did (shutdown, idle timeout, a limit), or the handler did. code and reason are the close the connection ended with ( 1006 when it was lost without one). hinoki.http.CloseCode ¶ Bases: IntEnum The status codes a handler is likely to send (RFC 6455, section 7.4). Rate limits ¶ hinoki.ratelimit.RateLimitPolicy ¶ Bases: Protocol Anything with a check method, def or async def . A sync check runs on the bounded executor and must use sync clients with finite timeouts; an async one runs on the event loop. hinoki.ratelimit.RateLimitContext dataclass ¶ RateLimitContext ( method : str , route : str , client : str | None , caller : Caller [ Any ] | None , lookup : Callable [[ type [ Any ]], Any ], ) What a policy may decide from: no headers, credentials, body or query. resource ¶ resource ( kind : type [ T ]) -> T The worker-owned resource of this type that a module provided (for example a Redis client or the Database ); LookupError if none. hinoki.ratelimit.RateLimit ¶ RateLimit ( limit : int , window : float , * , key : KeySource = "client" , tenant : Tenant | None = None , cost : int = 1 , scope : str | None = None , unknown_factor : int = 10 , headers : bool = False , on_error : Literal [ "closed" , "open" ] = "closed" , storage : Storage | None = None , clock : Callable [[], datetime ] | None = None , ) At most limit requests per window seconds for one key, counted in one shared table (or in memory, see storage ). A cell rate algorithm: a burst of limit is admitted at once and the sustained rate is limit per window . A refusal does not use up quota. The key is hashed in the native core, so a client address, user id or custom key never reaches SQL, logs or metrics. key is "client" (the trusted address, an IPv6 one by its /64), "caller" (the authenticated caller, the client for an anonymous request) or a plain function of the context returning a string. scope defaults to the method and the route, so routes count apart; give routes the same scope to share a quota. tenant adds a segment to the key. A request with no known client shares one bucket unknown_factor times as large. on_error="closed" answers 503 when storage is unavailable, "open" admits the request and counts it. headers=True adds RateLimit-Limit , RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset (whole seconds) to admitted and refused answers. clock returns an aware datetime ( hinoki.testing.ManualClock ); the default is the system clock. storage instance-attribute ¶ storage : Storage = storage or DatabaseLimits () limit instance-attribute ¶ limit = limit window instance-attribute ¶ window = _window_seconds ( window ) key instance-attribute ¶ key = key tenant instance-attribute ¶ tenant = tenant scope instance-attribute ¶ scope = scope headers instance-attribute ¶ headers = headers on_error instance-attribute ¶ on_error = on_error clock instance-attribute ¶ clock = clock rule instance-attribute ¶ rule = core . RateRule ( limit , self . window , cost , unknown_factor , on_error == "open" , ) attach_metrics ¶ attach_metrics ( metrics : RateLimitMetrics ) -> None Count this limiter's decisions into the server's metrics, replacing the metrics of an earlier worker in this process. release ¶ release () -> None Forget the limiters bound to a worker's database, and its metrics, when that worker shuts down; a later worker binds its own. Memory buckets stay with their MemoryLimits . decide async ¶ decide ( context : RateLimitContext ) -> core . RateDecision Count one hit and return the decision; raises core.RateLimitUnavailable when storage fails and on_error is closed. decide_sync ¶ decide_sync ( context : RateLimitContext ) -> core . RateDecision decide for a thread with no event loop. Raises RuntimeError on an event loop thread. header_items ¶ header_items ( decision : RateDecision , ) -> tuple [ tuple [ str , str ], ... ] The RateLimit-* headers of a decision, or none unless headers . refusal ¶ refusal ( decision : RateDecision ) -> TooManyRequests The TooManyRequests of a refused decision. check async ¶ check ( context : RateLimitContext ) -> None check_sync ¶ check_sync ( context : RateLimitContext ) -> None hinoki.ratelimit.DatabaseLimits dataclass ¶ DatabaseLimits ( table : str = "hinoki_rate_limits" , max_rows : int = 1000000 , timeout : float = 0.5 , sweep_every : int = 1000 , ) Buckets in a table of the worker's Database , shared by every worker. max_rows caps the table: once full, new keys share one overflow bucket per scope, unknown_factor times as large, until expired rows are swept. timeout (seconds, at most 5) bounds one check, the wait for a connection included. hinoki.ratelimit.MemoryLimits dataclass ¶ MemoryLimits ( max_rows : int = 100000 , sweep_every : int = 1000 ) Buckets in the memory of ONE worker: not shared, reset on restart. For development and tests. The buckets belong to this instance, created at the first request, so routes given the same instance and the same scope and tenant count together.

docs.text: Hinoki ( * , settings : object | None = None , include : Sequence [ Includable ] | None = None , modules : Sequence [ Module | type [ Module ]] = (), commands : Sequence [ Command | type [ Command ]] = (), on_startup : Sequence [ Hook ] = (), on_shutdown : Sequence [ Hook ] = (), events : Sequence [ Handlers ] | None = None , email_templates : Sequence [ TemplateBase ] = (), startup_url : str | None = None , runtime : RuntimeConfig | None = None , title : str | None = None , version : str | None = None , openapi_url : str | Unset | None = UNSET , docs_url : str | Unset | None = UNSET , redoc_url : str | Unset | None = UNSET , llms_url : str | Unset | None = UNSET , openapi_version : Literal [ "3.1" , "3.2" ] | None = None , rules : RuleSet | None = None , enforce_rules : bool = True , waivers : str | Path | None = None , parsers : Sequence [ Parser ] | None = None , renderers : Sequence [ Renderer ] | None = None , middleware : Sequence [ Middleware ] | None = None , ) A Hinoki application. Registering routes builds the native router; nothing connects to anything, so factories returning Hinoki are safe to import and call. The instance is itself an ASGI callable ( granian --interface asgi module:app ); the first call freezes the declarations. on_startup and on_shutdown list functions taking the worker's ModuleContext ( async def or def ). Startup hooks run once per worker after the modules have started; shutdown hooks run before they are closed, and only after a startup that completed. events lists the Handlers collections whose typed event handlers run, in this order (see hinoki.events ); an unlisted one does nothing. email_templates lists the mail.Template objects the application sends. They go to the email module the email: EmailSettings field implies; with your own EmailModule pass them there instead. File templates are read and checked when each worker starts. startup_url optionally reserves a public GET/HEAD endpoint that returns {"status": "ok"} after worker startup. It reports startup completion, not application, database, or event-loop health. waivers names the owner's waiver file applied to the startup rules; it must exist. Without it, hinoki-rules.toml at the project root is used.

docs.text: RouteGroup ( prefix : str = "" , * , access : Access | None = None , atomic : bool = False , errors : Sequence [ type [ APIError ]] = (), cors : Cors | None = None , include_in_schema : bool = True , tags : Sequence [ str ] = (), ) A function-based route group with a shared path prefix and defaults. Decorated functions belong to this group and the group can be included once in a Hinoki application. Use API for class-based resources. tasks = RouteGroup("/tasks", access=member_only, atomic=True, errors=(NotFound,)) @tasks.get("/") # GET /tasks async def listing(...): ... @tasks.post("/", status=201) # POST /tasks, atomic=True async def create(...): ... @tasks.get("/health", access=None) # public on purpose, overriding the group prefix is prepended to every path ( "/" means the prefix itself), access is the default policy (pass access=None on an action to make it public), atomic=True makes POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE transactional unless the action says atomic=False , errors are added to each action's own and cors is the default http.Cors ( cors=None on an action keeps the application's policy). include_in_schema=False leaves every action out of the OpenAPI document unless it says include_in_schema=True , and tags come before the tags of each action. The result is an ordinary action: rules, OpenAPI and the MCP see no difference.

docs.text: RateLimit ( limit : int , window : float , * , key : KeySource = "client" , tenant : Tenant | None = None , cost : int = 1 , scope : str | None = None , unknown_factor : int = 10 , headers : bool = False , on_error : Literal [ "closed" , "open" ] = "closed" , storage : Storage | None = None , clock : Callable [[], datetime ] | None = None , ) At most limit requests per window seconds for one key, counted in one shared table (or in memory, see storage ). A cell rate algorithm: a burst of limit is admitted at once and the sustained rate is limit per window . A refusal does not use up quota. The key is hashed in the native core, so a client address, user id or custom key never reaches SQL, logs or metrics. key is "client" (the trusted address, an IPv6 one by its /64), "caller" (the authenticated caller, the client for an anonymous request) or a plain function of the context returning a string. scope defaults to the method and the route, so routes count apart; give routes the same scope to share a quota. tenant adds a segment to the key. A request with no known client shares one bucket unknown_factor times as large. on_error="closed" answers 503 when storage is unavailable, "open" admits the request and counts it. headers=True adds RateLimit-Limit , RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset (whole seconds) to admitted and refused answers. clock returns an aware datetime ( hinoki.testing.ManualClock ); the default is the system clock.

docs.text: Tutorial ¶ Follow the Tracker, an API where members keep their own tasks, one layer per chapter. Each chapter walks through files of the checked-in example in examples/tracker and runs its commands, so every step runs as shown. Chapter 9 then adds an app to your own project. Chapter It covers You learn 1. Models tables, a foreign key, an index, a default order models and migrations 2. Schemas what clients send and receive strict validation, derived schemas 3. Endpoints the HTTP layer and explicit app mounts access, generated CRUD with filters, transactions, declared errors 4. Implement a business rule complete_task(...) and delete_task(...) why domain rules live in operations.py with ownership in SQL 5. Events between apps Created[Task] , Updated[Task] and activity decoupled in_transaction handlers and hinoki events 6. Rules checks that keep the layers apart hinoki check 7. Run and test it the manifest, settings, a server, tests hinoki dev , the test client 8. Validate input normalizers and checks field and cross-field errors 9. Projects and apps an app in your own project hinoki app create , planned migrations Chapters 1–7 cover the Tracker. Chapter 8 uses standalone examples, and chapter 9 continues the project from the Quick start . The Tracker's shape ¶ The Tracker is one project with three apps that depend on each other on purpose. Each app is a package with its own models, endpoints and migrations: tracker/ ├── main.py, settings.py the application and its typed settings ├── routes.py the project route map (GET /health and explicit app mounts) ├── middleware.py a project-wide middleware ├── rules.py architecture rules └── apps/ ├── members/ Member, the bearer token and the access policy ├── tasks/ Task: models, schemas, filters, operations, api └── activity/ Activity, written by listening to task events hinoki.toml registers the application, its route map, middleware, rules and apps, while tracker/routes.py decides where each exposed app is mounted: # examples/tracker/hinoki.toml [project] application = "tracker.main:app" routes = "tracker.routes:routes" middleware = [ "tracker.middleware:middleware" ] rules = [ "tracker.rules:policy" , "tracker.rules:layers" ] [[apps]] name = "members" models = "tracker.apps.members.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.members.migrations" requires = [] [[apps]] name = "tasks" models = "tracker.apps.tasks.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.tasks.migrations" requires = [ "members" ] [[apps]] name = "activity" models = "tracker.apps.activity.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.activity.migrations" events = "tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers" requires = [ "tasks" , "members" ] Inside the tasks app, the layers point one way: api.py HTTP: shapes, status codes, access, transactions ↓ operations.py business rules: plain async functions, no HTTP types ↓ models.py tables and relations activity reacts to what tasks announces, and tasks never imports it ( chapter 3 and chapter 5 ). Before you start ¶ Install Hinoki . Chapters 1–6 run in the Tracker's own directory of the checkout, which is a complete project with its own hinoki.toml : cd examples/tracker Commands there take no target: uv run hinoki check , uv run hinoki dev and uv run hinoki migrations apply read the manifest, as they do in your own project. They create examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 , which the repository ignores.
docs.title: Overview

docs.title: Tutorial

docs.text: The Tracker is one project with three apps that depend on each other on purpose. Each app is a package with its own models, endpoints and migrations: tracker/ ├── main.py, settings.py the application and its typed settings ├── routes.py the project route map (GET /health and explicit app mounts) ├── middleware.py a project-wide middleware ├── rules.py architecture rules └── apps/ ├── members/ Member, the bearer token and the access policy ├── tasks/ Task: models, schemas, filters, operations, api └── activity/ Activity, written by listening to task events hinoki.toml registers the application, its route map, middleware, rules and apps, while tracker/routes.py decides where each exposed app is mounted: # examples/tracker/hinoki.toml [project] application = "tracker.main:app" routes = "tracker.routes:routes" middleware = [ "tracker.middleware:middleware" ] rules = [ "tracker.rules:policy" , "tracker.rules:layers" ] [[apps]] name = "members" models = "tracker.apps.members.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.members.migrations" requires = [] [[apps]] name = "tasks" models = "tracker.apps.tasks.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.tasks.migrations" requires = [ "members" ] [[apps]] name = "activity" models = "tracker.apps.activity.models" migrations = "tracker.apps.activity.migrations" events = "tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers" requires = [ "tasks" , "members" ] Inside the tasks app, the layers point one way: api.py HTTP: shapes, status codes, access, transactions ↓ operations.py business rules: plain async functions, no HTTP types ↓ models.py tables and relations activity reacts to what tasks announces, and tasks never imports it ( chapter 3 and chapter 5 ).
docs.title: The Tracker's shape

docs.text: Install Hinoki . Chapters 1–6 run in the Tracker's own directory of the checkout, which is a complete project with its own hinoki.toml : cd examples/tracker Commands there take no target: uv run hinoki check , uv run hinoki dev and uv run hinoki migrations apply read the manifest, as they do in your own project. They create examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 , which the repository ignores.
docs.title: Before you start

docs.text: 1. Models ¶ A model declares a table. A relation is loaded only when you ask for it, never as a side effect of reading an attribute. The Tracker keeps one model per app, each in the app's models.py . The members app owns the table of people: # tracker/apps/members/models.py from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk @db . table ( "tracker_members" ) class Member ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) name : str = field ( max_length = 80 ) token_hash : str = field ( unique = True ) # SHA-256 hex digest, never the token The tasks app belongs to a member through a foreign key: # tracker/apps/tasks/models.py from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , OnDelete , field , foreign_key , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now from tracker.apps.members.models import Member @db . indexed ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ) @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" , "-id" ) @db . table ( "tracker_tasks" ) class Task ( Model , label = "Task" , plural = "Tasks" ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) owner_id : UUID = foreign_key ( Member , on_delete = OnDelete . RESTRICT , related_name = "tasks" ) title : str = field ( max_length = 120 ) priority : int = 3 done : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now ) completed_at : datetime | None = None pk(...) declares the primary key; field(...) adds column options such as max_length and unique . @db.indexed("owner_id", "created_at") adds a composite index. @db.ordered_by(...) sets the order of every query that does not call order_by . foreign_key(Member, ...) stores the owner's id. task.owner is fetched only when a query asks for it. Because tasks imports Member , its entry in hinoki.toml says requires = ["members"] . @db.table(...) pins the table name, because a Tracker rule requires it ( chapter 5 ). Without it, Hinoki derives <app>_<models> , as chapter 8 shows. The third app, activity , has an Activity model of the same kind: a line per task change. Chapter 3 shows how it gets written. Apply the migrations ¶ A migration is a SQL file generated from the models and checked in beside them. Each app has its own migrations/ directory. Tasks ships one: -- tracker/apps/tasks/migrations/0001-create-table-tracker-tasks.sql -- hinoki migration 0001-create-table-tracker-tasks -- generated from the models; review it. -- create table tracker_tasks CREATE TABLE "tracker_tasks" ( "id" UUID PRIMARY KEY , "owner_id" UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES "tracker_members" ( "id" ) ON DELETE RESTRICT , "title" varchar ( 120 ) NOT NULL , "priority" integer NOT NULL , "done" boolean NOT NULL , "created_at" timestamptz NOT NULL , "completed_at" timestamptz ); CREATE INDEX "ix_tracker_tasks_owner_id_created_at_e46b5006" ON "tracker_tasks" ( "owner_id" , "created_at" ); From examples/tracker , list and apply them: uv run hinoki migrations status uv run hinoki migrations apply database: sqlite:///…/examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default) members pending 0001-create-table-tracker-members tasks pending 0001-create-table-tracker-tasks activity pending 0001-create-table-tracker-activity database: sqlite:///…/examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default) members: 0001-create-table-tracker-members tasks: 0001-create-table-tracker-tasks activity: 0001-create-table-tracker-activity Each command first names the database it uses. With no database configured, that is .hinoki/local.sqlite3 beside hinoki.toml . apply runs the apps in requires order, so tracker_members exists before the table that references it. Migrations run only when you call apply ; an application never migrates at startup. When a model changes, uv run hinoki migrations plan tasks writes the next migration of that app. Review its SQL, then apply it. Recap ¶ A model is a typed class; decorators state table facts such as indexes and order. Each app owns its models and migrations; requires orders them. Migrations are reviewed files, applied by an explicit command. Relations are never loaded implicitly. Next: 2. Schemas .

docs.text: 2. Schemas ¶ A model describes a table; a Schema describes what crosses the API. A column reaches a client only when a schema names it. # tracker/apps/tasks/schemas.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import Field , Schema , derive from .models import Task class TaskIn ( Schema ): """What a client may set. The owner is the caller, never a field.""" title : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 120 )] priority : Annotated [ int , Field ( ge = 1 , le = 5 )] = 3 @derive ( Task , exclude = ( "owner_id" ,)) class TaskOut ( Schema ): """Every column of a task except its owner (derived from the model).""" TaskIn is strict: no coercion, no unknown keys, and every problem is reported with its path. Validation runs in Rust before your code does. priority is optional and, when sent, must be from 1 to 5. TaskOut takes its fields from Task , with the model's types and limits. exclude=("owner_id",) keeps the owner out. Relations are never derived; you name them on purpose. The owner is not a field of TaskIn , so a client cannot choose it. Server values passed to Task.acreate(data, owner_id=...) always win, and a schema never carries the primary key. Every response is a Schema , never a model, a dict or a dataclass. The members app does the same with MemberOut , which names id and name and so never sends the token digest. Schemas also support aliases, computed fields and tagged unions; see discriminated unions . Recap ¶ Input schemas list what a client may send, nothing more. Output schemas can be derived from a model, minus what must stay private. Ownership comes from the caller, never from the request body. Next: 3. Endpoints .

docs.text: 4. Implement a business rule ¶ Generated CRUD ( chapter 3 ) already handles listing, retrieving, creating and deleting rows. When an action encodes a domain rule — such as marking an open task done or refusing to delete a completed one — put that rule in operations.py instead of writing SQL or state checks directly inside the HTTP handler: Reuse across entry points : plain async def functions take owner_id and plain values, never a Request , so an endpoint, a management command, a test or an admin hook can call the same rule. Layer isolation : api.py stays responsible only for HTTP shapes, status codes, Access policies and atomic=True transaction boundaries, while chapter 6 enforces that operations.py never imports HTTP types. Single-statement ownership : writes include the owner in the WHERE clause so there is no race between reading a row, checking ownership and updating it. It starts with one scoped query that every action reuses: # tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py from uuid import UUID from hinoki import events from hinoki.events import Updated from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from hinoki.utils import utc_now from .errors import DoneTasksAreKept , TaskAlreadyDone from .models import Task def mine ( owner_id : UUID ) -> QuerySet [ Task ]: return Task . filter ( owner_id = owner_id ) Writes put the owner in the statement itself: # tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py (continued) async def complete_task ( owner_id : UUID , task_id : UUID ) -> Task : """Mark an own open task done in one statement.""" changed = await Task . aupdate_where ( { "id" : task_id , "owner_id" : owner_id , "done" : False }, { "done" : True , "completed_at" : utc_now ()}, ) if changed : # aupdate_where emits no model event, so announce the change ourselves. await events . emit ( Updated ( Task , changed [ 0 ], ( "done" , "completed_at" ))) return changed [ 0 ] await mine ( owner_id ) . filter ( id = task_id ) . aget () # missing or not yours: 404 raise TaskAlreadyDone () async def delete_task ( owner_id : UUID , task_id : UUID ) -> None : """Delete an own open task; completed ones are kept.""" removed = await Task . adelete ( id = task_id , owner_id = owner_id , done = False ) if removed : return await mine ( owner_id ) . filter ( id = task_id ) . aget () # missing or not yours: 404 raise DoneTasksAreKept () There is no gap between reading a row, checking its owner and writing it. Another member's task looks exactly like a missing one (404), so nothing leaks. Business failures are named after the rule they report. Each carries its HTTP status (409 for Conflict ) and a stable code: # tracker/apps/tasks/errors.py from hinoki import errors class TaskAlreadyDone ( errors . Conflict ): code = "task_already_done" message = "The task is already done." class DoneTasksAreKept ( errors . Conflict ): code = "done_tasks_are_kept" message = "Completed tasks are kept as a record and cannot be deleted." Recap ¶ Business rules such as complete_task(...) belong in operations.py , separate from HTTP handlers in api.py . Ownership is part of the WHERE clause, not a separate check. Errors are classes with a status and a stable code. Next: 5. Events between apps .

docs.text: 3. Endpoints ¶ The HTTP layer maps requests to operations and results to responses. It holds no business rule and no SQL. First, who may call. A bearer token resolves to a Member through its SHA-256 digest (the table never holds the token), and the policy names the permission that every task action requires. The policy lives in the members app, so every app reuses it: # tracker/apps/members/security.py """Authentication: an opaque bearer token resolved to a ``Member``.""" import hashlib from hinoki import Access , BearerAuth , Caller , Permission from .models import Member def hash_token ( token : str ) -> str : """The SHA-256 hex digest stored instead of the token (high-entropy, so no KDF).""" return hashlib . sha256 ( token . encode ()) . hexdigest () class MemberPermission ( Permission ): USE = "tracker:use" class MemberTokens ( BearerAuth [ Member ]): async def resolve_token ( self , token : str ) -> Caller [ Member ] | None : member = await Member . aget_or_none ( token_hash = hash_token ( token )) if member is None : return None return Caller ( id = str ( member . id ), user = member , permissions = { MemberPermission . USE } ) member_only = Access ( auth = MemberTokens (), permissions = [ MemberPermission . USE ]) Next, what a client may ask of the task list. A FilterSet declares each query parameter once; only what it declares is accepted: # tracker/apps/tasks/filters.py from datetime import datetime from hinoki.filters import Eq , FilterSet , In , Range , Search class TaskFilters ( FilterSet ): done : Eq [ bool ] priority : In [ int ] created_at : Range [ datetime ] completed_at : Eq [ datetime | None ] search = Search ( "title" ) ordering = ( "created_at" , "priority" , "title" ) Then the actions. List, retrieve, create and delete are generated from the model by @crud ; the one action it cannot know, complete , is handwritten in the same class: # tracker/apps/tasks/api.py """HTTP layer of the tasks app: generated CRUD plus one handwritten action.""" from uuid import UUID from hinoki import API , Caller , Includable , crud , errors , http from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from tracker.apps.members.models import Member from tracker.apps.members.security import member_only from . import operations from .errors import TaskAlreadyDone from .filters import TaskFilters from .models import Task from .schemas import TaskIn , TaskOut @crud ( Task , path = "" , read = TaskOut , create = TaskIn , delete = True , access = member_only , owner = "owner_id" , filters = TaskFilters , ) class Tasks ( API ): """The caller's own tasks: list (filtered), retrieve, create and delete.""" def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> QuerySet [ Task ]: return operations . mine ( caller . user . id ) async def remove ( self , item : Task , _scoped : QuerySet [ Task ], caller : Caller [ Member ] ) -> bool : await operations . delete_task ( caller . user . id , item . id ) return True @http . post ( "/ {item_id} /complete" , access = member_only , atomic = True , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone ), ) async def complete ( self , item_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : """Mark an own open task done.""" return TaskOut . from_model ( await operations . complete_task ( caller . user . id , item_id ) ) routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Tasks ] The hooks get_queryset and remove take a typed caller: Caller[Member] . That is valid because every generated action that calls them has the member_only policy, so the caller is never None ; Hinoki checks this when the class is declared and raises RegistrationError otherwise. For a resource that mixes public and protected actions, annotate Caller[Member] | None . See hooks in the CRUD guide. The project's tracker/routes.py defines the public GET /health check and mounts each exposed app explicitly with Mount(...) : # tracker/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , Mount , Schema , http from .apps.activity.api import routes as activity_routes from .apps.members.api import routes as members_routes from .apps.tasks.api import routes as tasks_routes class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) async def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) routes : list [ Includable ] = [ health , Mount ( "/members" , members_routes ), Mount ( "/tasks" , tasks_routes ), Mount ( "/activity" , activity_routes ), ] @crud(...) generates the list, retrieve, create and delete actions with the policy, the schemas and the filters you name. owner="owner_id" sets the owner of a created task to the caller, and read=TaskOut is the only shape that leaves the server. Writes of generated actions are transactional by default. get_queryset scopes every generated action to the caller, so another member's task is a 404. remove replaces the generated delete body with the operation, which keeps completed tasks. access= names a reusable policy. Actions are public unless they name one, so protect on purpose; a rule in the next chapter enforces it. atomic=True runs the handwritten write in a transaction. It commits after the response is encoded and rolls back before an error becomes HTTP. errors=(...) declares what an action may raise. The OpenAPI document, the MCP tool description and the strict test client all read it. caller: Caller[Member] is the authenticated caller, typed: caller.user is your Member . TaskOut.from_model(...) converts a row into the response. A handler never returns a model. The list accepts exactly the filters of TaskFilters , next to the pagination parameters: GET /tasks?done=false&priority=1,2&created_at.from=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z&search=docs&ordering=-created_at A name, an operator or an ordering key that TaskFilters does not declare is a 422 that lists every problem. See filter, order and search the list . The two smaller apps follow the same shape. members has one handwritten action, GET /members/me , and activity has a read-only generated list scoped to the caller: # tracker/apps/activity/api.py """HTTP layer of the activity app, mounted at ``/activity`` by hinoki.toml.""" from hinoki import API , Caller , Includable , crud from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from tracker.apps.members.models import Member from tracker.apps.members.security import member_only from .models import Activity from .schemas import ActivityOut @crud ( Activity , path = "" , read = ActivityOut , access = member_only ) class Feed ( API ): """The caller's activity, newest first. Read only.""" def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> QuerySet [ Activity ]: return Activity . filter ( member_id = caller . user . id ) routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Feed ] Declare request: Request as the first parameter only when you need headers, cookies or the raw body. File uploads are covered in upload files . Register the routes ¶ Nothing in main.py lists these routes. hinoki.toml points each app at its routes list and gives it the prefix ( /tasks , /members , /activity , by default /<app name> ), which is why path="" above repeats nothing ( chapter 6 ). Recap ¶ @crud generates the standard actions from the model, the policy, the schemas and a FilterSet ; a handwritten action sits beside them. Handlers call operations and convert rows with from_model . Every error an action raises is declared. Next: 4. Implement a business rule . In the guides: function-based APIs and class-based APIs .

List, retrieve, create and delete are generated from the model by @crud ; the one action it cannot know, complete , is handwritten in the same class: # tracker/apps/tasks/api.py """HTTP layer of the tasks app: generated CRUD plus one handwritten action.""" from uuid import UUID from hinoki import API , Caller , Includable , crud , errors , http from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from tracker.apps.members.models import Member from tracker.apps.members.security import member_only from . import operations from .errors import TaskAlreadyDone from .filters import TaskFilters from .models import Task from .schemas import TaskIn , TaskOut @crud ( Task , path = "" , read = TaskOut , create = TaskIn , delete = True , access = member_only , owner = "owner_id" , filters = TaskFilters , ) class Tasks ( API ): """The caller's own tasks: list (filtered), retrieve, create and delete.""" def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> QuerySet [ Task ]: return operations . mine ( caller . user . id ) async def remove ( self , item : Task , _scoped : QuerySet [ Task ], caller : Caller [ Member ] ) -> bool : await operations . delete_task ( caller . user . id , item . id ) return True @http . post ( "/ {item_id} /complete" , access = member_only , atomic = True , errors = ( errors . NotFound , TaskAlreadyDone ), ) async def complete ( self , item_id : UUID , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> TaskOut : """Mark an own open task done.""" return TaskOut . from_model ( await operations . complete_task ( caller . user . id , item_id ) ) routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Tasks ] The hooks get_queryset and remove take a typed caller: Caller[Member] . That is valid because every generated action that calls them has the member_only policy, so the caller is never None ; Hinoki checks this when the class is declared and raises RegistrationError otherwise. For a resource that mixes public and protected actions, annotate Caller[Member] | None . See hooks in the CRUD guide. The project's tracker/routes.py defines the public GET /health check and mounts each exposed app explicitly with Mount(...) : # tracker/routes.py from hinoki import Includable , Mount , Schema , http from .apps.activity.api import routes as activity_routes from .apps.members.api import routes as members_routes from .apps.tasks.api import routes as tasks_routes class Health ( Schema ): status : str @http . get ( "/health" ) async def health () -> Health : return Health ( status = "ok" ) routes : list [ Includable ] = [ health , Mount ( "/members" , members_routes ), Mount ( "/tasks" , tasks_routes ), Mount ( "/activity" , activity_routes ), ] @crud(...) generates the list, retrieve, create and delete actions with the policy, the schemas and the filters you name. owner="owner_id" sets the owner of a created task to the caller, and read=TaskOut is the only shape that leaves the server. Writes of generated actions are transactional by default. get_queryset scopes every generated action to the caller, so another member's task is a 404. remove replaces the generated delete body with the operation, which keeps completed tasks. access= names a reusable policy. Actions are public unless they name one, so protect on purpose; a rule in the next chapter enforces it. atomic=True runs the handwritten write in a transaction. It commits after the response is encoded and rolls back before an error becomes HTTP. errors=(...) declares what an action may raise. The OpenAPI document, the MCP tool description and the strict test client all read it. caller: Caller[Member] is the authenticated caller, typed: caller.user is your Member . TaskOut.from_model(...) converts a row into the response. A handler never returns a model. The list accepts exactly the filters of TaskFilters , next to the pagination parameters: GET /tasks?done=false&priority=1,2&created_at.from=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z&search=docs&ordering=-created_at A name, an operator or an ordering key that TaskFilters does not declare is a 422 that lists every problem. See filter, order and search the list . The two smaller apps follow the same shape. members has one handwritten action, GET /members/me , and activity has a read-only generated list scoped to the caller: # tracker/apps/activity/api.py """HTTP layer of the activity app, mounted at ``/activity`` by hinoki.toml.""" from hinoki import API , Caller , Includable , crud from hinoki.orm import QuerySet from tracker.apps.members.models import Member from tracker.apps.members.security import member_only from .models import Activity from .schemas import ActivityOut @crud ( Activity , path = "" , read = ActivityOut , access = member_only ) class Feed ( API ): """The caller's activity, newest first. Read only.""" def get_queryset ( self , caller : Caller [ Member ]) -> QuerySet [ Activity ]: return Activity . filter ( member_id = caller . user . id ) routes : list [ Includable ] = [ Feed ] Declare request: Request as the first parameter only when you need headers, cookies or the raw body. File uploads are covered in upload files .

docs.text: Nothing in main.py lists these routes. hinoki.toml points each app at its routes list and gives it the prefix ( /tasks , /members , /activity , by default /<app name> ), which is why path="" above repeats nothing ( chapter 6 ).

docs.text: @crud generates the standard actions from the model, the policy, the schemas and a FilterSet ; a handwritten action sits beside them. Handlers call operations and convert rows with from_model . Every error an action raises is declared. Next: 4. Implement a business rule . In the guides: function-based APIs and class-based APIs .

docs.text: 6. Rules ¶ Rules turn the project's promises into checks. A failure names the rule, the file and the line. The Tracker keeps its promises in tracker/rules.py , as two RuleSet values: policy says what an action, a schema and a model must declare, and layers says which module may import which. # tracker/rules.py from hinoki import rules PKG = "tracker" TASKS = f " { PKG } .apps.tasks" policy = rules . RuleSet ( rules . Actions . require_access ( match = f " { PKG } .*" , except_ = [ f " { PKG } .routes.health" ]), rules . Actions . require_permissions ( match = f " { PKG } .*" , except_ = [ f " { PKG } .routes.health" ] ), rules . Actions . forbid_model_responses ( match = f " { PKG } .*" ), rules . Actions . require_return_type ( match = f " { PKG } .*" ), rules . Actions . require_pagination ( match = f " { PKG } .*" ), rules . Transactions . require_atomic (), rules . Schemas . forbid_exposure ( "token_hash" ), rules . Schemas . require_string_limits (), rules . Models . require_explicit_table ( match = f " { PKG } .*" ), rules . Models . require_foreign_key_index ( match = f " { PKG } .*" ), ) layers = rules . RuleSet ( # api -> operations -> models, and tasks never imports its listener. rules . Imports . forbid ( source = f " { TASKS } .models" , target = f " { TASKS } .operations" ), rules . Imports . forbid ( source = f " { TASKS } .models" , target = f " { TASKS } .api" ), rules . Imports . forbid ( source = f " { TASKS } .operations" , target = f " { TASKS } .api" ), rules . Imports . forbid ( source = f " { TASKS } " , target = f " { PKG } .apps.activity" ), ) hinoki.toml lists both under rules in [project] , and the application merges them in that order, so a worker refuses to start while one is violated. main.py passes no rules= argument ( chapter 6 ). Run the check ¶ From examples/tracker : uv run hinoki check 14 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived The check reads the rules from the manifest, imports the models of every app and scans the tracker package for the import rules. Break a rule ¶ Take complete out of its transaction by changing atomic=True to atomic=False in its decorator in tracker/apps/tasks/api.py , then run the check again: tracker/apps/tasks/api.py:39: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /tasks/{item_id}/complete (Tasks.complete) does not declare atomic=True fix: add atomic=True to the action (or declare it on a RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) group) 14 rule(s): 1 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived The command exits with status 1. Put atomic=True back to restore the check. The import rules fail the same way. Add from tracker.apps.activity import models as the last line of tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py and the check reports it: tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py:46: HNK-IMP-001 [violated] tracker.apps.tasks.operations imports tracker.apps.activity, which is forbidden for tracker.apps.tasks fix: move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between (the check also lists the same line for tracker.apps.activity.models , which brings the total to 2 violated ). Remove the import to restore it. Waivers ¶ An accepted exception is a waiver in hinoki-rules.toml , with a reason, an owner and a bounded target. hinoki check and application startup apply the same waivers. The project owner writes waivers; tools and agents read them but never edit them to make a check pass. The Tracker needs none; the Blog example carries one. Recap ¶ Rules are Python values in the project, checked by hinoki check and at startup. Each failure has a stable id, a location and a fix. Exceptions are explicit, owned waivers. Next: 7. Run and test it .

docs.text: 7. Run and test it ¶ Settings ¶ Settings are a typed class. Tracker declares a database; with no value set it is local SQLite. Each field of DatabaseSettings is a TRACKER_DATABASE__<FIELD> variable, two underscores between the group and the field, so TRACKER_DATABASE__URL selects another database ( Configure a database ): # tracker/settings.py from hinoki import settings class TrackerSettings ( settings . AppSettings , prefix = "TRACKER_" ): database : settings . DatabaseSettings main.py declares the application at module level. It names no route, event handler, middleware or rule, because Hinoki() reads them from hinoki.toml : # tracker/main.py from hinoki import Hinoki from .commands import Seed from .settings import TrackerSettings def create_app ( settings : TrackerSettings | None = None ) -> Hinoki : """Routes, events, middleware and rules come from the manifest.""" return Hinoki ( settings = settings or TrackerSettings , title = "Tracker" , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , commands = [ Seed ], ) app = create_app () What the manifest ( the index ) supplies: hinoki.toml What Hinoki() loads [project] routes tracker/routes.py : GET /health and explicit Mount(...) entries for members , tasks and activity [[apps]] events the handlers of activity [project] middleware ApiVersion , which adds x-tracker-version to every answer of a matched route [project] rules policy and layers , checked at startup and by hinoki check Hinoki() fills each of include= , events= , middleware= and rules= from the manifest when you leave it out, and only in the module that [project] application names ( tracker.main ). An argument you pass yourself, even an empty one, replaces the manifest's list for that argument; do that only when you want an explicit application, such as a test that serves one app. create_app takes the settings so a test can point it at its own database. Hinoki(settings=TrackerSettings) reads the TRACKER_* variables at import; nothing connects until a worker starts. Serve it ¶ From examples/tracker : SQLite (default) PostgreSQL uv run hinoki migrations apply uv run hinoki manage seed uv run hinoki dev export TRACKER_DATABASE__URL = postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/tracker uv run hinoki migrations apply uv run hinoki manage seed uv run hinoki dev The migration commands, manage and the server all read the database setting of the application that hinoki.toml names, so TRACKER_DATABASE__URL alone configures all of them ( which database ). hinoki dev serves on http://127.0.0.1:8000 and reloads on change; open /docs . hinoki serve runs without reload and takes host, port and workers from the server settings ( serving ). Try it ¶ Every task route needs a member's token, and the Tracker has no sign-up route. hinoki manage seed is a management command of the example ( tracker/commands.py ) that creates the member Ada Demo and prints a random token once; the table stores only its SHA-256 digest, so the token cannot be shown again. Export it: member 'Ada Demo' created; token '<random token>' (shown once) export TOKEN = '<the printed token>' With the server running, call the API from a second terminal: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " \ -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"title":"Write docs","priority":2}' curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks?done=false&priority=1,2&search=docs&ordering=-created_at' \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/activity -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " The first call answers 201 with the new task, the second a page with it that matches the filters, and the third the created line that the activity app wrote. Without the header every one of them answers 401 . {"id":"…","title":"Write docs","priority":2,"done":false,"created_at":"…","completed_at":null} Completing the task answers 200 ; completing it again is a 409 task_already_done , and deleting a completed task a 409 done_tasks_are_kept : curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks/<id>/complete -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN " Test it ¶ The tests of the Tracker need no environment variable: the fixture in tracker_tests/conftest.py migrates each app, in the order of its requires , into a SQLite file in a temporary directory, creates the members Ann and Ben and builds the application with create_app(settings) around that file: # tracker_tests/conftest.py (excerpt) @pytest . fixture async def world ( tmp_path : Path ) -> AsyncIterator [ World ]: url = f "sqlite:// { tmp_path / 'tracker.sqlite3' } " database = await Database . connect ( url , max_size = 1 ) for name in ORDER : await migrator . apply ( database , APPS / name / "migrations" , namespace = name ) with use_database ( database ): ann = await Member . acreate ( name = "Ann" , token_hash = hash_token ( "ann-token" )) ben = await Member . acreate ( name = "Ben" , token_hash = hash_token ( "ben-token" )) database . close () settings = TrackerSettings . load ( overrides = { "database" : { "url" : url }}) async with ASGIClient ( create_app ( settings )) as client : yield World ( client , ann , ben ) Operations need no HTTP, so test them directly. Then drive the whole stack with the in-process client: # tracker_tests/trackerapitest.py (excerpt) async def test_completing_twice_is_a_conflict_and_done_tasks_are_kept ( world : World , ) -> None : task = await create ( world , "Ship" ) path = f "/tasks/ { task [ 'id' ] } " ann = "ann-token" done = await world . client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = ann ) again = await world . client . post ( f " { path } /complete" , token = ann ) removed = await world . client . delete ( path , token = ann ) assert ( done . status , done . body [ "done" ]) == ( 200 , True ) assert ( again . status , again . body [ "error" ]) == ( 409 , "task_already_done" ) assert ( removed . status , removed . body [ "error" ]) == ( 409 , "done_tasks_are_kept" ) Run all of them from the repository root: uv run --locked pytest examples/tracker/tracker_tests ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) fails a test when an action answers an error it did not declare. For tests without async , use SyncClient . See testing for disposable databases of other backends. Recap ¶ Settings are typed and read from prefixed environment variables. hinoki.toml wires routes, events, middleware and rules; main.py only configures the application. hinoki dev serves with reload; migrations stay a separate step. Test operations directly and the stack with ASGIClient . Next: 8. Validate input .

docs.text: 8. Validate input ¶ A Schema validates in three steps, all before your code runs: built-in constraints reject invalid input, normalizers make valid strings canonical, and checks reject values that are valid but not acceptable. Normalize and check fields ¶ # registration.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import ( Field , Invalid , Schema , errors , field_check , field_normalize , object_check , ) class Registration ( Schema ): username : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 , pattern = r "[a-z0-9_]+" )] email : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "email" )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 )] confirmation : str @field_normalize ( "email" ) def lowercase_email ( self , value : str ) -> str : return value . lower () @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "password_mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" ) # registration.py (continued) user = Registration . validate ( { "username" : "mari_23" , "email" : "Mari@Example.test" , "password" : "correct-horse-battery" , "confirmation" : "correct-horse-battery" , } ) assert user . email == "mari@example.test" try : Registration . validate ( { "username" : "mari_23" , "email" : "mari@example.test" , "password" : "password12345" , "confirmation" : "different-password" , } ) except errors . ValidationError as error : for detail in error . details : print ( detail . path , detail . code , detail . message ) password common_password choose a less common password confirmation password_mismatch passwords do not match Constraints come first: min_length , max_length , pattern , and format= ( email , url , slug , hex_color ); numbers take gt , ge , lt and le , and one_of fixes the allowed values. A failed constraint stops validation of that field. @field_normalize receives a valid string and returns a str ; the result is checked against the same constraints. It also runs for Schema(...) and from_model(...) . @field_check sees the final value of one field, @object_check the whole schema. Both raise Invalid(code, message) and return None . Normalizers and checks are synchronous and do no I/O. A rule that needs the database, such as "this email is not registered yet", belongs in an operation, where it can be race-safe. Ignore unknown fields ¶ Unknown fields are rejected by default. For an external payload that adds metadata you do not use, discard unknown keys on that Schema : # webhooks.py from hinoki import Schema , SchemaConfig , SchemaExtra class Webhook ( Schema , config = SchemaConfig ( extra = SchemaExtra . IGNORE )): event_id : str revision : int event = Webhook . validate ( { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 , "provider_data" : { "trace" : "abc" }} ) assert event . dump () == { "event_id" : "evt-1" , "revision" : 2 } Declared fields stay strict, and ignored keys are never stored or dumped. Constructor keywords and from_model(..., **extra) stay strict too, and each nested Schema applies its own policy. Validate model writes ¶ Data can also reach a table without an HTTP Schema : from a management command or the admin. Put the same constraints on the model: # catalog/models.py from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import Field , db from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk def trimmed ( value : str ) -> None : if value != value . strip (): raise ValueError ( "surrounding whitespace is not allowed" ) @db . table ( "catalog_products" ) class Product ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) sku : str = field ( max_length = 32 , constraints = Field ( min_length = 3 , pattern = r "[A-Z0-9-]+" ) ) name : str = field ( max_length = 120 , validators = ( trimmed ,)) price : float = field ( constraints = Field ( gt = 0 )) The checks run before acreate , asave and queryset aupdate , and their synchronous forms. An invalid write raises ModelValidationError (import it from hinoki.errors ) with structured details and sends no SQL. Rows that are read are not revalidated. See field constraints and validators . Recap ¶ Constraints, then normalizers, then checks; all before the handler. Unknown keys are an error unless a Schema opts out. Model constraints guard writes that bypass HTTP. Next: 9. docs.text: A Schema validates in three steps, all before your code runs: built-in constraints reject invalid input, normalizers make valid strings canonical, and checks reject values that are valid but not acceptable.
docs.title: 8. Validate input

docs.text: # registration.py from typing import Annotated from hinoki import ( Field , Invalid , Schema , errors , field_check , field_normalize , object_check , ) class Registration ( Schema ): username : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 3 , max_length = 32 , pattern = r "[a-z0-9_]+" )] email : Annotated [ str , Field ( format = "email" )] password : Annotated [ str , Field ( min_length = 12 )] confirmation : str @field_normalize ( "email" ) def lowercase_email ( self , value : str ) -> str : return value . lower () @field_check ( "password" ) def reject_common_password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if value . lower () in { "password12345" , "qwerty123456" }: raise Invalid ( "common_password" , "choose a less common password" ) @object_check def passwords_match ( self ) -> None : if self . password != self . confirmation : raise Invalid ( "password_mismatch" , "passwords do not match" , path = "confirmation" ) # registration.py (continued) user = Registration . validate ( { "username" : "mari_23" , "email" : "Mari@Example.test" , "password" : "correct-horse-battery" , "confirmation" : "correct-horse-battery" , } ) assert user . email == "mari@example.test" try : Registration . validate ( { "username" : "mari_23" , "email" : "mari@example.test" , "password" : "password12345" , "confirmation" : "different-password" , } ) except errors . ValidationError as error : for detail in error . details : print ( detail . path , detail . code , detail . message ) password common_password choose a less common password confirmation password_mismatch passwords do not match Constraints come first: min_length , max_length , pattern , and format= ( email , url , slug , hex_color ); numbers take gt , ge , lt and le , and one_of fixes the allowed values. A failed constraint stops validation of that field. @field_normalize receives a valid string and returns a str ; the result is checked against the same constraints. It also runs for Schema(...) and from_model(...) . @field_check sees the final value of one field, @object_check the whole schema. Both raise Invalid(code, message) and return None . Normalizers and checks are synchronous and do no I/O. A rule that needs the database, such as "this email is not registered yet", belongs in an operation, where it can be race-safe.

docs.text: 9. Projects and apps ¶ An app is a package with its own models, migrations and routes, registered in hinoki.toml . This chapter adds a billing app to the notes project from the Quick start . Create the app ¶ From the project root: uv run hinoki app create Prompt Default Answer App name billing Depends on (none) The command writes the package and registers it: notes/apps/billing/ ├── api.py endpoints of the app ├── routes.py the app’s route list, initially empty ├── models.py tables of the app └── migrations/ migration history [[apps]] name = "billing" models = "notes.apps.billing.models" migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations" requires = [] Hinoki reads apps only from hinoki.toml ; it never scans installed packages. If billing later references a model of another app, list that app in requires : migrations then run in dependency order. Add a model ¶ # notes/apps/billing/models.py """Models owned by this app.""" from datetime import datetime from uuid import UUID , uuid4 from hinoki import db from hinoki.orm import Model , field , pk from hinoki.utils import utc_now @db . ordered_by ( "-created_at" ) class Invoice ( Model ): id : UUID = pk ( default_factory = uuid4 ) reference : str = field ( max_length = 40 , unique = True ) paid : bool = False created_at : datetime = field ( default_factory = utc_now , index = True ) The table name is derived: billing_invoices , the app followed by the plural model name. @db.table("billing_invoices") pins it, so renaming the class keeps the physical name; the model rules below ask for it. Plan and apply the migration ¶ uv run hinoki migrations plan billing uv run hinoki migrations apply database: sqlite:///…/notes/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default) create table billing_invoices wrote notes/apps/billing/migrations/0001-create-table-billing-invoices.sql database: sqlite:///…/notes/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default) entries: nothing to apply billing: 0001-create-table-billing-invoices plan compares the models with the recorded migration state and writes the next migration; the number and the slug come from the change. Review the .sql file before you apply it. With more than one app, plan needs the app name; apply runs every app in dependency order. Where the data goes apply uses the application's database setting, so the variable that configures the server, such as NOTES_DATABASE__URL , also configures the migrations; plan , status and apply print the database they chose. With no database configured, apply creates .hinoki/local.sqlite3 beside hinoki.toml . HINOKI_DATABASE_URL overrides the setting for one run. If the application cannot be loaded, the commands stop (exit 2) instead of guessing. Migrations never run when the application starts. Check the project ¶ uv run hinoki check uv run pytest 8 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived notes/rules.py keeps two model rules commented out: rules.Models.require_explicit_table and rules.Models.require_foreign_key_index . hinoki check imports the models of every [[apps]] entry, so a project with no model at all would report them as unverifiable , which fails the check. Now that billing has Invoice , turn them on: # notes/rules.py (excerpt) from hinoki import rules project_rules = rules . RuleSet ( # …the rules the scaffold wrote… rules . Models . require_explicit_table ( match = "notes.*" ), rules . Models . require_foreign_key_index ( match = "notes.*" ), ) The check then reports the derived table name: notes/apps/billing/models.py:11: HNK-DB-001 [violated] Invoice uses the derived table name 'billing_invoices' fix: name the table with @db.table(...) or table=... on the model 10 rule(s): 1 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived Add @db.table("billing_invoices") above the class (the first line of its decorators) and the check passes. Pinning the derived name changes no table: migrations plan billing then reports no changes . Endpoints for billing go in notes/apps/billing/api.py , and notes/apps/billing/routes.py exports them. You decide where they are served by mounting them in notes/routes.py with Mount("/billing", billing_routes) , so paths inside the app never repeat the prefix, and notes/main.py loads notes/routes.py from hinoki.toml automatically: # notes/main.py (as hinoki new wrote it) from hinoki import Hinoki from notes.settings import ProjectSettings app = Hinoki ( settings = ProjectSettings , # NOTES_* variables and .env title = "Notes" , openapi_url = "/openapi.json" , docs_url = "/docs" , ) # routes, rules and middleware come from hinoki.toml Passing include= explicitly overrides [project] routes when you need it (for example in tests or conditional mounts). The same manifest can also list project-wide middleware , an events module per app and more than one rule set ( rules ), as the Tracker's hinoki.toml does. The project's rules (listed in hinoki.toml ) require every action to name an Access policy with permissions; build one as in chapter 3 . Recap ¶ hinoki app create writes an app and registers it in hinoki.toml . Table names, migration numbers and slugs are derived; you review the SQL. The project's routes.py mounts each exposed app explicitly; code inside the app never repeats the prefix.

docs.text: 5. Events between apps ¶ Creating a task and completing one both leave a line in the member's activity feed, but tasks does not know the feed exists. It announces: generated create emits Created[Task] , and complete_task ( chapter 4 ) emits Updated[Task] itself because aupdate_where emits no model event. The activity app listens: # tracker/apps/activity/events.py from hinoki import events from tracker.apps.tasks.models import Task from .models import Activity handlers = events . Handlers ( "activity" ) async def record ( task : Task , kind : str ) -> None : await Activity . acreate ( member_id = task . owner_id , task_id = task . id , kind = kind ) @handlers . in_transaction ( events . Created [ Task ]) async def task_created ( event : events . Created [ Task ]) -> None : await record ( event . instance , "created" ) @handlers . in_transaction ( events . Updated [ Task ]) async def task_updated ( event : events . Updated [ Task ]) -> None : await record ( event . instance , "updated" ) in_transaction runs the handler inside the transaction of the change, so the task and its activity line commit together or not at all. The handlers are registered by the events entry of the activity app in hinoki.toml ( chapter 7 ), and one command lists them: uv run hinoki events Created[Task] in_transaction activity async tracker.apps.activity.events.task_created Updated[Task] in_transaction activity async tracker.apps.activity.events.task_updated limits: events.handler_timeout=5.0, events.max_handlers=16, events.max_depth=4 declared in hinoki.toml: activity -> tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers The dependency points from activity to tasks only, which is also why activity lists requires = ["tasks", "members"] . Chapter 6 makes the other direction a failing check. See events for after_commit handlers and the limits. Recap ¶ An app announces what happened; another app listens without an import in the other direction. in_transaction keeps the main write and its audit trail atomic. hinoki events inspects the handlers declared in hinoki.toml . Next: 6. Rules .
